q: A nightly cron job runs ./backup.sh > /var/log/backup.log 2>&1 and both normal output and errors land in the log. A colleague 'simplifies' it to ./backup.sh 2>&1 > /var/log/backup.log. After the change, error messages print on the terminal instead of going to the log. Why?
options: Redirections are processed left to right: in the new order, 2>&1 first duplicates stderr to the terminal (stdout's current target), and only then is stdout sent to the file, so stderr never reaches the log
stderr cannot be merged into a file redirect at all; capturing stderr always requires running the command a second time
Redirection order is irrelevant, so the real problem must be that the log file needs the append operator >> instead of >
The shell requires 2>&1 to be quoted, otherwise it is parsed as two separate arguments and ignored
explain: The shell processes redirections strictly left to right, which is why order matters. In the original command, > /var/log/backup.log points stdout at the file first, then 2>&1 points stderr at wherever stdout currently goes (the file), so both streams land in the log. In the 'simplified' version, 2>&1 runs first and duplicates stderr to the terminal, which is stdout's target at that moment; the later > file only moves stdout. Option D is wrong because 2>&1 needs no quoting. Option B is wrong because merging stderr into stdout's destination is standard shell behavior. Option C is wrong because append vs truncate has nothing to do with which stream reaches the file.

q: An admin runs grep "error+" /var/log/app.log expecting to match the lines 'error', 'errorr', and 'errror', but gets zero output. The lines definitely exist. What is the pitfall and the fix?
options: The pattern needs grep -F, which enables regex repetition operators
The + operator only works at the start of a line, so the pattern should be rewritten as "^+error"
grep cannot match repeated characters at all; this requires awk or sed instead
In basic regular expressions (grep's default), + is a literal plus sign, so the pattern only matches the literal text 'error+'; use grep -E "error+" for extended regex where + means one-or-more
explain: Default grep uses basic regular expressions (BRE), where +, ?, |, and () are literal characters unless escaped or unless grep -E (extended regex) is used. So grep "error+" searches for the literal string 'error+', which appears nowhere, hence no output. With grep -E "error+", the + becomes a one-or-more quantifier and matches 'error', 'errorr', and 'errror'. Option A is backwards: grep -F disables regex entirely (fixed-string search), making it worse. Option B invents a nonexistent positional rule for +. Option C is false; grep handles repetition fine once the regex flavor is right (equivalently, grep "error\+" works in BRE on GNU grep).

q: An admin runs tar -xzf /backup/site.tar.gz -C /srv/restore and gets 'tar: /srv/restore: Cannot chdir: No such file or directory'. The archive itself is valid. What went wrong?
options: The -C directory must already exist; tar changes into it before extracting but will not create it, so run mkdir -p /srv/restore first
tar automatically creates any -C directory, so this error proves the archive is corrupt
The -C option must appear before -xzf in the option string, otherwise tar ignores it
--directory can only be used with -t (list mode), not with -x (extract mode)
explain: The -C / --directory option tells tar to chdir into that directory before extracting members, and tar does not create it for you; a missing target produces exactly this 'Cannot chdir' error. Creating it first with mkdir -p /srv/restore resolves it. Option C is wrong because tar option order is flexible (-C can come after the -f argument). Option B is wrong: tar never creates the -C directory. Option D is wrong: -C works with -x, -c, and -t alike.

q: Given ln /data/report /data/report.hard and ln -s /data/report /data/report.soft, the original /data/report is then deleted with rm. What is the state of the two links?
options: Both links keep working, because rm only unlinks names lazily and the kernel keeps serving both
The hard link breaks but the symlink survives, because symlinks cache a copy of the target's contents
Both links break, because rm destroys the underlying data blocks immediately
report.hard still opens the full data normally, while report.soft is now a dangling symlink pointing at a nonexistent path
explain: A hard link is simply another directory entry pointing at the same inode, and the data blocks are freed only when the last link to the inode is removed, so report.hard keeps working after the original name is deleted. A symlink stores only a path string, so once /data/report is gone, report.soft dangles and reads fail with 'No such file or directory'. Option C is wrong because rm decrements the link count rather than wiping blocks. Option A confuses lazy behavior that does not exist. Option B reverses both mechanisms: symlinks store no content copy.

q: An admin runs chmod 2750 /srv/projects. What are the resulting permissions and behavior?
options: drwxr-s--- : owner has rwx, group has r-x, others have nothing, and new files created inside inherit the directory's group via the setgid bit
2750 is identical to 0750 because the leading digit is ignored on directories
rwxrwxrwx with the sticky bit: everyone gets full access but only owners may delete
drwxr-xr-t : the directory is world-readable with the sticky bit set
explain: The leading 2 sets the setgid bit; on a directory, setgid causes new files and subdirectories to inherit the directory's group ownership instead of the creator's primary group. The remaining digits give rwx to owner, r-x to group, and nothing to others, shown as drwxr-s--- (the 's' marks setgid in the group execute slot). Option D describes 1755 (sticky bit, value 1, plus world read/execute). Option C describes 1777. Option B is wrong: the leading octal digit is exactly how setuid (4), setgid (2), and sticky (1) bits are set.

q: Which single command displays both stdout and stderr of ./deploy.sh live on the terminal AND saves both streams to deploy.log?
options: ./deploy.sh | tee deploy.log 2>&1
It is impossible: pipes can only carry stdout, so stderr can never reach tee
./deploy.sh 2>&1 | tee deploy.log
Use the script command instead, because tee cannot be combined with stderr redirection
explain: The 2>&1 placed before the pipe merges the command's stderr into its stdout, so the pipe carries both streams into tee, which writes them to the terminal and appends them to deploy.log. Option A is wrong: there the pipe still carries only stdout, and the trailing 2>&1 applies to tee itself, so deploy.sh's stderr goes to the terminal but never reaches the log. Option B is false precisely because 2>&1 exists to merge streams before the pipe. Option D is wrong; tee works fine once both streams are merged upstream of it.

q: Running grep -r "PermitRootLogin" * inside /etc/ssh finds nothing, yet grep -r "PermitRootLogin" /etc/ssh finds matches. What explains this?
options: The shell expands * before grep runs, and * omits dotfiles and dot-directories; passing the directory path itself avoids the glob and searches everything
grep -r cannot descend into subdirectories, so only the top level is ever searched
Hidden files are encrypted on RHEL and cannot be searched by grep at all
grep -R (capital R) is required for any recursive search; lowercase -r only searches one level
explain: Glob expansion is done by the shell, not grep: * expands to all non-dot entries in the current directory, so dotfiles and dot-directories are never handed to grep. Giving grep the literal path /etc/ssh lets grep's own recursion walk the entire tree including dot entries. Option B is false; -r is exactly the recursive flag. Option D confuses -R, which additionally follows symlinked directories during recursion. Option C invents a nonexistent encryption behavior.

q: An admin backs up /var/www with tar and restores it as a non-root user; all files are now owned by that user instead of apache. What happened, and what is the correct fix?
options: Running chmod -R on the tree will correct the ownership
Re-extracting with tar -p fixes ownership, because -p restores the recorded owners

tar records the original uid/gid, but only root can restore arbitrary ownership, so extraction as a normal user assigns everything to that user; re-extract as root or run chown -R apache:apache afterwards
tar never stores ownership information, so restored files always take the extracting user's ownership no matter what
explain: GNU tar stores numeric uid/gid in the archive, but the kernel only permits a superuser to chown files to another user, so non-root extraction silently assigns the extracting user's ownership. Extracting as root restores the recorded apache ownership automatically. Option D is false; ownership is part of the tar header. Option B confuses -p (--same-permissions), which concerns mode bits, not ownership (--same-owner, and it still needs root). Option A is wrong because chmod changes permission bits, never ownership; that is chown's job.

q: /srv/shared is drwxr-s--- root:devs (mode 2750, setgid set). New files created there are owned by group devs as expected, but their mode is -rw-r--r--, so group members cannot edit them. Why doesn't the setgid bit grant group write?
options: The directory should have been created with mode 2770, which forces new files to be group-writable
The setgid bit is broken on this directory and must be reapplied with chmod g+s
The umask only affects directories, never regular files

The setgid bit on a directory controls group ownership inheritance only; the permission bits of new files come from the mode 666 masked by the umask (022 gives 644), so lower the umask or add a default ACL such as setfacl -d -m g::rw /srv/shared
explain: Setgid on a directory affects which group new entries belong to; it says nothing about their permission bits. File modes start at 666 and the umask clears bits (022 yields 644), independent of the parent directory's mode. To get group-writable files, use a more permissive umask for the creators or set a default ACL (setfacl -d -m g::rwX) on the directory. Option B misdiagnoses working inheritance as broken. Option A confuses the directory's own 770 mode with the modes of files created inside it. Option C is backwards: umask affects both files (from 666) and directories (from 777).

q: An admin runs chmod 3770 /srv/team. What does the leading 3 do, and what is the full result?
options: 3770 is just 0770 with a comment digit; the leading 3 has no effect
3 = setuid (4) minus 1, giving the directory setuid behavior for all members
3 = setgid (2) + sticky bit (1): the directory is rwxrwx--- with group inheritance for new files, and only a file's owner (or root) may delete or rename entries inside
The sticky bit on a regular file prevents anyone but root from deleting it
explain: The leading octal digit is the sum of setuid (4), setgid (2), and sticky (1), so 3 = 2 + 1. On a directory, setgid makes new files inherit the directory's group, and the sticky bit restricts deletion/renaming to each file's owner. The 770 gives rwx to owner and group, nothing to others. Option B mangles the arithmetic (setuid is 4, and 3 contains no setuid). Option A denies the special-bits mechanism entirely. Option D misplaces the sticky bit's effect, which matters on directories, not regular files.

q: A user gets 'Permission denied' reading /srv/app/config.yaml even though the file is mode 644. namei -l /srv/app/config.yaml shows /srv as drwxr-x--- root root, and the user is not in group root. What is the diagnosis?
options: namei -l modifies permissions as a side effect, so rerunning it will fix the problem
Only the file's own permission bits matter, so the 644 mode must be a lie and the file is actually 600
Mode 644 is insufficient for reading; the file needs at least 664
Path resolution requires execute permission on every ancestor directory; namei -l pinpoints /srv as the blocker, so fix /srv's permissions or the user's group membership
explain: To reach a file, the kernel needs the execute (search) bit on each directory component of the path; without x on /srv, even a world-readable file inside is unreachable. namei -l lists ownership and mode for every component, making it the ideal diagnostic. Option B ignores directory traversal requirements. Option A is wrong: namei is a read-only diagnostic. Option C is wrong: 644 grants world read, which is sufficient once the path is traversable.

q: An admin runs chmod g+s /usr/local/bin/report-tool, owned by root:finance. A colleague claims this is 'the same as the setgid bit on /srv/shared'. What is the actual effect on the executable, and how does it differ?
options: On an executable, setgid makes the process run with the file's group (finance) as its effective group; on a directory, setgid instead makes new files inherit the directory's group
It is identical: both force group inheritance of newly created files
The setgid bit does nothing on regular files on Linux; it only has meaning on directories
It makes the binary run as root, equivalent to setuid
explain: Setgid has two distinct meanings by file type: on an executable it elevates the process's effective group to the file's group (like setuid does for the user), while on a directory it changes group-inheritance behavior for new entries. Here, anyone executing report-tool gains finance group privileges for that process. Option B collapses the two meanings incorrectly. Option C is false; setgid executables are a real (and security-sensitive) feature. Option D confuses setgid (g+s, group) with setuid (u+s, user).

q: Practice scenario: you SSH daily as 'admin' to db01.example.com using ~/.ssh/db_key. Which client-side config removes the need for '-i' every time?
options: Add alias sshdb='ssh -i ~/.ssh/db_key' to ~/.bashrc
In ~/.ssh/config add a block: Host db01 / HostName db01.example.com / User admin / IdentityFile ~/.ssh/db_key
Append the key path to ~/.ssh/known_hosts
Append "IdentityFile ~/.ssh/db_key" to /etc/ssh/ssh_config
explain: B is correct: ~/.ssh/config Host blocks are the standard per-user mechanism - HostName, User, and IdentityFile travel together and apply automatically to matching hosts. A edits the system-wide config, affecting all users and requiring root - the wrong scope for a personal key. B works but is fragile shell trickery that breaks scp, rsync, and Ansible invocations. D is nonsense: known_hosts stores server host keys, never client identity paths.

q: A task requires you to run /usr/local/bin/report.sh and append BOTH its standard output and its error messages to /var/log/report.log, without overwriting existing content. Which command accomplishes this?
options: /usr/local/bin/report.sh | tee -a /var/log/report.log 2>&1
/usr/local/bin/report.sh >> /var/log/report.log 2>&1
/usr/local/bin/report.sh 2> /var/log/report.log > /var/log/report.log
/usr/local/bin/report.sh > /var/log/report.log 2>&1
explain: B is correct: >> appends stdout to the log, and 2>&1 (placed AFTER the >> redirection) duplicates stderr onto that same appended stream, so both end up in the file without truncating it. D is wrong because > truncates the file instead of appending. C is wrong because 2> also truncates, and the ordering sends stderr to the file while stdout goes... both truncate the same file, which is undefined/racy behavior, not appending. A is wrong because tee -a only captures stdout; the 2>&1 applies to tee's own stderr handling oddly and errors from report.sh still go to the terminal, not the file.

q: You need to display only the lines in /var/log/messages that do NOT contain the word 'error' (case-insensitive), with line numbers, so you can scan for other problems. Which command does this?
options: grep -n -i error /var/log/messages | uniq
grep -n -i -x error /var/log/messages
grep -n -i -v error /var/log/messages
grep -n -c error /var/log/messages
explain: C is correct: -v inverts the match (shows non-matching lines), -i makes it case-insensitive, and -n adds line numbers. B is wrong because -x only matches whole lines that are exactly 'error', the opposite of what is wanted. D is wrong because -c prints only a count of matching lines, not the lines themselves. A is wrong because it shows only lines that DO contain 'error', and piping to uniq does not remove them.

q: A log file contains entries like '404-Page not found' and '200-OK'. You must print only lines that begin with exactly three digits followed by a dash. Which command works?
options: grep -E '^[0-9]{3}-' access.log
grep '^[0-9]{3}-' access.log
grep -F '^[0-9]{3}-' access.log
grep -G '^[0-9]{3}-' access.log
explain: A is correct: -E enables extended regex, where {3} is a valid interval quantifier, ^ anchors to line start, and [0-9] matches digits. B is wrong because basic grep (BRE) treats {3} as literal characters, so it would only match the literal string '{3}'. D is wrong because -G is just explicit basic regex, same problem as B (would need \{3\} in BRE). C is wrong because -F treats the whole pattern as a fixed literal string, so it searches for the literal characters ^[0-9]{3}-.

q: From your workstation you must check the status of the sshd service on server1.example.com as user admin, without opening an interactive shell, and have the output appear on your local terminal. Which command does this?
options: scp admin@server1.example.com systemctl status sshd
ssh admin@server1.example.com 'systemctl status sshd'
ssh -t admin@server1.example.com < systemctl status sshd
ssh 'systemctl status sshd' admin@server1.example.com
explain: B is correct: ssh user@host 'command' runs the quoted command on the remote host and returns its output locally, with no interactive session. A is wrong because scp copies files; it cannot execute remote commands. D is wrong because ssh expects the destination first; the quoted string in the destination position is parsed as a (nonexistent) hostname. C is wrong because the shell interprets < systemctl as input redirection of a local file named 'systemctl', which does not exist, before ssh even runs.

q: You must create a gzip-compressed tar archive named /backup/home-backup.tar.gz containing the entire /home directory, preserving permissions. Which command does this correctly?
options: tar -xzf /backup/home-backup.tar.gz /home
tar -cjf /backup/home-backup.tar.gz /home
tar -cz /backup/home-backup.tar.gz /home
tar -czf /backup/home-backup.tar.gz /home
explain: D is correct: -c creates, -z compresses with gzip, -f names the archive file, and /home is the source; permissions are preserved by default when creating as root. A is wrong because -x extracts instead of creating, so it would try to unpack (and fail or misbehave) rather than archive. B is wrong because -j uses bzip2 compression, producing a bzip2 file mislabeled .tar.gz. C is wrong because without -f, tar writes the archive to stdout (or errors about the archive device) instead of the named file.

q: The archive /tmp/webfiles.tar.gz must be extracted into /var/www/html, keeping the default directory structure inside the archive. Which command does this?
options: tar -tzf /tmp/webfiles.tar.gz -C /var/www/html
tar -xzf /tmp/webfiles.tar.gz -C /var/www/html
tar -czf /tmp/webfiles.tar.gz -C /var/www/html
tar -xzf /var/www/html < /tmp/webfiles.tar.gz
explain: B is correct: -x extracts, -z decompresses gzip, -f gives the archive, and -C changes to /var/www/html before extracting so contents land there. C is wrong because -c creates an archive, the reverse operation. D is wrong because -f /var/www/html tells tar the ARCHIVE is /var/www/html (a directory), and redirecting the file into stdin does not work without -f -; it fails. A is wrong because -t only lists archive contents without extracting anything.

q: Which statement about hard links and symbolic (soft) links on RHEL is TRUE?
options: A hard link can reference a file on a different filesystem than the link itself.
A symbolic link has its own inode and stores the path to its target; it can span filesystems.
A hard link can point to a directory, which is useful for linking whole directory trees.
Deleting the original file breaks a hard link, but a symbolic link survives.
explain: B is correct: a symlink is a separate inode containing the target's path text, and because it is path-based it can cross filesystem boundaries and point to directories. C is wrong because hard links to directories are forbidden on Linux (only . and .. exist, created by the filesystem). D is backwards: deleting the original leaves a hard link fully intact (data persists until the last link is removed), while a symlink becomes dangling/broken. A is wrong because hard links are inode-based and inodes are per-filesystem, so a hard link cannot cross filesystems.

q: A script /opt/tools/cleanup.sh must be readable and writable by its owner, readable by the group, and inaccessible to others. Which command sets exactly that?
options: chmod 600 /opt/tools/cleanup.sh
chmod 640 /opt/tools/cleanup.sh
chmod 660 /opt/tools/cleanup.sh
chmod 644 /opt/tools/cleanup.sh
explain: B is correct: 640 = rw- (6) for owner, r-- (4) for group, --- (0) for others, exactly the requirement. D is wrong because 644 gives others read access (r--), which must be denied. A is wrong because 600 removes group read access, which is required. C is wrong because 660 gives the group write access, more than the required read-only.

q: The file /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh is currently mode 644. You must add execute permission for the group only, leaving owner and others unchanged. Which command does this?
options: chmod +x /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh
chmod 755 /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh
chmod u+x,g+x /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh
chmod g+x /usr/local/bin/deploy.sh
explain: D is correct: g+x adds execute for the group class only, turning 644 into 654 with owner and others untouched. A is wrong because bare +x (equivalent to a+x) adds execute for user, group, AND others, changing more than the group. B is wrong because 755 sets rwxr-xr-x, which also grants execute to others and is an absolute mode reset, not a group-only addition. C is wrong because it also adds owner execute, which was not requested.

q: You need to read the manual page for the sshd_config FILE FORMAT (not the sshd daemon command). Which command opens the correct man page?
options: man 5 sshd_config
man 8 sshd_config
man sshd_config
info sshd_config
explain: A is correct: section 5 of the manual covers file formats and configuration files, so man 5 sshd_config opens the config-file reference directly. C is wrong because without a section, man opens the first match, which may be the sshd(8) daemon page or another section rather than the file format. B is wrong because section 8 covers system administration commands, which would show the daemon page, not the config file format. D is wrong because info uses a different documentation system; the canonical sshd_config reference lives in man section 5, and an info node for it does not exist. Section 2 — Operating Running Systems

q: Members of the group 'devs' cannot write to /shared, which shows 'drwxr-xr-x root root' in ls -ld. You need group collaboration with least privilege. Which fix is correct?
options: chmod g+w /shared
chgrp devs /shared && chmod 2770 /shared
chmod 777 /shared
chown alice /shared
explain: B is correct: chgrp gives the devs group ownership of the directory and 2770 grants rwx to owner and group, nothing to others, with the set-GID bit (the leading 2) so new files inherit the devs group. C is wrong because 777 grants read/write/execute to everyone on the system — it works but violates least privilege and is never the right answer on an exam. D is wrong because chowning to one user fixes it only for alice, not the whole devs group. A is wrong because adding group-write alone leaves the group as root (so devs still cannot write) and omits the set-GID bit, so new files would be created with the creator's primary group instead of devs.

q: Which command ensures that every new file created inside /shared automatically inherits the directory's group ownership, enabling collaboration?
options: chmod u+s /shared
chmod 2770 /shared
chmod 1770 /shared
chmod 0770 /shared
explain: B is correct: the leading '2' in 2770 is the set-GID bit on a directory, which makes new files and subdirectories inherit the directory's group rather than the creator's primary group. C is wrong because '1' is the sticky bit — it restricts deletion to file owners (like /tmp) and does nothing for group inheritance. A is wrong because 'u+s' is the set-UID bit, which on directories is ignored on Linux and does not affect group inheritance. D is wrong because 0770 sets the permissions but includes no special bit at all, so new files get the creator's primary group. Verify with 'ls -ld /shared', which shows an 's' in the group execute position (drwxrws---).

q: While working through a change ticket, an admin runs chmod 750 /srv/projects. Which nine-character permission string does ls -l show for it?
options: rwxrwx---
rwxr-x--T
rwxr-x-w-
rwxr-x---
explain: Octal 750 maps digit-by-digit to rwx triads (7=rwx, 5=r-x, 4=r--, 0=---, 6=rw-). The leading digit sets special bits: 4=setuid, 2=setgid, 1=sticky, shown as s or t in the matching execute position (uppercase when the underlying execute bit is absent). So 750 renders as rwxr-x---.

q: While working through a change ticket, an admin runs chmod 640 /opt/tools/report.sh. Which nine-character permission string does ls -l show for it?
options: rw-rw----
rw-r---w-
rw-r----T
explain: Octal 640 maps digit-by-digit to rwx triads (7=rwx, 5=r-x, 4=r--, 0=---, 6=rw-). The leading digit sets special bits: 4=setuid, 2=setgid, 1=sticky, shown as s or t in the matching execute position (uppercase when the underlying execute bit is absent). So 640 renders as rw-r-----.

q: During a routine maintenance window, an admin runs chmod 2750 /data/team. Which nine-character permission string does ls -l show for it?
options: rwxr-x---
rwxr-s-w-
rwxr-s---
rwxrws---
explain: Octal 2750 maps digit-by-digit to rwx triads (7=rwx, 5=r-x, 4=r--, 0=---, 6=rw-). The leading digit sets special bits: 4=setuid, 2=setgid, 1=sticky, shown as s or t in the matching execute position (uppercase when the underlying execute bit is absent). So 2750 renders as rwxr-s---.

q: While working through a change ticket, an admin runs chmod 1777 /srv/shared. Which nine-character permission string does ls -l show for it?
options: rwxrwxrwx
rwxrwxr-t
rwxrwxrwt
rwxr-xrwt
explain: Octal 1777 maps digit-by-digit to rwx triads (7=rwx, 5=r-x, 4=r--, 0=---, 6=rw-). The leading digit sets special bits: 4=setuid, 2=setgid, 1=sticky, shown as s or t in the matching execute position (uppercase when the underlying execute bit is absent). So 1777 renders as rwxrwxrwt.

q: During a routine maintenance window, an admin runs chmod 4755 /usr/local/bin/backup. Which nine-character permission string does ls -l show for it?
options: rwsrwxr-x
rwxr-xr-x
rwsr-xrwx
rwsr-xr-x
explain: Octal 4755 maps digit-by-digit to rwx triads (7=rwx, 5=r-x, 4=r--, 0=---, 6=rw-). The leading digit sets special bits: 4=setuid, 2=setgid, 1=sticky, shown as s or t in the matching execute position (uppercase when the underlying execute bit is absent). So 4755 renders as rwsr-xr-x.

q: While working through a change ticket, an admin runs chmod 700 /var/data. Which nine-character permission string does ls -l show for it?
options: rwx-----T
rwx----w-
rwx-w----
explain: Octal 700 maps digit-by-digit to rwx triads (7=rwx, 5=r-x, 4=r--, 0=---, 6=rw-). The leading digit sets special bits: 4=setuid, 2=setgid, 1=sticky, shown as s or t in the matching execute position (uppercase when the underlying execute bit is absent). So 700 renders as rwx------.

q: On a RHEL 10 admin workstation, an admin runs chmod 2770 /tmp/scratch. Which nine-character permission string does ls -l show for it?
options: rwxrws-w-
rwxr-s---
rwxrws---
rwxrwx---
explain: Octal 2770 maps digit-by-digit to rwx triads (7=rwx, 5=r-x, 4=r--, 0=---, 6=rw-). The leading digit sets special bits: 4=setuid, 2=setgid, 1=sticky, shown as s or t in the matching execute position (uppercase when the underlying execute bit is absent). So 2770 renders as rwxrws---.

q: In a hands-on lab exercise, an admin runs chmod 664 /home/team/docs. Which nine-character permission string does ls -l show for it?
options: rw-r--r--
rw-rw-r--
rw-rw-r-T
rw-rw-rw-
explain: Octal 664 maps digit-by-digit to rwx triads (7=rwx, 5=r-x, 4=r--, 0=---, 6=rw-). The leading digit sets special bits: 4=setuid, 2=setgid, 1=sticky, shown as s or t in the matching execute position (uppercase when the underlying execute bit is absent). So 664 renders as rw-rw-r--.

q: A file starts as mode 0644. An admin runs chmod g+w on it. What is the resulting octal mode?
explain: Symbolic chmod changes only the named class: g is the group triad. Applying '+w' to the 0644 triads gives 0664; the other classes are untouched, which rules out the choices that also alter a second triad.

q: chmod o+r is applied to /var/log/messages, whose current mode is 0600. What octal mode does stat report afterwards?
explain: Symbolic chmod changes only the named class: o is others triad. Applying '+r' to the 0600 triads gives 0604; the other classes are untouched, which rules out the choices that also alter a second triad.

q: Starting from mode 0755, an admin changes permissions with chmod g-w. Which octal mode results?
explain: Symbolic chmod changes only the named class: g is the group triad. Applying '-w' to the 0755 triads gives 0755; the other classes are untouched, which rules out the choices that also alter a second triad.

q: The file /srv/web/index.html has mode 0777. After running chmod o-w, what is its new mode in octal?
explain: Symbolic chmod changes only the named class: o is others triad. Applying '-w' to the 0777 triads gives 0775; the other classes are untouched, which rules out the choices that also alter a second triad.

q: A file starts as mode 0640. An admin runs chmod u+x on it. What is the resulting octal mode?
explain: Symbolic chmod changes only the named class: u is the owner triad. Applying '+x' to the 0640 triads gives 0740; the other classes are untouched, which rules out the choices that also alter a second triad.

q: chmod a+w is applied to /srv/web/index.html, whose current mode is 0444. What octal mode does stat report afterwards?
explain: Symbolic chmod changes only the named class: a is all three classes triad. Applying '+w' to the 0444 triads gives 0666; the other classes are untouched, which rules out the choices that also alter a second triad.

q: Which command line will append BOTH standard output and error output to /var/log/nightly.log without truncating it?
options: ./job.sh >> /var/log/nightly.log 2> /var/log/nightly.log
./job.sh >> /var/log/nightly.log 2>&1
./job.sh 2>&1 >> /var/log/nightly.log
./job.sh > /var/log/nightly.log 2>&1
explain: The >> operator appends stdout, and 2>&1 placed AFTER it duplicates stderr onto the same open file description, so both streams append. Using > would truncate the log first. Putting 2>&1 before the file redirection duplicates stderr to the terminal, and opening the same file twice with two redirections risks interleaved, clobbered writes.

q: Which command line will send standard output to results.txt while error messages still appear on the terminal?
options: ./check.sh &> results.txt
./check.sh 2> results.txt
./check.sh > results.txt 2>&1
./check.sh > results.txt
explain: A bare > redirects only stdout; stderr is untouched and keeps going to the terminal. &> and > file 2>&1 both merge stderr into the file, and 2> alone redirects the wrong stream.

q: Which command line will discard all error messages from a noisy command while keeping its normal output on screen?
options: ./scan.sh > /dev/null
./scan.sh 2> /dev/null
./scan.sh &> /dev/null
./scan.sh 2>&1 > /dev/null
explain: 2> /dev/null throws away only stderr, leaving stdout attached to the terminal. Sending stdout to /dev/null hides the output you want, and 2>&1 BEFORE > /dev/null still points stderr at the terminal's copy, so errors leak through; &> discards both streams.

q: Which command line will run a command so a copy of everything it prints, both streams, is saved to session.log while still displayed live?
options: ./deploy.sh 2>&1 | tee session.log
./deploy.sh | tee session.log
./deploy.sh 2> session.log | tee session.log
./deploy.sh > session.log | tee session.log
explain: tee duplicates a pipeline's stdout to a file and the screen. The command's stderr must first be merged into stdout with 2>&1 (placed before the pipe) or errors bypass tee entirely. Redirecting stdout to the file before the pipe leaves tee nothing to display, and 2> sends errors only to the file, not the screen.

q: Which command line will capture only the error output of a command into errors.log, with normal output discarded entirely?
options: ./audit.sh 2> errors.log
./audit.sh > /dev/null 2> errors.log
./audit.sh &> errors.log
./audit.sh 2>&1 > errors.log
explain: Two independent redirections are needed: stdout to /dev/null and stderr to errors.log. Using 2> alone leaves normal output on the terminal; &> merges both streams into the file; and 2>&1 before > errors.log leaves stderr pointing at the terminal.

q: Which command line will append only the error stream to /var/log/err.log while normal output appends to /var/log/out.log?
options: ./etl.sh > /var/log/out.log 2> /var/log/err.log
./etl.sh >> /var/log/out.log 2>> /var/log/err.log
./etl.sh 2>> /var/log/err.log
./etl.sh >> /var/log/out.log 2>&1
explain: Each stream gets its own append redirection: >> for stdout and 2>> for stderr. Single > truncates the logs, 2>&1 would merge errors into the output log instead of their own file, and redirecting only stderr leaves stdout going to the screen.

q: Which command will create a gzip-compressed archive named /backup/etc.tar.gz containing /etc?
options: tar -xzf /backup/etc.tar.gz /etc
tar -cjf /backup/etc.tar.gz /etc
tar -cf /backup/etc.tar.gz /etc
tar -czf /backup/etc.tar.gz /etc
explain: c creates, z selects gzip compression, and f names the archive file. x extracts instead of creating, j selects bzip2 (wrong compressor and extension pairing), and omitting z produces an uncompressed tar despite the .gz name.

q: Which command will extract a bzip2-compressed archive /tmp/data.tar.bz2 into /srv/restore, which already exists?
options: tar -xzf /tmp/data.tar.bz2 -C /srv/restore
tar -xjf /tmp/data.tar.bz2 /srv/restore
tar -xjf /tmp/data.tar.bz2 -C /srv/restore
tar -cjf /tmp/data.tar.bz2 -C /srv/restore
explain: x extracts, j matches the bzip2 compression of a .tar.bz2, and -C changes into the target directory before extracting. z would try gzip on a bzip2 archive, c creates rather than extracts, and without -C the trailing path is treated as an archive member name, not a destination.

q: Which command will list the contents of the xz-compressed archive /var/backups/full.tar.xz without extracting?
options: tar -tJf /var/backups/full.tar.xz
tar -xJf /var/backups/full.tar.xz
tar -tzf /var/backups/full.tar.xz
tar -cJf /var/backups/full.tar.xz
explain: t lists the table of contents, J matches xz compression, and f names the file. x would actually extract it, z claims gzip for an xz archive, and c would try to create a new archive over the path.

q: Which command will create an uncompressed archive of /home in /backup/home.tar?
options: tar -cf /backup/home.tar /home
tar -czf /backup/home.tar /home
tar -tf /backup/home.tar /home
tar -xf /backup/home.tar /home
explain: With no compression letter, cf simply creates a plain tar archive, which matches the .tar name. Adding z silently gzip-compresses it, t only lists, and x extracts.

q: Which command will extract /tmp/web.tar.gz into /var/www/html while preserving the archived permissions?
options: tar -czpf /tmp/web.tar.gz -C /var/www/html
tar -xzf /tmp/web.tar.gz -C /var/www/html --no-preserve
tar -xzpf /tmp/web.tar.gz -C /var/www/html
tar -xzpf /tmp/web.tar.gz /var/www/html
explain: x extracts, z matches gzip, p preserves the permissions recorded in the archive instead of applying the umask, and -C selects the destination. The create variant would overwrite the archive, and dropping -C makes the path a member name. (As root, tar preserves permissions by default; p makes it explicit for any user.)

q: Which command will see which files a gzip archive contains, showing the listing on screen like ls -l?
options: tar -czvf /backup/site.tar.gz
tar -xzvf /backup/site.tar.gz
tar -tzvf /backup/site.tar.gz --extract
tar -tzvf /backup/site.tar.gz
explain: t lists, z handles gzip, and v makes the listing verbose with sizes and permissions. x extracts the files for real, and c creates an archive. The --extract long option contradicts list mode.

q: Which command will create a gzip archive of /srv/data but leave out the /srv/data/tmp subdirectory?
options: tar -czf /backup/data.tar.gz --exclude=/srv/data/tmp /srv/data
tar -czf /backup/data.tar.gz /srv/data --skip=/srv/data/tmp
tar -xzf /backup/data.tar.gz --exclude=/srv/data/tmp /srv/data
tar -czf /backup/data.tar.gz -C /srv/data/tmp /srv/data
explain: --exclude=PATTERN is tar's mechanism for skipping paths while creating. --skip is not a tar option, x extracts instead of creating, and -C changes directory rather than excluding anything.

q: Which command will count how many lines in /var/log/secure contain the word 'Failed'?
options: grep -l 'Failed' /var/log/secure
grep -n 'Failed' /var/log/secure
grep -c 'Failed' /var/log/secure
grep -o 'Failed' /var/log/secure
explain: -c prints only the count of matching lines. -n prefixes line numbers to each match, -l prints just filenames with matches, and -o prints each matched string occurrence, none of which produce a single count.

q: Which command will search every file under /etc recursively and show only the names of files that mention 'chrony'?
options: grep -i 'chrony' /etc
grep -rl 'chrony' /etc
grep -c 'chrony' /etc/*
grep -r 'chrony' /etc
explain: -r recurses through the directory tree and -l lists only the filenames that contain a match. Without -l every matching line is printed; -c gives per-file counts; and without recursion only regular files in the top directory are searched, with /etc/* also failing on subdirectories.

q: Which command will show the lines of app.log that do NOT contain 'DEBUG', ignoring case?
options: grep -cvi 'debug' /var/log/app.log
grep -v 'DEBUG' /var/log/app.log
grep -iv 'debug' /var/log/app.log
grep -i 'DEBUG' /var/log/app.log
explain: Inversion needs -v and case-insensitivity needs -i; together they print non-matching lines regardless of case. Without -i, lines with lowercase 'debug' would still show; without -v there is no inversion; and adding -c reduces the output to a bare number.

q: Which command will match the pattern 'err[0-9]+' so that err7 and err42 match but the literal text err[0-9]+ does not need to exist?
options: grep -e 'err[0-9]+' /var/log/app.log
grep -F 'err[0-9]+' /var/log/app.log
grep 'err[0-9]+' /var/log/app.log
grep -E 'err[0-9]+' /var/log/app.log
explain: In basic regular expressions (grep's default) + is a literal plus sign; -E switches to extended regex where + is a one-or-more quantifier. -F treats the whole pattern as a fixed string, the opposite of what is wanted, and -e only marks the pattern argument without changing the regex flavor, so it stays basic.

q: Which command will print each matching line from messages together with the two lines that follow it?
options: grep -n 2 'panic' /var/log/messages
grep -A 2 'panic' /var/log/messages
grep -a2 'panic' /var/log/messages
grep -B 2 'panic' /var/log/messages
explain: -A NUM prints NUM lines of trailing context after each match. -B prints lines before the match instead, -n only adds line numbers, and -a is about treating binary files as text, not context.

q: Which command will find whole-word occurrences of 'cat' so that 'catalog' and 'concatenate' do not match?
options: grep -w 'cat' /var/log/app.log
grep -F 'cat' /var/log/app.log
grep -x 'cat' /var/log/app.log
grep '^cat$' /var/log/app.log
explain: -w requires the match to be bounded by non-word characters, so embedded occurrences inside longer words are skipped. ^...$ anchors to whole lines, -F changes nothing about word boundaries, and -x requires the entire line to equal the pattern.

q: Which command will find all regular files under /var larger than 100 MB?
options: find /var -type f -size -100M
find /var -type f -size +100M
find /var -size +100M -type d
find /var -type f -size 100M
explain: +100M means strictly larger than 100 MiB units; a bare 100M matches files that round to exactly 100, and -100M means smaller. The type must be f (regular file), not d (directory).

q: Which command will find files under /home modified within the last 7 days?
options: find /home -type f -mtime +7
find /home -type f -mmin -7
find /home -type f -mtime -7
find /home -type f -mtime 7
explain: -mtime -7 means modified less than 7*24h ago (within the last week). A bare 7 means exactly 7 days ago (in 24-hour buckets) and +7 means more than 7 days ago; -mmin counts minutes, so -7 minutes is far too narrow.

q: Which command will find files named exactly 'core' anywhere under / (case-sensitive)?
options: find / -iname 'core'
find / -name 'core'
find / -regex 'core'
find / -name 'core*'
explain: -name matches the basename exactly and case-sensitively. -iname is case-insensitive, the trailing * also matches names like core.1234, and -regex matches against the whole path with different semantics.

q: Which command will delete all empty regular files under /tmp/scratch?
options: find /tmp/scratch -type f -empty -delete
find /tmp/scratch -type f -size 0 -exec rm {} +
find /tmp/scratch -empty -delete
find /tmp/scratch -type f -empty -print
explain: -empty matches zero-length entries and -delete removes what matched, while -type f restricts the match to regular files so empty directories survive. -print only lists the matches, omitting -type f would also delete empty directories, and piping or guessing predicate names does not run any removal.

q: Which command will run chmod 640 on every .conf file under /srv/app?
options: find /srv/app -name '*.conf' -chmod 640
find /srv/app -name '*.conf' -exec chmod 640 {} \;
find /srv/app -name '*.conf' -exec chmod 640 \;
find /srv/app -name '*.conf' | chmod 640
explain: -exec runs the command per matched file with {} as the filename placeholder, terminated by \;. Piping filenames into chmod does nothing (chmod reads no stdin file list), omitting {} leaves chmod with no file operand, and -chmod is not a find predicate.

q: Which command will find all files under /data owned by user oracle?
options: find /data -user oracle
find /data -uid oracle
find /data -owner oracle
find /data -group oracle
explain: -user matches file ownership by user name (or numeric UID). -owner is not a find test, -uid is not either (numeric IDs go through -user/-group), and -group tests group ownership instead.

q: ls -li /data shows: 922337 -rw-r--r-- 2 root root 4096 report.txt; 922337 -rw-r--r-- 2 root root 4096 report.bak; 922340 lrwxrwxrwx 1 root root 10 latest -> report.txt. Which statement is TRUE?
options: All three names are hard links to one inode
report.bak is a symlink to report.txt because it was created second
report.txt and report.bak are hard links to the same inode; latest is a symlink
Deleting report.txt immediately frees the 4096 bytes of data
explain: Identical inode numbers (922337) with link count 2 mark hard links: two directory entries for one file. The lrwxrwxrwx entry with an arrow is a symbolic link with its own inode. Deleting one hard-link name only decrements the link count; the data survives until the last name is removed.

q: An admin creates ln -s /srv/app/current /srv/app/prod, then the target directory is renamed to /srv/app/v2. What happens when a user reads through /srv/app/prod?
options: It fails only until the nightly updatedb job rebuilds the link database
It fails with 'No such file or directory' because the symlink still stores the old path
It keeps working, because symlinks follow the inode, not the path
It silently redirects to /srv/app/v2 because the kernel tracks renames
explain: A symbolic link stores a pathname string, not an inode reference. Renaming the target leaves the stored path dangling, so lookups through the link fail until the link is recreated with ln -sfn pointing at the new path.

q: Which command creates a hard link named /backup/passwd.copy pointing at the same inode as /etc/passwd?
options: ln -s /etc/passwd /backup/passwd.copy
cp --link-deref /etc/passwd /backup/passwd.copy
link --symbolic /etc/passwd /backup/passwd.copy
ln /etc/passwd /backup/passwd.copy
explain: Plain ln without -s creates a hard link: a second name for the same inode, valid only within one filesystem. -s makes a symbolic link instead, and the cp/link option spellings shown are not real options.

q: A file shows link count 1 in ls -l and an admin needs a second name for it on the SAME filesystem that stays valid even if the original name is deleted. Which property decides between a hard link and a symlink here?
options: Only a symlink survives deletion of the original name
Hard links cannot exist on the same filesystem, only across filesystems
Either works for same-filesystem names, but only the hard link keeps the data alive by itself once the original name is removed; a symlink would dangle
The link count must be raised with chmod before linking
explain: A hard link IS the file under another name: the inode's link count rises, and data persists while any name remains. A symlink depends on the target path continuing to exist, and hard links are actually restricted TO the same filesystem, the reverse of one distractor.

q: A technician runs ./check_disks.sh and wants normal output added to the end of /var/log/disks.log instead of replacing the file, while errors still appear on screen. Which command does this?
options: ./check_disks.sh 2>> /var/log/disks.log
./check_disks.sh > /var/log/disks.log
./check_disks.sh < /var/log/disks.log
./check_disks.sh >> /var/log/disks.log
explain: The double greater-than operator appends standard output to an existing file without truncating it, and leaving standard error untouched keeps errors on the terminal. A single greater-than truncates first, the 2>> form redirects errors rather than output, and the less-than sign feeds the file in as input.

q: Which command runs ./probe.sh, throws away only its error messages, and shows its normal output on the terminal?
options: ./probe.sh 2> /dev/null
./probe.sh &> /dev/null
./probe.sh > /dev/null
./probe.sh 1> /dev/null
explain: File descriptor 2 is standard error, so redirecting it to /dev/null discards errors while standard output stays attached to the terminal. Redirecting descriptor 1 discards normal output instead, and the combined form discards both streams.

q: A build is started with make app 2>&1 > /tmp/build.log; the builder complains that errors appeared on screen but not in /tmp/build.log. What went wrong?
options: Standard error was duplicated to the original terminal before standard output was moved to the file
Make writes errors to file descriptor 3, which was never redirected in that command line
The log file needed to be created with touch before make could write errors to it
The greater-than sign truncates /tmp/build.log after make has already finished writing it
explain: Redirections are processed left to right, so 2>&1 first points standard error at the current standard output, the terminal, and only afterwards is standard output moved to the file. Putting the file redirection first and then 2>&1 would send both streams into the log.

q: Which pipeline counts how many lines of /etc/services contain the string tcp?
options: grep tcp /etc/services > wc -l
grep tcp /etc/services | wc -l
grep -c tcp /etc/services | wc -w
cat /etc/services | wc -l tcp
explain: The pipe sends the matching lines produced by grep to the standard input of wc, and the -l switch counts lines. Writing to a file named wc would be a redirection rather than a pipeline, and applying wc to the whole file counts lines that never matched.

q: An operator wants ./audit.sh output saved to /tmp/audit.txt, with any existing content kept and new output added below it on every run, including error messages. Which form using tee accomplishes this? (Choose two.)
options: ./audit.sh 2>&1 | tee -a /tmp/audit.txt
./audit.sh | tee -a /tmp/audit.txt 2> /dev/null
./audit.sh &> /tmp/audit.txt | tee -a /tmp/other.txt
./audit.sh | tee /tmp/audit.txt
explain: Merging standard error into standard output first and then piping through tee with its append switch writes both streams to the terminal and appends them to the file. Plain tee without the append flag truncates the file, the combined redirection form truncates the file and bypasses tee entirely, and in the last form the program's own errors are never merged into the pipe so they are not saved.

q: A command is run as sort < /tmp/names.txt > /tmp/sorted.txt. How are the two files used?
options: Both files are opened for appending so no earlier names or results are ever lost
/tmp/names.txt is used as an error log while sorting prints to /tmp/sorted.txt
/tmp/names.txt supplies standard input and /tmp/sorted.txt receives standard output
/tmp/names.txt receives standard output and /tmp/sorted.txt supplies standard input
explain: The less-than sign connects a file to standard input and the greater-than sign connects standard output to a file, truncating it first. Neither file is appended in this form, and standard error is not redirected at all here.

q: Which command creates a 200 MiB file named /tmp/swaptest.img filled entirely with zero bytes?
options: cat /dev/zero > /tmp/swaptest.img bs=1M count=200
dd if=/dev/null of=/tmp/swaptest.img bs=1M count=200
dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/swaptest.img bs=1M count=200
cp /dev/zero /tmp/swaptest.img bs=1M count=200
explain: Reading from /dev/zero yields an endless stream of null bytes, and dd with a 1 MiB block size and a count of 200 copies exactly 200 MiB into the output file. Reading from /dev/null yields immediate end of file, and the block options shown are dd options rather than cp or cat options.

q: Reading from /dev/null in a shell test, such as cat /dev/null, produces what result?
options: A listing of devices that are currently unused on the system
An error because /dev/null is a directory that cannot be read
No output and an immediate end-of-file condition
An endless stream of zero bytes until it is interrupted
explain: The /dev/null device discards anything written to it and signals end of file immediately when read, which is why it is used to silence output. The endless zero stream comes from /dev/zero, not /dev/null.

q: In a directory containing notes1.txt, notes2.txt, and notes10.txt, which pattern matches notes1.txt and notes2.txt but not notes10.txt?
options: notes{1,2,10}.txt
notes[12].txt.bak
notes?.txt
notes*.txt
explain: The question mark matches exactly one character, so it covers the single-digit names and excludes the two-digit name. The asterisk matches any number of characters including two digits, the brace form explicitly includes the longer name, and the .bak suffix matches nothing here.

q: A variable is set with REGION=us-east and an admin runs echo 'Region is $REGION'. Why does the output show the literal text $REGION?
options: The variable was exported, so the shell hides its value from echo commands
Single quotes prevent the shell from expanding variables inside them
Echo cannot display variables unless the -e option is supplied with the command
Double quotes are required before any variable can be created with an assignment
explain: Single quotes preserve every character literally, so no variable expansion occurs inside them, while double quotes still allow expansion. Exporting a variable does not hide it, and echo displays expanded values without needing a special option.

q: Which statement correctly describes who expands the pattern *.log in the command ls *.log?
options: The ls program searches the directory itself after receiving the pattern
The shell expands it to matching filenames before ls ever runs
Expansion happens inside ls only if the --glob option is given on the line
The kernel expands it only when the current directory contains hidden files
explain: Bash performs filename expansion, called globbing, and passes the resulting list of names as arguments before the command starts. Programs such as ls receive the expanded names, not the pattern itself.

q: An admin must pass a literal asterisk to a program, as in find a file actually named star*file, without the shell expanding it. Which techniques work? (Choose two.)
options: Enclose the name in single quotes, as in 'star*file'
Wrap only the asterisk in parentheses, as in star(*)file
Prefix the asterisk with a backslash, as in star\*file
Type the asterisk twice so the shell treats the pair as literal text
explain: Single quotes preserve the asterisk literally and a backslash escapes the following character, and both stop the shell from treating it as a glob pattern. Parentheses do not quote a character and instead introduce subshell syntax, and typing a character twice does not disable filename expansion.

q: Which pattern matches files named data_a.csv, data_b.csv, and data_7.csv, but not data_ab.csv or data_.csv?
options: data_*.csv
data_[a-z0-9].csv
data_[!a-z0-9].csv
data_?.csv.bak
explain: A bracket expression matches one character from the listed ranges, so a lowercase letter or a digit qualifies while two characters or none do not. The asterisk allows any length including empty, and the negated bracket class would exclude exactly the characters wanted.

q: A script sets MODE=debug on its first line without exporting it, then starts a child program that reports MODE is empty. What is the cause?
options: Child processes only inherit variables whose names are written in uppercase
Variables set inside a script are deleted when the script reaches its second line
Unexported shell variables are not inherited by child processes
The child program must be started with sudo before it can read any variables
explain: Only exported variables become part of a process environment and are passed to children; a plain assignment stays local to the current shell. Case does not control inheritance, and privilege tools do not change how environments are passed.

q: An admin adds a directory to PATH with PATH=$PATH:/opt/tools/bin and opens a new terminal, but the addition is gone. What should be done for persistence?
options: Create a file named PATH inside /opt/tools/bin containing the directory name
Use chmod to make the current shell executable by all users on the system
Add the PATH assignment to ~/.bashrc so it runs for each new interactive shell
Run export PATH once as root so the change is written into /etc/passwd
explain: Startup files such as ~/.bashrc are read when new interactive shells start, so placing the assignment there reapplies it each time. A one-time assignment in a single shell, regardless of privilege, disappears when that shell exits.

q: After typing a long command, which history shortcut re-runs the immediately previous command exactly as typed?
options: ^old^new
explain: The double exclamation mark expands to the previous command line in interactive bash history expansion. The dollar form expands to only the last argument of the previous command, not the whole command.

q: Which two actions make the alias ll='ls -l' available in future interactive shells for one user? (Choose two.)
options: Add the alias definition to that user's ~/.bashrc file
Define the alias in a file sourced from that user's ~/.bashrc
Export the alias with export ll so child shells inherit it like a variable
Write the alias into /etc/passwd next to the user's home directory entry
explain: Aliases defined in ~/.bashrc, or in another file that ~/.bashrc sources, are recreated each time an interactive shell starts. Aliases are not environment variables, so exporting one does not pass it on in that way, and account databases are not shell configuration.

q: A user types report-tool and bash reports command not found, yet ls shows /opt/reports/bin/report-tool exists and is executable. What is the most likely reason?
options: /opt/reports/bin is not listed in the PATH environment variable
Bash only searches /usr/bin and /bin and can never use directories under /opt
The file needs its setuid bit set before bash will run any program stored in /opt
The program must be renamed to remove the hyphen before the shell accepts it
explain: The shell searches only the directories listed in PATH when a command is given without a path, so an executable in an unlisted directory is not found. Running it by its full or relative path would work, and neither a special bit nor a rename is required.

q: Which command shows whether the name ll currently refers to an alias, a built-in, or an external program, along with what it resolves to?
options: which -a ll only, because type never reports aliases in bash
alias -p ll, because it also prints the full path of external binaries
type ll
hash ll, because it deletes the alias and prints its former definition
explain: The type command reports how bash interprets a name, showing alias definitions, whether a command is a built-in, or the path of an external program. The which utility knows nothing about aliases or built-ins because it only searches PATH.

q: An admin cannot remember which command compresses files with xz and wants to search short manual descriptions for the keyword xz. Which command does this?
options: man -k xz
man xz --sections
info --keyword xz
apropos -k xz --exact
explain: The -k option to man searches the manual page names and short descriptions, which is the same database used by apropos. It returns candidate pages to open, rather than opening one specific page directly.

q: Which command opens the manual page that documents the format of the /etc/fstab file itself?
options: man 5 fstab
man 8 fstab
man 1 fstab
man fstab --format
explain: Manual section 5 covers file formats and conventions, and fstab is a configuration file format, so its page lives there. Section 1 covers user commands and section 8 covers system administration commands, neither of which describes this file format.

q: On a minimal system, running a command with the --help option differs from opening its man page in which key way?
options: --help always opens the full manual in a pager, while man pages print only a one-line summary to the terminal screen
--help prints a brief built-in summary from the program itself, while a man page is a separate, fuller document that may not be installed
--help requires network access to fetch documentation, while man pages are generated live by the kernel each time
--help changes the program into documentation mode and alters files, while man never displays anything on screen
explain: Most programs implement --help themselves and print a concise usage summary, independent of whether manual pages are installed at all. Man pages are pre-written separate documents that are displayed locally and do not modify the system.

q: Which command counts how many lines in /var/log/secure contain the string Failed, without printing the lines themselves?
options: grep -l Failed /var/log/secure
grep -c Failed /var/log/secure
grep -n Failed /var/log/secure
grep -q Failed /var/log/secure
explain: The -c option suppresses normal output and prints a count of matching lines per file. The -n option prints line numbers alongside matches, -l prints only filenames, and -q prints nothing and communicates only through its exit status.

q: Which command lists only the names of files under /etc/default whose contents mention the string GRUB, searching recursively?
options: grep -ri GRUB /etc/default
grep -rl GRUB /etc/default
grep -rn GRUB /etc/default
grep -rc GRUB /etc/default
explain: Combining -r for recursive searching with -l, which prints only the names of files containing a match, gives exactly a filename list. The -c option prints counts, -n prints line numbers with matches, and neither replaces the filename-only behavior.

q: A file /tmp/hosts.txt contains the words cat, catalog, and scatter. Which command matches only the standalone word cat?
options: grep cat$ /tmp/hosts.txt
grep -F cat /tmp/hosts.txt
grep -w cat /tmp/hosts.txt
grep -x cat /tmp/hosts.txt.bak
explain: The -w option requires the pattern to form a whole word bounded by non-word characters, so the longer words containing the same letters are excluded. A fixed-string search still matches substrings, an anchored dollar sign requires end of line, and the backup filename is a different file.

q: Which command finds lines in /tmp/menu.txt containing either pizza or pasta, using extended regular expressions?
options: grep -F 'pizza|pasta' /tmp/menu.txt
grep 'pizza|pasta' /tmp/menu.txt
grep -E 'pizza|pasta' /tmp/menu.txt
grep -E 'pizza&pasta' /tmp/menu.txt
explain: In extended regular expressions the vertical bar is alternation, matching either alternative. In a basic expression and in a fixed-string search that character is treated literally, and the ampersand is not an alternation operator.

q: A pattern must match values such as color and colour in /tmp/words.txt. Which extended pattern does this with a single expression?
options: grep -E 'colou*r' /tmp/words.txt
grep -E 'colou?r' /tmp/words.txt
grep 'colou?r' /tmp/words.txt
grep -E 'colou+r' /tmp/words.txt
explain: In an extended expression the question mark makes the preceding element, here the letter u, optional, which covers both spellings. A plus requires at least one u, a star also permits several in a row, and in a basic expression the question mark is not special in that way without escaping.

q: Which command prints lines of /tmp/report.txt that do NOT end with the word DONE?
options: grep -v 'DONE$' /tmp/report.txt
grep -v '^DONE' /tmp/report.txt
grep -c 'DONE$' /tmp/report.txt
grep -i 'DONE$' /tmp/report.txt
explain: The dollar sign anchors the pattern to the end of the line and -v inverts the match, yielding lines that do not end with the word. The caret anchors to the start of the line instead, and the other options do not invert the selection.

q: An admin needs lines from /tmp/codes.txt where a dot is a literal character, such as 192.168, and must NOT be treated as any character. Which two approaches work? (Choose two.)
options: grep '192\.168' /tmp/codes.txt
grep '192.168' /tmp/codes.txt with no escaping at all
grep '192*168' /tmp/codes.txt
grep -F '192.168' /tmp/codes.txt
explain: A fixed-string search treats every character literally, and escaping the dot with a backslash in a regular expression also makes it literal, so both match only a real dot. An unescaped dot matches any single character, and an asterisk quantifies the preceding character instead of matching a dot at all.

q: Which pattern in a basic regular expression matches a line in /tmp/serials.txt that starts with three digits, using an interval expression?
options: grep '^[0-9]{3}' /tmp/serials.txt
grep '^[0-9]\{3\}' /tmp/serials.txt
grep -F '^[0-9]\{3\}' /tmp/serials.txt
grep '^[0-9]\{3\}$' /tmp/serials.txt.bak
explain: In basic regular expressions interval expressions are written with escaped braces, and the caret anchors the three-digit class to the start of the line. Unescaped braces are not an interval in a basic expression, a fixed-string search treats the whole pattern literally, and the backup path is a different file.

q: Which command searches /tmp/access.log for the string timeout regardless of capitalization, and shows the line number of each hit?
options: grep -cn timeout /tmp/access.log
grep -iv timeout /tmp/access.log
grep -in timeout /tmp/access.log
grep -in timeout /var/log/access.log
explain: The -i option makes matching case-insensitive and -n prefixes each matching line with its line number. The -c option replaces matches with a count, -v inverts the match, and the other path names a different file than the one specified.

q: In /tmp/fruit.txt, which extended pattern matches apple at the very end of a line and also lines containing exactly the single word apple alone?
options: grep -E 'apple*' /tmp/fruit.txt
grep -F 'apple$' /tmp/fruit.txt
grep -E '^apple.' /tmp/fruit.txt
grep -E 'apple$|^apple$' /tmp/fruit.txt
explain: The dollar anchor requires the word to finish the line, and the alternative with both anchors requires the word to be the entire line. A star after the final letter quantifies that letter rather than anchoring position, a fixed-string search treats the dollar literally, and the dot form matches other trailing characters.

q: Which command continuously shows new lines as they are appended to /var/log/cron by running jobs?
options: tail -F /var/log/cron --once
tail -f /var/log/cron
head -f /var/log/cron
watch head /var/log/cron
explain: The -f option to tail follows the file and prints new lines as they are appended, which is the standard way to watch a growing log. Head has no follow behavior for this purpose, and repeatedly printing the start of the file does not show the newest entries.

q: A list in /tmp/scores.txt holds one number per line in random order. Which command prints the values from largest to smallest as numbers, so 100 sorts above 99?
options: sort -n /tmp/scores.txt | head -1
sort -nr /tmp/scores.txt
uniq -r /tmp/scores.txt
sort -r /tmp/scores.txt
explain: Numeric sorting with -n compares values as numbers and adding -r reverses the order to descending, which places 100 before 99. Plain reverse sorting still compares characters, so 99 would come before 100, and showing only the first ascending value gives the smallest entry.

q: Why does uniq fail to remove all repeated lines from an unsorted file /tmp/dupes.txt unless it is sorted first?
options: Uniq compares only the first character of each line unless -a is supplied
Uniq deletes the whole file unless the input arrives through a pipeline
Sorting changes the inode of the file, which is what uniq actually examines
uniq only collapses lines that are identical and adjacent to each other
explain: Uniq examines neighboring lines and removes a line only when it matches the one immediately before it, so identical lines separated by other content survive. Sorting first groups duplicates together, which is why the two tools are so often piped together.

q: Which command extracts the first field of each line of /tmp/users.csv where fields are separated by commas?
options: awk -d, -f1 /tmp/users.csv
tr ',' ' ' < /tmp/users.csv
cut -d: -f1 /tmp/users.csv
cut -d, -f1 /tmp/users.csv
explain: The cut tool uses -d to name the delimiter and -f to select fields, so a comma delimiter with field 1 gives the first column. Using a colon would split on the wrong character, and tr only replaces characters without selecting fields.

q: Which command converts all lowercase letters in /tmp/draft.txt to uppercase and saves the result to /tmp/DRAFT.txt?
options: tr 'a-z' 'A-Z' < /tmp/draft.txt > /tmp/DRAFT.txt
cut -c1- /tmp/draft.txt > /tmp/DRAFT.txt
tr -d 'a-z' < /tmp/draft.txt > /tmp/DRAFT.txt
sed 'a-z' 'A-Z' /tmp/draft.txt > /tmp/DRAFT.txt
explain: Tr translates characters from the first set to the corresponding characters in the second set, so the lowercase range maps onto the uppercase range. The delete option would remove lowercase letters entirely instead of converting them.

q: Which command reports only how many words are in /tmp/essay.txt?
options: wc -c /tmp/essay.txt
wc -w /tmp/essay.txt
wc -m /tmp/essay.txt | wc -w
wc -l /tmp/essay.txt
explain: The -w option to wc counts words, while -l counts lines, -c counts bytes, and -m counts characters. Piping the character count onward would count words in that small output rather than in the essay itself.

q: Which command creates the nested path /opt/lab/week3/exercises in one step, succeeding even if some parent directories already exist?
options: mkdir -r /opt/lab/week3/exercises
mkdir -p /opt/lab/week3/exercises
touch -p /opt/lab/week3/exercises
mkdir /opt/lab/week3/exercises
explain: The -p option creates any missing parent directories and does not fail when parts of the path already exist. Plain mkdir fails if a parent is missing, touch creates files rather than directories, and mkdir has no recursive flag in that form.

q: Which command copies the directory /srv/templates and everything in it to /srv/templates-copy while preserving ownership, permissions, timestamps, and links as far as possible?
options: mv -a /srv/templates /srv/templates-copy
cp -a /srv/templates /srv/templates-copy
cp -p /srv/templates /srv/templates-copy
cp /srv/templates /srv/templates-copy
explain: The archive option combines recursive copying with preservation of attributes and links, which suits a faithful directory copy. A plain copy cannot copy a directory, preserve alone does not recurse, and moving would remove the original.

q: What happens when mv renames a file to a new name on the SAME filesystem?
options: A symbolic link to the old name is created so old scripts keep working
The file receives a new inode and its timestamps are reset to the current time
Only the directory entry changes; the inode and file contents stay the same
The file data is copied block by block and the original inode is deleted
explain: Within one filesystem a move is a rename: the directory entry is updated while the inode, data blocks, and timestamps remain untouched. Copying data and allocating a new inode happens only when moving across filesystems.

q: Which statement about rmdir /tmp/oldproject is correct?
options: It requires the -rf options before it will remove any directory at all
It succeeds only if /tmp/oldproject is an empty directory
It moves the directory to a trash location until the system is rebooted
It deletes the directory together with every file and subdirectory inside it
explain: Rmdir removes only empty directories and fails with an error when any content remains, which makes it a safer check than a recursive delete. Removing a populated tree requires a recursive removal tool instead.

q: An admin runs touch /tmp/marker.txt on a file that already exists with content. What is the effect?
options: The file is converted into a directory with the same name and timestamps
The file is truncated to zero bytes so it can serve as a fresh marker file
A second file named /tmp/marker.txt.1 is created next to the original file
Its access and modification timestamps are updated and its content is unchanged
explain: Touch on an existing file updates its timestamps to the current time without altering its data at all. It creates an empty file only when the name does not already exist, and it never truncates content.

q: Which two commands prompt for confirmation before deleting files, giving a chance to stop a mistake? (Choose two.)
options: rm -v /tmp/scratch/*.tmp
rm -i /tmp/scratch/*.tmp
rm -f /tmp/scratch/*.tmp
rm --interactive /tmp/scratch/*.tmp
explain: The -i option and its long form --interactive both ask before each removal, so a negative answer spares that file. Verbose mode only reports what was removed, and force mode does the opposite of prompting by suppressing questions and errors.

q: Two filenames are compared with ls -li and show the SAME inode number and a link count of 2. What does this prove?
options: They are hard links to the same file data
One is a symbolic link pointing at the other filename
They are copies whose contents happen to be identical today
They are on different filesystems that reused the same inode number
explain: Hard links are multiple directory entries for one inode, so they share an inode number and the link count reflects how many names point to it. A symbolic link has its own inode, and identical content in copies does not share an inode.

q: Which limitation applies to hard links but NOT to symbolic links?
options: A hard link cannot span two different filesystems
A hard link stores a pathname that can become stale after moves
A hard link breaks when the original filename is deleted
A hard link cannot point to a file that does not exist yet
explain: A hard link is a name for an inode within one filesystem, so it cannot reference an inode on another filesystem, while a symbolic link stores a path and can cross filesystems freely. Deletion breakage, dangling targets, and stale paths are symbolic-link behaviors, not hard-link ones.

q: A relative symbolic link /tmp/shortcuts/readme points to ../docs/readme.txt. The shortcuts directory is moved to /var/tmp/shortcuts. Why does the link now fail?
options: Its relative target is resolved from its new location, where ../docs/readme.txt no longer exists
Moving a directory always deletes every symbolic link stored anywhere inside it
The kernel converts relative links to hard links during a move, losing the target
Symbolic links stop working whenever their own permissions are changed by a move
explain: A relative symbolic link is interpreted relative to the directory containing the link, so moving that directory changes what the stored path resolves to. An absolute link would have been unaffected because its target path does not depend on location.

q: Which command gives /opt/scripts/nightly.sh mode 750 using octal notation?
options: chmod 750 /opt/scripts/nightly.sh
chmod 570 /opt/scripts/nightly.sh
chmod 075 /opt/scripts/nightly.sh
chmod 705 /opt/scripts/nightly.sh
explain: Octal digits map to owner, group, and others in order, and 7 means read, write, and execute, 5 means read and execute, and 0 means no access, giving rwxr-x---. The other digit orders assign those permission sets to the wrong classes.

q: A file is mode 664 and the umask is 002. An admin asks what mode a NEW regular file created by the same process would get, assuming the program requests 666. What is the answer?
options: 666, because umask only ever applies to directories and never to regular files
644, because every new file is forced to 644 by the kernel on RHEL systems
664, because the umask removes the write bit for others from the requested 666
622, because the umask is subtracted digit by digit from the requested mode
explain: A process requesting 666 with a umask of 002 loses the other-write bit indicated by the final umask digit while its group bits are left untouched, yielding 664 for the new regular file. The umask masks requested permission bits rather than performing ordinary subtraction, and it applies to files as well as directories.

q: Which command changes the owner of /var/data/import.csv to user analyst and its group to finance in one operation?
options: chgrp analyst:finance /var/data/import.csv
chown analyst:finance /var/data/import.csv
chown -g finance -u analyst /var/data/import.csv
chmod analyst:finance /var/data/import.csv
explain: Chown accepts an owner and group separated by a colon and changes both in a single command. The chgrp tool changes only group ownership and does not take an owner in that syntax, and chmod changes permissions rather than ownership.

q: The /tmp directory shows mode 1777. A user can create files there but cannot delete a file owned by another user. Which feature causes this?
options: The setgid bit on a directory restricts deletion to members of its owning group
The sticky bit on a directory restricts deletion to the file owner and root
World-write permission on a directory automatically locks every file inside it
Mode 1777 grants everyone execute permission, which blocks all deletions by design
explain: On a directory the sticky bit means only a file owner, the directory owner, or root may delete or rename files inside it, which protects shared spaces such as /tmp. Setgid on a directory controls group inheritance of new files instead.

q: The binary /usr/bin/passwd is mode 4755 and owned by root, yet ordinary users can update their own entries in a protected file by running it. Which feature makes this possible? (Choose two.)
options: The owner is root, so the program runs with root privileges while it executes
The trailing 55 makes the program a daemon that bypasses all permission checks
The leading 4 sets the sticky bit, which is what elevates the program's privileges
The leading 4 sets the setuid bit, so the program runs with the file owner's privileges
explain: A leading octal digit of 4 sets setuid, and because the file is owned by root the program executes with root privileges so it can update the protected password database in a controlled way. The sticky bit is the leading 1 digit and concerns directories, and permission digits grant no daemon behavior.

q: Which symbolic chmod command removes write permission for others and adds execute for the owner on /opt/bin/tool.sh, in one command?
options: chmod -w o,+x u /opt/bin/tool.sh
chmod others-w,owner+x /opt/bin/tool.sh
chmod o-w,u+x /opt/bin/tool.sh
chmod o+w,u-x /opt/bin/tool.sh
explain: Symbolic clauses name a class, an operator, and permissions, and comma-separated clauses apply together, so removing write from others and adding execute for the user does exactly what was asked. The reversed operators change the opposite permissions.

q: Which command finds all regular files under /var/log whose names end in .gz?
options: locate /var/log -type f -name '*.gz'
find /var/log -type f -name '*.gz'
find /var/log -name '*.gz' -type d
find /var/log -type f -name *.gz
explain: Quoting the pattern keeps the shell from expanding it so find itself matches each name, and -type f limits results to regular files. An unquoted pattern would be expanded by the shell first and break the search, and -type d would look for directories.

q: Which command finds files under /home larger than 500 MiB?
options: find /home -type f -length +500M
find /home -type f -size 500M
find /home -type f -size -500M
find /home -type f -size +500M
explain: With -size, a leading plus means strictly greater than the given amount, so +500M matches files larger than 500 MiB. No sign means exactly that size rounded up, a minus means smaller, and -length is not a find test.

q: Which command finds files under /srv/backups that were modified more than 30 days ago and deletes them after listing via -exec?
options: find /srv/backups -type f -mtime +30 -exec rm {} \;
find /srv/backups -type f -mtime 30 rm {} \;
find /srv/backups -type f -mtime -30 -exec rm {} \;
find /srv/backups -type f -atime +30 -delete-now
explain: The +30 form of -mtime matches files modified over 30 days ago, and -exec runs the given command with the braces replaced by each pathname, terminated by an escaped semicolon. The -30 form matches recent files, which would delete the wrong set.

q: Which command finds all directories owned by user guest under /tmp?
options: find /tmp -user guest -type l
find /tmp -type d -user guest
find guest -type d /tmp
find /tmp -type f -user guest
explain: Combining -type d for directories with -user for ownership restricts results to directories owned by that user. The path to search comes first in find syntax, and symbolic links or regular files are different types than requested.

q: Which command lists the contents of /backup/etc-backup.tar.xz WITHOUT extracting any files?
options: tar -xJf /backup/etc-backup.tar.xz
tar -cJf /backup/etc-backup.tar.xz
tar -tJf /backup/etc-backup.tar.xz -C /tmp
tar -tJf /backup/etc-backup.tar.xz
