explain: The -t option lists archive contents, -J selects xz decompression, and -f names the archive file, so nothing is written to disk. The -x option would extract, -c would create a new archive, and an extraction directory is irrelevant when only listing.

q: Which command creates a bzip2-compressed tar archive of /etc/NetworkManager at /backup/nm.tar.bz2?
options: tar -cjf /backup/nm.tar.gz /etc/NetworkManager
tar -cjf /backup/nm.tar.bz2 /etc/NetworkManager
tar -czf /backup/nm.tar.bz2 /etc/NetworkManager
tar -xjf /backup/nm.tar.bz2 /etc/NetworkManager
explain: The -c option creates, -j selects bzip2 compression, and -f names the output archive, matching the .bz2 suffix used. The -z option selects gzip instead, and -x extracts an existing archive rather than creating one.

q: What is the difference between running gzip on /tmp/notes.txt versus gzip -k on the same file?
options: Both delete the original, but -k keeps a second uncompressed copy in /var/tmp
gzip keeps the original and -k deletes it after compression completes successfully
gzip replaces the file with notes.txt.gz, while -k also keeps the original file
Neither deletes anything; gzip always leaves the original file untouched on disk
explain: By default gzip removes the input file after creating the compressed version, while the -k option tells it to keep the input file as well. This surprises users who expect the original to remain without asking for it.

q: Which two commands extract /opt/pkg/software.tar.gz into the already-existing directory /opt/pkg/unpacked, changing into that directory for extraction? (Choose two.)
options: tar -xzf /opt/pkg/software.tar.gz -C /opt/pkg/unpacked
tar -xzf /opt/pkg/unpacked -C /opt/pkg/software.tar.gz
tar -xzf /opt/pkg/software.tar.gz --dir /opt/pkg/unpacked
tar -C /opt/pkg/unpacked -xzf /opt/pkg/software.tar.gz
explain: The -C option changes to the named directory before extracting, and it may appear before or after the other options as long as the archive is named with -f. The reversed form names the directory as if it were the archive, and --dir is not the tar option for this.

q: An archive was made with absolute paths stripped, and tar warns it is removing the leading slash from member names when creating /backup/rootfs.tar from /etc/hosts style paths. Why does tar do this by default?
options: To convert every member into a symbolic link pointing back at the original file location
Because tar cannot store filenames longer than eight characters in any archive format it writes
Because gzip compression requires all member names to start with a dot character first
So extraction restores files relative to the current directory instead of overwriting absolute system paths
explain: Stripping the leading slash makes members relative, so a later extraction places them under the chosen directory rather than silently overwriting live system files at absolute paths. This is a deliberate safety default, not a format or compression limitation.

q: Practice scenario: a script with 'if [ $1 = prod ]; then ...' fails with '[: =: unary operator expected' when run with no arguments. What is the fix?
options: Quote the variable: if [ "$1" = prod ]
Use [[ $1 = prod ]] - the real bug is single brackets
Change = to -eq
Add set -u at the top of the script
explain: A is correct: unquoted $1 vanishes when empty, leaving '[ = prod ]' - a syntax error. Quoting gives '[ "" = prod ]', a valid false comparison. B's [[ ]] would also tolerate emptiness, but it misidentifies the root cause and is not POSIX sh. C makes things WORSE: set -u turns the unset $1 into a fatal error. D is for integer comparison; 'prod' is a string.

q: A script contains: total=0; for i in $(seq 1 4); do total=$((total + i)); done; echo $total. What does it print?
explain: The loop adds each integer from 1 through 4 into its accumulator, printing the sum 1+...+4 = 10. The other values come from adding the final value twice, an off-by-one, or printing the loop variable instead of the accumulator.

q: Consider this script: sum=0; for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do sum=$((sum+i)); done; echo "sum is $sum". What line appears on the terminal?
options: sum is 5
sum is 15
sum is 14
sum is 20
explain: The loop adds each integer from 1 through 5 into its accumulator, printing the sum 1+...+5 = 15. The other values come from adding the final value twice, an off-by-one, or printing the loop variable instead of the accumulator.

q: A script runs: acc=0; for i in {{1..6}}; do acc=$((acc + i)); done; echo $acc. What value is printed?
explain: The loop adds each integer from 1 through 6 into its accumulator, printing the sum 1+...+6 = 21. The other values come from adding the final value twice, an off-by-one, or printing the loop variable instead of the accumulator.

q: A script contains: for w in web db cache; do echo $w; done. How many lines does it print?
explain: The for loop iterates once per word in the list, and echo runs once per iteration, printing each word on its own line: 3 lines in total. Nothing extra is printed because the loop has no trailing echo.

q: A script contains: for w in alpha beta gamma; do echo $w; done. How many lines does it print?
explain: The for loop iterates once per word in the list, and echo runs once per iteration, printing each word on its own line: 3 lines in total. Nothing extra is printed because the loop has no trailing echo.

q: A script contains: i=0; while [ $i -le 20 ]; do echo $i; i=$((i + 5)); done. What is the LAST number printed?
explain: The counter starts at 0 and grows by 5 while it stays <= 20, giving the sequence 0, 5, 10, 15, 20. The loop stops before printing 25 because that value exceeds the limit.

q: A script contains: i=2; while [ $i -le 11 ]; do echo $i; i=$((i + 3)); done. What is the LAST number printed?
explain: The counter starts at 2 and grows by 3 while it stays <= 11, giving the sequence 2, 5, 8, 11. The loop stops before printing 14 because that value exceeds the limit.

q: x=10 and a script evaluates [ $x -gt 9 ]. A second script evaluates [ $x \> 9 ] with string comparison. Which statement is TRUE?
options: String comparison of 10 and 9 is true because longer strings are greater
The numeric test is true; the string test compares '10' with '9' character by character and is false because '1' sorts before '9'
The numeric test is false because -gt needs the variable quoted to work
Both tests are true because 10 is greater than 9 either way
explain: -gt performs integer comparison, so 10 -gt 9 is true. String comparison is lexicographic: '10' vs '9' compares '1' to '9' first, and '1' is smaller, so the string test is false. This is the classic reason numeric tests exist as separate operators.

q: A script runs: if [ -f /etc/app.conf ]; then echo present; else echo missing; fi. /etc/app.conf exists but is a DIRECTORY. What prints?
options: present, because -f tests existence of any kind
missing, because -f requires read permission as well
An error, because -f cannot be used on directories at all
missing, because -f tests for a regular file and the path is a directory
explain: -f is true only for regular files; directories need -d and any-kind existence is -e. The test simply evaluates false on a directory (no error), so the else branch runs.

q: count is unset (empty). A script runs [ $count -eq 0 ] without quotes. What happens?
options: It evaluates false silently and the script continues
The test errors with something like 'integer expression expected' or 'unary operator expected' because the expansion leaves [ -eq 0 ]
The shell assigns 0 to count automatically
It evaluates true, treating the empty value as 0
explain: Unquoted, an empty variable disappears from the command line, leaving a malformed test with a missing operand, so test reports a syntax-style error instead of comparing. Quoting "$count" or using a default like ${count:-0} avoids it.

q: A script must run /opt/fix.sh ONLY when the file /tmp/ready.flag exists. Which construct is correct?
options: [ -e /tmp/ready.flag ] || /opt/fix.sh
/opt/fix.sh && [ -e /tmp/ready.flag ]
[ -e /tmp/ready.flag ] && /opt/fix.sh
if [ -e /tmp/ready.flag ]; then /opt/fix.sh; else /opt/fix.sh; fi
explain: && runs the right-hand command only when the left side succeeds (exit 0), so the fix script runs exactly when the flag file exists. || would run it when the file is ABSENT, checking after running reverses cause and effect, and the if/else runs the script on both branches.

q: After running grep -q 'ERROR' app.log (no match found), a script echoes $?. What value does it see?
options: The exit code of the echo command instead
2, because no-match is an error condition
0, because the command itself ran successfully
1, because grep exits 1 when no lines match
explain: grep's contract: 0 when lines are selected, 1 when nothing matched, 2 for real errors like a missing file. $? captures the exit status of the most recently finished foreground command, which here is the grep.

q: Which test checks whether the string variable $mode is exactly 'prod'?
options: [ $mode -eq prod ]
test $mode = 'prod' -a $mode
[ "$mode" = "prod" ]
[ "$mode" == "prod" ] && [ $mode > 5 ]
explain: String equality inside [ ] uses a single = with both sides quoted so empty or space-containing values cannot break the syntax. -eq is numeric-only, and a bare trailing expression or an unquoted expansion is malformed. (Double == also works in bash's [ ], but the quoted single-= form is the portable test.)

q: A script is invoked as: ./deploy.sh web1 web2 web3. Inside the script, what does $0 expand to?
options: ./deploy.sh followed by all of its arguments as one string
./deploy.sh
The parent shell's name
web1
explain: $0 expands to the name the script was invoked as, here './deploy.sh'. The first positional parameter $1 is 'web1', and the full command line is not stored in any single special variable.

q: The command line './deploy.sh web1 web2 web3' launches a script. How many positional parameters does the script see in $#?
options: 3 including the script name
explain: $# is the number of positional parameters, which excludes the script name itself: 3 argument(s) were passed. $0 holds the script name separately and is not counted.

q: A script is invoked as: /opt/tools/audit.sh --full /var. Inside the script, what does $0 expand to?
options: /opt/tools/audit.sh followed by all of its arguments as one string
--full
/opt/tools/audit.sh
The parent shell's name
explain: $0 expands to the name the script was invoked as, here '/opt/tools/audit.sh'. The first positional parameter $1 is '--full', and the full command line is not stored in any single special variable.

q: The command line '/opt/tools/audit.sh --full /var' launches a script. How many positional parameters does the script see in $#?
options: 2 including the script name
explain: $# is the number of positional parameters, which excludes the script name itself: 2 argument(s) were passed. $0 holds the script name separately and is not counted.

q: A script is invoked as: bash cleanup.sh old.log. Inside the script, what does $0 expand to?
options: cleanup.sh
cleanup.sh followed by all of its arguments as one string
old.log
The parent shell's name
explain: $0 expands to the name the script was invoked as, here 'cleanup.sh'. The first positional parameter $1 is 'old.log', and the full command line is not stored in any single special variable.

q: The command line 'bash cleanup.sh old.log' launches a script. How many positional parameters does the script see in $#?
options: 1 including the script name
explain: $# is the number of positional parameters, which excludes the script name itself: 1 argument(s) were passed. $0 holds the script name separately and is not counted.

q: A script runs: cp /etc/hosts /tmp/hosts.bak; echo $?. The copy succeeds. What does the echo print, and why?
options: Nothing, because $? is only set inside functions
The PID of the cp process
0, because $? holds the exit status of the cp command and 0 means success
1, because echo is the second command run
explain: $? always expands to the exit status of the last completed foreground command. A successful cp exits 0. It is not a PID (that is $$ for the shell itself) and it works anywhere in the script.

q: Inside deploy.sh, the line echo "$$" prints 2417. What is 2417?
options: The script's inode number
The process ID of the shell running the script
The number of arguments the script received
The exit code of the previous command
explain: $$ expands to the PID of the current shell (for a script, the interpreter process running it). Exit status is $?, argument count is $#, and inode numbers never appear through a shell variable.

q: A script needs to pass all of its own arguments through to an inner command exactly as received, preserving multi-word arguments. Which expansion is correct?
options: ${args}
explain: "$@" expands each positional parameter as its own quoted word, preserving arguments that contain spaces. Unquoted $* (and even "$*") joins everything into a single word, $# is only a count, and ${args} is an ordinary (here unset) variable.

q: A case statement reads: case $1 in start) echo go;; stop) echo halt;; *) echo usage;; esac. The script is run as ./svc.sh restart. What prints?
options: usage, because 'restart' matches no listed pattern and falls to the * default
Nothing, because an unmatched case is a syntax error
go, because the first branch is the default
halt, because restart is closest to stop
explain: case tries patterns top to bottom; 'restart' matches neither start nor stop, so the catch-all * branch runs. An unmatched case without * would simply do nothing, not error.

q: A script contains: mkdir -p /tmp/work && cd /tmp/work || echo FAILED. /tmp/work already exists as a regular FILE. What happens?
options: mkdir overwrites the file with a directory and cd succeeds
The script aborts at mkdir before evaluating the rest
cd runs anyway because && only checks mkdir's output
mkdir fails, cd never runs, and FAILED is printed because the || branch catches the failed chain
explain: mkdir -p fails when the path exists as a non-directory file, so the && chain short-circuits (cd is skipped) and the || alternative executes. -p only suppresses the error when the path already exists AS a directory.

q: What does echo $(( 2 + 3 * 4 )) print?
options: An error, because spaces are not allowed inside $(( ))
14, because multiplication binds tighter than addition inside arithmetic expansion
Nothing, because $(( )) only works with variables
20, because shell arithmetic is strictly left to right
explain: Arithmetic expansion follows normal precedence: 3 * 4 is evaluated first (12), then + 2 gives 14. Constants are fine, and spaces inside $(( )) are allowed.

q: A script ends a validation block with exit 3. The calling wrapper checks the result. How does the wrapper see the 3?
options: In the script's stdout, which the wrapper must parse
In its $? immediately after running the script, as the script's exit status
Exit codes above 2 are discarded by the shell
Only through a shared environment variable the script exports
explain: exit N terminates the script with status N, and the parent reads it from $? (or tests it directly with if). Exit codes are not printed to stdout, values 0-255 are all valid, and children cannot export variables back to their parent.

q: Which line correctly makes a script print 'even' when the variable n holds an even number?
options: if [ $((n % 2)) -eq 0 ]; then echo even; fi
if [ $n % 2 = 0 ]; then echo even; fi
if (( n % 2 )); then echo even; fi
if [ $n -mod 2 -eq 0 ]; then echo even; fi
explain: The remainder must be computed with arithmetic expansion $((n % 2)) and then compared numerically with -eq. A bare % inside [ ] is not an operator, (( n % 2 )) is true when the remainder is NONZERO (odd), and -mod is not a test operator.

q: What is the purpose of the first line #!/bin/bash at the top of a script file?
options: It forces every user who runs the script to use an interactive bash shell
It makes the file executable without needing any permission change
It is a comment that documents who wrote the script and is ignored at runtime
It tells the kernel which interpreter to run the script with when the file is executed directly
explain: The shebang line is read by the kernel on direct execution to choose the interpreter, here /bin/bash, for the script contents. It is not merely documentation, it does not set the executable permission bit by itself, and it selects a non-interactive interpreter rather than an interactive shell.

q: A script named check.sh has correct contents but running ./check.sh fails with Permission denied. What is the most likely fix?
options: Run the script as root once so the permission is remembered for all users
chmod +x check.sh to add the executable permission, then run ./check.sh again
Add #!/bin/bash as the last line of the script so the shell can find it
Rename the file to check.bash so the extension grants execution rights
explain: Direct execution requires the executable bit on the file, and chmod +x adds it. The shebang belongs on the first line and does not grant permissions, file extensions do not control executability on Linux, and running as root does not permanently change the file mode for others.

q: A script starts with #!/bin/sh but the author runs it as bash deploy.sh. Which interpreter actually executes the script, and why?
options: Neither, because a mismatched invocation is rejected with an interpreter error
Both run in sequence, with sh checking syntax and bash executing the body
bash, because naming the interpreter on the command line overrides the shebang entirely
The shebang interpreter /bin/sh, because the shebang always wins over the command line
explain: When you invoke an interpreter explicitly, that interpreter reads and runs the file and the shebang is treated as an ordinary comment line. The shebang only matters when the file itself is executed directly, nothing runs the script twice, and no mismatch error is produced.

q: In a script, NAME=report and you need to build the string report_final.txt from the variable. Which expansion is safe and correct?
options: ${NAME}_final.txt
$NAME-final.txt is wrong here because the required separator is an underscore in the filename
$NAME_final.txt
$(NAME)_final.txt
explain: Braces in ${NAME} delimit exactly where the variable name ends, so the underscore and suffix become literal text. Without braces the shell looks for a variable named NAME_final, the hyphen form builds a different filename than the one required, and $( ) is command substitution rather than variable expansion.

q: What is printed by this inline script? ; X=world; echo 'Hello $X'; echo "Hello $X";
options: Hello world on both lines
An error, because a variable cannot be used inside single quotes at all
Hello $X on both lines
Hello $X on the first line and Hello world on the second line
explain: Single quotes preserve every character literally, so $X is printed as written, while double quotes allow expansion so the value world is substituted. Using a variable inside single quotes is perfectly legal, it simply is not expanded.

q: A script is invoked as ./backup.sh /data /mnt/usb verbose. Inside the script, what do $0, $# and $2 expand to?
options: $0 is the PID, $# is ./backup.sh, and $2 is /mnt/usb
$0 is backup, $# is 4 including the script name in the count of arguments shown, and $2 is /data
$0 is /data, $# is 2, and $2 is verbose
$0 is ./backup.sh, $# is 3, and $2 is /mnt/usb
explain: $0 holds the name used to invoke the script, $# counts only the positional arguments which are three here, and positional parameters are numbered from 1 so $2 is the second argument /mnt/usb. The script name is not counted in $#, $1 would be /data, and the PID is held by $$ rather than $0.

q: Immediately after running the command grep -q error app.log, a script tests the special variable $?. What does it contain?
options: The exit status of the grep command, 0 if a match was found and 1 if no match was found
The number of lines in app.log that contain the word error
The full text of the first matching line from app.log
The process ID of the grep command that just ran
explain: $? always expands to the exit status of the most recently completed foreground command, and grep uses 0 for match found and 1 for no match. It never contains counts, PIDs which are in $$, or any output text from the command.

q: Which special variable expands to the process ID of the shell running the script itself?
explain: $$ expands to the PID of the current shell or script process, which scripts commonly use for unique temporary filenames. $! is the PID of the most recent background job, $# is the argument count, and $@ expands to all positional parameters.

q: A script must ask the operator for a target directory and store the reply in the variable DEST. Which line does this with a visible prompt?
options: read DEST < prompt.txt
read -p "Target directory: " DEST
input -p "Target directory: " DEST
DEST=read "Target directory: "
explain: The read builtin with -p displays the prompt and stores the typed line into the named variable DEST. Redirecting from a file reads file contents rather than prompting, the assignment form tries to set DEST to a literal string rather than reading input, and input is not a shell builtin for this task.

q: Which test correctly checks that /etc/app/config.yaml exists and is a regular file?
options: [ -file /etc/app/config.yaml ]
[ -f /etc/app/config.yaml ]
[ -d /etc/app/config.yaml ]
[ -e -f /etc/app/config.yaml ]
explain: The -f test is true only when the path exists and is a regular file, which is exactly the check required. The -d test checks for a directory, test primaries are not stacked with two flags in one expression that way, and -file is not a valid test operator.

q: A script needs to branch when the directory /srv/uploads does NOT exist. Which condition expresses this correctly?
options: if [ -notdir /srv/uploads ]; then
if [[ -d /srv/uploads == 0 ]]; then
if [ ! -d /srv/uploads ]; then
if [ -d /srv/uploads = false ]; then
explain: Placing ! before the -d primary inside the test negates it, so the branch runs only when the path is not a directory. Comparing the test itself to a string or to 0 is not how test results work since the command communicates through its exit status, and -notdir is not a real primary.

q: Which test checks whether the string variable TOKEN is empty, handling the unset case safely in the intended sense of the test itself?
options: [ -e "$TOKEN" ]
[ $TOKEN = "" ]
[ -n "$TOKEN" ]
[ -z "$TOKEN" ]
explain: The -z primary is true when the length of the string is zero, which covers an empty or effectively empty value for this check. Comparing an unquoted possibly-empty variable to an empty string reproduces the classic unary-operator failure, -n tests the opposite condition of non-empty, and -e tests for a filesystem path rather than a string.

q: Inside a backup script, COUNT holds the number of files copied. Which condition is true when COUNT is greater than 100?
options: [ "$COUNT" -more 100 ]
[ "$COUNT" -gt 100 ]
explain: Integer comparisons inside test use the -gt family of operators, so -gt 100 is the correct greater-than test. A bare > inside [ ] is parsed as output redirection rather than comparison and would create a file named 100, and the other two spellings are not valid comparison operators.

q: What is the output of this inline script? ; N=5; if [ $N -lt 3 ]; then echo low; elif [ $N -lt 10 ]; then echo mid; else echo high; fi;
options: low and mid, because both conditions are partially true
low
high
mid
explain: With N equal to 5 the first test for less than 3 fails, the elif test for less than 10 succeeds, and only that branch runs, printing mid. The else branch is reached only when every earlier condition fails, and an if/elif chain executes at most one branch.

q: What does this inline script print? ; for W in alpha beta gamma; do echo $W; done | wc -l; Consider only the loop output count.
options: 3, because the loop iterates once for each word in the list
0, because a for loop over words requires an array to be defined first
1, because the list is treated as a single string
4, because the word done is also echoed on a final pass
explain: A for loop over an explicit word list iterates once per word, producing three echo lines for alpha, beta, and gamma. The list is split into separate words by the shell, the do/done keywords are syntax rather than data, and no array definition is needed for a simple word list.

q: Which loop processes every .log file in the current directory, including correctly handling the intent of iterating over matching files?
options: for F in $(ls *.log); do gzip $F; done is required because globbing does not work in loops
for F in *.log; do gzip "$F"; done
foreach F (*.log) gzip "$F"
for F = *.log; do gzip "$F"; done
explain: The shell expands the *.log glob into the list of matching filenames before the loop runs, and quoting the variable protects names containing spaces. Command substitution over ls output is not required and is more fragile, the assignment-style header is not valid for syntax, and foreach is a different shell's construct.

q: What is printed by this inline script? ; I=1; while [ $I -le 3 ]; do echo $I; I=$((I+1)); done;
options: Nothing, because a while loop cannot contain arithmetic expansion
1, then 2, then 3, each on its own line, and then the loop ends
An infinite loop printing 1 forever, because I never changes
1, then 2, then 3, then 4, because the test runs after the increment
explain: The counter starts at 1, the test allows values up to and including 3, and the arithmetic assignment increments I each pass, so it prints 1, 2, and 3 and then the test fails at 4. The increment does happen inside the loop so it is not infinite, and arithmetic expansion works fine within a while body.

q: A case statement reads: ; case $DAY in Mon) echo weekday;; Sat|Sun) echo weekend;; *) echo unknown;; esac; What prints when DAY=Sun?
options: weekday
weekend
weekend and unknown, because the default pattern also matches
unknown
explain: Sunday matches the Sat|Sun alternation pattern, so the weekend branch runs and the case stops at its closing double semicolon. The default star pattern is only used when no earlier pattern matches, and only one branch of a case is executed for a given value.

q: A deployment script finishes its checks and must signal failure to the calling automation with status 3. Which line does this?
options: return 3 at the top level of the script so the caller receives it
status=3 as the final line of the script
echo 3 and then let the script end normally
exit 3
explain: The exit builtin terminates the script immediately with the given status, which the caller reads through $?. return is only valid inside a function or a sourced script, echoing a number prints text but leaves the exit status as that of echo itself, and assigning a variable named status has no effect on the process exit code.

q: In the chain ./check.sh && ./deploy.sh || echo FAILED, when does the echo run?
options: When either check.sh fails, or check.sh succeeds but deploy.sh fails
Only when check.sh fails before deploy.sh is ever considered, in all cases and exclusively
Only when check.sh succeeds and deploy.sh also succeeds
Always, because || runs its right-hand side unconditionally after && completes
explain: The && runs deploy only if check succeeds, and the || runs the echo if the left side as a whole ends in failure, which covers check failing or deploy failing after a successful check. The echo does not run when both succeed, it is not limited strictly to the check step since a deploy failure also triggers it, and || is conditional rather than unconditional.

q: What is the value of R after this line runs? ; A=6; B=4; R=$((A * B - 5));
options: An error, because variables inside $(( )) must be written as $A and $B
24, because the subtraction is ignored inside arithmetic expansion
explain: Arithmetic expansion evaluates 6 times 4 minus 5, giving 19, with normal operator precedence. Inside $(( )) bare variable names are automatically dereferenced so the dollar form is not required, and the subtraction is a normal part of the expression rather than being ignored.

q: A function is defined as: ; greet() { echo "Hello $1"; }; What happens when the script later calls greet Admin?
options: It prints Hello Admin, because $1 inside a function refers to the function's own first argument
It prints Hello greet, because $1 inside a function is the function name
It fails, because functions cannot accept arguments in bash
It prints Hello followed by the script's first command-line argument, ignoring the word Admin
explain: Inside a function the positional parameters are temporarily replaced by the arguments passed to that function call, so $1 is Admin for this invocation. The script-level arguments are restored when the function returns, functions do accept arguments, and the function name itself is not a positional parameter.

q: A script contains the test [ $RETRIES -gt 5 ] and RETRIES is unset because an earlier config file failed to load. What failure is expected when the test runs?
options: The script exits immediately with status 127 before reaching the test
An integer expression expected style error, because the unquoted unset variable expands to nothing and leaves -gt without a left operand
The shell automatically treats the missing value as 0 and the test works normally
The test silently evaluates to false and the script continues with no message
explain: An unset variable expands to an empty string, and without quotes the test receives a malformed expression missing its left operand, producing an integer expression expected error. The shell supplies no automatic default of 0, the malformed test does not quietly become false, and the failure is in the test builtin rather than a command-not-found exit.

q: A script edited on a Windows workstation fails on RHEL with the error bad interpreter: /bin/bash^M: No such file or directory. What is the cause and fix?
options: The script is missing the executable bit; adding it with chmod +x resolves the interpreter error
The bash package is not installed; installing it creates the /bin/bash^M file the script requests
The file has CRLF line endings so the carriage return becomes part of the interpreter path; convert the file to Unix line endings, for example with dos2unix
The shebang must be changed to #!/usr/bin/bash because /bin/bash was removed in RHEL 10
explain: The ^M is a carriage return left by CRLF endings, and because it sits at the end of the shebang line the kernel looks for an interpreter whose name literally includes it. Converting to LF endings fixes the path, while permissions, a missing bash package, and the interpreter location are unrelated since /bin/bash exists on RHEL 10.

q: A script has no shebang and no executable bit, and a user runs it successfully with the command bash tools.sh. Why did it work despite the missing pieces?
options: Because bash was named explicitly, it simply reads the file as a list of commands and neither the shebang nor the executable bit is consulted
Because files ending in .sh are automatically executable on RHEL 10
Because bash silently adds a shebang and the executable bit to any file it is asked to run
Because the kernel supplies /bin/bash as a default interpreter for any text file
explain: Passing the file as an argument to bash means bash itself opens and interprets it, so kernel shebang handling and execute permission are never involved. Bash does not modify the file's contents or mode, the extension confers no rights, and direct execution of a shebang-less file depends on shell fallback behavior rather than a kernel default.

q: What is printed by this inline script? ; S=0; for N in 2 4 6; do S=$((S+N)); done; echo $S;
options: 6, because only the last value of N is kept
An error, because a for loop variable cannot be used in arithmetic
explain: The loop accumulates each value into S, computing 0 plus 2 plus 4 plus 6, so the final echo prints 12. The values are added rather than concatenated as text, earlier additions are retained rather than overwritten by the last iteration, and loop variables work normally in arithmetic expansion.

q: Which two statements about the [[ ]] construct are correct? (Choose two.)
options: It supports pattern matching with = and == against a glob pattern on the right-hand side
Word splitting and pathname expansion are not performed on words inside [[ ]], so unquoted variables are safer there
It is part of POSIX sh and behaves identically in every shell that provides test
It requires all string comparisons to use the -eq operator family
explain: Inside [[ ]] the shell does not word-split or glob-expand the arguments, and the equality operators perform glob pattern matching, both well-known advantages over the single-bracket form. The construct is a bash and ksh extension rather than POSIX sh, and -eq belongs to integer comparison rather than string comparison.

q: Which two expansions are command substitution? (Choose two.)
options: $(hostname)
A backtick expression such as `hostname` enclosed in backticks
$((hostname))
${hostname}
explain: Both the modern $( ) form and the older backtick form run a command and substitute its output. The brace form is parameter expansion of a variable with that name, and the double-parenthesis form is arithmetic expansion rather than command execution.

q: Which two test primaries are correctly paired with their meaning inside [ ]? (Choose two.)
options: -n string is true when the length of the string is zero
-x file is true when the file exists and is executable
-z string is true when the length of the string is zero
-d file is true when the file exists and is a regular file
explain: The -x primary tests executability and -z tests for a zero-length string, so both pairings are correct. The -d primary tests for a directory rather than a regular file, which is -f, and -n tests for a non-zero length, the opposite of the pairing claimed.

q: Which two statements about quoting in bash are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Double quotes allow variable expansion and command substitution while preventing word splitting of the result in most contexts
Double quotes preserve the dollar sign literally just like single quotes
Single quotes preserve the literal value of every character inside them, including the dollar sign
Single quotes allow variable expansion but block command substitution
explain: Double quotes are the grouping form that still permits expansions while protecting against splitting, and single quotes are fully literal so a dollar sign inside them is just a character. Single quotes block variable expansion as well, and double quotes do not make the dollar sign literal.

q: A while loop must read a hosts file line by line and process each entry in the current shell. Which form is the robust standard pattern?
options: read HOST < hosts.txt once, then loop over the single value with while
while read HOST; do process $HOST; done | hosts.txt
for HOST in read hosts.txt; do process "$HOST"; done
while read -r HOST; do process "$HOST"; done < hosts.txt
explain: Redirecting the file into the loop feeds each line to read in the current shell, and -r prevents backslash mangling while quoting protects the value. Piping the file name is not input redirection, the for form shown does not read file contents, and a single read outside a loop only consumes the first line.

q: A script ends with a successful echo as its very last command and contains no exit statement. What exit status does the script report to its caller?
options: The number of commands the script ran, counted automatically by the shell
An undefined status that callers are forbidden from testing
0, because a script without an explicit exit returns the status of its last command, and echo succeeded
1, because any script without an explicit exit is considered to have failed
explain: When no exit builtin is used, the script's exit status is the status of the last command executed, and a successful echo yields 0. There is no automatic failure default, the status is not a command count, and callers routinely and legitimately test this status.

q: The root password on a RHEL 10 system is lost. Which sequence correctly resets it?
options: Append single to the kernel line, which drops to a root shell that needs no password and no SELinux relabel
At the GRUB menu press e, append rd.break to the end of the linux line, press Ctrl+x, then run mount -o remount,rw /sysroot; chroot /sysroot; passwd; touch /.autorelabel; exit; exit
At the GRUB menu append rw init=/bin/bash, boot, run passwd, and reboot immediately with no further steps
Boot with rd.break and run passwd directly at the initramfs prompt without remounting or chrooting
explain: rd.break interrupts boot in the initramfs with the real root filesystem mounted read-only at /sysroot, so it must be remounted read-write first. chroot /sysroot is required so that passwd edits the real system's /etc/shadow rather than the initramfs. touch /.autorelabel is critical: without it, SELinux contexts on /etc/shadow are wrong and logins fail after the reset. Option C omits the remount (the filesystem is read-only) and the relabel step. Option D runs passwd against the initramfs, changing nothing persistent. Option A is wrong because sulogin/single still prompts for the root password on RHEL.

q: Which command shows only sshd service messages at error priority or worse, logged since 09:00 today?
options: journalctl -u sshd --until "09:00" -p err
journalctl -u sshd --since "09:00" -p err
journalctl -p err --since "09:00"
journalctl -u syslog --since "09:00" -p err
explain: The -u sshd flag scopes the query to the sshd unit, --since "09:00" sets the lower time bound (today at 09:00), and -p err filters to priority err and anything more severe (emerg through err). Option D uses the wrong unit name; there is no syslog unit holding sshd messages on a systemd-journal system. Option A uses --until, which sets the upper bound instead of the lower bound, returning everything before 09:00. Option C is not scoped to sshd, so it returns errors from every unit on the system.

q: An admin launches a heavy nightly report with nice -n 15 ./report.sh so it yields CPU to interactive work. A junior suggests nice -n -15 ./report.sh instead 'for maximum speed'. Who is right?
options: Both are equivalent because nice only affects disk I/O priority, not CPU scheduling
The admin's command is invalid because any nonzero nice value requires root privileges
The junior: negative nice values lower priority, so -15 is the polite choice
The admin: higher nice values mean lower CPU priority, and only root may assign negative values; -n 15 correctly deprioritizes the background job
explain: Nice values range from -20 (highest CPU priority) to 19 (lowest); a larger number means 'nicer' to other processes, i.e., less CPU. Only root can lower the nice value below 0 (raise priority), so the junior's -15 would fail with 'permission denied' for a normal user. Option C inverts the scale. Option A confuses nice with ionice, which handles I/O scheduling classes. Option B is wrong: any user may raise their own nice value (lower their priority); only decreasing it needs privilege. Verify with ps -o pid,ni,comm.

q: After running tuned-adm profile throughput-performance on a database server, which command confirms the active profile, and does the setting survive a reboot?
options: tuned-adm recommend both suggests and applies the profile in one step
The profile must be re-applied from cron at every boot or it is lost
tuned-adm active shows the current profile, and the setting persists across reboots because tuned records it as the active profile
Profile names must be given with a .conf suffix or tuned-adm silently ignores them
explain: tuned-adm active prints the currently applied profile, and tuned stores the selection so it is reapplied automatically after reboot. Option B is unnecessary work caused by misunderstanding tuned's persistence. Option A is wrong: tuned-adm recommend only prints a suggestion based on system role; it applies nothing. Option D is wrong: profile names are given bare (e.g., throughput-performance, balanced, virtual-guest).

q: A server wastes resources booting into a graphical desktop. The admin wants text-mode boot going forward and wants to switch immediately without rebooting. Which pair of commands does this?
options: systemctl set-default multi-user.target, which also switches the running system immediately
systemctl set-default graphical.target, because graphical.target is the text-mode runlevel 3 equivalent
Edit /etc/inittab and change the initdefault line, then run telinit 3
systemctl set-default multi-user.target (takes effect at next boot; verify with systemctl get-default) and systemctl isolate multi-user.target (switches right now)
explain: set-default rewrites the default.target symlink, which only affects the next boot; get-default confirms it. isolate switches the running system to the target immediately without a reboot. multi-user.target is the systemd equivalent of runlevel 3 (text), while graphical.target is runlevel 5. Option A is wrong because set-default never changes the current state. Option B swaps the targets. Option C describes the obsolete SysV mechanism; RHEL 9/10 use systemd targets, not /etc/inittab.

q: Journal logs are complete during the day but always missing after a reboot. /var/log/journal does not exist. What is the cause and the fix?
options: The journal is corrupt and the only fix is journalctl --flush on every boot

With the default Storage=auto, journald keeps logs only in volatile /run/log/journal when /var/log/journal is absent; create the directory with mkdir -p /var/log/journal (or set Storage=persistent) and restart systemd-journald
The logs are present but journalctl --since cannot read across reboots
journald is incapable of persistent storage by design; a third-party syslog is mandatory
explain: Storage=auto means persistent storage only if /var/log/journal exists; otherwise journald writes to /run/log/journal on tmpfs, which evaporates at reboot. Creating /var/log/journal (systemd-tmpfiles or the journald restart then owns it) makes logging persistent. Option D is false; persistent journals are a standard feature. Option C is wrong because time filtering has nothing to do with storage location. Option A misdiagnoses a configuration default as corruption.

q: On a new KVM virtualization host, the admin runs tuned-adm recommend and it prints 'virtual-host'. What did that command actually do?
options: It applied the virtual-host profile immediately and persistently
The recommend subcommand is deprecated and always prints the last-used profile
It analyzed the system role and printed the suggested profile; it applied nothing, and the admin must run tuned-adm profile virtual-host to apply it
It only works on bare-metal servers and its output on a VM should be ignored
explain: tuned-adm recommend queries system facts (including virtualization role) and prints a suggestion; it is read-only and changes nothing. Applying the suggestion requires tuned-adm profile . Option A confuses recommend with profile. Option D is wrong; recommendation works on virtual, physical, and cloud systems. Option B is false; recommend is a current, supported subcommand.

q: Practice scenario: /var is critically full and journalctl --disk-usage shows 4 GB of journals. What is the correct cleanup?
options: journalctl --rotate
rm -rf /var/log/journal/*
Delete /var/log/messages
journalctl --vacuum-size=500M, then set SystemMaxUse=500M in /etc/systemd/journald.conf
explain: D is correct: --vacuum-size trims archives to the target NOW, and SystemMaxUse caps future growth - immediate relief plus prevention. A manually deletes active journal files out from under journald; vacuum is the safe API. C removes the classic syslog file, which is not where the 4 GB is. D only rotates (closes the current file); it frees no space by itself.

q: A server must boot to the command-line multi-user environment by default instead of the graphical environment, persistently. Which command makes this change?
options: systemctl set-default multi-user.target
systemctl start multi-user.target
systemctl isolate multi-user.target
systemctl enable multi-user.target
explain: A is correct: set-default changes the default.target symlink so the system boots into multi-user.target on every future boot. C is wrong because isolate switches targets immediately for the current session only; it does not change the default for the next boot. D is wrong because targets are not 'enabled' like services; enable on a target unit does not set the boot default. B is wrong because start only activates the target right now and has no effect on the next boot.

q: A running server is at the graphical target. You need to switch it to rescue mode immediately for emergency maintenance, for this session only, without changing the default boot target. Which command does this?
options: systemctl rescue
systemctl set-default rescue.target && reboot
telinit 1
systemctl enable rescue.target
explain: A is correct: systemctl rescue isolates rescue.target immediately (equivalent to isolate), entering single-user maintenance mode for this session while leaving the default boot target untouched. B is wrong because it permanently changes the default target and reboots, which is neither session-only nor immediate. D is wrong because enabling a target does not activate it, and rescue.target is a special target not managed via enable. C is wrong because telinit maps to runlevel changes via systemd but runlevel 1 maps to rescue only through compatibility; the native, reliable command is systemctl rescue (telinit 1 actually does work via systemd-sysv, but it is the legacy path and less explicit; the exam expects systemctl rescue).

q: You have lost the root password on a RHEL 10 system. At the GRUB 2 boot menu, which kernel command-line addition is the documented method to interrupt the boot and gain a shell early enough to reset the password?
options: single
systemd.unit=emergency.target
rd.break
init=/bin/bash
explain: C is correct: adding rd.break to the kernel command line (on the linux line in the GRUB editor) interrupts the initramfs boot before the root filesystem is mounted, dropping to a dracut shell where you remount /sysroot read-write, chroot, and run passwd — the documented RHEL password-recovery procedure. D is wrong because init=/bin/bash bypasses systemd entirely, leaving filesystems and SELinux contexts unmanaged, and is not the documented RHEL method (it also breaks SELinux relabeling on reboot). A is wrong because 'single' is the legacy SysV runlevel word; it still requires the root password to enter single-user mode on RHEL. B is wrong because emergency.target also prompts for the root password, which is exactly what is lost.

q: A runaway process with PID 4312 is consuming 98% CPU. You want to ask it to terminate gracefully first, giving it a chance to clean up. Which command does this?
options: kill 4312
pkill -9 -P 4312
kill -9 4312
kill -KILL 4312
explain: A is correct: plain kill sends SIGTERM (signal 15) by default, which asks the process to terminate gracefully and lets it run cleanup handlers. C and D are wrong because -9/-KILL sends SIGKILL, which the kernel enforces immediately with no cleanup — the opposite of graceful, and the last resort. B is wrong twice over: -9 is SIGKILL (not graceful), and -P matches by parent PID, so it would target the wrong processes entirely.

q: A database backup job is already running as PID 8841 and is starving interactive users of CPU. You must lower its scheduling priority (make it nicer) while it runs, without killing it. Which command does this?
options: renice -n 10 -p 8841
nice --adjust 8841
nice -n 10 -p 8841
renice 10 8841
explain: A is correct: renice changes the nice value of an already-running process; -n 10 sets niceness 10 (lower priority) and -p 8841 selects the PID. C is wrong because nice only sets priority for a NEW command being launched, and -p is not a valid nice option. D is wrong because renice requires the -p flag to interpret the argument as a PID; without it the syntax is invalid (older syntax renice 10 -p 8841 is valid, but bare 'renice 10 8841' is not). B is wrong because nice --adjustment applies at launch of a new process, cannot target an existing PID, and the argument form is incorrect.

q: A file server handling heavy sequential I/O should use the throughput-optimized system tuning profile. Which command applies it?
options: tuned profile-set throughput-performance
tuned-adm active throughput-performance
systemctl set-profile throughput-performance
tuned-adm profile throughput-performance
explain: D is correct: tuned-adm profile activates a tuned profile immediately and persistently; throughput-performance is the real profile tuned for high-throughput workloads. B is wrong because tuned-adm active only DISPLAYS the currently active profile; it takes no profile argument. A is wrong because there is no 'tuned' command with a 'profile-set' subcommand; the tool is tuned-adm. C is wrong because systemd has no set-profile operation; tuning profiles are managed by the tuned daemon, not systemctl.

q: After a reboot, journalctl only shows logs since the current boot; older logs are gone. Which change makes the systemd journal persistent across reboots?
options: Add LogToDisk=true to /etc/systemd/system.conf
Set Storage=persistent in /etc/systemd/journald.conf and restart systemd-journald
Run journalctl --flush --persistent
Set Persistent=yes in /etc/rsyslog.conf and restart rsyslog
explain: B is correct: the journal stores on disk only when /var/log/journal exists or Storage=persistent is set in /etc/systemd/journald.conf; restarting systemd-journald (or rebooting) applies it, and logs then survive reboots. D is wrong because rsyslog.conf controls the traditional syslog daemon, not the systemd journal's storage. C is wrong because journalctl has no --persistent option (--flush only flushes runtime logs to disk once). A is wrong because /etc/systemd/system.conf has no LogToDisk option; journal storage is configured in journald.conf.

q: The web service failed at 03:12 last night. You need to see only the error-priority messages from the httpd unit since yesterday, newest last. Which command does this?
options: journalctl -u httpd --priority error --after yesterday
journalctl httpd -p 3 --from yesterday
journalctl -u httpd.service -l err -d yesterday
journalctl -u httpd -p err --since yesterday
explain: D is correct: -u httpd filters by the unit, -p err selects priority err and higher (emerg through err), and --since yesterday bounds the time range. A is wrong because --priority and --after are not valid journalctl options. B is wrong because the unit must be given with -u (a bare 'httpd' is treated as a match pattern, not a unit filter) and --from is not a valid option (--since is). C is wrong because -l is --full (no truncation), not a priority filter, and -d is not a date option.

q: A server currently boots into the graphical target, but you need it to boot into the multi-user (text) target automatically from now on. Which command makes this the persistent default?
options: systemctl isolate multi-user.target
systemctl set-default runlevel3
Edit /etc/inittab and change the initdefault line
systemctl set-default multi-user.target
explain: D is correct: 'systemctl set-default' changes the default.target symlink, making multi-user.target the persistent boot target across reboots. A is wrong because 'isolate' only switches targets immediately for the current session — the next reboot returns to whatever the default is. C is wrong because /etc/inittab is the RHEL 6 SysV mechanism; systemd ignores it on RHEL 9/10. B is wrong because 'runlevel3' is not a valid target name — the systemd target is literally called multi-user.target (runlevel3.target exists only as a compatibility alias). Confirm with 'systemctl get-default'.

q: Which command will see only error-or-worse messages from the httpd service logged since 09:00 today?
options: journalctl -u httpd -p err --until "09:00"
journalctl --errors httpd --since "09:00"
journalctl -u httpd -p err --since "09:00"
journalctl -p httpd --since "09:00" -u err
explain: -u selects the unit, -p err filters to priority err and above, and --since bounds the start of the window. --until would show everything BEFORE 09:00, and -p takes a priority, not a unit name; --errors is not a journalctl option.

q: Which command will follow the journal live as new entries arrive, like tail -f on the old log files?
options: journalctl -t -f /var/log/messages
journalctl -f
journalctl --follow-all-boots
journalctl --live
explain: -f makes journalctl follow the journal, printing new entries as they are written. There is no --live or --follow-all-boots option, and journalctl does not take log file paths the way tail does.

q: Which command will inspect the kernel messages from the PREVIOUS boot after a crash and reboot?
options: journalctl -k --since yesterday
journalctl -k -b 0
journalctl --kernel --last-boot
journalctl -k -b -1
explain: -b -1 selects the boot before the current one and -k limits output to kernel messages. -b 0 is the current boot, which no longer contains the crash; the other two spellings do not select a specific boot (and --last-boot is not an option).

q: Which command will reclaim journal disk space so the journal keeps at most the last 14 days?
options: journalctl --vacuum-days=14
journalctl --vacuum-time=14d
journalctl --rotate-now --delete-old
rm -rf /var/log/journal/*
explain: --vacuum-time= removes archived journal files older than the given span (a size-based sibling, --vacuum-size=, also exists). The other option spellings do not exist, and deleting journal files by hand can corrupt the journal's bookkeeping.

q: Which command will show everything the journal recorded during the boot before last, newest entries first?
options: journalctl -b -1 -r
journalctl --boot=-2 --reverse-all
journalctl -b -2 -r
journalctl -b 2 -r
explain: Negative offsets count back from the current boot: -2 is two boots ago, and -r reverses the output order. -b -1 is only the previous boot, a bare 2 is not how boots are addressed, and --reverse-all is not an option.

q: Which command will check how much disk space the journal is using before changing retention?
options: journalctl --usage-report
du -sh /var/log/journal (only)
journalctl --size
journalctl --disk-usage
explain: --disk-usage reports the total size of active and archived journal files as the journal itself accounts for them. The du path can approximate it but misses journald's accounting and fails when journal files live elsewhere; --size and --usage-report are not options.

q: An admin needs to ask a runaway process (PID 4312) to shut down gracefully, letting it clean up and close files first. Which action is correct?
options: kill -STOP 4312 (sends SIGSTOP)
kill -HUP 4312 (sends SIGHUP)
kill 4312 (sends SIGTERM, signal 15)
kill -9 4312 (sends SIGKILL)
explain: A bare kill sends SIGTERM (15), the polite termination request a process can handle to clean up. SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught and risks data loss, SIGHUP conventionally means hangup/reload, and SIGSTOP only freezes the process.

q: An admin needs to force-kill a completely hung process (PID 9021) that ignores normal termination requests. Which action is correct?
options: kill -USR1 9021
kill -TERM -9 9021
kill 9021
kill -9 9021
explain: SIGKILL (9) is delivered by the kernel and cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored, making it the last resort for a hung process. Plain kill sends catchable SIGTERM, the -TERM -9 combination is malformed, and SIGUSR1 is application-defined.

q: An admin needs to make a daemon (PID 777) reload its configuration without restarting it, the conventional way. Which action is correct?
options: kill -CONT 777
kill -INT 777
kill -USR2 777
kill -HUP 777
explain: SIGHUP is the long-standing convention for 'reload your configuration' for daemons (systemd's reload does exactly this). SIGCONT resumes a stopped process, SIGINT is the terminal interrupt, and SIGUSR2 has no standard reload meaning.

q: An admin needs to temporarily freeze a batch job (PID 5150) without terminating it, so it can be resumed later. Which action is correct?
options: kill -STOP 5150, then kill -HUP 5150 to resume
kill -STOP 5150, then kill -CONT 5150 to resume
kill -19 5150 twice to toggle pause
kill -PAUSE 5150, then kill -RESUME 5150
explain: SIGSTOP freezes a process and SIGCONT resumes it; the pair is how job control pauses work without losing state. SIGHUP would typically terminate or reload the process, and PAUSE/RESUME are not signal names; signal 19 IS SIGSTOP on x86_64 but sending it again does not resume anything.

q: An admin needs to send the same interrupt that pressing Ctrl+C in the terminal produces, to PID 3333. Which action is correct?
options: kill -TSTP 3333
kill -TERM 3333
kill -QUIT 3333
kill -INT 3333
explain: Ctrl+C delivers SIGINT (2) to the foreground process group. SIGTERM is the generic kill default, SIGQUIT (Ctrl+\) also dumps core, and SIGTSTP (Ctrl+Z) suspends rather than interrupts.

q: An admin needs to terminate every process whose command name is 'runaway' in one command. Which action is correct?
options: killall runaway
pkill -x runaway --count
kill runaway
killall -u runaway --all
explain: killall takes a process NAME and signals all matching processes. Bare kill needs numeric PIDs, the killall -u form targets a user's processes (and the flags shown are wrong), and pkill --count only counts matches instead of killing (plain pkill runaway would also work, but it is not among the choices as written).

q: ps aux shows this row: root 4312 98.2 0.4 882340 31204 ? R Sep12 41:33 /usr/bin/runaway --mode=all. Answer: which process is consuming the most CPU and what is its PID?
options: The runaway process, PID 4312, at 0.4% CPU
The runaway process, PID 4312, at 98.2% CPU
The runaway process, PID 98, at 4312% CPU
root's shell, PID 4312, at 0.4% CPU
explain: In ps aux output the columns are USER, PID, %CPU, %MEM, VSZ, RSS, TTY, STAT, START, TIME, COMMAND. The row shows PID 4312 with %CPU 98.2 and %MEM 0.4 — the distractors swap the PID with the CPU figure or read the memory column as CPU.

q: ps aux shows this row: alice 2210 0.1 1.9 882340 31204 ? R Sep12 41:33 /usr/bin/python3 /srv/app/worker.py. Answer: how much memory (as %MEM) the worker is using and who owns it?
options: 2210% of memory, owned by alice
1.9% of memory, owned by root
0.1% of memory, owned by alice
1.9% of memory, owned by alice
explain: The %MEM column (fourth field) reads 1.9 and the USER column reads alice. The 0.1 figure is %CPU, and 2210 is the PID, not a memory value.

q: ps aux shows this row: mysql 8841 12.0 8.5 882340 31204 ? R Sep12 41:33 /usr/libexec/mysqld --datadir=/var/lib/mysql. Answer: the command being run and its user?
options: The datadir path, running as PID 8841
/usr/libexec/mysqld, running as root
mysqld_safe, running as the mysql user
/usr/libexec/mysqld, running as the mysql user
explain: COMMAND is the final column (everything after TIME), and USER is the first: mysqld runs as the dedicated mysql account. The datadir is an argument to the command, not the command itself.

q: Which ps invocation lists every process on the system in the BSD-style full listing most admins use for triage?
options: ps -p all
ps aux
ps -list
ps --everything --full
explain: ps aux is the classic BSD-syntax combination (a = all users, u = user-oriented format, x = include processes without a controlling terminal). The other spellings are not valid ps options.

q: A process shows STAT 'Z' in ps output. What does that mean and what resolves it?
options: It is a kernel thread consuming no resources that can be killed with -9
It is a zero-priority process waiting for renice
It is a zombie: the process has exited but its parent has not read its exit status; only the parent reaping it (or dying) clears it
It is a stopped process that kill -CONT will fix
explain: Z marks a zombie — a dead process whose exit status still sits in the process table until the parent wait()s for it. Zombies consume no CPU or memory, cannot be killed (they are already dead), and renice/CONT do not apply.

q: An admin needs to handle this tuning task: a database server doing heavy sequential disk I/O that should favor throughput over latency. Which command is correct?
options: tuned-adm set throughput-performance
tuned-adm profile powersave
tuned-adm profile virtual-guest
tuned-adm profile throughput-performance
explain: throughput-performance tunes the kernel and I/O settings for maximum throughput, the standard pick for storage/database workloads. powersave throttles for energy, virtual-guest assumes a VM guest role, and tuned-adm has no 'set' verb (profiles are applied with 'profile').

q: An admin needs to handle this tuning task: confirm which tuned profile is currently in effect after a colleague changed it. Which command is correct?
options: systemctl show tuned -p Profile
cat /proc/tuned/profile
tuned-adm active
tuned-adm status --profile
explain: tuned-adm active prints the current profile (and whether it verifies). The other paths and options do not exist; systemctl can show the service state but not the active profile name in that form.

q: An admin needs to handle this tuning task: a KVM virtualization HOST (hypervisor) — which profile does tuned itself usually suggest?. Which command is correct?
options: network-throughput
virtual-host
desktop
virtual-guest
explain: tuned-adm recommend typically returns virtual-host on a hypervisor (it optimizes for hosting guests) and virtual-guest inside a VM. desktop targets interactive responsiveness, and network-throughput is a different specialization.

q: An admin needs to handle this tuning task: verify that the running system settings actually match the selected profile after manual changes were made. Which command is correct?
options: tuned-adm diff
tuned-adm profile --audit
tuned-adm verify
tuned-adm check --strict
explain: tuned-adm verify compares the live system settings against the active profile and reports deviations. The other verbs are not tuned-adm subcommands.

q: An admin needs to handle this tuning task: disable tuned entirely so no profile is applied. Which command is correct?
options: tuned-adm off
tuned-adm profile none --now
systemctl mask tuned (only)
tuned-adm disable --all
explain: tuned-adm off removes the active tuning and stops applying profile settings. Masking the service prevents it starting but is not the documented way to clear an applied profile, and the other two spellings are invented.

q: An admin needs to make the server always boot to the text-only multi-user environment instead of the graphical desktop. Which action is correct?
options: systemctl set-default runlevel3.target
systemctl isolate multi-user.target
systemctl enable multi-user.target
systemctl set-default multi-user.target
explain: set-default changes the default target the system boots into (it re-points the default.target symlink). isolate switches the CURRENT session only and does not persist; runlevel3.target is not the target's name; and targets are not 'enabled' like services.

q: An admin needs to immediately drop a running system into rescue mode for emergency maintenance, without rebooting. Which action is correct?
options: systemctl set-default rescue.target
init 1 --isolate
systemctl rescue --now
systemctl isolate rescue.target
explain: isolate starts the rescue target and stops everything not part of it, right now. set-default would only change the NEXT boot, and the other two are not valid commands (the legacy runlevel tool exists but takes just a number and is not the systemd way).

q: An admin needs to check what the system's current default boot target is. Which action is correct?
options: systemctl show-default-target
systemctl is-default
ls -l /etc/systemd/system/default.target (only)
systemctl get-default
explain: get-default prints the target the default.target symlink points to. The other verbs do not exist, and inspecting the symlink manually is indirect (it also lives under /usr/lib/systemd/system in some layouts).

q: An admin needs to understand the difference: a system was booted with the emergency target instead of rescue. What is true?. Which action is correct?
options: They are identical; emergency is just the newer name for rescue
Emergency mode mounts almost nothing (root starts read-only) and starts no services; rescue mode mounts local filesystems and starts basic services before the single-user shell
Emergency mode requires the graphical target to be installed
Rescue mode is the more minimal of the two and starts no shell
explain: rescue.target pulls in basic services and mounted filesystems for single-user work; emergency.target is the bare minimum — a root shell with the root filesystem initially read-only. They are distinct targets, and neither needs the graphical stack.

q: An admin needs to temporarily boot THIS ONCE into the multi-user target from the GRUB menu, leaving the default unchanged. Which action is correct?
options: Press e and change the default.target symlink from the GRUB shell
Append target=multi-user to the kernel command line
Append systemd.unit=multi-user.target to the kernel command line for that boot
Append runlevel=3 to the kernel command line
explain: systemd.unit= on the kernel command line overrides the unit systemd activates for that boot only. There is no runlevel= or bare target= kernel parameter, and the symlink cannot be edited from the GRUB menu.

q: An admin needs to see which target the system is currently running under, and which units belong to it. Which action is correct?
options: systemctl whoami-target
systemctl list-units --type=target (and systemctl status on the active target)
runlevel --target
systemctl get-current-target
explain: list-units --type=target shows the loaded targets including the active one. The other verbs are invented; the legacy runlevel command only prints the previous/current SysV runlevel pair, not systemd target membership.

q: An admin needs to reset a forgotten root password, the standard RHEL 10 way. Which approach is correct?
options: Append single to the kernel line and run passwd in the shell that appears, no other steps
Append rd.break, then run passwd directly at the initramfs prompt
Append init=/bin/bash, run passwd, and reboot immediately
At GRUB press e, append rd.break to the linux line, boot with Ctrl+x, then remount /sysroot rw, chroot, passwd, and touch /.autorelabel before exiting
explain: rd.break stops in the initramfs with the real root mounted read-only at /sysroot, so it must be remounted rw and chrooted into before passwd edits the right shadow file; the /.autorelabel touch makes SELinux relabel the changed files on the next boot. 'single' is legacy wording, init=/bin/bash skips the chroot and relabel (and the root fs starts read-only there too), and passwd at the initramfs prompt edits the wrong root.

q: An admin needs to make boot messages visible in detail for troubleshooting instead of the graphical splash and quiet mode. Which approach is correct?
options: Append splash=off --debug to the kernel command line
Append verbose=1 to the kernel command line
Remove rhgb and quiet from the kernel command line for that boot
Press Tab at the GRUB menu and type 'show messages'
explain: rhgb (graphical boot) and quiet are what suppress the messages on RHEL; removing them for the boot shows the full kernel and systemd output. The parameter spellings shown in the other choices are not the RHEL mechanism.

q: An admin needs to boot directly into a root shell as PID 1 for deep filesystem repair. Which approach is correct?
options: Append init=/bin/bash to the kernel line; remember the root filesystem starts read-only and must be remounted rw before changes
Append rd.shellonly=1 to the kernel line
Append init=/bin/bash; changes apply immediately because the root fs is mounted rw
Append shell=/bin/bash to the kernel line
explain: init= replaces PID 1 with the given program — here bash — giving a bare root shell. The root filesystem is mounted read-only in this path, so a remount is required before edits. The other parameter names are invented.

q: An admin needs to after editing /etc/default/grub, the change does not appear at boot. What was missed?. Which approach is correct?
options: Running grub2-install again on the boot disk
Rebooting twice; the first boot only stages the new configuration
Regenerating the GRUB configuration with grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
Running systemctl daemon-reload so systemd picks up the grub defaults
explain: /etc/default/grub is only the input template; grub2-mkconfig renders it into the grub.cfg the bootloader actually reads. daemon-reload concerns systemd units, no staging boot exists, and grub2-install rewrites boot code, not the menu configuration.

q: An admin needs to set the default kernel to the second entry in the GRUB menu persistently. Which approach is correct?
options: grubby --set-default-index=1 (or grubby --set-default with the kernel path)
grub-setdefault 1 at the GRUB console
grubby --default-kernel=2
Edit GRUB_DEFAULT=2nd in /etc/default/grub only, with no regeneration
explain: grubby manages the bootloader entries directly: --set-default-index counts from 0, so index 1 is the second kernel. Editing /etc/default/grub alone changes nothing until mkconfig runs, and the other command spellings do not exist.

q: An admin needs to A system drops to an emergency shell during boot right after /etc/fstab was edited. What is the most likely cause, and the first fix?. Which approach is correct?
options: SELinux relabeled the files and emergency mode clears after one more reboot on its own
GRUB lost its configuration and must be reinstalled
A bad fstab entry (wrong device/UUID or options) fails a local filesystem mount; correct the entry or add nofail, then reboot
The default target was changed to emergency.target by the edit
explain: systemd treats failed fstab mounts as boot-critical and drops to emergency mode for repair. Fixing the entry (or marking it nofail) resolves it; fstab edits never change the default target or GRUB's own configuration, and a relabel does not repair a mount failure.

q: An admin needs to launch the nightly report generator so it yields CPU to interactive users, with niceness 10. Which statement/action is correct?
options: nice --priority=high ./report.sh
nice -n -10 ./report.sh
renice -n 10 ./report.sh
nice -n 10 ./report.sh
explain: nice -n ADDS to the niceness of the new process; positive values make it NICER (lower scheduling priority), which is what 'yield CPU' means. A negative adjustment would raise its priority, renice works on already-running processes, and --priority=high is not a nice option.

q: An admin needs to raise the scheduling priority of the already-running backup job, PID 8841, whose current niceness is 0, setting niceness to -5. Which statement/action is correct?
options: renice -n -5 -p 8841 (requires root, since decreasing niceness raises priority)
renice --lower 5 -p 8841
nice -n -5 -p 8841
renice -n 5 -p 8841
explain: renice changes a running process; a target niceness of -5 is a DECREASE from 0, i.e. higher priority, which only root may grant. nice cannot touch existing PIDs, and +5 would lower the priority instead.

q: An admin needs to interpret values: process A has niceness -10 and process B has niceness 15. Which gets CPU preference under contention?. Which statement/action is correct?
options: Process A: lower niceness means higher scheduling priority
They are equal; niceness only affects I/O
Process B: higher niceness means higher priority
Process B, because positive values outrank negative ones
explain: Niceness is inverted: -20 is the highest priority and +19 the lowest. A's -10 strongly outranks B's +15. Niceness affects CPU scheduling, not I/O directly.

q: An admin needs to lower the priority of a running compile job, PID 6123, by setting its niceness to 12 as its owner (not root). Which statement/action is correct?
options: nice -n 12 -p 6123 — nice accepts a PID for running jobs
renice -n -12 -p 6123 — the sign must be flipped for a decrease
renice -n 12 -p 6123 — but it will fail; only root can renice at all
renice -n 12 -p 6123 — allowed, because owners may increase niceness (lower priority) on their own processes
explain: Unprivileged users can renice their own processes as long as niceness only INCREASES (priority decreases); decreasing it back requires root. nice starts new commands and takes no -p PID.

q: An admin needs to find the niceness of a running process from the command line. Which statement/action is correct?
options: systemctl show <PID> -p Nice alone works for any process
cat /proc/sys/kernel/nice/<PID>
nice --show <PID>
ps -o pid,nice,comm -p <PID> (the NI column), or the NI column in top
explain: ps exposes niceness as the NI field (also shown by top). There is no nice --show, /proc/sys/kernel/nice does not exist, and systemctl's Nice property applies to service units, not arbitrary PIDs (the general answer is ps/top).

q: An admin needs to A user runs nice -n -10 ./myjob.sh without root and it runs with niceness 0 anyway or errors. Why?. Which statement/action is correct?
options: nice requires the CAP_NICE capability granted by sudoers only
The shell resets niceness for scripts but not for binaries
Only root can start a process with negative niceness (raised priority); unprivileged users may only increase niceness from the default 0 upward
Negative niceness values are invalid on RHEL 10
explain: The kernel enforces it: decreasing niceness below the current value is a privileged operation (CAP_SYS_NICE, held by root). Negative values are perfectly valid for root, and the rule applies to scripts and binaries alike.

q: At the GRUB 2 boot menu on RHEL 10, you highlight the normal entry and want to temporarily edit its kernel command line for this boot only. What do you press and what happens after editing?
options: Press c to edit the entry, then type boot to start with the edited parameters
Press Tab to open the editor, then press Esc twice to boot with the edited parameters
Press Enter to boot first, then edit /boot/grub2/grub.cfg from the login prompt to apply the change to this boot
Press e to edit the entry in place, make the change, then press Ctrl+X or F10 to boot with the edited parameters
explain: Pressing e opens the highlighted entry for in-memory editing and Ctrl+X or F10 boots using those temporary parameters, leaving the on-disk configuration unchanged. The c key opens a GRUB command prompt rather than the entry editor, booting first makes the edit too late for that boot, and Tab only completes or lists commands in the prompt.

q: A RHEL 10 server must boot just once into rescue mode for filesystem work, without changing its normal default target. Which kernel command-line addition at the GRUB menu achieves this?
options: Append single and delete the rhgb quiet parameters from the line
Append init=/bin/bash and remount the root filesystem read-only
Append systemd.unit=rescue.target to the linux line for that boot only
Append systemd.unit=multi-user.target and set a one-time password for root
explain: Adding systemd.unit=rescue.target as a temporary GRUB edit tells systemd to activate the rescue target for that boot only, and the default target is untouched. Booting to the multi-user target is a normal boot rather than rescue, init=/bin/bash bypasses systemd entirely instead of starting the rescue target, and the historical single keyword plus display options does not select the rescue target.

q: During a root password reset using rd.break, you have set the new password inside the chroot. Why must you also run touch /.autorelabel before rebooting?
options: Because GRUB will refuse to boot an entry that was edited unless /.autorelabel exists
Because SELinux would otherwise deny login with the changed password files until a full filesystem relabel occurs on the next boot
Because rd.break leaves the root filesystem mounted read-only until a relabel is requested
Because the password file is only written to disk when an autorelabel is triggered
explain: Changing /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow in the rd.break chroot leaves those files with incorrect or missing SELinux contexts, so creating /.autorelabel forces a relabel at boot that restores correct contexts and allows logins. The password change itself is already written, the filesystem remount state is unrelated to the label file, and GRUB does not check for that file.

q: An administrator runs systemctl get-default and sees graphical.target. The server is a headless database host. What does this output actually tell you?
options: The system cannot boot to a text console until the graphical packages are removed
The display manager service is enabled and has started successfully
The graphical desktop is currently running and consuming resources right now
The system will activate the graphical target at a normal boot unless a temporary kernel override is used
explain: get-default reports the target systemd selects at boot time, which is a statement about future boots rather than current state. Current state is shown by tools that inspect the running system, the display manager could be disabled or failed despite this default, and a text console remains available regardless of the default target.

q: Without rebooting, you run systemctl isolate multi-user.target on a workstation currently in the graphical target. What is the expected result?
options: The default target is permanently changed to multi-user.target for all future boots
The command fails because targets can only be changed at boot time
All services are stopped and the machine drops to a root shell with filesystems unmounted
Graphical-only services are stopped and the system settles into the multi-user target for this session
explain: isolate starts the named target and stops units not part of it, so graphical-only units stop for the current session only. It does not rewrite the default target symlink, it does not unmount filesystems or drop to a maintenance shell the way emergency mode does, and isolate is specifically designed to switch targets on a running system.

q: What is the key difference between the rescue target and the emergency target on RHEL 10?
options: Rescue is for graphical systems only, while emergency is for text-mode systems only
Rescue mounts local filesystems and starts basic services before giving a root shell, while emergency mounts root read-only with almost nothing started
Rescue prompts for the root password, while emergency never requires any authentication
Rescue requires a network connection for remote rescue media, while emergency works only from local media
explain: The rescue target mounts local filesystems and initializes basic system plumbing before the root shell, whereas the emergency target is more minimal, mounting root read-only and starting almost nothing. Neither depends on rescue media or on whether a desktop is installed, and both maintenance modes normally ask for the root password.

q: Which file or link does systemctl set-default multi-user.target actually change on RHEL 10?
options: It edits the GRUB configuration so the kernel is passed multi-user as an argument
It writes the target name into /etc/inittab for systemd to read at boot
