It repoints the /etc/systemd/system/default.target symlink to the multi-user target unit
It creates a new unit file named default.target inside /usr/lib/systemd/system
explain: set-default works by changing the default.target symlink under /etc/systemd/system to point at the chosen target unit. It does not touch the bootloader configuration, it does not create or overwrite vendor unit files under /usr/lib, and RHEL 10 does not use /etc/inittab to select the boot target.

q: Which single command reports the target that RHEL 10 will boot to by default?
options: systemctl isolate --show
runlevel --default
systemctl get-default
systemctl status default
explain: systemctl get-default prints the name of the target linked as the default, which is exactly the persistent boot target. There is no default unit to show status for in that form, isolate is used to switch targets rather than report the default, and runlevel reports runlevel history rather than the configured default target.

q: You run ps aux and see this line: ; user bob; PID 2190; %CPU 2.1; %MEM 41.7; VSZ 8823100; RSS 3340012; TTY ?; STAT Sl; COMMAND /usr/bin/java -jar analytics.jar; Which conclusion is correct?
options: The process started with PID 41 because %MEM is 41.7
The Java process is the memory concern on this host because it holds about 41.7 percent of physical memory, shown by %MEM and its large RSS
The process is stopped and waiting for the terminal because STAT shows Sl
The Java process is the CPU concern because its VSZ is the largest number on the line
explain: %MEM and RSS describe resident physical memory use, so a value near 42 percent identifies this process as the memory consumer. VSZ is virtual address space and often vastly overstates real memory use, the S in STAT means sleeping and l means multithreaded rather than stopped, and the PID is the dedicated PID column value of 2190.

q: Inside top, the summary shows load average: 2.40, 1.85, 1.20 on a 2-CPU virtual machine. How should this be interpreted?
options: Exactly 2 processes are running now and 0.40 of a process is waiting on disk only
Recent demand averaged over 1 minute is slightly above the 2 CPUs available, and the trend over 5 and 15 minutes is falling
The machine has run 2.40 processes since boot and will run out of PIDs soon
Memory is 2.40 times oversubscribed and a swap storm is in progress
explain: Load average counts runnable plus uninterruptible processes averaged over 1, 5, and 15 minutes, so 2.40 on 2 CPUs means modest oversubscription that is easing across the longer windows. It is not a cumulative process count, it says nothing directly about memory or swap, and it is an average rather than an instantaneous split of running versus waiting tasks.

q: Which signal does a plain kill 6020 command send by default, and what is its conventional number?
options: SIGHUP, signal 1, which tells the process to reload its configuration
SIGTERM, signal 15, which asks the process to terminate and lets it clean up first
SIGINT, signal 2, which simulates pressing Ctrl+C in the terminal
SIGKILL, signal 9, which terminates the process immediately with no cleanup
explain: A kill with no signal argument sends SIGTERM number 15, the polite termination request that well-behaved programs can handle for cleanup. SIGKILL number 9 is the uncatchable forced kill, SIGHUP number 1 is conventionally a hangup or reload signal, and SIGINT number 2 is the terminal interrupt generated by Ctrl+C.

q: A stuck indexer process, PID 7731, ignored a normal kill request five minutes ago and still holds a lock file. What is the appropriate next step?
options: Send the uncatchable forced termination with kill -9 7731, accepting that it gets no chance to clean up
Raise its nice value so the scheduler eventually starves it to a stop
Send SIGHUP repeatedly until the process notices and exits
Delete its entry under /proc/7731 to remove the process from the table
explain: Once a process has ignored SIGTERM, SIGKILL via kill -9 is the standard escalation because the kernel terminates it without asking. Repeated hangup signals are equally ignorable, renicing changes scheduling priority but never stops a process, and entries under /proc are a kernel view that cannot be deleted to kill anything.

q: A developer starts a build with nohup ./build.sh > build.log 2>&1 & and then logs out completely. Why does the build keep running?
options: nohup raises the process priority so logout cannot preempt it
nohup converts the job into a systemd service that restarts on failure
nohup makes the process ignore SIGHUP, which the shell would otherwise deliver when the session hangs up
nohup copies the process under PID 1 immediately so the session no longer owns it
explain: nohup specifically arranges for the command to ignore the hangup signal sent when a controlling terminal or session ends, and the redirection sends its output to a file instead of the closed terminal. The process is not immediately reparented as a service, priority is irrelevant to hangups, and no unit file or restart policy is created.

q: In an interactive shell you press Ctrl+Z on a running tar job, see [1]+ Stopped, and want it resumed in the background so you can keep typing. What do you enter?
options: fg %1
bg %1
disown %1
jobs -r
explain: bg with the job spec resumes a stopped job in the background, freeing the terminal while the job continues. fg would resume it in the foreground and retake the terminal, jobs merely lists job state without resuming anything, and disown only removes a job from the shell job table rather than restarting it.

q: An operator wants a newly launched compression job to be a good neighbor on a busy login host, so it should get CPU only when little else wants it. Which launch is correct?
options: nice -n -19 xz -9 bigfile.img
nice -n 19 xz -9 bigfile.img
renice -n 19 xz -9 bigfile.img
nice -n 0 xz -9 bigfile.img
explain: Higher nice values mean lower scheduling priority, so nice -n 19 launches the job at the lowest priority and makes it yield to other work. A negative value would give it higher priority than normal, renice adjusts processes that are already running rather than launching a command, and a value of 0 leaves the priority unchanged.

q: A regular (non-root) user lowered her own running process to nice 10, then tries to bring it back to nice 0 to finish faster. What happens and why?
options: The shell silently clamps the request and leaves the value at 19 instead
The change succeeds but only takes effect after the process is restarted
The attempt is denied because only root may decrease a nice value, which would raise the process priority
The change succeeds because a user may always restore her own process to its original priority
explain: On Linux an unprivileged user may only increase the nice value of her own processes, making them nicer, and may never decrease it to gain priority; that direction requires root. There is no exception for returning to an earlier value, the restriction is enforced immediately rather than at restart, and no silent clamping to a different value occurs.

q: On an 8-CPU RHEL 10 host, top reports load average: 13.60, 12.90, 11.75 sustained across all three windows. What is the best assessment?
options: The load proves memory exhaustion, so adding RAM is the only correct response
The host is healthy because load under 16 is always acceptable regardless of CPU count
The host is heavily oversubscribed, with far more runnable or blocked work than 8 CPUs can service, and the condition is persistent rather than a spike
The host has exactly 13 processes in total and the rest of the numbers are percentages
explain: Load must be judged against CPU count, and values near 12 to 14 sustained on 8 CPUs mean a persistent queue of work waiting for CPU or uninterruptible I/O. There is no universal safe number independent of core count, the figures are averages rather than a process census, and high load alone cannot diagnose memory as the cause.

q: Which command gives you the load averages together with uptime and logged-in user count in one line of output?
options: journalctl -n 1
systemctl status
cat /proc/meminfo
uptime
explain: The uptime command prints how long the system has run, how many users are logged in, and the 1, 5, and 15 minute load averages on one line. The memory file reports memory counters without load, systemctl status summarizes services, and journal output shows log records rather than system load.

q: An admin needs the journal entries from the previous boot only, because the machine crashed before the current boot. Which command does this?
options: journalctl -b -1
journalctl -k -p emerg
journalctl --since-boot=-1
journalctl -b 0 --reverse-all
explain: journalctl -b -1 selects the boot before the current one, with negative offsets counting backwards and -b 0 or plain -b meaning the current boot. The other options are invented flags or, in the case of kernel emergency priority filtering, show only a narrow slice of the current boot rather than the whole previous boot.

q: You suspect a storage driver problem on the current boot and want only kernel messages. Which journalctl invocation shows them?
options: journalctl -p kernel
journalctl -k
journalctl --dmesg-only
journalctl -u kernel.service
explain: The -k option restricts journal output to kernel messages for the selected boot, equivalent in scope to reading the kernel ring buffer through the journal. There is no kernel.service unit to query, kernel is not a valid priority name for -p, and the last option is not a real journalctl flag.

q: A support engineer wants to watch new log entries arrive live during a service restart test, similar to tail -f on a log file. Which command provides this?
options: journalctl -f
journalctl --tail-live
journalctl -u --watch
journalctl -n 0 -r
explain: The -f option makes journalctl follow the journal, printing new entries as they are written until interrupted. The other spellings are not real journalctl options, and reversing or limiting output shows existing entries rather than streaming new ones.

q: To investigate delays, you need journal entries for the crond unit between 14:00 and 15:00 today only. Which command is correct, assuming today is the current date?
options: journalctl -u crond -p 14:00-15:00
journalctl --unit=crond --grep 14:00
journalctl -u crond --since 14:00 --until 15:00
journalctl -u crond --today 14-15
explain: Time windowing is done with --since and --until, which accept clock times for the current day, combined here with -u crond to limit output to that unit. Priority filtering does not accept times, --grep matches message text rather than timestamps, and there is no --today option that takes an hour range.

q: Which journalctl command shows only messages at warning priority or more severe for the current boot?
options: journalctl -b -p warning
journalctl -b -p 5..7
journalctl -b -x warning
journalctl --severity warning+
explain: With -p warning, journalctl shows messages at warning priority and every more severe level, which is the documented meaning of specifying a single priority. Priority numbers run from emerg at 0 as most severe, so a range of 5 to 7 would select the least severe levels instead, and the remaining options are not valid journalctl syntax.

q: An admin wants journals automatically trimmed so entries older than two weeks are discarded during vacuum operations. Which command applies that retention limit now?
options: systemctl clean journald --older-than=2weeks
journalctl --rotate --max-age=14
journalctl --vacuum-size=2weeks
journalctl --vacuum-time=2weeks
explain: --vacuum-time removes archived journal files whose entries are older than the given age, so 2weeks expresses a time-based retention. --vacuum-size takes a byte size rather than a duration, the rotate option merely archives the current file without an age policy in that form, and the systemctl clean form shown is not how journal vacuuming is invoked.

q: You edit /etc/systemd/journald.conf and set Storage=persistent, then restart systemd-journald, yet after reboot only the current boot is still visible. What else was most likely missing?
options: The default target was graphical instead of multi-user, which disables journal storage
The machine needed a tuned profile applied for journal files to survive
The /var/log/journal directory did not exist, so the journal had nowhere persistent to write on disk
The rsyslog service was not enabled to copy journal entries to text files
explain: Persistent storage requires the /var/log/journal directory to exist so journald can place files on disk rather than only in the volatile /run location. Text log forwarding is a separate feature, the boot target has no effect on journal storage, and tuned profiles do not control journal persistence.

q: An administrator wants all tuned adjustments removed so the host runs with no tuning profile at all. Which command does this?
options: tuned-adm reset now
tuned-adm profile default
tuned-adm disable --all
tuned-adm off
explain: tuned-adm off deactivates tuning and restores the unprofiled state. There is no shipped profile literally named default to switch to for this purpose, and the disable and reset forms shown are not tuned-adm subcommands.

q: After hand-editing several sysctl values, an admin runs tuned-adm verify and it reports that the system settings do not match the active profile. What does this result mean?
options: The profile is scheduled to apply at the next reboot but is not active yet
The tuned daemon is stopped and no profile has ever been applied
The active profile file is corrupt and tuned must be reinstalled
Current kernel and system settings have drifted from what the active profile prescribes, for example due to manual changes
explain: verify compares the live system configuration against the active profile prescriptions, so a mismatch indicates drift such as manual sysctl edits after the profile was applied. It does not diagnose package corruption or a stopped daemon, and an active profile is by definition already applied rather than pending a reboot.

q: A latency-sensitive network appliance must shave microseconds off packet handling and keep the CPU from idling down. Which tuned profile is the right pick?
options: throughput-performance
desktop
network-latency
powersave
explain: The network-latency profile is designed for low-latency workloads, disabling power-saving behaviors that add wake-up delay. Throughput-performance favors bulk transfer over response time, powersave does the opposite of keeping CPUs responsive by aggressively saving power, and the desktop profile targets interactive desktop responsiveness rather than network latency.

q: A RHEL 10 virtual machine running under KVM should use the tuning intended for a guest system rather than for the hypervisor host. Which profile fits?
options: virtual-host
virtual-guest
throughput-performance
network-throughput
explain: The virtual-guest profile tunes a system running as a virtual machine guest. The virtual-host profile is for the machine running the hypervisor itself, and the throughput-oriented profiles are generic performance choices that are not specifically guest-tuned.

q: Which tuned profile is the sensible general-purpose choice for a RHEL 10 office workstation where responsiveness and power use should be balanced?
options: throughput-performance
realtime
powersave-max
balanced
explain: The balanced profile is the general-purpose tuned profile that trades off performance and power saving for typical interactive use. There is no shipped profile with the max name shown, throughput-performance sacrifices power saving for bulk performance, and the realtime profile is a specialized low-latency configuration not intended for ordinary workstations.

q: A profile was applied weeks ago, but tuned-adm verify now fails even though nobody re-applied a different profile. Which explanation is most plausible?
options: verify only works immediately after applying a profile in the same login session
Runtime settings were changed after the profile was applied, for example by manual sysctl edits or another tool, so live values no longer match the profile
Profiles expire after a fixed number of days and must be renewed with tuned-adm
The profile was automatically replaced by the balanced profile at the last update
explain: verify checks live settings against the active profile, so post-application changes from administrators or other management tools cause exactly this drift failure. Profiles do not expire on a timer, verify is meant to be run at any time, and tuned does not silently swap the active profile during package updates.

q: An operator must warn logged-in users and schedule a reboot in 20 minutes for kernel work. Which command does this correctly?
options: reboot --delay 20 -m System rebooting for kernel maintenance
shutdown -r +20 System rebooting for kernel maintenance in 20 minutes
shutdown -r 20:00 --no-wall System rebooting for kernel maintenance
systemctl reboot --when=+20min
explain: The shutdown command with -r and a +20 time schedules the reboot 20 minutes ahead and broadcasts the trailing message to logged-in users as a wall message by default. A bare clock time is interpreted as a specific time of day rather than in 20 minutes and contradicts the no-wall intent, and neither reboot nor systemctl reboot accepts the delay syntax shown.

q: A shutdown was scheduled for midnight, but the maintenance window is cancelled at 23:10. Which command cancels the pending shutdown?
options: systemctl cancel shutdown.target
shutdown --abort-pending
kill the shutdown process with kill -9
shutdown -c
explain: shutdown -c is the documented way to cancel a previously scheduled shutdown, and it also notifies users that it was cancelled. The other spellings are not the shutdown cancellation interface, and killing a process is not reliable here because the scheduled action is tracked by systemd rather than a single killable countdown process.

q: Which file under /proc would you read to learn how much memory the kernel believes is available for starting new applications without swapping?
options: /proc/uptime, reading the second value
/proc/meminfo, reading the MemAvailable field
/proc/loadavg, reading the fourth field
/proc/cpuinfo, reading the cache size field
explain: MemAvailable in /proc/meminfo estimates memory available for new workloads without swapping, accounting for reclaimable caches. The processor file describes CPUs, the fourth loadavg field counts currently runnable and total scheduling entities rather than memory, and the second uptime value is accumulated idle time.

q: You cat /proc/loadavg and see: ; 0.42 0.58 0.61 2/847 29144; What is the last field, 29144?
options: The number of kernel threads currently running
The total number of processes created since boot
The number of processes currently in uninterruptible sleep
The PID of the most recently created process
explain: In /proc/loadavg the first three fields are the load averages, the fourth shows running over total scheduling entities, and the fifth and last field is the PID of the most recently created process. It is not a count of sleeping processes, a since-boot total, or a kernel thread count.

q: A runaway reporting process is pegging all CPUs and the box is becoming unresponsive. Which triage order is best practice?
options: Immediately SIGKILL every process owned by that user to be safe
Raise its nice value to 19 and wait for it to finish on its own, however long that takes
Identify it with top or ps, try a graceful SIGTERM so it can clean up, and escalate to SIGKILL only if it refuses to exit
Reboot the server first, then investigate the journal after it comes back
explain: Sound triage identifies the offender first, attempts a graceful termination that allows cleanup, and reserves the uncatchable SIGKILL for processes that ignore the polite request. Killing all of a user's processes destroys unrelated work, rebooting first discards evidence and disrupts everything, and merely renicing a runaway does not stop it or protect the system promptly.

q: You need to terminate every running copy of a misbehaving helper named metrics-agent, regardless of PID. Which command targets them by name?
options: kill metrics-agent
systemctl kill metrics-agent
killall metrics-agent
pkill --pid metrics-agent
explain: killall sends a signal to all processes whose name matches the given command name, which is exactly the by-name termination needed. Plain kill requires numeric PIDs, the pkill form shown invents an option and still treats the argument incorrectly, and systemctl kill operates on services and units rather than arbitrary process names.

q: Which pkill usage terminates processes whose full command line contains the string nightly-etl, including ones started with long argument lists?
options: pkill -f nightly-etl
pkill -n nightly-etl
pkill nightly-etl --full-args
pkill -x nightly-etl
explain: The -f option makes pkill match against the full command line rather than just the process name, so patterns appearing in arguments are found. The invented flag form is invalid, -n selects only the newest matching process instead of all of them, and -x requires an exact full name match which is the opposite of a substring search in arguments.

q: You run ps -eo pid,ppid,stat,cmd and see a process with STAT Z whose parent is a long-running application. Why does kill -9 on that PID have no effect?
options: The process is protected by SELinux and requires root to signal it
The process is a zombie that has already exited; only its parent can reap its exit status to remove the entry
The PID has been recycled and now belongs to the kernel itself
The process is in uninterruptible disk sleep and will accept the signal after the I/O completes
explain: A zombie is a process that has already terminated and remains only as an exit-status entry until its parent collects it, so there is nothing left to kill. This state is unrelated to SELinux permissions, disk sleep is the D state rather than Z, and PID recycling does not turn a zombie entry into a kernel process.

q: What is PID 1 on a RHEL 10 system, and what happens to orphaned processes?
options: PID 1 is systemd, and orphaned processes are reparented to it so they are properly reaped
PID 1 is the kernel scheduler, and orphaned processes are terminated immediately
PID 1 is sshd, and orphaned processes are adopted by the next user who logs in
PID 1 is the first login shell, and orphaned processes keep their dead parent PID forever
explain: On RHEL 10 systemd runs as PID 1 and adopts processes whose parents exit, ensuring their exit statuses are reaped. The kernel itself is not a userspace PID 1 process, orphans are neither instantly killed nor left parentless forever, and sshd plays no adoption role.

q: A server booted with noisy storage errors scrolling past, but rhgb quiet hides the details you need on the next boot. What GRUB-level change helps you see full boot messages for troubleshooting?
options: Delete the splash image file from the GRUB themes directory
Append systemd.unit=emergency.target to drop straight to a shell before drivers load
Set the default target to rescue so boot messages are written to the journal
Temporarily remove rhgb quiet from the linux line when editing the entry at the GRUB menu
explain: Removing rhgb quiet for that boot disables the graphical boot splash and verbose suppression, so kernel and service messages print to the console for troubleshooting. Dropping to the emergency target changes the whole boot mode rather than just visibility, the default target does not control boot verbosity, and theme files do not govern kernel message display.

q: After editing a GRUB entry in place, which action actually boots the system using your edited kernel parameters?
options: Press Esc to return to the menu and then wait for the timeout to expire
Press Enter on the edited line inside the editor
Press Ctrl+X or F10 while in the GRUB editor
Save the entry permanently with Ctrl+S, then select it from the menu
explain: In the GRUB editor, Ctrl+X or F10 boots immediately with the in-memory edited parameters. Returning to the menu discards the temporary edit path described, Enter inside the editor inserts a newline rather than booting, and there is no in-editor save shortcut that makes the edit permanent.

q: A database service was restarted at 02:00 and has been misbehaving since. Which command reviews only that unit's messages from the current boot, in the order they occurred?
options: journalctl -u mariadb -b
journalctl -u mariadb --boot=all-boots
journalctl --service mariadb -r -b
journalctl -b -u mariadb.service.d
explain: Combining -u with the unit name and -b restricts output to that unit during the current boot in chronological order. The boot flag shown in the second option is not valid syntax, --service is not the journalctl unit option and -r would reverse the order, and the drop-in directory name is not a unit selector.

q: Which two settings together make journal storage persistent across reboots on RHEL 10? (Choose two.)
options: Set Storage=persistent (or auto with the directory present) in /etc/systemd/journald.conf and restart systemd-journald
Enable the rsyslog service so it archives the journal to /var/log/messages
Add a tmpfiles rule that copies /run/log/journal to /var at shutdown
Create the /var/log/journal directory so journald has an on-disk location
explain: Persistence requires both an on-disk home, the /var/log/journal directory, and configuration that tells journald to use persistent storage, after which the daemon is restarted. Rsyslog forwarding is a separate legacy logging path and is not what makes the journal itself persistent, and no shutdown copy rule is part of the mechanism.

q: Which two commands each terminate every process whose name is backup-agent? (Choose two.)
options: killall backup-agent
kill backup-agent
systemctl stop backup-agent
pkill backup-agent
explain: Both killall and pkill in their basic form match processes by name and signal all of them, so either terminates every backup-agent process. Plain kill requires numeric PIDs and rejects a name argument, and systemctl stop works on service units rather than arbitrary processes matched by name.

q: Which two commands each display the system load averages? (Choose two.)
options: uptime
cat /proc/meminfo
df -h
cat /proc/loadavg
explain: Both uptime and the contents of /proc/loadavg present the 1, 5, and 15 minute load averages. The memory information file reports memory counters with no load figures, and df reports filesystem space usage only.

q: Which two targets each provide a single-user-style maintenance environment on RHEL 10? (Choose two.)
options: multi-user.target
graphical.target
emergency.target
rescue.target
explain: Both the rescue and emergency targets are maintenance modes that provide a root shell with progressively fewer services started. The multi-user target is a normal full boot without graphics, and the graphical target is a normal boot with a desktop, so neither is a single-user maintenance environment.

q: Which two methods each let a long-running command survive the user logging out of the terminal session? (Choose two.)
options: Start it in the background and use the shell disown builtin so the shell stops sending it a hangup
Start it in the foreground and press Ctrl+Z before logging out
Start it with a higher nice value so logout cannot affect it
Start it under nohup so it ignores the hangup signal
explain: nohup protects a process by ignoring SIGHUP, and disown removes a job from the shell job table so the shell does not hang it up at exit; both are established ways to survive logout. Scheduling priority has nothing to do with hangup delivery, and merely stopping a foreground job with Ctrl+Z leaves it in the job table and vulnerable at logout.

q: Which two tuned-adm commands are valid ways to inspect tuning state on a host? (Choose two.)
options: tuned-adm active
tuned-adm verify
tuned-adm show-kernel
tuned-adm ps
explain: tuned-adm active reports the applied profile and tuned-adm verify checks whether live settings conform to that profile, so both inspect tuning state. The other two spellings are not tuned-adm subcommands at all.

q: Which command-line addition boots RHEL 10 straight to a root shell in the emergency target, skipping most initialization?
options: Append rd.break and continue without entering any password
Append systemd.unit=emergency.target to the linux line at the GRUB menu
Append init=/sbin/systemd-rescue to the linux line
Append systemd.unit=multi-user.target and log in as root at the console
explain: Passing systemd.unit=emergency.target overrides the default target for that boot and brings the system up in the minimal emergency environment with a root shell. The multi-user target is a complete normal boot, rd.break stops in the initramfs rather than the emergency target and is part of the password-reset flow, and the init path shown is not a real binary.

q: In top, the Tasks line reads: ; Tasks: 214 total, 1 running, 213 sleeping, 0 stopped, 0 zombie; CPU shows 96.2 id. An admin claims the box is CPU-bound. Is that claim supported, and why?
options: No, 96.2 percent idle CPU with only 1 running task shows the processor is mostly waiting, so the bottleneck lies elsewhere
No, because a system with any sleeping tasks can never be CPU-bound in any circumstance
Yes, 213 sleeping tasks are all consuming CPU in the background
Yes, 214 total tasks proves the CPUs are saturated regardless of the idle figure
explain: The idle percentage directly measures unused CPU, so 96.2 percent idle with a single running task contradicts a CPU-bound diagnosis. A large task count alone says nothing about CPU use, sleeping tasks consume no CPU while asleep, and the general statement in the last option overreaches even though the claim is unsupported here.

q: You need to follow the journal for the postfix unit live during a mail test, seeing new entries as they happen. Which command does this?
options: journalctl -u postfix -f
journalctl -f -u postfix.service.log
journalctl -u postfix --live
tail -f /var/log/journal/postfix
explain: Combining -u for the unit with -f to follow gives a live stream of that unit's new journal entries. The --live spelling is not a journalctl option, the unit name does not take a log-file suffix, and journal files are binary stores that are not tailed per unit as plain text.

q: An admin lowers a running batch process from nice 5 to nice 12 with renice, then checks with ps and sees the change already reflected. What does this confirm about renice?
options: renice changes the scheduling priority of an already-running process immediately, without a restart
renice changes the priority only for child processes the batch job forks later
renice restarts the process automatically with the new priority, losing in-memory state
renice only records the value and applies it the next time the process is scheduled after reboot
explain: renice adjusts the nice value of a live process in place and the kernel scheduler honors it right away, which is why ps shows the new value without any restart. It neither defers to a reboot nor restarts the process, and it acts on the specified process itself rather than only its future children.

q: An admin tries to create a single 3.5 TB partition on /dev/sdb with fdisk and cannot. What is the limitation and the correct tool?
options: fdisk cannot create any partition larger than 1 TB under any circumstances
The DOS/MBR partition table uses 32-bit sector addresses, capping partitions at 2 TiB; use gdisk or parted with a GPT label instead
The filesystem must be created before partitioning, so run mkfs.xfs first
The kernel cannot address disks larger than 2 TB regardless of partition table type
explain: MBR's 32-bit LBA fields max out at 2 TiB per partition, so a 3.5 TB single partition is impossible with a DOS label. GPT uses 64-bit addresses and removes the limit; gdisk (GPT fdisk) or parted with mklabel gpt handles it. Option A understates fdisk wildly. Option C reverses the order: partitioning precedes filesystem creation. Option D is wrong; the limit is in the partition table format, not the kernel.

q: An admin runs pvcreate /dev/sdc on a brand-new empty disk, then notices fdisk -l shows no partitions on /dev/sdc. Is something wrong?
options: Yes: pvcreate silently failed, because physical volumes must always be partitions like /dev/sdc1
Yes: running pvcreate on a whole disk destroys the disk's firmware and it must be replaced
Yes: the command must be re-run as pvcreate /dev/sdc1 or the volume group cannot use the space
No: pvcreate works on a whole disk or a partition, and a whole-disk physical volume legitimately has no partition table; the LVM metadata sits directly on the disk
explain: LVM physical volumes can be built on whole disks or on partitions; on a whole disk there is simply no partition table, which is normal and expected. The pvcreate metadata occupies the start of the device directly. Option A is wrong because the command succeeds on whole disks. Option C would require creating a partition first, which is valid but unnecessary. Option B is nonsense; pvcreate only writes metadata sectors. (Caution: on a disk with existing data, whole-disk pvcreate would destroy it, so verify the disk is empty first.)

q: An admin runs fallocate -l 2G /swapfile && mkswap /swapfile && swapon /swapfile, but swapon fails with 'swap file has holes'. What is the robust fix?
options: Delete it and recreate with dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapfile bs=1M count=2048 so every block is physically allocated, then chmod 600 /swapfile, mkswap /swapfile, and swapon /swapfile
Use fallocate -p to punch more holes, which paradoxically satisfies the allocator
Ignore the error: holes in swap files are harmless and swapon will use the file anyway
Swap files are unsupported on XFS, so a dedicated partition is the only option
explain: fallocate can create files with unwritten extents (holes), especially on XFS, and the kernel's swap code refuses such files because it needs guaranteed block mappings. dd writes real zeros to every block, producing a fully allocated file. chmod 600 is required practice (swapon warns about insecure permissions), then mkswap formats and swapon activates it. Option C is wrong: swapon refuses to activate. Option B is backwards: -p punches holes, the exact problem. Option D is false; fully allocated swap files work on XFS.

q: In gdisk, an admin changes a new partition's type code to 8E00 before running pvcreate on it. What does 8E00 signify, and is it mandatory?
options: 8E00 designates a RAID partition; LVM partitions use FD00
8E00 is the GPT type code for 'Linux LVM'; it documents intent for administrators and tools, but pvcreate works regardless of the type code
pvcreate refuses to run unless the partition type is exactly 8E00
GPT disks have no type codes, so the setting is meaningless
explain: GPT partition type GUIDs (shown abbreviated by gdisk) label a partition's intended use; 8E00 = Linux LVM. LVM itself does not check the type code, so pvcreate succeeds either way, but correct typing keeps the layout self-documenting and avoids confusion with other tools. Option C overstates it as a hard requirement. Option A swaps the codes: FD00 is Linux RAID. Option D is false; type codes are a fundamental GPT feature.

q: After parted -s /dev/sdb mklabel gpt mkpart primary 1MiB 100%, pvcreate /dev/sdb1 fails with 'Device /dev/sdb1 not found'. The parted command reported success. What happened?
options: The -s flag makes parted print commands without executing them
The kernel has not re-read the new partition table, so /dev/sdb1 does not exist yet; run partprobe /dev/sdb (or reboot) to make the kernel rescan
mkpart requires a filesystem type argument or no device node is created
Partition numbers start at 0, so the device is actually /dev/sdb0
explain: parted updates the on-disk table, but existing device nodes only appear after the kernel re-reads the table; partprobe triggers that rescan immediately. Option A is wrong: -s means script/non-interactive mode, and it does execute. Option C is wrong: the filesystem-type hint in mkpart is optional and unrelated to node creation. Option D is wrong: Linux partition numbers start at 1.

q: A new disk was added to the system, but lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/vgdata/lvdata fails with 'Insufficient free space'. What step was skipped?
options: Unmounting the filesystem, because lvextend -r requires the filesystem to be offline
Running lvextend before pvcreate, which is the required order
Rebooting, because LVM cannot see new disks until a reboot
vgextend vgdata /dev/sdX1: the new physical volume must first be added to the volume group, because lvextend allocates from the VG's free extents
explain: LVM is layered: physical volumes feed free extents into the volume group, and logical volumes allocate from the VG. Until vgextend adds the new PV's extents to vgdata, the VG has no free space to give. The correct order is pvcreate, then vgextend, then lvextend. Option C is unnecessary; a rescan (or reboot) may be needed to see the disk, but the error here is VG free space. Option B reverses the required order. Option A is wrong: -r (--resizefs) is designed for online resizing.

q: Two swap areas exist and the admin wants /dev/sdb2 used before the swap file. The fstab line is /dev/sdb2 none swap sw,pri=10 0 0. How is priority verified, and which value wins?
options: The lower number wins: pri=10 makes /dev/sdb2 the last resort
Run swapon -s (or swapon --show): the Priority column lists each area, and the higher number is used first
fstab cannot set swap priority; it requires a sysctl setting
Priority can only be set on zram devices, not on partitions or files
explain: The pri=N mount option sets swap priority, and swapon -s/--show displays the resulting Priority column so you can confirm. The kernel prefers the highest-priority area first. Option D is false; pri works on partitions, files, and zram alike. Option A inverts the ordering. Option C is wrong; fstab's options field is exactly where pri belongs.

q: You have attached a new blank disk /dev/sdb. Before creating partitions, you must write a GPT partition table to it. Which command does this?
options: parted /dev/sdb mktable gpt
parted /dev/sdb mklabel gpt
fdisk /dev/sdb gpt
gdisk /dev/sdb -g
explain: B is correct: parted's mklabel command writes a new partition table label, and 'gpt' selects the GUID Partition Table format. A is wrong because parted has no 'mktable' subcommand; the command is mklabel. C is wrong because fdisk does not take a table-type argument; (and classic fdisk is MBR-oriented — gdisk/parted are the GPT tools). D is wrong because gdisk is interactive/menu-driven and has no -g flag for writing a label; in gdisk you would use the 'o' command interactively or use sgdisk --clear.

q: You need to confirm that /dev/sdc actually uses a GPT partition table and see its existing partitions. Which command shows both?
options: df -h /dev/sdc
ls -l /dev/sdc*
mount | grep sdc
parted /dev/sdc print
explain: D is correct: parted /dev/sdc print displays the partition table type (e.g., 'Partition Table: gpt') along with all partitions, sizes, and flags. B is wrong because ls only shows device nodes, revealing nothing about the table type or partitions' contents. A is wrong because df shows mounted filesystems' usage, not partition tables, and fails on unmounted disks. C is wrong because mount only lists currently mounted filesystems, saying nothing about the underlying table type.

q: /dev/sdd has a GPT table with three partitions, and partition 3 is no longer needed. The other partitions contain live data. Which command removes ONLY partition 3?
options: parted /dev/sdd rm 3
parted /dev/sdd delete 3
parted /dev/sdd rm 1
wipefs -a /dev/sdd3
explain: A is correct: parted's rm subcommand takes the partition NUMBER, so rm 3 deletes only partition 3, leaving partitions 1 and 2 and their data intact. C is wrong because rm 1 would delete partition 1, destroying the wrong data. B is wrong because parted has no 'delete' subcommand; the command is rm. D is wrong because wipefs -a only erases filesystem signatures on that partition, it does not remove the partition entry from the table (and is the wrong tool for the job).

q: You created partition /dev/sdb1 and want to use it as LVM physical storage. What is the correct FIRST LVM step?
options: pvcreate /dev/sdb1
vgextend vgdata /dev/sdb1
vgcreate vgdata /dev/sdb1
lvcreate -n lvdata -L 5G /dev/sdb1
explain: A is correct: pvcreate initializes the partition as an LVM physical volume, which must happen before any volume group can use it. C is wrong because vgcreate requires its devices to already be physical volumes; running it on a raw partition fails. D is wrong because lvcreate allocates from a volume group, not from a raw partition, and no VG exists yet. B is wrong because vgextend adds a PV to an existing VG — it both assumes a VG exists and requires the device to already be a PV.

q: Volume group vgdata already exists on /dev/sdb1. You have prepared a new physical volume /dev/sdc1 and must add its space to vgdata WITHOUT destroying existing data. Which command does this?
options: vgextend vgdata /dev/sdc1
lvextend -L +10G /dev/vgdata/lv0
pvcreate vgdata /dev/sdc1
vgcreate vgdata /dev/sdc1
explain: A is correct: vgextend adds an initialized physical volume to an existing volume group, growing its free space non-destructively. D is wrong because vgcreate creates a NEW volume group and would fail since vgdata already exists. B is wrong because lvextend grows a logical volume, not the volume group; it cannot add a new disk's space to the VG. C is wrong because pvcreate initializes a device as a PV — vgdata is a VG name, not a device, so the syntax is invalid and it does not attach anything to the group.

q: Volume group vgdata has 20 GB free. You must create a 10 GB logical volume named lvweb inside it. Which command does this?
options: lvcreate -L 10G -n lvweb /dev/sdb1
lvcreate -n vgdata -L 10G lvweb
lvcreate -n lvweb -L 10G vgdata
lvadd -n lvweb -L 10G vgdata
explain: C is correct: -n names the new LV (lvweb), -L 10G sets its size, and the final argument is the volume group it is carved from (vgdata). B is wrong because the name and VG arguments are swapped; it would try to create an LV named 'vgdata' in a VG called 'lvweb', which does not exist. A is wrong because lvcreate allocates from a volume group, not from a raw PV device like /dev/sdb1. D is wrong because there is no 'lvadd' command; LV creation is lvcreate.

q: Logical volume /dev/vgdata/lvweb (ext4, mounted at /web) is running out of space, and vgdata has free extents. You must grow the LV by 5 GB AND resize the filesystem in one operation, without unmounting. Which command does this?
options: extendfs -r /dev/vgdata/lvweb 5G
lvextend -r -L +5G /dev/vgdata/lvweb
lvresize +5G /dev/vgdata/lvweb
lvextend -L +5G /dev/vgdata/lvweb
explain: B is correct: -L +5G grows the LV by 5 GB, and -r (--resizefs) automatically grows the ext4 filesystem to fill it while mounted — the complete non-disruptive operation. D is wrong because without -r the LV grows but the filesystem stays its old size, so /web gains no usable space until a separate resize2fs is run. C is wrong because lvresize also needs -r to resize the filesystem, and the size argument requires -L/+ syntax (bare '+5G' is invalid). A is wrong because there is no 'extendfs' command on RHEL; filesystem resizing is done via resize2fs/xfs_growfs or the -r flag.

q: Logical volume /dev/vgdata/lvold is unmounted and its data is no longer needed. You must remove the LV itself (the VG and its other LVs must remain). Which command does this?
options: lvremove /dev/vgdata/lvold
vgremove /dev/vgdata/lvold
lvdelete /dev/vgdata/lvold
lvreduce --remove /dev/vgdata/lvold
explain: A is correct: lvremove deletes the named logical volume (prompting for confirmation unless -y) while leaving the VG and other LVs untouched. C is wrong because there is no 'lvdelete' command in LVM. B is wrong because vgremove deletes an entire VOLUME GROUP, which would destroy the other LVs too — and it takes a VG name, not an LV path. D is wrong because lvreduce shrinks an LV's size; it has no --remove option and does not delete the volume.

q: You ran mkswap on /dev/sdb2 and added it to /etc/fstab. The swap space is still not active. Which command activates it now?
options: swapon /dev/sdb2
swapoff -a && swapon -a
mkswap -a /dev/sdb2
systemctl start swap
explain: A is correct: swapon activates a prepared swap device immediately; mkswap only writes the swap signature, and the fstab entry only takes effect at boot or via swapon -a. C is wrong because mkswap has no -a option and re-running mkswap would just rewrite the signature without activating anything. B is wrong because swapoff -a would deactivate currently active swap first — disruptive and unnecessary — when a single swapon suffices. D is wrong because there is no generic 'swap' systemd unit to start; swap devices are managed via swapon or their fstab entries.

q: A new disk /dev/sdd is installed. You must add ALL of its space to the existing logical volume /dev/vgdata/lvweb (ext4, mounted) without losing data and without unmounting. Which sequence is correct?
options: pvcreate /dev/sdd → vgcreate vgdata /dev/sdd → lvextend -r /dev/vgdata/lvweb
vgcreate vgdata /dev/sdd → lvextend -r -L +100%FREE /dev/vgdata/lvweb
vgextend vgdata /dev/sdd → lvextend -r -L +5G /dev/vgdata/lvweb
pvcreate /dev/sdd → vgextend vgdata /dev/sdd → lvextend -r -l +100%FREE /dev/vgdata/lvweb
explain: D is correct and complete: pvcreate initializes the whole disk as a PV, vgextend attaches it to the existing vgdata, and lvextend -r -l +100%FREE grows the LV by all new free extents while resizing ext4 online. B is wrong because vgcreate fails (vgdata already exists) and -L cannot be combined with a +100%FREE relative value (-l is the extent-based option). A is wrong because vgcreate fails on the existing VG name, so the LV never gets the new space. C is wrong because vgextend requires the device to already be a PV; without pvcreate first, it errors out.

q: Volume group vgdata is empty (all LVs removed) and must be deleted entirely. Which command removes the volume group?
options: vgremove vgdata
vgdelete vgdata
pvremove vgdata
vgreduce --removemissing vgdata
explain: A is correct: vgremove deletes the named volume group (it requires no LVs to remain, prompting for confirmation). B is wrong because there is no 'vgdelete' command. C is wrong because pvremove removes LVM metadata from physical volume DEVICES (e.g., /dev/sdb1), not volume groups, and takes device paths. D is wrong because vgreduce --removemissing only drops missing PVs from a VG; it does not delete the VG itself.

q: After removing an LV, vgdata has scattered free extents. You must grow /dev/vgdata/lvdb to consume ALL remaining free space in the VG and resize its XFS filesystem online. Which command does this?
options: lvextend -l 100%FREE /dev/vgdata/lvdb
lvresize -r --use-all /dev/vgdata/lvdb
lvextend -r -L +100%FREE /dev/vgdata/lvdb
lvextend -r -l +100%FREE /dev/vgdata/lvdb
explain: D is correct: -l (lowercase L) takes extents, and +100%FREE means all free extents in the VG; -r resizes the XFS filesystem online via xfs_growfs. C is wrong because -L (uppercase) takes absolute/relative SIZES like +5G; combining -L with the %FREE extent syntax is invalid. A is wrong because without -r the LV grows but the XFS filesystem does not, leaving the new space unusable (and the missing + makes it 'set to exactly 100%FREE' semantics, which is not the intent). B is wrong because lvresize has no --use-all option; the correct form would be lvresize -r -l +100%FREE.

q: The logical volume /dev/vg0/lv_data is full. It holds an XFS filesystem mounted at /data. Which single command extends the LV by 5 GiB AND grows the XFS filesystem to use the new space?
options: xfs_growfs /data
lvextend -L +5G /dev/vg0/lv_data && resize2fs /dev/vg0/lv_data
lvextend -r -L +5G /dev/vg0/lv_data
lvresize -L 5G /dev/vg0/lv_data
explain: C is correct: '-L +5G' adds 5 GiB to the current LV size, and '-r' (--resizefs) automatically grows the filesystem afterward using the correct tool for the filesystem type (xfs_growfs for XFS). B is wrong because resize2fs only works on ext2/ext3/ext4 — it cannot grow XFS. A is wrong because xfs_growfs only expands the filesystem to fill the existing LV; if the LV itself was never extended, there is no new space to claim. D is wrong because '-L 5G' without the plus sets the LV to an absolute size of 5 GiB — if the LV is larger than that, this shrinks it, and XFS cannot be shrunk, so this risks data loss.

q: vgs shows volume group vgdata with a physical extent size of 4 MiB, and an LV in it occupies 2560 extents. What is the LV's size?
options: 5 GiB
10 GiB
20 GiB
2560 GiB
explain: LV size = extents x PE size = 2560 x 4 MiB = 10240 MiB = 10 GiB. The extent COUNT alone is not a size, and the doubled/halved values come from arithmetic slips.

q: In volume group vgapp the physical extent size is 4 MiB. A logical volume there spans 1280 extents. How much space does that LV occupy?
options: 5 GiB
2.5 GiB
10 GiB
1280 GiB
explain: LV size = extents x PE size = 1280 x 4 MiB = 5120 MiB = 5 GiB. The extent COUNT alone is not a size, and the doubled/halved values come from arithmetic slips.

q: An admin checks vgdb: each physical extent is 8 MiB, and one LV holds 640 of them. What capacity does the LV report?
options: 2.5 GiB
5 GiB
10 GiB
640 GiB
explain: LV size = extents x PE size = 640 x 8 MiB = 5120 MiB = 5 GiB. The extent COUNT alone is not a size, and the doubled/halved values come from arithmetic slips.

q: On vgweb (extent size 4 MiB), lvs lists a volume using 512 extents. Calculate the volume's size.
options: 512 GiB
1 GiB
2 GiB
4 GiB
explain: LV size = extents x PE size = 512 x 4 MiB = 2048 MiB = 2 GiB. The extent COUNT alone is not a size, and the doubled/halved values come from arithmetic slips.

q: vgs shows volume group vgstore with a physical extent size of 16 MiB, and an LV in it occupies 320 extents. What is the LV's size?
options: 320 GiB
5 GiB
10 GiB
2.5 GiB
explain: LV size = extents x PE size = 320 x 16 MiB = 5120 MiB = 5 GiB. The extent COUNT alone is not a size, and the doubled/halved values come from arithmetic slips.

q: In volume group vgvirt the physical extent size is 4 MiB. A logical volume there spans 2048 extents. How much space does that LV occupy?
options: 2048 GiB
8 GiB
4 GiB
16 GiB
explain: LV size = extents x PE size = 2048 x 4 MiB = 8192 MiB = 8 GiB. The extent COUNT alone is not a size, and the doubled/halved values come from arithmetic slips.

q: Volume group vgdata totals 100 GiB with 30 GiB allocated to logical volumes. An admin runs lvcreate -l 100%FREE -n lvnew vgdata. How large is lvnew?
options: 35 GiB
30 GiB
100 GiB
70 GiB
explain: 100%FREE means all currently UNALLOCATED extents: 100 - 30 = 70 GiB. It does not mean the whole VG (existing LVs keep their space) and it is not split or halved.

q: Volume group vgapp totals 200 GiB with 45 GiB allocated to logical volumes. An admin runs lvcreate -l 100%FREE -n lvnew vgapp. How large is lvnew?
options: 45 GiB
155 GiB
200 GiB
77 GiB
explain: 100%FREE means all currently UNALLOCATED extents: 200 - 45 = 155 GiB. It does not mean the whole VG (existing LVs keep their space) and it is not split or halved.

q: Volume group vgdb totals 50 GiB with 12 GiB allocated to logical volumes. An admin runs lvcreate -l 100%FREE -n lvnew vgdb. How large is lvnew?
options: 38 GiB
12 GiB
19 GiB
50 GiB
explain: 100%FREE means all currently UNALLOCATED extents: 50 - 12 = 38 GiB. It does not mean the whole VG (existing LVs keep their space) and it is not split or halved.

q: Which command(s) will prepare the partition /dev/sdc1 so LVM can use it as a physical volume?
options: pvcreate /dev/sdc1
vgcreate /dev/sdc1
lvcreate /dev/sdc1
pvscan --initialize /dev/sdc1
explain: pvcreate writes the LVM metadata header that marks a device as a physical volume. vgcreate builds a volume group FROM existing PVs, lvcreate carves logical volumes out of a VG, and pvscan only reports what already exists.

q: Which command(s) will create a volume group named vgapp from physical volumes /dev/sdb1 and /dev/sdc1?
options: lvcreate -n vgapp /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
vgcreate vgapp /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
vgcreate /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1 vgapp
pvcreate vgapp /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
explain: vgcreate's first argument is the new VG name, followed by the member PV devices. Putting devices first reads them as the VG name position, and the other two commands operate at the wrong LVM layer.

q: Which command(s) will add the prepared physical volume /dev/sdd1 to the existing volume group vgdata?
options: vgcreate vgdata /dev/sdd1
pvadd vgdata /dev/sdd1
lvextend vgdata /dev/sdd1
vgextend vgdata /dev/sdd1
explain: vgextend adds PVs to an existing VG. vgcreate would try to create a new group with a taken name, lvextend grows logical volumes (not groups), and pvadd is not an LVM command.

q: Which command(s) will create a 20 GiB logical volume named lvweb in volume group vgapp?
options: lvcreate --size=20G --name=lvweb --vg=vgapp
lvcreate -L 20G -n lvweb /dev/vgapp
vgcreate -L 20G -n lvweb vgapp
lvcreate -L 20G -n lvweb vgapp
explain: lvcreate takes -L for size, -n for the LV name, and the VG as the bare final argument. The /dev/ path form is how you REFERENCE an LV afterward, not how you name its VG at creation, and there is no --vg option.

q: Which command(s) will grow logical volume /dev/vgdata/lvdata by 10 GiB AND grow its filesystem in the same operation?
options: lvextend -r -L +10G /dev/vgdata/lvdata
lvextend -L +10G /dev/vgdata/lvdata
lvextend -r -L 10G /dev/vgdata/lvdata
lvresize --growfs -L +10G /dev/vgdata/lvdata
explain: -r (--resizefs) makes lvextend resize the contained filesystem after extending the block device. Without it df keeps showing the old size. Note -L +10G (relative) versus -L 10G (absolute total of 10 GiB), and lvresize has no --growfs flag.

q: Which command(s) will safely retire physical volume /dev/sdb1 from vgdata, moving its extents to the group's other disks first?
options: pvmove /dev/sdb1, then vgreduce vgdata /dev/sdb1, then pvremove /dev/sdb1
pvremove /dev/sdb1, then vgreduce vgdata /dev/sdb1
lvmove /dev/sdb1, then vgreduce vgdata /dev/sdb1, then pvremove /dev/sdb1
vgreduce vgdata /dev/sdb1, then pvremove /dev/sdb1 (pvmove is optional)
explain: Extents in use must be evacuated with pvmove BEFORE the PV leaves the VG, or the data on them is lost. vgreduce alone refuses (or would orphan data), pvremove first destroys the metadata while the VG still references it, and lvmove is not a real command.

q: Which command(s) will see which physical volumes belong to vgdata and how much free space the group has?
options: lvs vgdata --pvs
pvcreate --show vgdata
vgs vgdata and pvs (or vgdisplay vgdata)
lsblk --vg vgdata
explain: vgs/vgdisplay report VG size and free extents; pvs lists the member PVs. lvs lists logical volumes, and the other two spellings are not real options.

q: Which command(s) will shrink the risk before reducing an LV: an LV must be made smaller, and it holds an ext4 filesystem. What is the correct order??
options: Unmount, fsck, resize2fs to the smaller size first, then lvreduce — and never attempt this on XFS, which cannot shrink
Shrink with xfs_growfs, then lvreduce
Run lvreduce -r and let it shrink the filesystem automatically in all cases
lvreduce first, then resize2fs to fit
explain: For ext4 the filesystem must be shrunk BEFORE the block device, or the tail of the filesystem is amputated. (lvextend -r handles the grow direction; shrink support via -r exists for some filesystems but the safe exam procedure is filesystem-first, unmounted.) XFS cannot be shrunk at all.

q: lsblk shows: sda 8:0 0 100G 0 disk; sda1 8:1 0 1G 0 part /boot; sda2 8:2 0 99G 0 part; vgdata-lvroot 253:0 0 40G 0 lvm /; vgdata-lvswap 253:1 0 4G 0 lvm [SWAP]. Which device holds the root filesystem, and what type is it?
options: sda2 directly, a plain partition
vgdata-lvroot, an LVM logical volume built on partition sda2
vgdata-lvswap, an LVM logical volume
sda, the whole disk
explain: The TYPE column marks vgdata-lvroot as 'lvm' and its mountpoint is /. sda2 is the partition (TYPE part) that serves as the LVM physical volume beneath it; sda itself has no filesystem mounted at /, and lvswap is the swap LV.

q: lsblk shows: nvme0n1 259:0 0 500G 0 disk; nvme0n1p1 259:1 0 600M 0 part /boot/efi; nvme0n1p2 259:2 0 2G 0 part /boot; nvme0n1p3 259:3 0 497.4G 0 part. How many partitions does the disk have, and which is the EFI system partition?
options: Two partitions; nvme0n1p2 is the EFI partition
Four partitions, counting nvme0n1 itself
Three partitions; nvme0n1p1 is the EFI system partition (mounted at /boot/efi)
Three partitions; nvme0n1p3 is the EFI partition because it is largest
explain: NVMe partition names append pN to the disk name: p1, p2, p3 are three partitions. The one mounted at /boot/efi (600M, the conventional ESP size) is the EFI system partition; the disk row itself is not a partition.

q: lsblk -f shows: sdb1 xfs 9f3c... /data; sdc1 with no FSTYPE and no mountpoint; sdd1 vfat. What is the most likely state of sdc1?
options: It is corrupted and must be reformatted immediately
It is a swap device because swap has no FSTYPE
It has no filesystem signature — it is blank or an unformatted/LVM member, so it cannot be mounted as-is
It is mounted but lsblk hides mounted filesystems
explain: lsblk -f reports the filesystem type it detects; an empty FSTYPE means no recognizable filesystem (raw disk, new partition, or an LVM PV — check with pvs). Swap would show FSTYPE 'swap', and absence of a mountpoint alone would not blank the type.

q: An admin needs to activate the swap file /swapfile immediately AND make it persistent across reboots. Which approach is correct?
options: mkswap /swapfile; swapon /swapfile; add '/swapfile none swap defaults 0 0' to /etc/fstab
swapon /swapfile only; fstab picks it up automatically at the next swapon -a
mkswap /swapfile; mount /swapfile; add the fstab entry
chmod 600 /swapfile; systemctl enable swapfile.swap (a unit is always auto-created)
explain: A swap area needs formatting (mkswap), activation now (swapon), and an fstab line for boot persistence. It is never 'mounted', no unit is auto-created, and without swapon the area sits unused until reboot despite the fstab entry.

q: An admin needs to give the swap partition /dev/sdb2 priority over the swap file so the kernel uses it first. Which approach is correct?
options: Add pri=10 to the partition's fstab options (higher than the file's priority) or swapon -p 10 /dev/sdb2
Set the partition type to 'swap-priority' with parted
Kernel always prefers partitions; nothing to configure
Add the partition's line AFTER the file's line in fstab; order decides usage
explain: Swap areas of equal priority are used round-robin/striped; a HIGHER pri value wins. Fstab line order does not set preference, and there is no such partition type flag.

q: An admin needs to list the active swap areas together with their sizes and current usage. Which approach is correct?
options: free -p
lsblk --swap
systemctl list-units --type=swap only shows sizes
swapon --show (or cat /proc/swaps)
explain: swapon --show lists each active swap device/file with size, used amount, and priority; /proc/swaps has the same data. free shows only totals, and the systemctl view lists units without per-area size/usage columns.

q: An admin needs to A swap file was created with fallocate and mkswap succeeds, but swapon fails with 'file has holes'. What is the fix?. Which approach is correct?
options: Format it with mkswap --holes-ok
Defragment the swap file with xfs_fsr first
Run swapon --force-holes /swapfile
Recreate the file with dd (or cp) so it is fully allocated with no holes, chmod 600 it, then mkswap and swapon again
explain: Swap files must not be sparse or COW: fallocate on some filesystems leaves unwritten extents that the kernel rejects. Writing the file out with dd avoids holes. The --force-holes and --holes-ok options do not exist.

q: Which TWO statements about swap on RHEL 10 are true? (Choose two.)
options: Swap files must have restrictive permissions (0600) or swapon warns and other users could read swapped memory contents
Two swap areas with the same priority are filled strictly in fstab order, first one completely, then the next
A swap area defined only in /etc/fstab but never activated stays inactive until boot or swapon -a
Increasing RAM removes the need for any swap entry in fstab; the kernel auto-creates swap in /tmp
explain: An fstab entry alone does not activate swap in the running system — swapon (or a reboot) does. Swap files hold raw memory pages, hence the 0600 requirement. The kernel never auto-creates swap files, and equal-priority areas are used in a striped round-robin, not filled sequentially.

q: An admin needs to write a GPT partition table on the blank disk /dev/sdb using parted, non-interactively. Which action is correct?
options: fdisk --write-gpt /dev/sdb
parted -s /dev/sdb mklabel mbr --gpt
gdisk -t gpt /dev/sdb
parted -s /dev/sdb mklabel gpt
explain: parted's mklabel gpt writes the GUID partition table (-s runs scripted). fdisk can also create GPT (its g command) but takes interactive input, gdisk edits GPT but has no -t gpt write switch like that, and mbr contradicts the goal.

q: An admin needs to in gdisk, mark a new partition as an LVM physical volume later — which type code does the admin enter?. Which action is correct?
options: 0700 (Microsoft basic data)
8300 (Linux filesystem)
EF00 (EFI system)
8E00 (Linux LVM)
explain: gdisk type 8E00 designates Linux LVM. 8300 is a plain Linux filesystem partition, EF00 is the EFI system partition, and 0700 is Microsoft basic data.

q: An admin needs to make partition changes on a disk with mounted partitions take effect in the kernel without rebooting. Which action is correct?
options: fdisk -r /dev/sdb
partprobe /dev/sdb (or reboot if the kernel still refuses)
systemctl restart systemd-udevd only
mount -a --reread
explain: partprobe asks the kernel to re-read the partition table. mount -a mounts fstab entries but does not rescan partitions, and the other spellings are not real mechanisms (udevd restart alone does not re-read the table).

q: An admin needs to create a 50 GiB primary partition at the start of GPT disk /dev/sdc with parted in one command. Which action is correct?
options: parted -s /dev/sdc mkpart primary 1MiB 50GiB
parted -s /dev/sdc mkpart 50GiB
parted -s /dev/sdc mkpart primary 0 50G --type=lvm
parted /dev/sdc new 50G
explain: parted mkpart takes a partition name/type followed by START and END positions; starting at 1MiB aligns the partition properly. The other forms omit required arguments or use verbs parted does not have.

q: An admin needs to A blank 3 TB disk must hold a single data partition. fdisk refuses to use the space beyond about 2 TB. Why, and what is the fix?. Which action is correct?
options: The partition must be created as a logical volume; primary partitions cap at 2 TiB
XFS filesystems are limited to 2 TiB, so format it ext4 instead
The disk needs a firmware update to unlock the third terabyte
fdisk created a DOS/MBR table, which caps partitions at 2 TiB; recreate the table as GPT (parted mklabel gpt or gdisk) and repartition
explain: MBR partition entries store 32-bit sector counts, limiting a partition to 2 TiB with 512-byte sectors. GPT removes that ceiling. The limit is the table format, not the disk firmware, the filesystem, or primary-vs-logical status.

q: pvs shows: PV /dev/sdb1, VG vgdata, PSize 100.00g, PFree 0.00g; PV /dev/sdc1, VG vgdata, PSize 100.00g, PFree 42.00g. An admin wants to lvextend an LV in vgdata by 30 GiB. Will it work?
options: No: PFree must be equal on all PVs before extending
Yes: the VG has 42 GiB free (on sdc1), which covers the 30 GiB extension regardless of which PV the extents come from
No: sdb1 is full, and LVs can only grow onto the same PV
Yes, but only by 0 GiB until sdb1 is emptied with pvmove
explain: Free extents are a VG-level pool: lvextend draws from any PV in the group. sdb1 being full matters only for pvmove/evacuation scenarios, not for growth.

q: vgs shows vgdata with VFree 0 while lvs shows three LVs not using the full disk sizes the admin expected. pvs reveals a fourth PV is NOT listed. What is the most likely story?
options: vgs under-reports free space until a vgchange -ay runs
The LVs have snapshots consuming the missing space invisibly
LVM hides PVs whose names sort last
A disk was added physically but never pvcreate'd/vgextend'ed into the group, so its space is invisible to LVM
explain: LVM only knows devices explicitly initialized (pvcreate) and added (vgextend). A cabled disk that skipped those steps contributes nothing — the classic 'where did my new disk go' case.

q: An admin runs pvcreate on /dev/sdb (the whole disk) that previously held a partition table, and pvcreate warns about a partition table signature. What is the safe interpretation?
options: pvcreate detected an existing signature (wipefs-style warning): proceeding ERASES that table; the admin should confirm the disk is really the blank target before answering yes
The warning is cosmetic; pvcreate never destroys data
The disk is defective and must be replaced
The warning means /dev/sdb is already an active PV of another VG
explain: LVM (via the wipe checks) warns before overwriting signatures — a last chance to catch a wrong-device mistake. Confirming wipes the table; this is a data-safety checkpoint, not a hardware verdict.

q: Which statement about thin provisioning in LVM is correct at the EX200 level?
options: Thin pools cannot hold snapshots
Thin provisioning is the default for every lvcreate

Thin volumes are carved from a thin POOL LV; they can be over-provisioned (virtual sizes summing beyond the pool), and the pool must be monitored because running out of pool space corrupts thin volumes
Thin volumes reserve their full size immediately, like regular LVs
explain: Thin LVs allocate extents on write from a shared pool, enabling overcommit and fast snapshots — with the operational duty to watch pool usage. Regular (thick) LVs remain the default.

q: An LV named /dev/vg0/lvdata must be removed permanently. It is currently mounted at /data. What is the correct sequence?
options: Set the LV inactive with lvchange -an and deletion is complete
lvremove -f /dev/vg0/lvdata (fstab cleanup is optional and unrelated)
rm the device node, then vgchange --refresh
Unmount /data (and remove/adjust its fstab entry), then lvremove /dev/vg0/lvdata
explain: lvremove refuses (or dangerously forces) removal of an active, mounted LV; unmounting first is the procedure, and the fstab entry must go or the next boot tries to mount a ghost. Deactivation alone is not removal.

q: fdisk is used to partition a disk and the admin presses 'g' at the main prompt before creating partitions. What did 'g' do?
options: It printed the geometry report and changed nothing
It converted the table to GPT only in the running kernel
It created a new DOS/MBR table
It created a new empty GPT partition table on the disk (wiping the old table from memory until 'w' writes it)
explain: Modern fdisk supports both formats: 'o' makes a DOS table and 'g' makes a GPT table. As with all fdisk edits, nothing touches the disk until 'w' writes (and 'q' abandons).

q: An admin creates a snapshot with lvcreate -s -n lvdata_snap -L 5G /dev/vg0/lvdata. What does the 5G represent?
options: Reserved journal space for the snapshot's metadata only
The size of a full second copy of the data, made instantly
The maximum size the snapshot's filesystem may report
The size of the copy-on-write (COW) exception store: it holds the ORIGINAL versions of blocks changed on the source LV while the snapshot lives
explain: A traditional LVM snapshot stores only changed-block originals in its COW area, which is why creation is instant and why a snapshot dies if changes exceed the COW size. It is a point-in-time view, not a clone.

q: lvs shows: lvdata vg0 -wi-ao---- 50.00g; lvdata_snap vg0 swi-a-s--- 5.00g with Origin lvdata. What is true?
options: lvdata_snap is a snapshot of lvdata whose exception store is 5 GiB; the 's' in its attributes marks snapshot state
The two LVs are mirrors of each other
lvdata_snap is a thin pool because of the s attribute
lvdata is a snapshot of the 5 GiB lvdata_snap
explain: The Attr column encodes the volume type: 's' marks a snapshot (and 'S' an invalid one), and the Origin column names the source LV. Size flows from the origin (50G) to the smaller COW store (5G), not the reverse.

q: Why does an LV sometimes appear as /dev/mapper/vg--data-lv--files with doubled hyphens in /proc/mounts?
options: Device-mapper names escape hyphens inside VG/LV names by doubling them: VG 'vg-data' and LV 'lv-files' become vg--data-lv--files
It is filesystem corruption in /proc/mounts
It indicates the LV is clustered
The doubling marks a snapshot relationship
explain: In /dev/mapper naming, a single hyphen separates VG from LV, so literal hyphens inside either name are escaped as double hyphens. The /dev/vg-data/lv-files path remains the friendly form.

q: A VG's LVs are all present in /dev but show as 'NOT available' in lvs (Attr first letter is not 'a' in the state position) after the VG was exported on another host. What reactivates them?
options: systemctl restart lvm2-monitor only
lvchange --refresh-all
pvscan --activate-all-now
vgchange -ay vgname (activates the group's logical volumes)
explain: vgchange -ay is the activation switch for a volume group (used after import or when devices appear late). The monitor service watches events but is not the manual activation mechanism.

q: An admin adds a SECOND swap partition to share load with the first. Both fstab lines have no pri= option. How does the kernel use them?
options: It stripes/interleaves swap I/O across both areas, because equal-priority swap areas are used in round-robin fashion
It refuses two swap areas without priorities
It uses only the larger of the two
It fills the first completely, then uses the second
explain: Same-priority swap areas are used in parallel (striped), which can improve swap throughput on separate devices. Sequential fill is what different priorities (or equal pri with the areas on one disk path) approximates.

q: A technician must partition a new 4 TiB disk /dev/vdc as a single device for data. The disk currently has an MBR table. What must happen first so the full capacity can be used?
options: Create an extended partition, because extended partitions bypass the 2 TiB MBR limit
Run pvcreate on the whole disk, because LVM converts MBR to GPT automatically
Replace the MBR table with a GPT table, because MBR addressing limits usable space to about 2 TiB
Format the disk with XFS first, because XFS removes the MBR size limit
explain: GPT must replace MBR to use space beyond about 2 TiB, because MBR partition entries cannot address the rest. An extended partition only works around the four-primary limit, XFS is created after partitioning, and pvcreate writes an LVM label without converting the partition table.

q: On /dev/nvme1n1, an administrator needs to inspect the existing partition layout and table type before making changes. Which command provides that information with parted?
options: parted /dev/nvme1n1 print
lsblk --partitions-only /dev/nvme1n1
fdisk -l /dev/nvme1n1p1 --create
parted /dev/nvme1n1 mklabel gpt
explain: Running parted with the print operation displays the disk model, table type such as gpt, and each partition's start, end, and size. Using mklabel would rewrite the table, while limiting the view to a single partition or a block listing does not show the table type in the same way.

q: In gdisk on /dev/sde, a new partition will hold Linux swap. Which type code should be assigned to that partition?
explain: The 8200 code identifies Linux swap in gdisk. The 8E00 code identifies an LVM physical volume, 8300 is a general Linux filesystem partition, and 0700 is associated with Microsoft basic data, so none of those describe swap.

q: After using parted interactively to add /dev/vdb3 on a running system, the kernel still does not show the new partition. What is the correct next step?
options: Unmount all filesystems on /dev/vdb and run mkfs on /dev/vdb3
Run pvscan --cache /dev/vdb so LVM creates the missing partition device
Run partprobe /dev/vdb so the kernel re-reads the partition table without rebooting
Delete and recreate the volume group that will use /dev/vdb3
explain: partprobe informs the kernel of partition table changes so new partition device nodes appear without a reboot. LVM scanning does not create kernel partitions, formatting cannot succeed on a device node that does not exist, and volume group work comes after the partition is visible.

q: A blank partition /dev/sdc2 must be initialized for LVM use. Which command writes the LVM physical volume label to it?
options: lvcreate --physical /dev/sdc2
pvcreate /dev/sdc2
parted /dev/sdc2 set lvm on only, with no other command needed
vgcreate vgstore /dev/sdc2
explain: pvcreate prepares a block device as a physical volume by writing the LVM label and metadata area. vgcreate expects an already prepared physical volume, lvcreate makes logical volumes inside a group, and a parted flag alone does not initialize the device for LVM.

q: When creating volume group vgapps, the administrator wants a physical extent size of 16 MiB instead of the default. Which command does this?
options: vgcreate --extent-count 16 vgapps /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
vgcreate -s 16M vgapps /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
pvcreate -s 16M /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1, then vgcreate vgapps /dev/sdb1
lvcreate -s 16M vgapps /dev/sdb1 /dev/sdc1
explain: Extent size is a volume group property set with the -s option of vgcreate at creation time, and all logical volume sizes in that group become multiples of it. pvcreate does not set the group extent size, and the count and lvcreate variants misuse options that do not define extent size.

q: Inline output reads: vgs; VG #PV #LV #SN Attr VSize VFree; vgstore 3 2 0 wz--n- 297.00g 45.00g. How much space in vgstore is still available for new or larger logical volumes?
options: 3, because three physical volumes are present
explain: The VFree column shows unallocated space in the volume group, here 45.00g, regardless of total size. VSize is the group's total capacity, subtracting free from total gives allocated space, and the physical volume count does not itself state free capacity.

q: Inline output reads: pvs; PV VG Fmt Attr PSize PFree; /dev/sdd1 vgbackup lvm2 a-- 100.00g 0; /dev/sde1 vgbackup lvm2 a-- 100.00g 62.00g. Which statement is correct?
options: /dev/sde1 still contributes 62.00g of unallocated space to vgbackup, while /dev/sdd1 is fully allocated
vgbackup has 200.00g free because PSize values are added together
/dev/sdd1 must be removed because its PFree value is zero
Both physical volumes are empty because PFree is shown per volume group
explain: PFree is the unallocated portion of each physical volume, so the second device has 62.00g free and the first has none free but may hold live logical volumes. A zero PFree does not mean empty or removable, and adding PSize values gives total size rather than free space.

q: Volume group vgapps uses 4 MiB extents. An administrator needs a 2 GiB logical volume named lvlogs. Which lvcreate command uses extent count to do this?
options: lvcreate -L 512 -n lvlogs vgapps
lvcreate --extents 2048 -n lvlogs vgapps
lvcreate -l 2G -n lvlogs --name lvlogs vgapps
lvcreate -l 512 -n lvlogs vgapps
explain: With 4 MiB extents, 512 extents provide 2048 MiB, which is 2 GiB, and the lowercase -l option takes an extent count. Uppercase -L takes a size with units so 512 alone is not 2 GiB, -l does not accept a G suffix, and 2048 extents would provide 8 GiB.

q: Volume group vgstore has ample free space. Which command creates a 25 GiB logical volume named lvcache?
options: lvcreate -L 25G -n lvcache vgstore
mkfs.xfs -L 25G /dev/vgstore/lvcache before creating the volume
lvcreate -l 25G -n lvcache vgstore
lvcreate -L +25G --new lvcache vgstore
explain: The -L option with an absolute size and -n for the name creates the requested logical volume in the named group. Lowercase -l expects a count of extents, a leading plus is used when extending rather than creating, and a filesystem can only be made after the volume exists.

q: Logical volume /dev/vgapps/lvapp is currently 30 GiB and must become exactly 45 GiB. Its filesystem is unmounted and vgapps has enough free space. Which command sets that final size without growing the filesystem?
options: lvcreate -L 45G -n lvapp vgapps
lvextend -l 45 /dev/vgapps/lvapp
lvextend -L +45G /dev/vgapps/lvapp
lvextend -L 45G /dev/vgapps/lvapp
explain: An -L value without a plus sign is an absolute target size, so 45G makes the volume exactly 45 GiB. Adding +45G would grow it to 75 GiB, -l 45 means only 45 extents, and lvcreate would attempt to make a second volume with a conflicting name.

q: An XFS logical volume /dev/vgstore/lvmedia is mounted at /srv/media and vgstore has free extents. Which single command grows the volume to use all remaining free space and grows the filesystem?
options: xfs_growfs /dev/vgstore/lvmedia with no volume change first
lvextend -L +100%FREE /dev/vgstore/lvmedia, then reboot
lvextend -r -l +100%FREE /dev/vgstore/lvmedia
lvresize --filesystem-only -l +100%FREE /dev/vgstore/lvmedia
explain: The -r flag resizes the filesystem together with the volume, and -l +100%FREE consumes all remaining free extents in the group. A size option does not accept the percent-free syntax, a filesystem-only step cannot create space, and xfs_growfs alone cannot enlarge the underlying volume.

q: An administrator plans to shrink /dev/vglab/lvtest from 50 GiB to 20 GiB. It holds XFS and is currently mounted. What is the correct assessment?
options: XFS cannot be shrunk, so the volume must not be reduced in place; back up, recreate at the smaller size, and restore
Unmount it and run lvreduce -f, because forcing bypasses the filesystem limitation
Run lvreduce -r -L 20G while mounted, because -r makes XFS shrink safely
Run xfs_growfs -d /srv/test first, because that tool shrinks XFS on demand
explain: XFS supports growing while mounted but does not support shrinking, so reducing the logical volume in place would destroy data beyond the new end. The -r and force options do not add shrink support, and xfs_growfs only grows a filesystem, which is why a backup and recreate workflow is required.

q: All data on logical volume /dev/vgops/lvscratch is backed up, the volume is unmounted, and it must be deleted while keeping vgops and its other volumes. Which command and warning apply?
options: lvremove /dev/vgops/lvscratch, and confirm removal because the volume and its contents are destroyed
vgremove /dev/vgops/lvscratch, and no confirmation is needed because only metadata changes
lvremove --shrink /dev/vgops/lvscratch, which preserves the data in free extents
pvremove /dev/vgops/lvscratch, after mounting it read-only
explain: lvremove deletes a single logical volume after a confirmation prompt, and the data on it is lost. vgremove targets a whole group, pvremove targets physical volumes, and there is no shrink mode that deletes a volume while preserving its contents in free space.
