q: What is the correct order to completely decommission LVM on /dev/sdf1, whose volume group vgarchive contains one unmounted logical volume lvarchive?
options: vgremove vgarchive first, then pvremove /dev/sdf1, then lvremove the logical volume
pvremove /dev/sdf1, then lvremove the logical volume, then vgremove vgarchive
lvremove the logical volume, then vgremove vgarchive, then pvremove /dev/sdf1
swapoff the volume, then delete the partition with parted only
explain: LVM teardown proceeds top-down: logical volumes are removed first, then the empty volume group, then the physical volume label. Removing the physical volume or group first is blocked or unsafe while volumes exist, and deleting only the partition leaves stale LVM metadata behind.

q: Physical volume /dev/sdd1 in vgstore must be emptied so the disk can be removed, and its extents are in use. Which command migrates its data to other physical volumes in the same group?
options: vgreduce --move /dev/sdd1 vgstore
pvremove --migrate /dev/sdd1
lvmove /dev/sdd1 vgstore
pvmove /dev/sdd1
explain: pvmove relocates allocated extents from the specified physical volume to other physical volumes in the volume group while the data stays online. After the move completes, vgreduce can remove the empty device; the other command names and options shown do not perform that migration.

q: After pvmove finishes, /dev/sdd1 shows PFree equal to PSize in pvs output for vgstore. Which command removes that now-empty physical volume from the group?
options: vgreduce vgstore /dev/sdd1
vgremove vgstore /dev/sdd1
lvextend vgstore /dev/sdd1 --release
pvcreate --remove vgstore /dev/sdd1
explain: vgreduce removes one or more empty physical volumes from an existing volume group. vgremove deletes an entire group, pvcreate initializes rather than detaches devices, and lvextend grows logical volumes rather than shrinking group membership.

q: A new 200 GiB disk /dev/sdg has been partitioned as /dev/sdg1. Existing mounted ext4 volume /dev/vgapps/lvapp at /srv/app must gain all of that disk's space with no data loss. Which is the correct order of steps?
options: lvcreate the new space, then merge it with lvapp using pvcreate /dev/sdg1
pvcreate /dev/sdg1; vgextend vgapps /dev/sdg1; lvextend -r -l +100%FREE /dev/vgapps/lvapp
mkfs.ext4 /dev/sdg1; mount it over /srv/app; copy the volume group metadata
vgextend vgapps /dev/sdg1; pvcreate /dev/sdg1; lvextend -r /dev/vgapps/lvapp
explain: The new partition must first become a physical volume, then join the group to increase free extents, and only then can the logical volume and its filesystem grow into that space. Extending the group before pvcreate fails, and formatting or mounting the partition separately does not add its space to the existing volume.

q: Partition /dev/sdb2 must become swap and be active immediately but not yet persistent. Which sequence is correct?
options: mkfs.swap /dev/sdb2; swapadd /dev/sdb2
pvcreate /dev/sdb2; swapon --lvm /dev/sdb2
mkswap /dev/sdb2; swapon /dev/sdb2
dd if=/dev/zero of=/dev/sdb2; mount -t swap /dev/sdb2 none
explain: mkswap writes the swap signature and swapon activates the area for the current boot, with persistence requiring a separate fstab entry. The other sequences use non-existent tools or options, confuse LVM preparation with swap preparation, or try to mount swap as a regular filesystem.

q: A swap file at /swapdir/extra.swap must be created safely. Which sequence avoids the holes problem and sets safe permissions?
options: truncate -s 2G /swapdir/extra.swap; chmod 644 /swapdir/extra.swap; swapon --file /swapdir/extra.swap
fallocate -l 2G /swapdir/extra.swap; chmod 777 /swapdir/extra.swap; swapon /swapdir/extra.swap
dd if=/dev/zero of=/swapdir/extra.swap bs=1M count=2048; chmod 600 /swapdir/extra.swap; mkswap /swapdir/extra.swap; swapon /swapdir/extra.swap
touch /swapdir/extra.swap; mkswap /swapdir/extra.swap; mount /swapdir/extra.swap
explain: Writing the file fully with dd avoids sparse holes that swapon rejects, restrictive 600 permissions protect swap contents, and mkswap must run before swapon. Sparse allocation helpers can leave holes, world-readable or executable permissions expose swapped memory, and swapon still needs a prepared swap signature.

q: Inline output reads: swapon --show; NAME TYPE SIZE USED PRIO; /dev/vdc3 partition 4G 0B 100; /swapdir/extra.swap file 2G 0B -2. Which swap area will the kernel prefer?
options: Neither, because a priority of 100 is invalid and both are ignored
Both equally, because USED is 0B for both areas
/swapdir/extra.swap, because files are always preferred over partitions
/dev/vdc3, because its priority 100 is higher than the file's -2
explain: Higher numeric swap priority is used first, and automatically assigned priorities are negative, so the partition at 100 is preferred over the file at -2. The file is not inherently preferred, 100 is a valid administrator-set priority, and equal usage at this moment does not mean equal preference.

q: An entry in /etc/fstab reads: /dev/vgswap/lvswap none swap sw,pri=50 0 0. What does the pri=50 setting control?
options: The order in which this swap area is used relative to other swap areas, with higher values preferred
The size of the swap area is limited to 50 percent of the logical volume
The process priority of every program whose pages are placed in this swap area
The swap area is checked 50 times during boot before other filesystems
explain: The pri option sets the swap area's priority so the kernel fills higher-priority areas first; it can also be set with swapon -p. It does not cap the area's size, control boot checks, or change the scheduling priority of processes using swapped pages.

q: Extending /dev/vgapps/lvapp fails and reports insufficient free space, while vgs shows VFree of 0 for vgapps and a new disk is attached but unused. What is the root cause?
options: The logical volume name is too short, so lvextend cannot calculate extents
The new disk was never added to the volume group, so the volume has no new extents to allocate
The mount point /srv/app is busy, which prevents any volume extension
The filesystem is XFS, and XFS always reports insufficient free space when a volume is half full
explain: A logical volume can only grow into free extents already inside its volume group; attaching a disk to the machine does not add it. The disk must be prepared and added with pvcreate and vgextend first, while filesystem type, name length, and a busy mount point do not cause this specific allocation error.

q: Inline output reads: lsblk; NAME MAJ:MIN RM SIZE RO TYPE MOUNTPOINTS; nvme0n1 259:0 0 500G 0 disk; nvme0n1p1 259:1 0 1G 0 part /boot; nvme0n1p2 259:2 0 499G 0 part; vgroot-lvroot 253:0 0 80G 0 lvm /. Which device is partition 2 of the NVMe disk?
options: vgroot-lvroot, because it occupies most of the disk
nvme0n1p2
nvme0n1-2
sda2, because NVMe devices are renamed after boot
explain: NVMe partition naming appends p plus the partition number to the whole-disk name, giving nvme0n1p2 for partition 2. The hyphen form is not a device name, NVMe devices are not renamed to sda style, and the lvm device is a logical volume built on storage rather than the partition itself.

q: Inline output reads: lsblk; sda 500G disk; sda1 200G part /srv/files; sda2 300G part; vgmedia-lvfilms 120G lvm /srv/films. Which statement is correct?
options: sda1 is a logical volume because it has a mount point
sda2 is a partition that likely serves as an LVM physical volume for the volume shown, while sda1 is directly mounted
vgmedia-lvfilms is a partition of sda named films
The whole disk sda can be formatted safely because its children are listed separately
explain: The TYPE column distinguishes a directly mounted partition from an lvm device; a logical volume appearing alongside a large unmounted partition indicates that partition underlies LVM. Having a mount point does not make a partition a logical volume, the films device is type lvm not part, and formatting the parent disk would destroy its children.

q: An administrator needs a thin pool named pool0 of 60 GiB in vgstore, from which thin volumes will later be provisioned. Which command creates the pool?
options: lvcreate -V 60G --thinpool pool0 vgstore
vgcreate --thin pool0 -L 60G vgstore
lvcreate -L 60G --thinpool pool0 vgstore
pvcreate --thinpool 60G /dev/vgstore/pool0
explain: Creating a thin pool uses lvcreate with a real size via -L and the --thinpool option naming the pool. The -V option specifies a virtual size for a thin volume inside an existing pool, while physical and volume group creation tools do not create thin pools.

q: Thin pool pool0 in vgstore has 60 GiB of real capacity. Which command creates a thin logical volume named lvthin with a virtual size of 120 GiB?
options: lvcreate -L 120G -T vgstore/pool0 -n lvthin
lvcreate -V 120G --thinpool lvthin vgstore
thincreate -s 120G vgstore/pool0 lvthin
lvcreate -V 120G -T vgstore/pool0 -n lvthin
explain: A thin volume is created with -V for its virtual size, which may exceed the pool's physical capacity, plus -T to select the pool. Using -L would request real allocation, --thinpool creates a pool rather than a volume in one, and the thincreate name is not the LVM command used here.

q: A disk with an MBR table already has four primary partitions and unallocated space remains. What is the supported way to add more partitions without converting the table?
options: Run parted and create a fifth primary partition, because parted ignores the MBR limit
Replace one primary partition slot with an extended partition and create logical partitions inside it
Use gdisk to add the partitions, because it silently converts only the free space
Set the new partition type to GPT while leaving the rest of the disk as MBR
explain: MBR allows at most four primary partitions, so one slot must become an extended container holding logical partitions if the table is not converted. Tools cannot create a fifth primary on MBR, and a single disk cannot mix MBR and GPT tables for different regions of free space.

q: Using parted on /dev/vdd, an administrator wants one partition that starts at 1 MiB and consumes the rest of the disk. Which command line does this?
options: parted -s /dev/vdd create 1MiB 100% --type primary
parted -s /dev/vdd mkpart primary 0 100
parted -s /dev/vdd mkpart primary 1MiB 100%
parted -s /dev/vdd mklabel gpt 1MiB 100%
explain: In parted, mkpart takes the partition type followed by start and end positions, and 100% as the end uses the remainder of the disk. Starting at 0 can create alignment problems and is not the requested start, while create and mklabel are not the operations that add a partition with those arguments.

q: Which command opens the GPT partition editor on /dev/sdf without altering the disk until changes are written?
options: parted /dev/sdf mklabel gpt --force
fdisk --gpt-only /dev/sdf --write-now
gdisk /dev/sdf
sgdisk --clear /dev/sdf
explain: gdisk is the interactive GPT editor and defers changes until they are written with w. The fdisk option shown is not how that tool is invoked, mklabel immediately prepares a new table, and sgdisk --clear would erase the existing GPT structures.

q: An administrator wants volume group vgmedia built from both /dev/sdb4 and /dev/sdc4 in one step, after both were prepared. Which command is correct?
options: vgcreate vgmedia /dev/sdb4, then vgcreate vgmedia /dev/sdc4
pvcreate vgmedia /dev/sdb4 /dev/sdc4
vgcreate vgmedia /dev/sdb4 /dev/sdc4
lvcreate vgmedia /dev/sdb4 /dev/sdc4
explain: vgcreate accepts multiple prepared physical volumes and includes all of them in the new group at creation. Running vgcreate twice for the same group is wrong because the second device should be added with vgextend, and the other tools create different LVM layers.

q: Logical volume /dev/vgswap/lvswap is active swap and must be removed. What must happen immediately before lvremove can succeed?
options: Run swapoff /dev/vgswap/lvswap and remove or update its fstab entry so it is not reactivated
Extend it to use all free space so removal prompts are skipped
Run mkswap /dev/vgswap/lvswap again to clear its contents
Unmount it with umount, because swap areas are unmounted like filesystems
explain: An active swap area must be deactivated with swapoff before its volume can be removed, and its persistent fstab entry should be cleaned up to avoid a failed activation later. Re-running mkswap keeps it a swap area, swap is not unmounted with umount, and extending it does not help removal.

q: Volume group vgapps has 4 MiB extents and an administrator must add exactly 3 GiB to a volume using an extent count. How many extents should be requested with -l?
options: 750 extents, because 3 GiB is treated as 3000 MiB for LVM math
3000 extents, because each extent holds 1 MiB by definition
768 extents, because 3 GiB is 3072 MiB divided by 4 MiB per extent
96 extents, because 3 GiB divided by 32 MiB metadata equals 96
explain: LVM sizes use binary units here: 3 GiB equals 3072 MiB, and 3072 divided by the 4 MiB extent size equals 768 extents. The decimal and one-megabyte assumptions give wrong counts, and metadata size does not enter the extent calculation.

q: Running vgextend vgstore /dev/sdh1 fails because the device has no LVM label. What is the missing prerequisite?
options: Run partprobe /dev/sdh1, because partition devices need probing individually
Run mkfs.xfs /dev/sdh1 first, because vgextend requires a filesystem
Run lvcreate on /dev/sdh1 to reserve it for the group
Run pvcreate /dev/sdh1 first, then repeat the vgextend command
explain: vgextend can only add devices that have already been initialized as physical volumes with pvcreate. Creating a filesystem would be overwritten and is not required, partprobe targets the parent disk's table, and lvcreate makes volumes inside a group rather than preparing member devices.

q: What does pvremove /dev/sdh1 actually do when the device is no longer part of any volume group?
options: It removes the partition from the partition table on the parent disk
It erases the LVM physical volume label so the device can be reused without stale metadata warnings
It securely wipes every byte of user data from the entire device
It exports the volume group configuration to a backup file
explain: pvremove clears the LVM label and metadata identifying the device as a physical volume, so other tools no longer treat it as an LVM member. It does not perform a full secure erase, does not edit the parent disk's partition table, and does not export group configuration.

q: Which statements about swap on a production RHEL 10 server are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Disabling all swap permanently is required before any logical volume can be extended
Swap provides overflow space when RAM is exhausted, but it is not a substitute for adequate physical memory
Swap should always be sized at exactly four times installed RAM on every workload
An active swap area can be inspected with swapon --show, including its type, size, and priority
explain: Swap acts as slower overflow for memory pressure and does not replace RAM, and swapon --show reports each active area's name, type, size, use, and priority. There is no universal four-times rule for modern workloads, and swap state has no bearing on extending unrelated logical volumes.

q: Which commands correctly report free space available inside a volume group? (Choose two.)
options: vgdisplay, reading the Free PE / Size information for the group
df -h, reading available space on a mounted filesystem
free -h, reading the available column for physical memory
vgs, reading the VFree column for the group
explain: Both vgs and vgdisplay expose unallocated extents in a volume group, which is the space available for logical volume work. The df tool reports filesystem usage rather than group allocation, and free reports memory and swap rather than LVM capacity.

q: An administrator is preparing /dev/sdi1, /dev/sdj1, and /dev/sdk1 as a new volume group vgpool. Which sequence is correct? (Choose two.)
options: Run mkswap on each partition so LVM recognizes them as member devices
Run vgcreate vgpool /dev/sdi1 /dev/sdj1 /dev/sdk1 after the physical volumes exist
Run pvcreate on all three partitions before creating the group that uses them
Run lvcreate -L 10G vgpool first so the group is created automatically with default extents
explain: Physical volumes must be initialized before a group can be built from them, and a single vgcreate naming all prepared devices creates vgpool correctly. lvcreate cannot run before its group exists, and swap signatures do not prepare a device for LVM membership.

q: Which actions are valid ways to grow a logical volume and its filesystem together? (Choose two.)
options: lvextend -r -l +100%FREE /dev/vgapps/lvapp to consume all remaining free extents in the group
xfs_growfs alone on an unmounted device to enlarge both the volume and the filesystem
lvextend -r -L +8G /dev/vgapps/lvapp for an ext4 or XFS filesystem with free extents available
pvcreate on a mounted filesystem to add its partition directly to the volume
explain: Using lvextend with -r grows the logical volume and resizes its filesystem in one operation, whether the growth is given as a size increment or as all remaining free extents. Growing XFS requires a mounted filesystem and does not enlarge the volume itself, and pvcreate would destroy a filesystem rather than extend it.

q: Which statements about GPT compared with MBR are correct? (Choose two.)
options: GPT keeps backup partition table structures, improving recovery from damage to the primary copy
MBR supports more partitions than GPT when an extended partition is used
GPT requires every partition to be an LVM physical volume
GPT supports disks larger than 2 TiB and far more than four partitions without extended or logical structures
explain: GPT removes the roughly 2 TiB MBR ceiling and the four-primary limitation, and it maintains a backup header and partition array. An extended MBR layout still cannot match GPT's partition count or size support, and GPT partitions may hold any filesystem or purpose, not only LVM.

q: A volume group shows plenty of total size but an lvcreate for 80 GiB fails. pvs shows every physical volume with small PFree values that sum to only 30 GiB. What is the best explanation?
options: Most of the group's capacity is already allocated to existing logical volumes, so only about 30 GiB is actually free
The new volume name conflicts, which lvcreate reports as a space error
The physical volumes need mkfs run on them before their free space counts
The physical extent size is too large, which hides the remaining 50 GiB from lvcreate
explain: Total group size includes space already assigned to logical volumes; lvcreate can only use unallocated extents, shown as PFree per device and VFree for the group. Extent size affects rounding, not tens of gigabytes, a name conflict gives a different error, and formatting physical volumes would erase LVM data.

q: An administrator runs lvcreate -L 40G -n lvbuild vgapps and gets an error that the name already exists, because a volume of that name is present but unused and unmounted. What is the cleanest resolution if that old volume's data is not needed?
options: Rename the volume group so the duplicate name is hidden
Run pvremove on one physical volume to free the name
Remove the old volume with lvremove /dev/vgapps/lvbuild, then repeat the lvcreate command
Use lvcreate -f, because the force flag overwrites an existing logical volume in place
explain: Logical volume names must be unique within a group, so the unwanted existing volume must be removed before a new one can take its name. Renaming the group does not resolve the collision, removing a physical volume endangers group data, and lvcreate does not overwrite an existing volume in place.

q: A server has /dev/vdb1 as a physical volume in vgfleet. The disk /dev/vdb is failing and a replacement /dev/vdc1 of equal size has been added to the group. Which is the correct order of steps to retire the failing disk?
options: lvremove all volumes; pvremove /dev/vdb1; restore every volume from scratch
pvmove /dev/vdb1 /dev/vdc1; vgreduce vgfleet /dev/vdb1; pvremove /dev/vdb1
vgreduce vgfleet /dev/vdb1; pvmove /dev/vdb1 /dev/vdc1; pvremove /dev/vdb1
pvremove /dev/vdb1; pvmove /dev/vdb1 /dev/vdc1; vgcreate vgfleet /dev/vdc1
explain: Data must be migrated off the failing device with pvmove while it is still a group member, then the empty device is removed from the group with vgreduce, and finally its label is cleared with pvremove. Reducing or label-removing first would strand allocated extents, and deleting all volumes is unnecessary downtime and data loss.

q: Which command shows logical volumes with their sizes, volume group, and attributes in a compact list for vgstore only?
options: vgs --logical vgstore
lvs vgstore
lsblk --lvm vgstore --sizes-only
pvs vgstore --volumes
explain: lvs lists logical volumes and can be limited to a named volume group, showing each volume's attributes, size, and origin information. The vgs and pvs tools report on groups and physical volumes respectively, and lsblk shows the block tree rather than the LVM logical volume report.

q: An administrator created a partition with parted on /dev/vde while filesystems from that disk were mounted, and parted warned the kernel could not be informed. When will the new partition reliably become usable?
options: Immediately after running pvcreate, because LVM forces a kernel table reload
After running mkswap on an unrelated partition to trigger device scanning
After a reboot, or after the busy partitions are unmounted so partprobe can update the kernel's table
Never; the partition table change is discarded whenever that warning appears
explain: When partitions on a disk are in use, the kernel may refuse the re-read, so the change appears after reboot or once the disk is no longer busy and partprobe succeeds. LVM and swap tools do not force the kernel to adopt a new table, and the warning does not mean the on-disk table change was discarded.

q: A swap partition /dev/vdc3 is in /etc/fstab but after boot swapon --show does not list it, and journal messages mention a failed swap unit. The partition exists. What should be checked first?
options: Whether the partition has a mount point directory created under /swap
Whether XFS quotas are enabled on the root filesystem
Whether mkswap was ever run on /dev/vdc3 and whether the fstab entry references the correct device or UUID
Whether the volume group containing /dev/vdc3 has free extents
explain: A partition without a swap signature cannot be activated, and a stale device or UUID reference in fstab points the boot process at the wrong target, so verifying the signature and the entry is the first step. Swap areas have no mount point directory, and quotas or volume group free space are unrelated to a plain partition's swap activation.

q: An administrator wants to temporarily disable all swap to move a swap volume, without rebooting. Which command does this?
options: swapoff -a
swapon -a --disable
systemctl stop swap.target --now, with no other step
umount swap
explain: The swapoff command with -a deactivates all active swap areas listed in the system, allowing their backing volumes to be manipulated. There is no disable flag on swapon for this purpose, swap is not unmounted, and stopping a systemd target alone does not deactivate already active swap areas.

q: A thin pool shows high data percentage in lvs output and thin volumes are starting to report write errors, even though df inside each filesystem shows space remaining. What is the most likely cause?
options: The filesystems need fsck because thin volumes always corrupt at high usage
Swap is full, which thin pools use as backing store
The thin pool's actual physical space is exhausted, because virtual sizes overcommit the pool and filesystems cannot see the shortfall
The volume group extent size is mismatched with the pool's chunk size in a way that hides errors
explain: Thin provisioning lets virtual volume sizes exceed the pool's real capacity, so when the pool itself fills, writes fail even though each filesystem believes it still has room based on its virtual size. The remedy is growing the pool or freeing data, not running filesystem checks, adjusting extent math, or adding swap.

q: On a disk /dev/vdf, an administrator must verify a partition is aligned and see free regions between partitions before adding another. Which parted operation shows start and end positions along with free space?
options: fdisk --list-free /dev/vdf
lsblk -f /dev/vdf --free
parted /dev/vdf check free
parted /dev/vdf print free
explain: The print free operation in parted lists existing partitions and the unallocated regions between them with their boundaries, which supports alignment and placement decisions. The other commands and options shown are not the parted operation that reports free regions in that form.

q: ln /data/fast/file.db /backup/file.db fails with 'Invalid cross-device link'. /data and /backup are separate filesystems. What is the explanation and the correct approach?
options: The file is too large for a hard link, which is limited to 2 GB per link
The -P flag is required on ln when linking across mount points
/backup must be remounted read-write before any link can be created
Hard links cannot span filesystems because a hard link is just another directory entry pointing at an inode, and inodes are only unique within one filesystem; use cp -a to copy or ln -s for a symlink
explain: A hard link shares the target's inode number, and inode numbers are meaningful only within their own filesystem, so the kernel rejects cross-filesystem hard links with EXDEV ('Invalid cross-device link'). A symlink works because it stores a path string, or cp -a duplicates the data. Option A invents a size limit that does not exist. Option B confuses ln with cp's -P (no-dereference) flag. Option C is unrelated; a read-only mount would produce a different error.

q: After vgextend vgdata /dev/sdd1 and lvextend -L +20G /dev/vgdata/lvdata, df -h /data still shows the old size, though lvs shows the LV grew. What was missed?
options: The logical volume grew but the filesystem inside it did not; rerun with lvextend -r (or run xfs_growfs /data) to resize the filesystem into the new space
A reboot is required before the kernel notices the larger logical volume
df cannot display LVM-backed filesystems and a different tool must be used
The vgextend must have failed, because lvextend cannot succeed after a failed vgextend
explain: A logical volume and the filesystem on top of it are separate layers: lvextend grows the block device, but the filesystem keeps its old geometry until resized. The -r (--resizefs) flag makes lvextend grow the filesystem in the same operation (xfs_growfs /data or resize2fs for ext4 does it manually). Option D contradicts the evidence that lvs shows growth. Option B is wrong; LV resizing is online. Option C is false; df works fine on LVM.

q: An admin adds UUID=4a2b-... /data xfs defaults 0 0 to /etc/fstab. How should the entry be tested without rebooting?
options: A reboot is the only way to test an fstab change
Run mount -a to mount all fstab entries not already mounted, and optionally findmnt --verify to validate the fstab syntax beforehand
Run systemctl daemon-reload, which is required after every fstab edit
Run mount -a, which remounts every filesystem including ones already mounted
explain: mount -a processes every fstab entry that is not already mounted, so it exercises the new line exactly as boot would. findmnt --verify parses fstab and reports errors (bad UUID, bad options) before anything is mounted. Option A wastes a reboot and risks a failed boot. Option D is wrong: mount -a skips filesystems that are already mounted. Option C is wrong because fstab is not a systemd unit file; daemon-reload is irrelevant to it.

q: An admin runs resize2fs /dev/vgdata/lvdata on an XFS filesystem and gets an error. What is the correct way to grow it?
options: Run resize2fs -x, which is the XFS-compatible variant of the command
resize2fs is for ext4; grow XFS with xfs_growfs /data, passing the mount point while the filesystem is mounted (XFS can only grow, never shrink)
Shrink it first with xfs_shrinkfs, then resize2fs will succeed
XFS cannot be grown while mounted; unmount it first and then run resize2fs
explain: resize2fs only understands ext2/3/4. XFS grows with xfs_growfs, which takes the mount point (not the device path), operates online, and only grows: XFS has no shrink support. Option D is wrong on both counts (XFS grows mounted, and resize2fs never works on XFS). Option A invents a -x flag. Option C invents xfs_shrinkfs, which does not exist.

q: An NFS entry in /etc/fstab mounts fine when run manually with mount /data, but the system drops to emergency mode at boot. Which fstab option fixes this?
options: Removing NFS entries from fstab entirely, since NFS cannot be listed there
noauto, which prevents the mount from ever being attempted
Changing the pass field to 1 so the filesystem is checked earlier
_netdev, which tells systemd to order the mount after the network is online instead of attempting it before networking is up
explain: Without _netdev, systemd treats the mount as a local filesystem and tries it before network-online.target, so the NFS mount fails and boot drops to emergency mode. The _netdev option marks it network-dependent and orders it after networking. Option B would stop the boot mount altogether, defeating the purpose. Option A is false; NFS in fstab is standard practice. Option C confuses the fsck pass field with mount ordering.

q: Each user needs their NFS home directory auto-mounted at /home/ from server:/export/home/ on demand. Which autofs map entry implements this?
options: * -fstype=nfs,rw,nfsvers=4 server:/export/home/& in a map file referenced from /etc/auto.master
& -fstype=nfs,rw server:/export/home/*, reversing the wildcard and substitution roles
One static fstab line per user, since autofs cannot generate per-user mounts
Autofs does not support wildcards; a script must create each mount in advance
explain: In autofs maps, * is the wildcard matching any requested key (the username), and & substitutes that key into the location, so a single line serves every user on demand. The map is referenced from /etc/auto.master (e.g., /home /etc/auto.home). Option C scales terribly and mounts everything at boot. Option B reverses the syntax: & is the substitution, not the match. Option D is false; wildcard maps are a core autofs feature.

q: A new data disk gets the fstab entry UUID=9f3c-... /data xfs defaults 0 0. Why are the last two fields 0 0?
options: XFS requires 0 0 or the mount fails
Pass 0 disables mounting of the filesystem entirely
The fifth field (dump) 0 skips the obsolete dump backup utility, and the sixth field (pass) 0 skips boot-time fsck; only / uses 1 and fsck-worthy filesystems use 2
The last two fstab fields are optional comments and are ignored
explain: Field five controls the dump backup program (0 = ignore; dump is obsolete). Field six sets fsck order at boot: 1 for the root filesystem, 2 for other filesystems that should be checked, 0 to skip. Data disks and non-filesystem entries (like swap) conventionally use 0 0. Option A is wrong; the fields are generic, not XFS-specific. Option B confuses pass with the mount itself. Option D is wrong; all six fields are meaningful.

q: xfs_growfs /dev/vgdata/lvdata fails with 'is not a mounted XFS filesystem', yet df shows the filesystem mounted at /data. What is the mistake?
options: The filesystem must be unmounted before growing
xfs_growfs expects the mount point, not the device path: run xfs_growfs /data
XFS filesystems cannot be grown at all once created
The device path needs a -m flag to indicate it is mounted
explain: Unlike resize2fs, which takes a device path, xfs_growfs takes the mount point of a mounted XFS filesystem and grows it to fill the enlarged block device. Option A is backwards: xfs_growfs requires the filesystem to be mounted. Option D invents a flag. Option C is false; online growth is a headline XFS feature (only shrinking is unsupported).

q: After adding a new export to /etc/exports, NFS clients get 'access denied by server'. The export syntax is correct. What was forgotten?
options: Setting the exported directory to mode 777, because NFS requires world-writable exports
Running exportfs -rav to make the kernel's export table pick up the change (and verifying firewalld allows nfs, mountd, and rpc-bind)
Nothing: /etc/exports is re-read automatically on every client request
Restarting NetworkManager, which manages NFS exports
explain: /etc/exports is only read when exports are (re)published; exportfs -r re-exports everything, -a covers all entries, and -v makes it verbose so you can confirm. The kernel export table is what the server enforces, not the text file. Additionally, firewalld must allow the nfs, mountd, and rpc-bind services or clients cannot connect. Option C is false; no auto-reload exists. Option D is irrelevant to NFS serving. Option A is wrong and dangerous; permissions do not cause 'access denied by server'.

q: The autofs maps are configured and /etc/auto.master looks right, but nothing ever mounts and systemctl is-active autofs reports inactive. What is the fix?
options: Run systemctl enable --now autofs so the automount daemon runs and persists; then trigger a mount by accessing the mount point and check journalctl -u autofs on failure
Autofs only mounts at boot time, so a reboot is required after any map change
Add matching entries to /etc/fstab, because autofs requires fstab entries to function
Reinstall the OS, because a failed autofs state cannot be recovered
explain: autofs is an on-demand mounter driven by the automount daemon; if the service is inactive, no triggering happens at all. enable --now both starts it and makes it persistent, and simply listing the mount directory triggers the mount. Option B is wrong: autofs mounts on access, not at boot. Option C defeats autofs' purpose (fstab mounts eagerly at boot). Option D is absurd; this is a service-state issue.

q: Practice scenario: you ran lvextend -L +10G /dev/vg0/lv_data on an XFS filesystem mounted at /data, but df still shows the old size. What is missing?
options: xfs_growfs /data
Reboot the server
resize2fs /dev/vg0/lv_data
vgextend vg0 /dev/sdb1
explain: A is correct: lvextend grows the block device, but XFS needs xfs_growfs on the MOUNT POINT to expand the filesystem into the new space - two separate steps. A is the ext4 tool; running resize2fs on XFS fails. C is unnecessary - XFS grows online. D extends the volume GROUP with a new PV, which is irrelevant since the LV already grew.

q: Practice scenario: after adding a new disk entry to /etc/fstab, the server drops to emergency mode on boot. What is the recovery?
options: Reinstall the kernel
From emergency mode, run blkid, correct the UUID in /etc/fstab, then reboot
Delete /etc/fstab and reboot
Run fsck on the root filesystem
explain: B is correct: a wrong UUID in fstab is the classic emergency-mode cause; blkid shows the disk's REAL UUID so you can fix the entry and boot cleanly. B would leave nothing mounted properly - fstab is required. C checks filesystem integrity, which is not the problem (the device simply does not exist under that UUID). D is drastic and irrelevant to a config typo.

q: You need /dev/sdb1 (UUID 4f2c1a9e-7b3d-4e8f-9c1a-2d5e6f708192, ext4) to mount at /data on every boot, referenced by UUID so it survives device-name changes. Which /etc/fstab line is correct?
options: /dev/sdb1 /data ext4 defaults 0 2
UUID=4f2c1a9e-7b3d-4e8f-9c1a-2d5e6f708192 /data ext4 defaults 0 2
LABEL=4f2c1a9e-7b3d-4e8f-9c1a-2d5e6f708192 /data ext4 defaults 0 2
UUID=4f2c1a9e-7b3d-4e8f-9c1a-2d5e6f708192 /data defaults ext4 0 2
explain: B is correct: UUID= references the filesystem by its persistent UUID, followed by mount point, fstype (ext4), options (defaults), dump (0), and pass (2) in the proper field order. A is wrong because /dev/sdb1 is a kernel device name that can change across boots or when disks are added — exactly what UUID mounting avoids. C is wrong because LABEL= expects a filesystem LABEL, not a UUID string; this UUID was never set as a label, so the mount would fail. D is wrong because the fields are out of order: the third field must be the filesystem type (ext4), not the options.

q: You have just edited /etc/fstab to add a new mount. You must verify the entry mounts correctly WITHOUT rebooting. Which command does this?
options: fstab --check
mount -a
mount --verify
systemctl daemon-reload
explain: B is correct: mount -a mounts all filesystems listed in /etc/fstab that are not already mounted (and not marked noauto), immediately surfacing any syntax or device errors. D is wrong because daemon-reload only reloads systemd unit files; fstab is parsed by the mount command and systemd-fstab-generator at boot, not by daemon-reload. A is wrong because there is no 'fstab' command. C is wrong because mount has no --verify option; verification is done by attempting the mount with mount -a.

q: Before writing a UUID-based /etc/fstab entry for /dev/sdb1, you need to discover the filesystem's UUID. Which command reliably reports it?
options: df --uuid /dev/sdb1
blkid /dev/sdb1
fdisk -l /dev/sdb1
lsblk -o NAME,SIZE /dev/sdb1
explain: B is correct: blkid queries block-device attributes and prints the UUID (and TYPE/LABEL) of the filesystem on the device. C is wrong because fdisk -l shows the partition table layout, not filesystem UUIDs. D is wrong because those lsblk columns show only name and size; UUID requires -o +UUID explicitly. A is wrong because df has no --uuid option; df reports mounted filesystem usage, not UUIDs. Section 4 — File Systems

q: You need to format a new partition /dev/sdb1 with the XFS filesystem and give it the label DATA. Which command does this correctly on RHEL?
options: mkfs -t ext4 -L DATA /dev/sdb1
format -t xfs /dev/sdb1
mkfs.xfs -L DATA /dev/sdb1
mkfs.xfs -l DATA /dev/sdb1
explain: C is correct: mkfs.xfs creates an XFS filesystem, and -L sets the filesystem label (uppercase L). A is wrong because -t ext4 creates an ext4 filesystem, not XFS. D is wrong because lowercase -l in mkfs.xfs controls the log section size, not the label — the filesystem would be created unlabeled and '-l DATA' is not a valid log-size value. B is wrong because there is no 'format' command on RHEL; mkfs is the tool. Note that on RHEL 10 XFS remains the default filesystem for new installs.

q: Which /etc/fstab entry correctly mounts the XFS filesystem labeled DATA at /data persistently across reboots?
options: LABEL=DATA /data xfs defaults 0 1
LABEL=DATA /data xfs defaults 0 0
/data LABEL=DATA xfs defaults 0 0
LABEL=DATA /data ext4 defaults 0 0
explain: B is correct: fstab field order is , and LABEL= is a valid way to identify the device. C is wrong because the first two fields are reversed — the device must come before the mount point. D is wrong because the filesystem type must match the actual filesystem (xfs, not ext4), or the mount will fail at boot. A is wrong because the pass field (fsck order) should be 0 for non-root filesystems; pass 1 is reserved for the root filesystem. After editing fstab, run 'systemctl daemon-reload' and 'mount -a' to verify before rebooting.

q: You need to list the NFS exports shared by server 192.168.10.5 and then mount its /srv/share export at the local directory /mnt/share. Which sequence accomplishes this?
options: showmount -a 192.168.10.5, then mount -t nfs 192.168.10.5:/srv/share /mnt/share
nfsstat -e 192.168.10.5, then mount -t nfs 192.168.10.5:/srv/share /mnt/share
showmount -e 192.168.10.5, then mount -t nfs 192.168.10.5:/srv/share /mnt/share
showmount -e 192.168.10.5, then mount -t nfs4 //192.168.10.5/srv/share /mnt/share
explain: C is correct: 'showmount -e ' queries the server's mountd and lists its exported directories, and 'mount -t nfs server:/export /mountpoint' performs the client-side NFS mount. B is wrong because nfsstat shows NFS statistics, not the export list — it has no -e export-listing function. D is wrong because '//server/share' is SMB/CIFS syntax; NFS uses 'server:/export' with a colon, not double slashes. A is wrong because 'showmount -a' lists hosts that currently have mounts on the server (active clients), not the available exports. The NFS client also needs the nfs-utils package installed.

q: You want autofs to provide on-demand NFS mounts under /misc, using /etc/auto.misc as the map file. Which line belongs in /etc/auto.master?
options: /etc/auto.misc /misc
* -fstype=nfs,rw server:/share
/- /etc/auto.misc
/misc /etc/auto.misc
explain: D is correct: an indirect map entry in auto.master has the form ' ', so '/misc /etc/auto.misc' tells automount to manage on-demand mounts beneath /misc using that map. A is wrong because the fields are reversed — the mount point always comes first. C is wrong because '/-' is the syntax for a direct map, where the map file itself contains full absolute paths; /etc/auto.misc is an indirect map. B is wrong because that is map-file content (a wildcard key with mount options), not a master-map line. After editing, restart with 'systemctl restart autofs' and test with 'ls /misc/'.

q: An NFS mount in /etc/fstab causes the boot to hang when the NFS server is unreachable. Which mount option fixes the boot ordering so the mount is only attempted after the network is up?
options: Remove the entry and mount it from rc.local instead
ro
_netdev
noauto
explain: C is correct: '_netdev' marks the filesystem as network-dependent, so systemd orders the mount unit after network-online.target instead of trying it before networking is ready. A proper entry looks like 'server:/data /mnt/data nfs defaults,_netdev 0 0'. D is wrong because noauto means the filesystem is never mounted automatically at boot — the mount would simply never happen. B is wrong because 'ro' only makes the mount read-only; it has no effect on boot ordering or network dependency. A is wrong because rc.local is a fragile legacy hack — systemd mount units with _netdev are the supported, deterministic mechanism. Pairing _netdev with x-systemd.automount is an even more robust pattern for flaky NFS servers. Section 5 — Deploy, Configure & Maintain Systems

q: An /etc/fstab line reads: UUID=9f3c-77 /data xfs defaults 0 0. What does it mean?
options: the entry is a comment template and is ignored until the zeros are replaced
the filesystem is mounted at boot by systemd from fstab, and the two zeros mean: not dumped by dump(8), and no fsck pass at boot
the two zeros mean 0 MB reserved and 0 inodes reserved
the filesystem is mounted read-only and checked every boot
explain: Field 5 is the dump flag (0 = never include in dump backups) and field 6 is the fsck pass order (0 = do not check at boot, typical for XFS whose check runs differently). Defaults are read-write mount options, so the entry is fully live.

q: An /etc/fstab line reads: server:/export /mnt/nfs nfs _netdev,noauto,x-systemd.automount 0 0. What does it mean?
options: a local bind mount of /export that systemd generates from the server name
an automounted CIFS share, because automount implies SMB
an NFS share mounted at boot before networking is up
an NFS share that mounts on first access via a systemd automount unit, with _netdev marking it network-dependent
explain: _netdev tells systemd the mount needs networking; noauto + x-systemd.automount defers the actual mount until first access through an automount unit. It is NFS (type field), mounted only after the network is available, not before.

q: An /etc/fstab line reads: /dev/sdb1 /backup ext4 defaults 1 2. What does it mean?
options: checked first at boot (pass 1) and excluded from dumps
a local ext4 filesystem included in dump backups and checked in fsck pass 2 (after the root filesystem's pass 1)
mounted with a 1-second timeout and 2 retries
backed up twice and checked once per the two numbers
explain: Field 5 = 1 enables dump; field 6 = 2 is the fsck order for non-root filesystems (root takes pass 1). The numbers are flags/order, not timeouts, retries, or counts of operations.

q: Which fstab entry will mount the XFS filesystem with UUID 4a2b-91 at /data on every boot, identified by UUID?
options: LABEL=4a2b-91 /data xfs defaults 0 0
UUID=4a2b-91 /data xfs defaults 0 0
UUID 4a2b-91 /data xfs defaults 0 0
/data 4a2b-91 xfs defaults 0 0 (device and mount point swapped)
explain: The device field comes first and accepts the UUID= form with an equals sign, then the mount point, type, options, dump and pass fields. Swapping device and mount point breaks the entry, the bare 'UUID 4a2b-91' lacks the required equals sign, and LABEL= expects a filesystem label, not a UUID value.

q: Which fstab entry will keep the system booting normally even if the /archive disk is absent or fails?
options: Add the noerror option to its fstab entry
Set its fsck pass field to 9
Add the nofail option to its fstab entry
Prefix the device field with a minus sign
explain: nofail tells systemd not to treat a failed mount of that entry as a boot failure. The other option names and tricks do not exist or address a different problem (fsck order does not affect mount failure handling).

q: Which fstab entry will verify a just-edited fstab completely WITHOUT rebooting?
options: systemctl daemon-reload (only)
mount -o remount / (only)
findmnt --verify plus mount -a to apply all entries now
fsck -a and then reboot anyway
explain: findmnt --verify parses fstab and warns about errors; mount -a then mounts everything not already mounted, surfacing failures immediately. daemon-reload alone does not test the entries (systemd regenerates mount units on reload, but the mount test is mount -a), and a root remount tests nothing new.

q: Which fstab entry will mount an NFS export at boot without risking a long boot hang when the server is down?
options: Mount it from /etc/rc.d/rc.local with a plain mount command
Use type nfs4 with the sync-now option
List the NFS entry FIRST in fstab so it is tried before local disks
Use the export in fstab with _netdev and a background/automount strategy (e.g. noauto,x-systemd.automount) so boot does not block on it
explain: Network mounts belong after networking (_netdev) and should not block boot; an automount unit mounts on demand. Putting the entry first changes nothing about blocking, the option named does not exist, and rc.local mounts block just the same.

q: getfacl /srv/team shows: user::rwx; user:alice:r-x; group::rwx; mask::rwx; other::---. What can alice do in /srv/team?
options: Read and traverse (execute) but not write, per her named-user entry of r-x
Nothing, because other::--- blocks everyone not in the group
Write only, because named users override the mask to write
Read, write and traverse, because the mask is rwx
explain: A named user entry applies directly to alice: r-x. The mask caps the effective rights of named users and the owning group, but the ENTRY itself is what grants alice r-x here; other:: applies to people with no earlier match.

q: getfacl /data/share shows: group::rw-; mask::r--; and ls -l shows group permissions r--. The owning group complains it cannot write despite group::rw-. Why?
options: ls -l is authoritative and the ACL is stale decoration
Group entries in ACLs never grant write on directories
The directory needs the setgid bit before group rights apply
The ACL mask is r--, so the EFFECTIVE rights of the owning group (and named users/groups) are reduced to read-only; fix with setfacl -m m::rw- /data/share
explain: When an ACL exists, ls -l's group column displays the MASK, and the mask is the ceiling for named entries and the owning group. group:: says rw- but mask r-- makes the effective permission r--. Raising the mask restores write.

q: Which command grants user bob read+execute on /srv/docs WITHOUT changing anyone else's access, using an ACL?
options: setfacl -m u:bob:r-x /srv/docs
setfacl -m o::r-x /srv/docs
chown bob /srv/docs && chmod 750 /srv/docs
chmod o+rx /srv/docs
explain: setfacl -m u:bob:r-x adds a named-user entry for bob only. chmod o+rx widens access for EVERY outsider, o:: edits the other class, and chown changes ownership with side effects far beyond the request.

q: Which command makes files created later inside /srv/proj inherit a default ACL granting the qa group read/write?
options: setfacl -m g:qa:rw- /srv/proj (this alone makes new files inherit it)
setfacl --default-all g:qa:rw /srv/proj
setfacl -d -m g:qa:rw- /srv/proj
chmod g+rw /srv/proj and setgid
explain: Only DEFAULT ACL entries (-d) on a directory are inherited by newly created files and directories. A plain access ACL entry applies to the directory itself, and mode bits/setgid govern group ownership, not inherited ACL entries.

q: An admin must REMOVE bob's named ACL entry from /srv/docs while leaving the rest of the ACL intact. Which command?
options: setfacl -m u:bob:: /srv/docs
setfacl -b /srv/docs
setfacl -x u:bob /srv/docs
chmod --remove-acl u:bob /srv/docs
explain: -x deletes the named entry. -b strips the ENTIRE ACL (all extended entries), the -m form shown has invalid syntax (an empty permission set is written ---, not ::), and chmod has no --remove-acl option.

q: Which command/approach will grow the XFS filesystem mounted at /data after its logical volume was extended?
options: resize2fs /dev/vgdata/lvdata
mkfs.xfs -f /dev/vgdata/lvdata
xfs_growfs /dev/vgdata/lvdata while unmounted
xfs_growfs /data (while the filesystem is mounted)
explain: XFS grows online with xfs_growfs given the MOUNT POINT, and the filesystem must be mounted. resize2fs is the ext-family tool and refuses XFS; running xfs_growfs unmounted fails, and mkfs would destroy the data.

q: Which command/approach will grow an ext4 filesystem on /dev/vgapp/lvweb to fill its (already extended) logical volume?
options: resize2fs /dev/vgapp/lvweb
tune2fs --resize /dev/vgapp/lvweb
xfs_growfs /web
e2fsck -grow /dev/vgapp/lvweb
explain: resize2fs is the ext2/3/4 resizer and can grow a mounted ext4 filesystem online. xfs_growfs only speaks XFS, and the fsck/tune2fs forms shown are not resize mechanisms.

q: Which command/approach will temporarily mount the ISO image /opt/rhel.iso at /mnt/iso for reading?
options: mount -t iso /opt/rhel.iso /mnt/iso
mount --bind /opt/rhel.iso /mnt/iso
mount -o loop,ro /opt/rhel.iso /mnt/iso
mount -o img /opt/rhel.iso /mnt/iso
explain: A regular file is attached through a loop device with -o loop, and ro keeps it read-only as ISOs are. -t expects a filesystem type (iso9660, not 'iso'), --bind mirrors a directory tree rather than interpreting an image, and -o img is not an option.

q: Which command/approach will list what the NFS server 192.168.10.5 exports before trying to mount anything?
options: showmount -e 192.168.10.5
mount -t nfs --list 192.168.10.5
exportfs -l 192.168.10.5 (run on the client)
nfsstat --server 192.168.10.5
explain: showmount -e queries the server's export list from the client. exportfs manages exports ON the server, and the other two spellings do not list exports.

q: Which command/approach will An autofs indirect map file /etc/auto.home contains: * -fstype=nfs,rw server:/export/home/&. A user cds into /home/alice (the master map mounts the map at /home). What happens??
options: The wildcard mounts every user's home simultaneously at login
autofs mounts the whole /export/home at /home and alice is a plain subdirectory
Nothing mounts until the user runs mount /home/alice manually
autofs mounts server:/export/home/alice at /home/alice on demand; * matches the key and & expands to that same key
explain: In an indirect map the key (alice) is matched by *, and & in the location expands to the key, so only alice's export is mounted, on first access. autofs never pre-mounts all keys, and the mount is triggered by access, not a manual mount.

q: Which command/approach will diagnose: df -h shows /var at 68% but users cannot create files there; df -i shows IUse% at 100%. What is wrong and the fix??
options: The journal filled /var; journalctl --vacuum fixes inode exhaustion
The filesystem is out of INODES (too many small files); free or remove files (or recreate with more inodes) — more blocks will not help
Quotas are misconfigured; run quotaoff to release inodes
The filesystem is out of blocks; extend the LV and grow the filesystem
explain: File creation needs BOTH a free block and a free inode. df -i at 100% with block space free is classic inode exhaustion from masses of tiny files. Growing the filesystem adds blocks, not a proportional inode fix on an existing ext filesystem, and the journal/quota paths do not address inode count.

q: Which TWO statements about growing filesystems on RHEL are true? (Choose two.)
options: ext4 filesystems can be grown online with resize2fs after the underlying device is enlarged
XFS filesystems can be grown while mounted but cannot be shrunk
xfs_growfs takes the block device path of an unmounted filesystem
resize2fs works on XFS as long as the filesystem is unmounted first
explain: XFS is grow-only and grows online via the mount point; ext4 grows with resize2fs (online for growing). xfs_growfs requires a MOUNTED filesystem and its mount point, and resize2fs never operates on XFS.

q: Which find command lists files anywhere under / that have the setuid or setgid bit set (a standard security sweep)?
options: find / -special 6000
find / -perm /6000 -type f
find / -perm 6000 -type f
find / -perm -6000 -type f
explain: Slash notation /6000 means ANY of the listed bits may be set (setuid 4000 OR setgid 2000). A bare 6000 demands the mode equal 6000 exactly, and -6000 requires BOTH bits set — each misses most results.

q: Which find command matches files whose permissions are AT LEAST 640 (all of the 640 bits present, possibly more)?
options: find /data -perm /640
find /data -perm -640
find /data -perm 640
find /data -perm +640
explain: The minus prefix requires ALL specified bits to be present while allowing extras. Bare 640 is an exact match, /640 is any-of, and +640 is obsolete syntax not used by GNU find on RHEL.

q: An NFS export line in /etc/exports reads: /srv/share 10.0.0.0/24(ro,sync,no_subtree_check). What do clients on that network get?
options: Access for any host, because the network in the line is ignored
Read-only access to the export, with writes acknowledged only after data is committed to stable storage (sync)
Read-write access, because sync implies commit speed
Read-only access only until they remount with rw locally
explain: ro is read-only and cannot be overridden by a client-side rw mount option; sync is about write durability semantics on the server, not about granting write permission.

q: What does root_squash (the NFS default) do, and when is no_root_squash justified?
options: It compresses root-owned files to save space; no_root_squash disables compression
It prevents root from logging into the NFS client at all
It maps client-side root to an anonymous UID (nobody) on the server; no_root_squash trusts client root fully and is only defensible for tightly controlled, trusted clients like diskless boot servers
It is a firewall rule for port 2049
explain: root_squash is the safeguard that stops 'root on a client' from meaning 'root on the server's files'. Squashing is about UID mapping, not compression, logins, or firewalling.

q: After editing /etc/exports, which command makes the running NFS server apply the new export list without a full service restart?
options: exportfs -r (re-export all entries from /etc/exports)
nfsstat --export
mount -a on the server
systemctl reload nfs-server is impossible; only exportfs -x works
explain: exportfs -r re-reads /etc/exports and updates the kernel's export table. (A service reload works too on RHEL since it calls exportfs, but exportfs -r is the direct mechanism; mount -a is a client-side action.)

q: Which mount option pair, added to an fstab entry for a removable backup disk, prevents a missing disk from stalling or breaking the boot?
options: defaults,required
optional,ignore-missing
soft,timeo=5 (NFS options, applied to the local disk)
nofail (systemd will not treat the failed mount as a boot failure); x-systemd.device-timeout can shorten the wait further
explain: nofail is the systemd-era answer for non-critical mounts. The NFS soft/timeo knobs do not apply to local device mounts, and the other strings are invented options.

q: A filesystem must be remounted read-only RIGHT NOW without unmounting it (an application holds files open). Which command?
options: mount --readonly-now /data
mount -o ro /data (a second mount on top)
umount -o ro /data
mount -o remount,ro /data
explain: remount changes the options of the live mount in place — the standard way to flip ro/rw, tighten noexec, and similar — without disturbing open file handles beyond the new policy.

q: What does the noexec mount option do, and on which mount is it a classic hardening choice?
options: It refuses direct execution of binaries from that filesystem; classic on /tmp (and other world-writable mounts)
It hides executables from ls output
It stops systemd from running services whose binaries live anywhere
It prevents files from being created executable by tar
explain: noexec makes execve fail for files on that mount — scripts/binaries dropped into /tmp cannot be run directly (interpreters can still read scripts, a known limit). It does not hide files or affect creation modes.

q: An /etc/auto.master line reads: /shares /etc/auto.shares --timeout=300. What does it establish?
options: A cron-style rescan of shares every 300 seconds
An indirect autofs mount point at /shares whose keys come from the /etc/auto.shares map, unmounting after 300 seconds idle
The NFS server exports /shares using auto.shares as its exports file
A direct mount of /etc/auto.shares at /shares every 300 seconds
explain: auto.master lines bind a mount-point directory to a map file; --timeout is the idle unmount delay for automounted entries. The map's keys become subdirectories of /shares.

q: Which line in an autofs DIRECT map (mounted via /- in auto.master) mounts server:/export/tools at the absolute path /opt/tools?
options: /opt/tools automount server:/export/tools
/opt/tools -fstype=nfs,rw server:/export/tools
tools -fstype=nfs,rw server:/export/tools (key only)
* /opt/tools server:/export/tools
explain: Direct maps use the full absolute path as the key (indirect maps use bare keys relative to their mount point). The value is options plus location, in the same shape as indirect entries.

q: tune2fs -l /dev/sdb1 shows 'Mount count: 24' and 'Maximum mount count: 25'. What will happen soon for this ext4 filesystem, and the modern caveat?
options: tune2fs automatically extends the filesystem at 25 mounts
The disk fails SMART at 25 mounts
A full fsck will be triggered at a coming boot when the count is reached — though many modern installs set the max to -1/0 and rely on other checks, so the admin should verify before relying on it
The filesystem becomes read-only at 25 mounts
explain: Mount-count-based checking schedules an fsck when the counter passes the maximum; nothing becomes read-only or grows. (Intervals and defaults vary; the mechanism is what the item tests.)

q: Which command changes the LABEL of the ext4 filesystem on /dev/sdb1 to 'DATA' (compare: XFS uses xfs_admin -L)?
options: blkid --set-label DATA /dev/sdb1
tune2fs -L DATA /dev/sdb1 (or e2label /dev/sdb1 DATA)
xfs_admin -L DATA /dev/sdb1
mkfs.ext4 -L DATA --relabel /dev/sdb1
explain: For ext filesystems the label tool is tune2fs -L (e2label is the dedicated shortcut). xfs_admin speaks only XFS, mkfs would reformat, and blkid reports rather than writes labels.

q: A systemd mount unit for the path /srv/data MUST be named what, and why?
options: srv_data.mount
srv-data.mount — mount unit names are derived from the mount point path with slashes turned into dashes
mount.srv.data.service
data-srv.mount
explain: systemd derives mount unit names from the Where= path by escaping: /srv/data becomes srv-data.mount. fstab entries are translated into such units automatically, which is also why path precision in fstab matters.

q: A filesystem will not unmount: umount reports 'target is busy'. Which TWO-step approach identifies the culprit and, if needed, detaches safely?
options: kill -9 on PID 1 to reset mount state
rmdir /data to force the issue
mount --force-unmount /data as the first step
fuser -vm /data (or lsof +D /data) to find the processes; if it must go now, umount -l performs a lazy unmount that detaches the namespace entry immediately and cleans up when references drop
explain: Busy mounts are held by processes (cwd, open files, submounts). fuser/lsof expose them; a lazy unmount (-l) is the safe forced option. There is no --force-unmount spelling, and the other two are destructive nonsense.

q: An XFS filesystem had an unclean shutdown and now refuses xfs_repair immediately after boot attempts. What must happen BEFORE xfs_repair can run?
options: xfs_repair must be run with the filesystem mounted read-write
fsck.xfs from boot already repaired it; xfs_repair is only a viewer
The log/journal must be replayed by mounting the filesystem (or the admin zeroes the log with xfs_repair -L as a last resort, accepting possible data loss); xfs_repair refuses a dirty log otherwise
The LV must be extended first
explain: xfs_repair requires an unmounted filesystem with a clean log; replay happens by mounting. -L forces log zeroing when replay is impossible, at real risk. fsck.xfs is famously a near-no-op stub at boot.

q: Which command forces a FULL check of an unmounted ext4 filesystem even if it is marked clean?
options: e2fsck -a /dev/vg0/lvdata
tune2fs -c 1 /dev/vg0/lvdata then mount it
fsck.ext4 --force-online /dev/vg0/lvdata
e2fsck -f /dev/vg0/lvdata
explain: -f forces checking regardless of the clean flag, on an UNMOUNTED filesystem. -a (preen) still respects the clean state, and checking a mounted ext filesystem is unsafe.

q: An application writing to an NFS mount mounted 'hard' hangs indefinitely when the server dies, while the same app on a 'soft' mount gets I/O errors. Which behavior is generally preferred for data-critical writes, and why?
options: soft: errors are always safer than hangs
hard with a 0 timeout, which means it never actually waits
Neither; NFSv4 disables both options
hard: the client retries forever until the server returns, so writes complete rather than silently failing — the hang IS the protection; soft risks silent data corruption on timeout
explain: With hard mounts the process blocks in uninterruptible sleep until the server recovers, preserving write semantics. Soft mounts surface errors after retrans attempts, which many applications mishandle — trading availability for corruption risk.

q: The autofs maps were edited (/etc/auto.home) but users still get the old mount behavior. What applies the change?
options: Nothing — autofs re-reads maps on every access, so the problem must be elsewhere
Restart (or reload) the autofs service: systemctl restart autofs (reload re-reads maps for automount-managed points)
Run automount --recompile-maps
Reboot; autofs maps are read at kernel load only
explain: automount reads maps when it starts (and on reload for changes it can apply live); a plain edit alone does not retarget already-managed mount points. Restarting the service is the reliable apply step during troubleshooting.

q: Which statement about default ACLs on a directory is TRUE for files created inside it?
options: Default ACLs apply only to subdirectories, never to files
A new file's ACL is the intersection of the creating program's requested mode and the directory's default ACL (the default ACL acts like a mask ceiling), so files rarely get the default ACL verbatim
New files receive an exact copy of the default ACL regardless of requested mode
chmod on the directory rewrites the default ACL
explain: Default ACLs are inherited as a starting point but are ANDed with the mode the application requests (open(2) semantics), then the mask settles effective rights. They DO apply to files, and chmod touches the mask/access entries, not the default ACL set.

q: A bind mount is needed so /srv/ftp/pub also appears at /var/ftp/pub, persistently. What are the pieces?
options: A second xfs mount of the same device with a different path in fstab, no bind flag
An autofs direct map is the only persistent way
ln -s is sufficient and is the same mechanism
mount --bind /srv/ftp/pub /var/ftp/pub now, plus an fstab line '/srv/ftp/pub /var/ftp/pub none bind 0 0' for persistence
explain: Bind mounts make the same directory tree visible at a second path; the fstab 'bind' form persists them. A symlink is not a mount (different semantics for chrooted daemons like FTP), and mounting one block device twice read-write invites corruption outside bind form.

q: What does 'cat /proc/mounts' (or findmnt) give an admin that 'mount' alone used to hide, during fstab debugging?
options: A list of mounts that failed at boot with reasons
Only NFS mounts; local mounts are excluded
The fstab file annotated with errors
The kernel's ACTUAL current mount table, including real options in force — the ground truth to compare against what fstab/systemd intended
explain: /proc/mounts is the live kernel state (findmnt formats it well). Boot failures' reasons live in the journal; fstab syntax issues show via findmnt --verify. Ground truth first, intentions second.

q: An admin sets atime behavior: a database volume should not update access times on reads. Which fstab option, and the default behavior caveat?
options: atime=none as an ext4-only option
noatime for the mount; by default RHEL uses relatime, which already limits atime updates to once a day or when the file changes
strictatime, which disables atime updates
lazyatime=off in the kernel, set via fstab field 5
explain: noatime fully suppresses access-time updates (a classic database/throughput tweak). The RHEL default relatime already reduces the cost, which is why noatime's gain is workload-dependent; strictatime is the FULL-update mode, the opposite.

q: Which TWO are legitimate reasons an automount (autofs) share fails to appear when a user enters the directory? (Choose two.)
options: Indirect maps always require the user to run mount first, by design
The autofs service is not running, so no automounter is watching the trigger directory
The map entry's server/export does not resolve or is not exported by the server
The user's primary group is not the group that owns /etc/auto.master
explain: autofs needs its daemon running to intercept the first access, and the target must actually be exported and reachable. Map file ownership by group is irrelevant, and requiring a manual mount defeats the entire mechanism.

q: A new partition /dev/vdb2 must receive an ext4 filesystem with the label ARCHIVE2026. Which command does this correctly?
options: xfs_admin -L ARCHIVE2026 /dev/vdb2 after formatting with mkfs.ext4
mkfs.ext4 -L ARCHIVE2026 /dev/vdb2
mkfs -t ext4 --label-first ARCHIVE2026 /dev/vdb2 --no-format
mkfs.xfs -L ARCHIVE2026 /dev/vdb2, then tune2fs converts it to ext4
explain: The -L option of the ext4 formatter sets the filesystem label while creating an ext4 filesystem on the device. Formatting as XFS is a different filesystem that tune2fs cannot convert, xfs_admin only manages XFS filesystems, and the invented label-first and no-format flags do not create the requested filesystem.

q: An existing unmounted ext4 filesystem on /dev/vgapps/lvlogs needs its label changed to LOGS2026. Which command does this?
options: blkid -L LOGS2026 /dev/vgapps/lvlogs --write
xfs_admin -L LOGS2026 /dev/vgapps/lvlogs
tune2fs -L LOGS2026 /dev/vgapps/lvlogs
setfacl -m label:LOGS2026 /dev/vgapps/lvlogs
explain: tune2fs adjusts ext family filesystem parameters, including setting the label with -L on an unmounted filesystem. xfs_admin works only on XFS, setfacl changes access lists rather than labels, and blkid reports identifiers instead of relabeling a filesystem.

q: An XFS filesystem on /dev/vgstore/lvmedia is unmounted and its label must be set to MEDIA. Which command does this?
options: e2label MEDIA /dev/vgstore/lvmedia
xfs_admin -L MEDIA /dev/vgstore/lvmedia
mkfs.xfs -L MEDIA /dev/vgstore/lvmedia, preserving existing data
tune2fs -L MEDIA /dev/vgstore/lvmedia
explain: xfs_admin manages XFS filesystem labels and requires the filesystem to be unmounted for a label change. tune2fs and e2label are for ext filesystems, and re-running mkfs.xfs would destroy the existing filesystem rather than simply relabel it.

q: A removable drive partition /dev/sdc1 will be shared with non-Linux systems and must be formatted as FAT with a label. Which command is appropriate?
options: mkfs.vfat -n SHARED /dev/sdc1
mkfs.ext4 -n SHARED /dev/sdc1
tune2fs -t vfat /dev/sdc1
mkfs.xfs --fat -n SHARED /dev/sdc1
explain: The vfat formatter creates a FAT filesystem and its -n option sets the volume label for broad compatibility with other operating systems. The ext4 and XFS formatters create Linux filesystems instead, and tune2fs cannot convert an existing filesystem to vfat.

q: An administrator mounts /dev/vgapps/lvapp at /srv/app for a test and does not want executables to run from it or setuid programs to be honored. Which mount command applies both restrictions?
options: mount -o noexec,nosuid /dev/vgapps/lvapp /srv/app
mount -o exec,suid,dev /dev/vgapps/lvapp /srv/app
mount --secure-only /dev/vgapps/lvapp /srv/app
mount -o ro,noexec /dev/vgapps/lvapp /srv/app, because ro also disables setuid
explain: The noexec option prevents execution of binaries on the filesystem and nosuid ignores setuid and setgid bits, and both can be combined in one -o list. The opposite options explicitly allow those behaviors, the secure-only flag is not a mount option, and read-only mounting does not by itself define setuid handling.

q: A mounted filesystem at /opt/vendor must be switched to read-only without unmounting it or interrupting its mount point. Which command does this?
options: mount -o remount,ro /opt/vendor
mount --bind -o ro /opt/vendor /opt/vendor, as the only supported method
echo ro > /proc/mounts, then run mount -a
umount -o ro /opt/vendor, then mount it again later
explain: A remount with ro changes the mount options in place on the existing mount point without removing it. Unmounting ends the mount entirely, a bind remount is not the only supported method, and editing the kernel's mounts listing directly is not a way to change mount state.

q: A directory /srv/source must also appear at /srv/mirror as the same content, not a copy. Which mount approach provides this?
options: ln /srv/source /srv/mirror, because hard links work for directories
mount -t tmpfs /srv/source /srv/mirror
cp -r /srv/source /srv/mirror on an hourly cron job
mount --bind /srv/source /srv/mirror
explain: A bind mount makes the same directory tree visible at a second mount point, so changes appear in both places because it is one filesystem object. Hard links cannot be created for directories in this way, copying creates a separate snapshot that diverges, and tmpfs would create a new empty memory filesystem.

q: An /etc/fstab line reads: UUID=7c1a-4412 /srv/files xfs defaults 0 2. What do the final two fields mean?
options: Mount retry count of 0 and a priority of 2 for parallel mounting
Backup level 0 and a requirement to check it twice per boot
Dump frequency of 0, meaning the dump tool skips it, and fsck pass order 2, meaning it is checked after the root filesystem
Filesystem size of 0 and a two-second mount timeout
explain: In fstab, the fifth field controls use by the dump backup utility and the sixth field is the fsck pass order at boot, where 1 is normally root, 2 is other filesystems to check, and 0 skips checking. The fields do not describe size, timeouts, retries, or checking something twice in one boot.

q: A data filesystem should not prevent a server from booting if its external disk is missing. Which fstab option should be added to its entry?
options: _netdev
noexec
x-mount.required, with a value of false
nofail
explain: The nofail option lets the boot continue and reports the mount as failed without dropping the system into an emergency state when that device is absent. The _netdev option delays mounting until networking is up, noexec only restricts execution, and the invented required option is not the standard fstab mechanism for this.

q: After editing /etc/fstab, an administrator wants to validate the file's syntax and check for errors without mounting anything new. Which command does this?
options: blkid --verify /etc/fstab
findmnt --verify
fsck --fstab-check
mount --verify-only /etc/fstab
explain: findmnt in verify mode parses fstab, checks fields and targets, and warns about problems without performing the mounts. The other commands and options shown are not the dedicated fstab verification tool provided for this pre-boot check.

q: A server boots to emergency mode immediately after an administrator added a line for a USB disk to /etc/fstab and rebooted without testing. The disk is now unplugged. What is the best recovery sequence?
options: Disable systemd so fstab is ignored on future boots
Run fsck on the USB disk from another machine and plug it back in permanently
Boot or log in to emergency mode, remount root read-write if needed, fix or add nofail to the bad fstab entry, then run mount -a and reboot to verify
Delete /etc/fstab entirely and reinstall the operating system
explain: Emergency mode from a bad fstab entry is recovered by correcting the entry from the console, making a missing non-critical device nofail or removing the line, and testing with mount -a before rebooting. Deleting fstab or disabling the init system is destructive, and requiring the removable disk to stay attached defeats the purpose of the fix.

q: An administrator grew logical volume /dev/vgstore/lvmedia but df -h /srv/media still reports the old filesystem size, and the filesystem was never resized because the extend command omitted -r. The filesystem is XFS and is mounted. What is the correct follow-up?
options: xfs_growfs /srv/media
resize2fs /srv/media
xfs_growfs /dev/vgstore/lvmedia --unmounted
mkfs.xfs /dev/vgstore/lvmedia to reinitialize at the new size
explain: For XFS, xfs_growfs is run against the mount point of the mounted filesystem to expand it into the enlarged volume. resize2fs only works on ext filesystems, running the XFS tool against the device path in that form produces the not-a-mounted-filesystem complaint, and reformatting would erase the data.

q: Why does resize2fs fail when an administrator runs it against an XFS filesystem?
options: resize2fs only supports ext2, ext3, and ext4 filesystems; XFS is grown with xfs_growfs instead
resize2fs requires the filesystem to be labeled RESIZE before it will work
XFS filesystems are always mounted read-only, so no resize tool can run
The command fails because XFS uses UUIDs and resize2fs only accepts labels
explain: The resize2fs utility is specific to the ext filesystem family and refuses other types, while XFS has its own grow tool used on a mounted filesystem. XFS is normally mounted read-write, labels are not a prerequisite for the tool, and the failure is about filesystem type rather than identifier style.

q: An ext4 filesystem on /dev/vgapps/lvapp was extended at the volume level while unmounted. Which command grows the filesystem to fill the volume?
options: resize2fs /dev/vgapps/lvapp
xfs_growfs /dev/vgapps/lvapp
tune2fs --grow /dev/vgapps/lvapp
fsck.ext4 --resize /dev/vgapps/lvapp
explain: resize2fs expands an ext filesystem to use the larger underlying device, and it can run after a volume extension. xfs_growfs is XFS-specific, and neither tune2fs nor fsck provides the grow operation described by the invented options.

q: When does fsck normally run automatically on a local filesystem?
options: Whenever df reports a filesystem over ninety percent full
During boot, according to the fstab pass field and filesystem state, or when an unclean or error state is detected
Only when an administrator runs mount -a after editing fstab
Every hour from a cron job on all mounted filesystems
explain: Filesystem checks are scheduled at boot based on the pass number and on conditions such as an unclean shutdown or a filesystem flagging errors, and running them on mounted read-write filesystems is avoided. Disk fullness alone does not trigger a check, and mount -a mounts entries rather than performing scheduled checks.

q: An administrator must check an ext4 filesystem that may be corrupted. It is currently mounted read-write at /srv/app and actively used. What is the safe approach?
options: Run fsck only on the mount point directory while users keep writing
Stop services, unmount /srv/app, then run fsck on the device before remounting it
Remount it read-only and run a full repair fsck while writes continue in the background
Run fsck -y on the mounted device immediately, because the -y flag makes it safe
explain: Repairing a filesystem requires it to be unmounted (except for a root filesystem handled from a special boot environment), because fsck must work on a quiescent filesystem. Running repair on a live mounted filesystem can cause corruption, whether invoked on the device or its mount point, and read-only remounting with background writes is contradictory.

q: Before writing an fstab entry, an administrator needs the UUID, filesystem type, and label of /dev/vdb2 in one view. Which command reports all of that?
options: findmnt /dev/vdb2, because it lists the UUID of unmounted devices
blkid /dev/vdb2
tune2fs -U /dev/vdb2, because it prints all filesystem metadata
lsblk /dev/vdb2 --sizes-only, with no filesystem columns
explain: blkid probes a block device and prints its UUID, type, label, and related filesystem identifiers whether or not it is mounted. A sizes-only listing omits filesystem details, findmnt describes mounts rather than unmounted devices, and tune2fs is ext-specific and its -U option sets rather than simply reports a UUID.

q: Inline output reads: lsblk -f; NAME FSTYPE LABEL UUID MOUNTPOINTS; vdb2 xfs FILES 9d44-2210 /srv/files; vdb3 ext4 LOGS 51aa-90bc. Which fstab reference is most robust for the XFS filesystem if device names may change?
options: TYPE=xfs, because filesystem type is unique on this system
LABEL=LOGS, because it is the shortest entry in the output
/dev/vdb2, because lsblk shows it first
explain: Referencing the XFS filesystem by its UUID survives device name changes, and the output pairs that UUID with the xfs filesystem labeled FILES. The device path is exactly what may change, LOGS belongs to the ext4 filesystem rather than the XFS one, and filesystem type is not a unique identifier.

q: A client must list what a file server at 10.20.30.40 exports via NFS. Which command does this?
options: showmount -e 10.20.30.40
exportfs -l 10.20.30.40
nfsstat --exports 10.20.30.40
mount -t nfs --list 10.20.30.40
explain: The showmount command with -e queries the server's mount daemon and lists its exported directories and allowed clients. The mount command mounts rather than lists exports, exportfs is a server-side administration tool, and nfsstat reports statistics rather than the export list.

q: Which command mounts the NFS export /exports/team from server nfs01.example.com at local directory /mnt/team as an NFS filesystem?
options: mount -t nfs /exports/team nfs01.example.com:/mnt/team
showmount nfs01.example.com:/exports/team /mnt/team
mount --nfs-server nfs01.example.com /exports/team /mnt/team
