mount -t nfs nfs01.example.com:/exports/team /mnt/team
explain: An NFS mount source is written as server colon export path, the -t nfs option selects the filesystem type, and the final argument is the local mount point. Reversing the source and target, using showmount to mount, or using the invented server flag does not perform the mount.

q: An NFS fstab entry causes very long boot delays whenever the server is down, because the mount retries in the foreground. The administrator wants background retries instead. Which option helps, alongside _netdev?
options: sync, because synchronous writes move retries to a helper service
hard, because hard mounts always retry in the background
nofail, as the only option that changes retry behavior
bg
explain: The bg option makes a failed NFS mount attempt retry in the background so boot is not blocked waiting in the foreground, and it is commonly paired with _netdev for network filesystems. nofail affects boot failure handling rather than retry placement, hard describes retry persistence rather than backgrounding, and sync concerns write behavior.

q: What is the practical difference between hard and soft NFS mounts when a server stops responding?
options: A hard mount mounts over UDP only and a soft mount mounts over TCP only
A hard mount retries indefinitely and blocks the process until the server returns, while a soft mount returns an error after its timeout and retransmission limits
A soft mount never loses data and a hard mount always corrupts files
There is no difference; the options are aliases kept for compatibility
explain: With a hard mount, operations retry until the server responds, preserving the expectation that writes eventually complete but hanging the client process; with a soft mount, the operation fails back to the application after the configured attempts, risking data issues. They are not aliases and the distinction is not about transport protocol alone.

q: Which /etc/exports-shaped line, seen from the server side, helps a client administrator understand why only one network can mount an export read-write while others cannot?
options: /exports/team *(rw) with a comment saying other networks are read-only
fstab /exports/team nfs rw 0 0 for the 192.168.40.0/24 network
mount /exports/team 192.168.40.0/24 rw
explain: An exports line lists the exported path followed by client specifications with their options in parentheses, so different networks can be granted rw or ro explicitly. A wildcard rw grant contradicts the read-only intent, and lines shaped like mount or fstab entries do not belong in the exports file and grant nothing.

q: An autofs setup must mount NFS shares under /shared using the map file /etc/auto.shared. Which line belongs in /etc/auto.master?
options: /etc/auto.shared /shared nfs defaults
/shared /etc/auto.shared
auto.master /shared --map=/etc/auto.shared --enable
mount autofs /shared /etc/auto.shared
explain: An auto.master line gives the master mount point first and the map file that provides its entries second, optionally with options. The reversed or invented forms do not match the file's format, and a manual mount command does not configure the automounter.

q: In an indirect autofs map /etc/auto.team, what does an entry whose key is * with a location of nfs01:/exports/& accomplish?
options: It permanently mounts all exports at boot under the literal directory named *
It disables autofs for every user whose name matches the server
It mounts nfs01:/exports/<key> on demand, substituting the requested subdirectory name for the ampersand and wildcard
It exports every directory on the local machine to nfs01
explain: In an indirect map, a wildcard key matches any requested name under the master mount point and the ampersand in the location expands to that key, giving per-user or per-name on-demand mounts. It does not turn the client into a server, does not mount everything permanently at boot, and does not disable the service.

q: An administrator needs autofs direct mounts defined in /etc/auto.direct to appear at their absolute paths across the filesystem. Which auto.master entry enables a direct map?
options: /+ /etc/auto.direct --absolute
/etc/auto.direct /- autofs direct
/direct /etc/auto.direct, with keys given as absolute paths inside the file
/- /etc/auto.direct
explain: Direct maps are declared in auto.master with the special mount point /- , meaning each key in the map file is itself the absolute mount point. Using an ordinary directory as the master point creates an indirect map instead, and the other syntaxes are not how direct maps are declared.

q: Autofs maps were edited, but users still see the old behavior and a newly added share does not appear. The autofs service is running. What should be done?
options: Delete the master mount point directory and recreate it while users are logged in
Restart or reload the autofs service so it re-reads auto.master and its maps, for example systemctl restart autofs
Run mount -a, because autofs entries are processed from /etc/fstab
Reboot every NFS client, because autofs only reads maps during the kernel boot phase
explain: The automounter reads its configuration when the service starts, so map and master changes require restarting or reloading autofs to take effect. Mount -a handles fstab entries rather than autofs maps, and neither a client-wide reboot nor deleting active mount directories is the required or safe step.

q: With autofs running and maps that look correct, browsing to /shared/team shows an empty directory and nothing mounts, and no error appears. What is a productive debugging step?
options: Add the share to /etc/fstab as a permanent mount and abandon autofs debugging
Check the autofs service logs and test the underlying NFS mount manually with showmount and a manual mount to separate autofs problems from NFS problems
Increase the number of percent signs in the map file so autofs retries harder
Format the local /shared directory, because an empty listing means filesystem corruption
explain: Verifying the export is visible with showmount and that a manual NFS mount works isolates whether the failure is in autofs map handling or in the NFS service itself, and service logs show map lookup errors. Replacing autofs with fstab avoids the task, and neither invented map syntax nor formatting a mount point addresses the cause.

q: What does enabling ghosting for an autofs mount point provide to users browsing the directory?
options: The mount points remain visible after autofs is stopped permanently
The managed directories appear in listings even before they are mounted, though accessing one still triggers the actual mount
Files are copied locally in advance so no network mount ever occurs
Hidden files from the NFS server are revealed without permissions
explain: Ghosting makes autofs create placeholder entries for map keys so users can see available shares in a listing before triggering a mount on access. It does not pre-copy data, does not bypass server permissions or hidden file rules, and the placeholders depend on the automounter running.

q: Inline output reads: getfacl /srv/team/report.txt; # file: srv/team/report.txt; # owner: ana; # group: leads; user::rw-; user:mateo:r--; group::r--; mask::r--; other::---. What effective access does user mateo have, and why?
options: Read and write, because the owning group entry is combined with named user entries
Read only, because mateo's named user entry is r-- and the mask r-- does not reduce it further
Write only, because the mask overrides the named user entry to its opposite
No access, because other is --- and named users fall back to other
explain: A named user ACL entry grants that user the listed permissions, here read, and the mask caps the effective rights of named users and the owning group without raising them, so read remains read. Named user entries take precedence over group and other checks, and the mask limits rather than inverts permissions.

q: User priya must be granted read and execute access to /srv/team/runbook without changing the file's group or mode for everyone else. Which command adds that ACL entry?
options: chmod 755 /srv/team/runbook, then add priya to every group on the system
setfacl -x u:priya /srv/team/runbook
chown priya /srv/team/runbook, then set the mode to 500
setfacl -m u:priya:rx /srv/team/runbook
explain: The setfacl modify operation with a user entry adds a named user ACL granting exactly read and execute to that person without disturbing other entries. Changing the mode alters access broadly, the -x operation removes entries rather than adding them, and changing ownership is a heavier change than the requirement allows.

q: An administrator must remove the ACL entry for user mateo from /srv/team/report.txt, leaving all other ACL entries intact. Which command does this?
options: setfacl -m u:mateo:--- /srv/team/report.txt only, because zero permissions delete the entry
chmod 640 /srv/team/report.txt, because mode changes delete named users
setfacl -x u:mateo /srv/team/report.txt
setfacl -b /srv/team/report.txt
explain: The -x operation deletes the specified ACL entry for that user while preserving the rest of the access list. The -b operation strips all ACL entries, a mode change does not selectively remove a named user, and setting an entry to no permissions leaves an explicit entry in place rather than removing it.

q: Every new file created inside /srv/projects should automatically grant the auditors group read access, regardless of which team member creates it. Which mechanism provides this?
options: Setting the setgid bit alone, because setgid also creates group ACL entries
A cron job that runs chmod on the directory every night
A default ACL on the directory, set with setfacl -m d:g:auditors:r-- /srv/projects
Making /srv/projects world-readable with chmod o+r recursively each hour
explain: A default ACL on a directory is inherited as the access ACL by new files and as the default ACL by new subdirectories, applying the auditors entry automatically at creation. Scheduled chmod jobs are after-the-fact and racy, world-readable is broader than required, and setgid controls group ownership inheritance rather than ACL entries.

q: Inline output reads: getfacl /srv/projects/plan.txt; user::rw-; user:luis:rwx; mask::r--; group::r--; other::---. The file mode appears as -rw-r-----+ in a long listing. What are luis's effective rights?
options: Read only, because the mask of r-- limits the effective rights of the named user entry despite it listing rwx
Execute only, because the mask is subtracted from the entry in reverse order
Read, write, and execute, because a named user entry ignores the mask
No rights, because the plus sign means ACLs are disabled on this file
explain: The mask entry caps the effective permissions of named users, named groups, and the owning group, so an rwx entry masked by r-- yields effective read, which getfacl also reports as effective rights. Named entries do not bypass the mask, the plus sign indicates an ACL is present, and masking is an intersection rather than a subtraction or reversal.

q: A user reports a filesystem at /srv/archive shows 100 percent full in df -h, yet large deletions freed little usable space for new small files, and df -i shows IUse% at 100%. What is the actual problem?
options: The filesystem is mounted read-only, which df -h misreports as full
Inode exhaustion: the filesystem has run out of inodes from very many small files, even though data blocks remain
The volume group has no free extents, which blocks file creation inside an existing filesystem
Swap is exhausted, so the kernel refuses to allocate file metadata
explain: Each file consumes an inode, and a filesystem crowded with tiny files can exhaust inodes while blocks remain; df -i exposes this with IUse% at 100%. The other explanations describe mount state, volume allocation, or memory conditions that do not match the inode saturation shown in the output.

q: An administrator needs to find which directory tree under /var is consuming the most disk space. Which command summarizes usage by subdirectory?
options: df -i /var, sorted by inode count
ls -R /var, reading file sizes line by line manually
findmnt /var --used, with subdirectories ranked
du -sh /var/* or du -h --max-depth=1 /var
explain: The du tool totals the disk usage of directory trees, and limiting depth or globbing subdirectories ranks the biggest consumers under /var. df reports whole-filesystem totals and inode counts rather than per-directory usage, and the other listings do not aggregate sizes by tree.

q: Which statements about growing filesystems are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Ext4 filesystems are grown with resize2fs after the underlying device or volume has been enlarged
XFS filesystems can be shrunk with xfs_growfs by adding a minus sign to the size
XFS filesystems are grown while mounted with xfs_growfs given the mount point
resize2fs is the correct grow tool for XFS, Btrfs, and ext4 alike
explain: XFS growth happens online via its mount point with xfs_growfs, and ext growth uses resize2fs once more block space exists beneath it. XFS cannot be shrunk with its grow tool or otherwise in place, and resize2fs is limited to the ext family rather than all filesystem types.

q: Which fstab practices reduce boot failures and ease verification? (Choose two.)
options: Referencing filesystems by UUID or label instead of changeable kernel device names
Giving every data filesystem a pass value of 1 so all are checked first in parallel
Testing changes with mount -a and findmnt --verify before rebooting
Mounting NFS shares without _netdev so they are attempted before networking starts
explain: Stable identifiers keep entries valid when device enumeration changes, and testing with mount -a plus verification catches errors while the administrator is still logged in to fix them. A pass of 1 is reserved for the root filesystem, and NFS entries need _netdev so they wait for networking rather than failing early.

q: Which statements about NFS client mounts are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The client must run exportfs to publish its local directories before mounting a server's export
A hard mount returns an I/O error immediately the first time a server stops responding
showmount -e against the server lists the exports that server offers to clients
An NFS entry in fstab should include _netdev so mounting waits until the network is available
explain: Network filesystems in fstab need _netdev for correct boot ordering, and showmount queries a server's exports from the client side. A hard mount retries rather than failing immediately, and exportfs is a server-side tool for managing that machine's exports, not a client prerequisite.

q: Which statements about ACLs are correct? (Choose two.)
options: The mask entry limits the effective rights of named users, named groups, and the owning group
An ACL can grant a specific named user access without changing the file's owner or group
A default ACL on a directory is inherited by newly created files inside it
Removing all ACLs with setfacl -b also removes the basic owner, group, and other mode entries
explain: Default ACLs propagate to new children of a directory, the mask caps effective rights for the middle ACL classes, and named entries grant individual access independently of ownership. Stripping ACLs with -b removes the extended entries but leaves the standard mode-based entries that map to owner, group, and other.

q: Which statements about autofs are correct? (Choose two.)
options: After editing maps, the autofs service must be restarted or reloaded before the changes take effect
An indirect map mounts shares beneath a single master mount point using keys from the map file
Entries for NFS shares in auto.master should use the filesystem type tmpfs
Autofs mounts every share permanently at boot, which is why it saves no resources
explain: Indirect maps attach all their mounts under one master directory keyed by map entries, and the daemon must re-read its configuration after edits. Autofs mounts on demand and expires idle mounts rather than holding everything permanently, and map locations describe the remote NFS source rather than a local tmpfs type.

q: At concept level, what is Stratis on RHEL 10?
options: A backup daemon that ships filesystem snapshots to a cloud service automatically
A local storage management system that layers filesystems over pooled block devices with features such as thin provisioning and snapshots managed through stratis commands
A replacement network protocol for NFS used to export pooled disks
A kernel option that converts any XFS filesystem into a compressed volume
explain: Stratis provides managed local storage pools and filesystems with thin provisioning, snapshots, and monitoring through its daemon and command line tools. It is not a network export protocol, not a filesystem conversion flag, and not an automatic cloud backup service.

q: At concept level, what does VDO provide on RHEL 10?
options: Automatic mirroring of a volume to a second server for high availability
A filesystem checker specialized for virtual disk images
Inline deduplication and compression at the block layer to reduce physical space used by data with repeated or compressible content
A virtual desktop service for remote graphical sessions
explain: Virtual Data Optimizer sits below the filesystem and reduces stored data through deduplication and compression, which suits volumes holding many similar images or datasets. It does not provide remote desktops, cross-server mirroring, or filesystem checking.

q: A filesystem is mounted at /srv/app with the nodev option. A backup tool complains that a device node it created inside /srv/app does not function. What explains this?
options: Device nodes only work on the root filesystem regardless of mount options
The nodev option deleted the device file, so it must be recreated after every reboot
The backup tool needs the filesystem remounted with the sync option to activate device nodes
nodev prevents device special files on that filesystem from being used as devices, so the node is ignored by the kernel
explain: The nodev mount option makes the kernel refuse to open device special files residing on that filesystem, a common hardening setting for data mounts. The file itself is not deleted, the behavior is controlled per mount rather than only on root, and write synchronization has no effect on device node handling.

q: An administrator runs umount /srv/app and receives a target is busy error. Which approach correctly identifies what is keeping it busy before retrying?
options: Delete the mount point directory so processes lose their reference to it
Run mount -a, because remounting all filesystems clears busy states
Run umount with a kill-all flag to terminate the filesystem driver
Use fuser -m /srv/app or lsof on the mount point to find processes holding it open, then stop or move those processes
explain: Tools such as fuser and lsof reveal the processes with open files or working directories on the mount, allowing a controlled shutdown or change of directory before unmounting. There is no kill-all unmount flag of that form, deleting the directory does not release references and is unsafe, and mounting everything again does not clear busy processes.

q: Inline output reads: findmnt /srv/files; TARGET SOURCE FSTYPE OPTIONS; /srv/files /dev/vdb2 xfs rw,relatime,seclabel,attr2. Later the administrator needs the same filesystem mounted read-only at boot. Which fstab change accomplishes this?
options: Add ro to the options field of the /srv/files entry in /etc/fstab and test with mount -a after remounting
Rename the mount point to /srv/files-ro, because the suffix controls access mode
Set the pass field to ro so fsck mounts it read-only
Change the FSTYPE field to ro, because findmnt shows options in that column position
explain: Read-only at boot is expressed by putting ro in the fourth, options, field of the fstab entry, and the change should be tested before relying on it. The filesystem type field must stay xfs, the pass field is a numeric check order, and mount point names have no effect on access mode.

q: A Stratis pool is nearly full even though the filesystems in it report plenty of unused space in df. At concept level, why can this happen?
options: Stratis filesystems are thinly provisioned, so the shared pool's real capacity can be exhausted while individual filesystems still show their larger virtual sizes
The pool is actually an NFS export, and its space is counted on the server instead
Stratis reserves ninety percent of every pool permanently, so reported fullness is always expected
df under-reports XFS usage whenever a pool is present, by design
explain: Because Stratis provisions filesystems thinly from a common pool, the sum of virtual filesystem sizes can exceed real pool capacity, and pool exhaustion is the binding limit regardless of per-filesystem free space shown. The space is local rather than on an NFS server, and no fixed ninety percent reservation explains the discrepancy.

q: An administrator wants a quick comparison of two mounted filesystems showing type and options for both in one table. Which command provides it?
options: findmnt, listing TARGET, SOURCE, FSTYPE, and OPTIONS columns for the mounts
cat /etc/fstab, because it shows the currently active mount options
blkid with no arguments, filtered by eye for mount state
du -h on both mount points and comparing the totals
explain: findmnt displays the live mount table with source, type, and effective options, and it can filter by filesystem type. blkid reports device identifiers rather than live mount options, fstab shows intended rather than actual state, and du reports space usage rather than mount configuration.

q: systemctl is-active nginx reports active, but after every reboot the site is down, and systemctl is-enabled nginx reports disabled. What is the correct fix, and what do the two commands mean?
options: Run systemctl start nginx: that single command both starts it now and enables it for boot
Run systemctl daemon-reload: the enabled state is cached and only a reload applies it
Run systemctl mask nginx: masking forces the service to stay running across reboots
Run systemctl enable nginx: is-active describes whether the unit is running right now, while is-enabled describes whether it starts automatically at boot
explain: is-active answers 'is it running now?' and is-enabled answers 'will it start at boot?' by checking for the wants-symlink; they are independent states, which is exactly why a service can be active yet disabled. systemctl enable nginx creates the symlink so it starts on future boots. Option A is wrong because start only affects the current runtime state. Option C is backwards: mask prevents a unit from ever starting. Option B is wrong because daemon-reload only re-reads unit files; it does not change enablement.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: An admin runs systemctl disable --now cups, yet the service keeps starting whenever a print job is submitted. What is the cause and fix?
options: The SysV chkconfig command must be used instead of systemctl for persistent disablement
The disable command is broken on RHEL and services can only be stopped, never disabled
A reboot is required before any disable takes effect
The cups.socket unit is still enabled and socket-activation starts the service on demand; also run systemctl disable --now cups.socket
explain: Many services ship a .socket unit, and an enabled socket will start its service on incoming connections regardless of the service unit's own enabled state. Disabling (and stopping) cups.socket as well removes the trigger. Option B is false; disable works normally. Option A is wrong because chkconfig is the legacy SysV tool and simply redirects to systemctl on modern RHEL. Option C is wrong: --now stops it immediately and disable takes effect at once for future boots.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: After systemctl enable httpd, the website is still down until the next reboot. Which command both enables the service for boot and starts it immediately?
options: systemctl start --enable httpd
systemctl daemon-reload httpd
systemctl enable httpd, which already implies starting it now
systemctl enable --now httpd
explain: enable only creates the boot-time symlink and changes nothing about the running state, which is why the site stayed down. The --now flag tells systemctl to also start the unit immediately, combining both operations. Option C states the exact misconception that caused the outage. Option A uses invalid syntax (--enable is not a start flag). Option B only reloads unit definitions and never starts anything.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: Practice scenario: a cron job runs but behaves as if commands are missing - 'backup: command not found' in the mail. The script works interactively. What is the cause and fix?
options: cron cannot run scripts in /usr/local/bin; move it to /bin
cron runs with a minimal PATH; use absolute paths (e.g. /usr/local/bin/backup) or set PATH at the top of the crontab
The script needs a .sh extension to run from cron
Add SHELL=/bin/bash - the default sh cannot find commands
explain: B is correct: cron's default PATH is tiny (/usr/bin:/bin); interactive shells get a rich PATH from profiles that cron never sources - absolute paths or an explicit PATH= line fixes it. A is superstition; extensions do not matter, the shebang and exec bit do. C is false - cron can run anything executable given a correct path. D misdiagnoses: the shell is not the problem, the search path is (and cron's default sh is fine for most scripts).
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: Practice scenario: a service starts fine with 'systemctl start myapp' but is dead after every reboot. What was missed?
options: systemctl daemon-reload
systemctl enable myapp (or enable --now to do both at once)
Adding it to /etc/rc.local
systemctl mask myapp
explain: B is correct: start affects only the current runtime; enable creates the boot-time symlink - the classic started-vs-enabled split. A only reloads unit files after edits; there were no edits. B does the opposite of what is wanted (mask forbids starting entirely). D is a legacy SysV hack; systemd enable is the correct mechanism.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: Practice scenario: dnf repolist shows zero repos and installs fail with 'Failed to download metadata'. The repo file's baseurl reads http://mirror.exmaple.com/rhel10. What is the diagnosis?
options: Typo in baseurl ('exmaple'); fix it, then dnf clean all && dnf repolist
Run dnf update to refresh the mirror list
The GPG key is missing; set gpgcheck=0
The repo needs enabled=0 to activate
explain: A is correct: 'exmaple' is a DNS typo - metadata cannot download from a nonexistent host; fixing the URL and cleaning the stale cache resolves it (repolist -v would show the failing URL). A disables signature verification, a security downgrade that fixes nothing about DNS. B cannot help: dnf update needs the same unreachable metadata. C is backwards - enabled=0 DISABLES the repo.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: Practice scenario: a 'systemctl --user enable mytimer' timer never fires unless the user is logged in. What enables it at boot without a login?
options: Add the timer to /etc/crontab
systemctl --user start mytimer
loginctl enable-linger
systemctl enable mytimer (system scope)
explain: C is correct: the per-user manager stops at logout; enable-linger keeps the user manager (and its timers) alive across boot and logout. B targets the system instance, which knows nothing of the --user unit. C is a different scheduler entirely - a rewrite, not a fix. D starts it now, but it still dies at logout.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You need the chrony time service to start now AND start automatically on every future boot. Which single command does both?
options: systemctl start chronyd
chkconfig chronyd on && service chronyd start
systemctl enable chronyd
systemctl enable --now chronyd
explain: D is correct: enable --now both enables the unit (creates the symlink for future boots) and starts it immediately in one operation. A is wrong because start only affects the current session; the service will not start on next boot. C is wrong because enable only configures future boots; the service is not running now. B is wrong because chkconfig and service are the legacy SysV tools; on a systemd-based RHEL they are compatibility shims and not the native, expected method.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You must reboot the server in 10 minutes and warn all logged-in users with the message 'Kernel upgrade'. Which command does this?
options: reboot +10 'Kernel upgrade'
shutdown -r +10 'Kernel upgrade'
shutdown -h +10 'Kernel upgrade'
systemctl reboot --delay 10
explain: B is correct: shutdown -r schedules a reboot (-r) in 10 minutes (+10) and broadcasts the quoted wall message to all logged-in users. A is wrong because reboot takes no time argument; it reboots immediately and sends no warning. C is wrong because -h halts/powers off the machine instead of rebooting. D is wrong because systemctl reboot has no --delay option; it reboots immediately. Section 3 — Configuring Local Storage
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You need /usr/local/bin/backup.sh to run automatically every day at 2:30 AM using cron. Which crontab entry is correct?
options: 2 30 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
30 2 * * 0 /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
* 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
30 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh
explain: D is correct: cron fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week — so '30 2 * * *' means minute 30 of hour 2, every day. A is wrong because hour 30 does not exist (hours are 0-23); cron would reject or misbehave with this entry. B is wrong because day-of-week 0 means Sunday only, so this runs weekly, not daily. C is wrong because minute '*' means every minute during the 2 AM hour — the script would launch 60 times. Always use absolute paths in cron entries and redirect output to a log or /dev/null so mail does not pile up.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You need /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh to run exactly once at 11:00 PM tonight. Which command schedules this one-time job?
options: batch 23:00
Add it to root's crontab with a time of 23:00
echo /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh | at 23:00
explain: D is correct: the 'at' daemon schedules one-time jobs — piping the command into 'at 23:00' queues it to run once at 11 PM. C is wrong because atq only lists the pending at queue; it does not accept a time argument or schedule anything. A is wrong because 'batch' executes jobs when the system load average drops below a threshold — it ignores any time you give it. B is wrong because cron is for recurring schedules; a crontab entry would run every night at 23:00, not just once. Note the atd service must be running: 'systemctl enable --now atd'.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You want to use a systemd timer (not cron) to run a backup every night. Which pair of unit files do you need to create?
options: mybackup.service and mybackup.cron
mybackup.timer and mybackup.target
mybackup.service and mybackup.timer
An entry in /etc/crontab only
explain: C is correct: a systemd timer setup needs a .service unit describing what to run and a .timer unit with the same base name describing when to run it (via OnCalendar=). You then enable and start the timer, not the service: 'systemctl enable --now mybackup.timer'. A is wrong because there is no .cron unit type in systemd. D is wrong because /etc/crontab is the legacy cron mechanism, not a systemd timer. B is wrong because .target units group other units for boot milestones — a timer must be paired with the .service it triggers. Verify timers with 'systemctl list-timers'.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You installed httpd and need it to start automatically on every boot. Which command configures this persistence?
options: systemctl start httpd
systemctl enable httpd
systemctl mask httpd
chkconfig httpd on
explain: B is correct: 'systemctl enable' creates the symlinks that wire the service into the boot target, so it starts on every future boot. A is wrong because 'start' only launches the service right now — after a reboot it will not come up. C is wrong because 'mask' does the opposite: it links the unit to /dev/null so it can never be started, even manually. D is wrong because chkconfig is the RHEL 6 SysV tool; RHEL 9/10 use systemd. The common pattern is 'systemctl enable --now httpd', which both persists and starts it immediately.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You added 'server 192.168.1.1 iburst' to /etc/chrony.conf and restarted chronyd. Which command verifies that the client is actually synchronizing to that time source?
options: systemctl status chrony
ntpq -p
chronyc sources
timedatectl set-ntp true
explain: C is correct: 'chronyc sources' queries the chronyd daemon and shows each configured source with its state — a '^*' marker indicates the source currently selected for synchronization. B is wrong because ntpq is the query tool for the old ntpd daemon, which is not used on RHEL 8/9/10 (and usually not installed). D is wrong because 'timedatectl set-ntp true' only enables NTP synchronization; it does not report which sources are in use. A is wrong on two counts: it only shows whether the daemon process is running, not sync status, and the service is named 'chronyd', not 'chrony' — 'systemctl status chrony' would fail. 'chronyc tracking' is a useful companion showing stratum and offset.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You need the GRUB boot menu timeout to be 10 seconds, persistently. Which procedure is correct on RHEL?
options: Run grub2-install --timeout=10 /dev/sda
Set GRUB_TIMEOUT=10 in /etc/default/grub, then run grub2-mkconfig -o /boot/grub2/grub.cfg
Run update-grub
Edit /boot/grub2/grub.cfg directly and set timeout=10
explain: B is correct: /etc/default/grub holds the canonical GRUB settings, and grub2-mkconfig regenerates the real boot configuration from those settings plus the scripts in /etc/grub.d/. D is wrong because grub.cfg is auto-generated — hand edits are overwritten the next time grub2-mkconfig runs (e.g., during a kernel update). A is wrong because grub2-install writes the bootloader to disk; it has no --timeout option and does not manage menu settings. C is wrong because update-grub is a Debian/Ubuntu convenience wrapper that does not exist on RHEL. The same workflow applies to kernel command-line changes via GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX. Section 6 — Managing Software
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You copied a repository to /mnt/repo on the local filesystem and need dnf to use it. Which /etc/yum.repos.d/local.repo content is valid?
options: name=Local Repo baseurl=file:///mnt/repo enabled=1 gpgcheck=0
[local] name=Local Repo baseurl=file:///mnt/repo enabled=1 gpgcheck=0
[local] name=Local Repo baseurl=file:///mnt/repo enabled=0 gpgcheck=0
[local] name=Local Repo baseurl=/mnt/repo enabled=1 gpgcheck=0
explain: B is correct: a repo file needs a [section] header, a baseurl with a proper URI scheme (file:// followed by the absolute path, hence three slashes), enabled=1 so dnf actually uses it, and gpgcheck=0 when the repo has no signed metadata. A is wrong because without the [local] section header, dnf ignores the entire stanza. C is wrong because enabled=0 disables the repo — dnf will not pull anything from it. D is wrong because baseurl requires a URI scheme; a bare path without file:// will not resolve. Verify with 'dnf repolist' and clear stale metadata with 'dnf clean all' if the repo was just populated (run createrepo_c on /mnt/repo first if it lacks repodata).
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You need to list every file installed on the system by the httpd package. Which rpm command does this?
options: rpm -qi httpd
rpm -ivh --list httpd
rpm -qf /usr/sbin/httpd
rpm -ql httpd
explain: D is correct: '-q' queries the rpm database and '-l' lists all files belonging to the named installed package. A is wrong because '-i' shows informational metadata about the package (version, description, build date), not its file list. C is wrong because '-f' works in reverse — given a file path, it tells you which package owns it; it does not list a package's files. B is wrong because '-ivh' means install with verbose output and hashes, and '--list' is not a valid companion flag for installs. Related queries worth knowing: 'rpm -qa' lists all installed packages and 'rpm -qc httpd' lists only its config files.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You downloaded foo-1.0.rpm to your home directory and want to install it with automatic dependency resolution from your configured repos. Which command is correct?
options: rpm -e foo-1.0.rpm
dnf install ./foo-1.0.rpm
rpm -ivh foo-1.0.rpm
tar -xzf foo-1.0.rpm
explain: B is correct: 'dnf install' on a local .rpm path treats it as a package to install and resolves its dependencies from the enabled repositories automatically (the ./ prefix disambiguates it from a repo package name). C is wrong because rpm -ivh installs the single file with no dependency resolution — if libraries are missing, the install fails or leaves broken deps. A is wrong because '-e' erases (uninstalls) a package; it does the opposite of what is wanted. D is wrong because an rpm is not a tarball — tar cannot install it, register it in the rpm database, or run its scriptlets. After installing, 'rpm -qi foo' confirms the install.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: You need to add the Flathub repository so you can install flatpak applications. Which command correctly adds the remote?
options: flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo
dnf config-manager --add-repo https://flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo
flatpak remote-add flathub
flatpak repo-add flathub https://flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo
explain: A is correct: 'flatpak remote-add' registers a new remote, '--if-not-exists' makes the command idempotent, and the .flatpakrepo URL provides the remote's configuration. D is wrong because 'repo-add' is not a flatpak subcommand — the subcommand is 'remote-add'. B is wrong because dnf config-manager manages dnf/yum repositories in /etc/yum.repos.d, which flatpak never reads. C is wrong because remote-add requires the repository URL argument; without it the command errors out. After adding, install with 'flatpak install -y flathub ' and list remotes with 'flatpak remotes'. Section 7 — Basic Networking
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: A crontab line's schedule fields read: 30 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/job.sh. When does the job run?
options: 30 minutes past every hour
02:30 every Sunday
The 30th day of February at 02:00
02:30 every day
explain: Cron fields are minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. 30 in the minute field and 2 in the hour field with wildcards elsewhere means 02:30 daily. The distractors misread field order or field meaning.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: A crontab line's schedule fields read: 0 4 * * 0 /usr/local/bin/job.sh. When does the job run?
options: Every 4 hours on the hour
04:00 on day 0 of each month
04:00 every day
04:00 every Sunday
explain: The fifth field is day-of-week, where 0 (and 7) is Sunday. Day-of-month is the wildcarded third field here, so the day restriction comes from Sunday. The distractors misread field order or field meaning.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: A crontab line's schedule fields read: */15 * * * * /usr/local/bin/job.sh. When does the job run?
options: Every 15 minutes, around the clock
Every 15 hours
Only during the first 15 minutes of each hour
At minute 15 of every hour
explain: */15 in the minute field steps through 0, 15, 30 and 45 of every hour. It is a step value, not a single minute and not an hours field. The distractors misread field order or field meaning.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: A crontab line's schedule fields read: 0 0 1 * * /usr/local/bin/job.sh. When does the job run?
options: At 01:00 on the first Sunday
Midnight every day
Midnight on January 1st only
Midnight on the first day of every month
explain: Minute 0, hour 0, day-of-month 1, any month, any weekday: the job fires at 00:00 on the 1st of each month. The month field being * means it is not limited to January. The distractors misread field order or field meaning.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: A crontab line's schedule fields read: 15 3 * * 1-5 /usr/local/bin/job.sh. When does the job run?
options: 03:15 Monday through Friday
03:15 on Fridays only
03:15 on the 1st through 5th of the month
Every weekday at 15:03
explain: The 1-5 range sits in the day-of-week field (1=Monday .. 5=Friday), and the time fields read minute 15, hour 3. Day ranges in the third field would be day-of-month, which is * here. The distractors misread field order or field meaning.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: A crontab line's schedule fields read: @weekly /usr/local/bin/job.sh. When does the job run?
options: Once a week at midnight on Sunday (equivalent to 0 0 * * 0)
Once a week at a random load-balanced time
A synonym for */7 in the day field
Every Sunday at noon
explain: Cron's @weekly nickname expands to 0 0 * * 0 — midnight at the start of Sunday. It is fixed, not randomized, and not a step syntax. The distractors misread field order or field meaning.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: Which entry/action will run /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh at 23:15 on the last day-of-month slot cron can express simply: the 1st and 15th of each month?
options: 15 23 1-15 * * /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh
15 23 1,15 * * /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh
15 23 * * 1,15 /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh
23 15 1,15 * * /usr/local/bin/cleanup.sh
explain: Minute comes before hour (15 23), and the day list 1,15 belongs in the day-of-month (third) field. Putting 1,15 in the weekday field means Monday and the 15th weekday value (invalid interpretation), and 1-15 would run on fifteen days, not two.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: Which entry/action will run a job once at boot using cron, accepting that cron's timing guarantee is 'when crond starts'?
options: @boot /usr/local/bin/startup-check.sh in the crontab
A cron line cannot run at boot; use a systemd timer instead in all cases
0 0 * * * /usr/local/bin/startup-check.sh --boot
@reboot /usr/local/bin/startup-check.sh in the crontab
explain: @reboot is cron's special string for jobs run when the cron daemon starts. @boot does not exist, and while a systemd unit is often the better engineering choice, cron CAN express this.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: Which entry/action will edit the crontab belonging to the service account 'backup' as root?
options: crontab -e backup
crontab --user-file /var/spool/cron/backup -e
vi /etc/crontab and add 'backup' as a field
crontab -u backup -e
explain: crontab -u USER -e edits that user's personal crontab. /etc/crontab is the system file whose lines carry an extra user column — a different mechanism; the other spellings are invalid.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: Which entry/action will keep a cron job's output from generating mail while still logging its own errors to a file?
options: Add the flag --quiet to the crontab line
Set MAILTO=off in the crontab
Cron never mails output; nothing to do
Append >>/var/log/job.log 2>&1 to the command in the crontab line (cron mails whatever a job leaves on stdout/stderr)
explain: crond mails any unredirected stdout/stderr to the crontab owner, so redirecting both streams to a log file silences the mail and keeps a record. MAILTO= (empty) also suppresses mail, but 'off' is not special; there is no --quiet crontab flag.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: A systemd timer unit contains: OnCalendar=*-*-* 02:30:00. What schedule does that express?
options: Every day at 02:30:00
At 02:30 on weekdays only
Every 2 hours 30 minutes
Only on the 2nd and 30th of each month
explain: OnCalendar is a wall-clock pattern year-month-day hour:minute:second; wildcards make it daily at 02:30. It is not an interval and carries no weekday restriction.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: A systemd timer unit contains: OnCalendar=Mon *-*-* 04:00:00. What schedule does that express?
options: Every Monday at 04:00
The first Monday of each month at 04:00
Every day at 04:00, named Mon for the unit author
Every month on the 4th at 04:00
explain: A leading weekday name restricts the calendar expression to Mondays; with wildcarded date fields it fires every Monday at 04:00, not just the first.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: A systemd timer unit contains: OnUnitActiveSec=15min with OnBootSec=2min in the same timer. What schedule does that express?
options: The service can only run once per boot because OnBootSec is set
The service runs every 15 minutes of uptime, ignoring boot
The service runs 2 minutes after boot, then re-runs 15 minutes after each previous activation finishes starting
The timer alternates between 2-minute and 15-minute delays
explain: Monotonic timers measure from boot (OnBootSec) or from the unit's last activation (OnUnitActiveSec). Together they give a first run shortly after boot and a repeating cadence thereafter.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: A systemd timer unit contains: Persistent=true in a timer whose OnCalendar time passed while the machine was off. What schedule does that express?
options: The missed run is triggered immediately at the next boot
The run is skipped forever; Persistent only affects logging
systemd refuses to enable timers with Persistent=true
The timer fires twice at the next scheduled time to catch up
explain: Persistent=true makes a calendar timer fire immediately on next activation if its scheduled time passed while the timer (or machine) was off — the key advantage over plain cron for laptops and downed servers.
domain: Domain 6: Deploy, Configure and Maintain Systems

q: systemctl is-active httpd prints 'active', but systemctl is-enabled httpd prints 'disabled', and the service is down after every reboot. What is the complete fix?
options: systemctl mask httpd to lock it into the boot sequence
systemctl start httpd again after each reboot; enablement is automatic once a service runs
systemctl daemon-reload; enablement state is cached and stale
systemctl enable httpd (or enable --now to also start it immediately); the service was only ever started manually and was never enabled for boot
explain: is-active reports the runtime state; is-enabled reports boot persistence. A service can be started by hand yet never enabled, so it vanishes at reboot. enable creates the [Install] symlinks; start does not.

q: An admin runs systemctl enable httpd and the command succeeds, but the web app is still unreachable until the next reboot. Why?
options: The enable symlinks need a daemon-reload before they take effect
enable only wires the service into the boot sequence; it does not start it now — use systemctl start httpd or enable --now
systemctl delays service starts by one boot by design
httpd must be unmasked before enable can work
explain: enable and start are independent axes in systemd: enable = start at boot, start = run now. enable --now does both. No reload or unmasking is involved when enable itself succeeded.

q: A service was disabled with systemctl disable --now appd, yet it still starts whenever a client connects to its port. What mechanism explains this, and the durable fix?
options: Socket activation: the appd.socket unit is still enabled and starts the service on demand; disable/stop the .socket unit as well
The service is respawned by cron's @reboot table
A masked dependency restarts it; mask the client package
The disable did not persist; rerun it with --permanent
explain: With socket activation, systemd listens on the .socket unit and launches the service on first connection, regardless of the service's own enablement. The socket is the thing to disable. --permanent is not a systemctl flag.

q: systemctl status appd shows 'failed (Result: exit-code)' right after a config edit, and journalctl -u appd shows the daemon rejecting its config. The admin fixes the config; what clears the failed state so start works cleanly?

systemctl reset-failed appd (then systemctl start appd); the failed state latches until reset or a successful start
systemctl daemon-reexec appd
The failed state can only clear at reboot
explain: reset-failed clears the latched failure state of a unit. Editing the config fixed the cause; a plain start would also retry, but reset-failed is the explicit clear, and no state file should ever be deleted by hand.

q: Which TWO actions together make a service both run NOW and start automatically at every future boot? (Choose two.)

systemctl start appd
explain: start handles the present, enable handles boot persistence; enable --now is the combined one-command form. mask PREVENTS a unit from starting at all, and daemon-reload only re-reads unit files.

q: [Unit] Description=Report Service; After=network.target; [Service] ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/reportd; Restart=on-failure; [Install] WantedBy=multi-user.target. The file is saved as /etc/systemd/system/reportd.service. What else is required before systemctl enable reportd works?

q: In a service unit, what does the [Install] section's WantedBy=multi-user.target actually do?

It starts the service immediately when the file is saved
It sets the service's runlevel to 5
explain: WantedBy creates the enablement relationship: systemctl enable adds a symlink under <target>.wants/. It does not start anything by itself, and multi-user.target corresponds to the text-mode target (runlevel 3 conceptually, not 5).

q: A unit file placed in /etc/systemd/system overrides one with the same name in /usr/lib/systemd/system. Why does that matter for vendor units?

Admins can customize a packaged service by copying and editing its unit in /etc/systemd/system without their changes being overwritten by package updates
It means packaged units are never used on RHEL
Overriding a unit requires masking the vendor copy first

q: Which command will see the transaction history and undo the most recent dnf transaction?

dnf rollback --last undoes any transaction cleanly

q: A .repo file stanza reads: [localrepo]; name=Local Repo; baseurl=file:///mnt/repo; enabled=1; gpgcheck=0. What does gpgcheck=0 mean and what is the risk?
options: Packages from this repo are installed without signature verification — acceptable only for a trusted local repo; gpgcheck=1 with a gpgkey is the safe default
Updates from this repo are disabled until gpgcheck is raised
The repo is used only for group installs
gpgcheck counts how many times packages are checksummed

q: A repo stanza has enabled=0. dnf install of a package that only exists there fails with 'No match'. Why, and the one-command remedy at install time?

q: An admin needs to verify that chronyd is actually synchronized and see which source it is using. Which action is correct?

q: An admin needs to point chronyd at the internal time server 192.168.1.10, preferring fast initial correction. Which action is correct?

Run timedatectl set-ntp-server 192.168.1.10
Edit /etc/ntp.conf, which chronyd reads by default

q: An admin needs to set the system timezone to America/New_York and confirm it. Which action is correct?

The kernel image the bootloader will load by default at the next boot
The newest kernel installed, regardless of boot order

q: What is the effect of GRUB_TIMEOUT=0 in /etc/default/grub followed by grub2-mkconfig, and the risk?

GRUB waits forever at the menu
Timeout 0 disables GRUB entirely and boots via systemd-boot

q: An administrator needs the vsftpd service running right now, but does NOT want it to start at boot. Which command achieves only the immediate start?

explain: Masking links the unit to /dev/null so systemd refuses manual and automatic starts; disabling only removes boot enablement, and stopping only affects the current run.

q: A unit file was edited on disk to change its ExecStart line, but systemctl start still launches the old command. What must be run before starting the service again?

q: Inline unit content reads: [Unit]; Description=Inventory API; After=network-online.target; [Service]; ExecStart=/opt/inventory/bin/api --port 8443; Restart=on-failure; User=inventory; [Install]; WantedBy=multi-user.target. What does the WantedBy line accomplish when the unit is enabled?

It creates the boot-time link that starts the service with the multi-user target
It restarts the service automatically after a crash

q: A custom unit placed in /etc/systemd/system/worker.service and a vendor unit with the same name in /usr/lib/systemd/system/worker.service both exist. Which one does systemd load?

The unit in /etc/systemd/system because administrator files take precedence over vendor files

The unit in /usr/lib/systemd/system because vendor files are authoritative

q: systemctl status mariadb shows Active: failed (Result: exit-code) after a configuration error was fixed. Which command clears that recorded failure without changing enablement?

q: An administrator runs systemctl is-enabled firewalld and gets enabled, yet systemctl is-active firewalld returns inactive. What is the accurate interpretation?

The service is configured to start at boot but is not running right now

Masking only hides the service from status output

q: In a service unit, what is the effect of Type=forking compared with the default simple type?

Systemd disables logging for the service

q: What should be expected from a service unit with Type=oneshot used for a boot-time configuration task?

q: A service configured with Restart=always exits after an explicit systemctl stop during maintenance. Why does it not restart despite the setting?

An explicit stop tells systemd the shutdown is intentional, so restart policy is not applied to that stop
The service must also set Type=notify to respect stop

q: What is the purpose of After=postgresql.service in the [Unit] section of an application that needs its database ready first?

It copies the database unit settings into this unit

It makes postgresql restart whenever this application restarts

q: An administrator disables the bluetooth service with systemctl disable bluetooth. Which statement correctly describes the result?

The currently running instance is always force-killed immediately
The unit file is deleted from disk permanently

q: Which two actions are required after creating a brand-new unit file at /etc/systemd/system/reportgen.service so it both loads correctly and starts at boot? (Choose two.)

Run systemctl mask reportgen.service to register the file

q: An administrator places a file in /etc/cron.d/nightly-check containing: 0 4 * * * /usr/local/sbin/check.sh. Why does the job never run compared with a similar per-user entry?

q: What does the special string @daily in a crontab accomplish?

Runs the command once per day at midnight, equivalent to 0 0 * * *
Runs the command every hour on the hour
Runs the command every minute during daylight hours

Cron strips execute permissions from scripts at runtime
Cron runs with a minimal environment and a short default PATH that may not include /opt/tools/bin

/etc/crontab lines include a username field before the command

q: An admin runs nmcli con mod net0 ipv4.addresses 10.0.5.20/24 ipv4.gateway 10.0.5.1, then nmcli con up net0, but the interface still gets a DHCP address. What was missed?

explain: NetworkManager's ipv4.method defaults to auto (DHCP); configuring addresses without switching the method to manual leaves DHCP in charge. Make resolv.conf immutable with chattr +i so NetworkManager cannot touch it
Store DNS in the NetworkManager connection profile with nmcli con mod net0 ipv4.dns "10.0.5.2 10.0.5.3" (then nmcli con up net0); never hand-edit the NM-managed resolv.conf

explain: On RHEL, /etc/resolv.conf is generated by NetworkManager from the active connection profiles, so manual edits are overwritten whenever the connection is (re)activated. Persistent DNS belongs in the profile via ipv4.dns (or ipv4.ignore-auto-dns yes to ignore DHCP-provided servers). Option B is a hack that breaks legitimate updates and can confuse NM. Option D is fragile to ordering and profile changes. Option A denies the observed behavior; the file is managed, not static.

q: A NIC has two connection profiles: 'Wired connection 1' (active) and 'corp-lan' (configured but inactive). The admin runs nmcli con mod corp-lan ipv4.addresses 10.0.5.20/24, then nmcli con up corp-lan, and networking flaps between configurations. What is the correct approach?

Rebooting is the only way to resolve conflicting profiles
Set connection.autoconnect no on all profiles, because autoconnect is irrelevant to static addressing
NetworkManager cannot hold two profiles for one device; both must be deleted and recreated as one
explain: nmcli con mod edits a specific stored profile, and only the active profile's settings affect the live interface; editing an inactive profile changes nothing until it is activated. With two profiles for one NIC, autoconnect priority decides which wins at boot, so leaving both set to autoconnect yes causes flapping: keep autoconnect yes on the intended profile and no on the other. Option D is false; multiple profiles per device are normal (e.g., home vs office). Option C is backwards: autoconnect is exactly the mechanism arbitrating between profiles. Option B is unnecessary; nmcli con up/down and autoconnect settings resolve it live.

explain: C is correct: it sets the address and gateway, flips ipv6.method to manual (required - with method auto NetworkManager ignores the static address), and reactivates the connection. A is wrong because it flips ipv4.method to manual, breaking the requirement that IPv4 stay on DHCP. C appends the address but leaves ipv6.method at auto, so the static config is never applied. A is futile: NM rewrites resolv.conf on every activation. B is overkill; reactivating the connection applies it. C is false - custom DNS with DHCP is exactly what ignore-auto-dns is for.

q: Using nmcli, you need to set a static IPv4 address 192.168.1.10/24 with gateway 192.168.1.1 and DNS 8.8.8.8 on connection 'eth0', then apply it. Which sequence is correct?
options: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8 ipv4.method manual && nmcli con up eth0
nmcli dev mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.10/24 ipv4.method manual
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8 && nmcli con up eth0
ifconfig eth0 192.168.1.10 netmask 255.255.255.0
explain: A is correct: 'nmcli con mod' sets the connection profile properties, 'ipv4.method manual' is mandatory to disable DHCP (without it, DHCP would override your static values), and 'nmcli con up' reactivates the profile so the changes apply. C is wrong because omitting 'ipv4.method manual' leaves the method at 'auto', so DHCP remains in control and your static address is ignored. D is wrong because ifconfig is deprecated on RHEL, makes only transient changes, and cannot set gateway or DNS. B is wrong because 'nmcli dev mod' modifies device-level state, not connection profile properties — ipv4.addresses is a connection setting, so this command fails. Verify with 'nmcli con show eth0' and 'ip addr'.

q: You need the 'eth0' connection to obtain its IPv6 address automatically via SLAAC/DHCPv6. Which nmcli command configures this?
options: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.method auto && nmcli con up eth0
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.method disabled && nmcli con up eth0
Add IPV6INIT=no to /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-eth0
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv6.addresses ::1/128 ipv6.method manual
explain: A is correct: 'ipv6.method auto' enables automatic IPv6 configuration (router advertisements/SLAAC and DHCPv6 as offered), and bringing the connection up applies it. B is wrong because 'disabled' turns IPv6 off entirely on that connection — the opposite of what is wanted. C is wrong on two counts: it disables IPv6, and /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-* files are the legacy format that NetworkManager no longer prefers on RHEL 9/10 (keyfiles under /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections are canonical). D is wrong because ::1/128 is the IPv6 loopback address — assigning it to eth0 is invalid and 'manual' requires real addresses. Check the result with 'ip -6 addr show eth0'.

q: You need to set the system's hostname to server1.example.com persistently. Which command is the correct, supported method?
options: hostname server1.example.com
uname -n server1.example.com
hostnamectl set-hostname server1.example.com
echo server1.example.com > /proc/sys/kernel/hostname
explain: C is correct: hostnamectl updates /etc/hostname and the running kernel hostname in one step, persisting across reboots. A is wrong because the 'hostname' command only sets the transient hostname — it is lost on the next reboot. D is wrong because writing to /proc only changes the running kernel value; /proc is a virtual filesystem that resets at boot. B is wrong because uname only displays system information; it has no option to set the hostname. Verify with 'hostnamectl' (shows static, transient, and pretty names).

q: You added an entry for dbserver to /etc/hosts. Which command tests name resolution exactly the way applications resolve it (honoring /etc/nsswitch.conf order)?
options: getent hosts dbserver
nslookup dbserver
host dbserver
ping -c1 dbserver
explain: A is correct: getent queries the name service switch, so it consults /etc/hosts first (per the default 'files dns' order in nsswitch.conf) and falls back to DNS — exactly what applications do. B is wrong because nslookup talks directly to DNS and bypasses /etc/hosts entirely, so it would not see your hosts-file entry. C is wrong for the same reason: 'host' is a pure DNS lookup utility that ignores /etc/hosts. D is wrong because ping's job is ICMP reachability; while it does resolve the name as a side effect, it sends packets and is not a name-resolution diagnostic — use getent for lookups. This distinction matters on the exam: an entry in /etc/hosts is invisible to nslookup/host.

q: What is the usable host range of 192.168.10.0/26?
explain: 192.168.10.0/26 spans 192.168.10.0 (network) through 192.168.10.63 (broadcast). Neither endpoint is assignable to a host, leaving 192.168.10.1 through 192.168.10.62 — 62 usable addresses.

q: How many usable host addresses does 192.168.10.0/26 provide?
explain: The block holds 64 addresses total; subtracting the network and broadcast addresses leaves 62 usable host addresses.

q: What is the usable host range of 10.0.5.64/27?
explain: 10.0.5.64/27 spans 10.0.5.64 (network) through 10.0.5.95 (broadcast). Neither endpoint is assignable to a host, leaving 10.0.5.65 through 10.0.5.94 — 30 usable addresses.

q: How many usable host addresses does 10.0.5.64/27 provide?
explain: The block holds 32 addresses total; subtracting the network and broadcast addresses leaves 30 usable host addresses.

q: What is the usable host range of 172.16.4.128/25?
explain: 172.16.4.128/25 spans 172.16.4.128 (network) through 172.16.4.255 (broadcast). Neither endpoint is assignable to a host, leaving 172.16.4.129 through 172.16.4.254 — 126 usable addresses.

q: How many usable host addresses does 172.16.4.128/25 provide?
explain: The block holds 128 addresses total; subtracting the network and broadcast addresses leaves 126 usable host addresses.

q: What is the usable host range of 192.168.1.0/30?
explain: 192.168.1.0/30 spans 192.168.1.0 (network) through 192.168.1.3 (broadcast). Neither endpoint is assignable to a host, leaving 192.168.1.1 through 192.168.1.2 — 2 usable addresses.

q: How many usable host addresses does 192.168.1.0/30 provide?
explain: The block holds 4 addresses total; subtracting the network and broadcast addresses leaves 2 usable host addresses.

q: What is the usable host range of 10.10.0.0/24?
explain: 10.10.0.0/24 spans 10.10.0.0 (network) through 10.10.0.255 (broadcast). Neither endpoint is assignable to a host, leaving 10.10.0.1 through 10.10.0.254 — 254 usable addresses.

q: How many usable host addresses does 10.10.0.0/24 provide?
explain: The block holds 256 addresses total; subtracting the network and broadcast addresses leaves 254 usable host addresses.

q: An admin configures a host as 192.168.20.70/26 with gateway 192.168.20.65. Will it work?
options: No: the gateway must be the .64 address
No: .70 is the broadcast address of its block
Yes: the /26 block is .64–.127, so .70 and gateway .65 are both usable hosts in the same subnet
Yes, but only because gateways may live in any subnet
explain: 192.168.20.64/26 spans .64 (network) to .127 (broadcast); usable hosts are .65–.126, so both the host (.70) and gateway (.65) fit, and a gateway must always be inside the host's own subnet.

q: An admin configures a host as 10.1.1.200/25 with gateway 10.1.1.100. What is the problem?
options: The gateway must end in .1 by rule
The gateway is in the OTHER half of the /24: 10.1.1.200 sits in .128–.255, whose usable range is .129–.254, so 10.1.1.100 is unreachable at layer 2
Nothing; /25 subnets share one gateway at .100
The host address is the subnet's broadcast address
explain: A /25 splits 10.1.1.0/24 into .0–.127 and .128–.255. The host .200 belongs to the second block, whose gateway must also be in .129–.254. A gateway outside the local subnet can never be ARPed, so all off-subnet traffic fails.

q: Which of these addresses can be assigned to a host interface in 172.20.8.0/27?
explain: 172.20.8.0/27 spans .0 (network) through .31 (broadcast); usable hosts are .1–.30, so .17 qualifies. .32 begins the NEXT subnet entirely.

q: Which command will set a static IPv4 address 192.168.30.10/24, gateway 192.168.30.1 and DNS 192.168.30.1 on connection 'eth0'?
options: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.30.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.30.1 ipv4.dns 192.168.30.1
nmcli dev set eth0 ipv4.addresses 192.168.30.10/24 ipv4.gateway 192.168.30.1 ipv4.dns 192.168.30.1
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.method static ipv4.ip 192.168.30.10/24 ipv4.gw 192.168.30.1
Edit /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-eth0; nmcli cannot set DNS
explain: Static addressing in nmcli requires ipv4.method manual (there is no 'static' method value) plus the ipv4.addresses/gateway/dns properties, and con mod edits the PROFILE. Device-level 'dev set' does not exist for these properties, and ifcfg files are the legacy mechanism NetworkManager has replaced.

q: Which command will make connection 'corp-lan' come up automatically at boot?
options: nmcli dev autoconnect eth0 yes
nmcli con mod corp-lan connection.autoconnect yes
nmcli con mod corp-lan connection.autoconnect true --save
Add ONBOOT=yes to /etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/ifcfg-corp-lan
explain: connection.autoconnect is the profile property that controls activation at boot; it takes yes/no. The ifcfg ONBOOT knob belongs to the legacy scripts, and 'dev autoconnect' is not an nmcli form.

q: Which command will apply the changes just made with con mod to the live interface?
options: systemctl reload NetworkManager applies profile edits to interfaces
nmcli dev reapply exists but requires a reboot after con mod
nmcli con up eth0 (reactivating the profile applies the stored settings)
nmcli con reload eth0 applies edits to the running connection automatically
explain: Editing a profile changes stored configuration; the running connection keeps its old settings until the profile is reactivated with con up (dev reapply can apply many settings without a full reactivation, but it is the con up path that is guaranteed — and neither reload variant touches the live interface).

q: Which command will create a brand-new ethernet connection profile named 'backup-net' bound to device ens3 with DHCP addressing?
options: nmcli dev add ens3 con-name backup-net
nmcli con add type ethernet con-name backup-net ifname ens3 ipv4.method auto
nmcli con add ifname ens3 --dhcp backup-net
nmcli con new ethernet backup-net ens3 dhcp
explain: con add creates profiles; type, con-name and ifname are its core arguments, and ipv4.method auto is DHCP. The other forms invent subcommands and flags nmcli does not have.

q: Which command will show the detailed settings of connection 'eth0', including its DNS and routes?
options: nmcli dev show --connection eth0
nmcli con cat eth0
nmcli profile print eth0
nmcli con show eth0
explain: con show <name> dumps the full stored profile. dev show reports DEVICE state, not the profile's stored settings, and cat/print are not nmcli verbs.

q: Which command will remove the DNS server 8.8.8.8 from connection eth0's list, keeping the others?
options: nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.dns-remove 8.8.8.8
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.dns '' (clears only 8.8.8.8)
nmcli con mod eth0 -ipv4.dns 8.8.8.8
nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.dns ~8.8.8.8
explain: Prefixing a multi-value property with - removes one value (+ adds one). Assigning a new list replaces the whole list, and setting it empty clears ALL DNS servers, not just the named one.

q: Which command will check which connection profile is active on device eth0 and its current IP?
options: ifconfig eth0 (the supported RHEL 10 tool)
nmcli device status (profile per device) and nmcli device show eth0 (IP4.ADDRESS lines)
nmcli con active-only eth0
cat /etc/sysconfig/network (shows the active profile)
explain: device status maps devices to their active connections; device show gives the live addressing. ifconfig is net-tools legacy (not installed by default on RHEL 10), and /etc/sysconfig/network does not hold per-device profile state.

q: Which command will switch device eth0 from its current profile 'Wired connection 1' to the stored profile 'corp-lan'?
options: nmcli dev profile eth0 corp-lan
nmcli con switch corp-lan
nmcli con up corp-lan ifname eth0
nmcli con mod eth0 profile corp-lan
explain: Activating a different profile on the device is con up <profile> ifname <device>. Profiles are not swapped with mod, and there is no switch verb.

q: An admin edits connection profile 'eth0' with nmcli con mod to change its IPv4 address, then checks with ip addr and sees the OLD address. Which TWO facts explain this? (Choose two.)
options: nmcli con mod silently failed because the admin was not root and printed no error
ip addr caches output and must be run with --refresh after NetworkManager changes
NetworkManager keeps the live device state separate from profile files until activation
con mod changes the stored profile; the running connection keeps its settings until reactivated (con up)
explain: Profile edits and live device state are different layers in NetworkManager: the edit is saved, and only a reactivation (or dev reapply for supported properties) pushes it to the interface. nmcli does error out on permission problems, and ip addr reads live kernel state with no cache.

q: ss -tulpn shows: tcp LISTEN 0 4096 0.0.0.0:22 0.0.0.0:* users:(("sshd",pid=910,fd=3)). What is listening, and from where is it reachable?
options: sshd on UDP port 22, this host only
sshd (TCP, port 22), reachable on all local IPv4 addresses
The ss daemon itself, on TCP port 910
A process with PID 22, reachable on all addresses
explain: The row's Netid column (shown at the line start as tcp) plus Local Address:Port 0.0.0.0:22 mean TCP port 22 on every IPv4 address; the users field names sshd with pid 910. Port and PID live in different columns.

q: ss -tulpn shows: udp UNCONN 0 0 127.0.0.1:323 0.0.0.0:* users:(("chronyd",pid=731,fd=5)). What does the local address tell you about exposure?
options: The service binds only to loopback (127.0.0.1), so it is not reachable from other hosts
The service listens on all interfaces because the peer column is 0.0.0.0:*
UDP port 323 is exposed to the LAN because chronyd is a time server
UNCONN means the port is firewalled and safe
explain: Binding is decided by the LOCAL address: 127.0.0.1 is loopback-only regardless of the wildcard peer column. UNCONN is simply the normal state label for connectionless UDP sockets.

q: ip route shows: default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 proto dhcp metric 100; 192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.50. How does this host reach 8.8.8.8?
options: Directly, because 8.8.8.8 is in 192.168.1.0/24
Via the kernel route marked proto kernel
Via the default route: forwarded to gateway 192.168.1.1 out eth0
It cannot; no route to 8.8.8.8 is listed, so the packet is dropped
explain: Any destination outside the connected 192.168.1.0/24 network matches the default route and is sent to the gateway. The proto kernel route is the connected subnet route itself, and a missing explicit route never means 'dropped' when a default exists.

q: A host can ping its gateway 192.168.1.1 but cannot ping anything by name or off-subnet IP. Its ip route output shows NO default route. What is the first fix?
options: Fix /etc/hosts, which stores the default gateway
Add/restore the default gateway on the connection (e.g. nmcli con mod eth0 ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 and reactivate)
Add a host route for every external server the host needs
Restart the DNS service on the gateway
explain: Without a default route the host can only reach its own subnet; name resolution is a red herring (even raw off-subnet IPs fail). The gateway belongs in the connection profile, not /etc/hosts.

q: getent hosts db01 returns '10.0.3.21 db01' even though no DNS server knows that name. Where did the answer come from, and what does that prove?
options: From the gateway's hosts file, proxied by getent
From the DNS cache in systemd-resolved only
getent invented it from the search domain
From /etc/hosts, via the files source in nsswitch — proving local files resolution is consulted (and here answered) without DNS
explain: getent queries the Name Service Switch sources in order; a hit from /etc/hosts (files) never touches DNS. It is the precise way to test resolution 'as applications see it'.

q: A host resolves names for the LAN but all external lookups time out. /etc/resolv.conf points at 192.168.1.1, and the gateway pings fine. What is the most likely layer at fault?
options: The DNS service/path: the resolver at 192.168.1.1 is not answering (or UDP/TCP 53 is filtered) — connectivity itself works since the gateway answers pings
The hosts file shadows all external names
The default route is missing, because external names fail
The NIC's MTU blocks DNS packets specifically
explain: Diagnosis by elimination: local pings work (link + IP fine), a default gateway exists (the resolver is ON the gateway), so the failure is in DNS service itself, not routing or the hosts file.

q: Which is the correct triage order for 'users cannot reach the web app at https://app.example.com' from a RHEL host?
options: Replace /etc/resolv.conf with a public resolver as step one
Resolve the name (getent/dig), then check route/reachability to the IP (ping, ss/curl to the port), then check local firewall/name-service extras
Check SELinux audit logs before any network test
Reboot NetworkManager first, then test
explain: Name → route → service port mirrors the dependency stack: each layer must work before the next is testable, and changing configuration before isolating the layer destroys evidence.

q: A laptop user on a RHEL workstation has an /etc/hosts entry '10.9.9.9 printer' and DNS also has a printer record with a DIFFERENT address. getent hosts printer returns 10.9.9.9. What does nsswitch have to do with this?
options: getent always prefers /etc/hosts regardless of configuration
DNS records expire, so files win by default
The hosts line in /etc/nsswitch.conf lists files before dns, so /etc/hosts wins and DNS is never asked
The workstation is offline, so DNS silently fell back
explain: Resolution order is configurable: 'hosts: files dns' in nsswitch means the local file short-circuits the lookup. Change the order (or the file) and the answer changes — there is no hard-coded preference inside getent.

q: An interface shows TWO IPv6 addresses: fe80::1ff:fe23:abcd/64 and 2001:db8:5::10/64. Which statement is correct?
options: fe80:: is the loopback address for IPv6
The 2001:db8 address is a documentation-range address that cannot route on the real internet (in this example)
fe80::/64 is the link-local address (valid only on this link, used for neighbor discovery and as the SLAAC base); 2001:db8::/32-range address is the global-scope one used for routed traffic
Both are global addresses; the fe80 one is just shorter
explain: fe80::/10 is link-local scope — never routed. 2001:db8::/32 is the documentation prefix (TEST-NET for v6), widely used in examples precisely because it is reserved. Loopback in IPv6 is ::1.

q: A host is configured as 172.16.40.77/24. How many usable host addresses exist in its subnet?
options: 254 usable addresses, from 172.16.40.1 through 172.16.40.254
128 usable addresses, from 172.16.40.1 through 172.16.40.128
256 usable addresses, from 172.16.40.0 through 172.16.40.255
252 usable addresses, from 172.16.40.2 through 172.16.40.253
explain: A /24 leaves 8 host bits, giving 256 total addresses; subtracting the network address 172.16.40.0 and broadcast 172.16.40.255 leaves 254 usable. Counting all 256 as usable ignores the reserved network and broadcast addresses, and the smaller counts belong to longer prefixes such as /25.

q: What are the network and broadcast addresses for 192.168.50.130/26?
options: Network 192.168.50.128 and broadcast 192.168.50.191
Network 192.168.50.64 and broadcast 192.168.50.127
Network 192.168.50.0 and broadcast 192.168.50.255
Network 192.168.50.128 and broadcast 192.168.50.255
explain: A /26 block is 64 addresses wide, so blocks start at .0, .64, .128 and .192; 130 falls in the .128 block, which ends at .191 as broadcast. The /24 boundaries would apply only without subnetting, and the .64 block ends before this address begins.

q: A small segment uses 10.20.8.16/27. Which address is the broadcast address for that subnet?
explain: A /27 block contains 32 addresses; starting at network .16, the last address .47 is broadcast. The .31 value would be broadcast for a /27 block starting at .0, .255 belongs to a /24, and .16 is the network address itself.

q: Two servers must use a /30 for a point-to-point link starting at 203.0.113.8. Which pair can be assigned to the two interfaces?
explain: A /30 has 4 addresses: network .8, usable .9 and .10, broadcast .11, so .9 and .10 are the only assignable pair. Using the network or broadcast address on an interface is invalid, and .13 lies in the next /30 block.

q: A workstation is set to 192.168.90.45/25 with gateway 192.168.90.200. Why will off-subnet traffic fail?
options: The gateway must always end in .1 in a /25 subnet
The gateway 192.168.90.200 is outside the workstation subnet, which spans .0 through .127
A /25 subnet cannot have a default gateway at all
The workstation address is the broadcast address for its subnet
