explain: A /25 starting at .0 covers .0 to .127 with usable .1 to .126, so a gateway at .200 is unreachable because the host would need the gateway to reach it. Gateways need not end in .1, /25 networks routinely use gateways, and .45 is an ordinary usable host address.

q: Which address is link-local IPv6 that a host can auto-configure without any router or server?
explain: Addresses in fe80::/10 are link-local, valid only on the local link and auto-configured on every IPv6 interface. The 2001:db8 address is global documentation space, ::1 is loopback, and ff02::1 is a multicast group, none of which serve as a host link-local unicast address.

q: An admin pings ::1 successfully but cannot reach any other IPv6 host. What does the successful test prove?
options: That SLAAC has assigned a global address
Only that the local IPv6 loopback and stack are working
That the default IPv6 gateway is correctly configured
That DNS for IPv6 records is working
explain: The ::1 address is IPv6 loopback, so reaching it tests only the local stack. It says nothing about a gateway, a globally routable address from SLAAC or manual configuration, or name resolution, which must be checked separately with ip address, ip -6 route and resolver tools.

q: On a RHEL 10 host, which ipv6.method value makes NetworkManager use SLAAC and stateless or stateful DHCPv6 as advertised by the router?
options: auto
link-local
disabled
manual
explain: Setting ipv6.method to auto follows router advertisements for SLAAC and DHCPv6. Manual requires statically listed addresses, disabled turns IPv6 off for the profile, and link-local keeps only fe80 addresses without global autoconfiguration.

q: Which command creates a new NetworkManager profile named lab-net for device ens192 with a static address 10.99.0.20/24, gateway 10.99.0.1 and DNS 10.99.0.5, without yet activating a different profile?
options: nmcli con add lab-net ip 10.99.0.20 mask 255.255.255.0 gw 10.99.0.1
ip addr add 10.99.0.20/24 dev ens192 persistent
nmcli con add con-name lab-net ifname ens192 type ethernet ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 10.99.0.20/24 ipv4.gateway 10.99.0.1 ipv4.dns 10.99.0.5
nmcli device add ens192 ipv4 10.99.0.20/24 gateway 10.99.0.1
explain: nmcli con add with con-name, ifname, type ethernet and ipv4.method manual creates the persistent profile with the requested addressing. Device add syntax does not create profiles, mask-style arguments are not nmcli syntax, and ip addr add changes only runtime state that vanishes on reboot or reactivation.

q: Output reads: DEVICE ens224; TYPE ethernet; STATE connected; CONNECTION uplink-a; DEVICE lo; TYPE loopback; STATE connected; CONNECTION lo. Which statement is correct?
options: ens224 has no profile and is unmanaged
ens224 is up and bound to the active profile uplink-a
lo is the default route device for ens224
Profile uplink-a is inactive and must be deleted
explain: nmcli device status lists STATE connected and names the CONNECTION profile in use, so ens224 is active via uplink-a. The loopback row is independent, and nothing in this output indicates an unmanaged device or an inactive uplink-a profile.

q: An admin runs: nmcli con mod backup-nic ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 172.31.5.15/24. The address does not appear in ip addr output. What is the most likely reason?
options: The profile backup-nic is not the active profile on the device, or it has not been reactivated with nmcli con up after the edit
ipv4.method manual prevents addresses from ever being shown by ip addr
The /24 suffix must be removed before NetworkManager will apply an address
ip addr only shows DHCP-assigned addresses
explain: Editing a profile changes stored configuration; the running device changes only when that profile is activated or reactivated. Manual method does apply listed addresses once active, ip addr shows static and dynamic addresses alike, and the CIDR suffix is required syntax for ipv4.addresses.

q: Which nmcli command assigns two DNS servers, 1.1.1.1 and 9.9.9.9, to the active profile named primary?
options: echo nameserver 1.1.1.1 9.9.9.9 >> /etc/resolv.conf
nmcli device set primary dns 1.1.1.1,9.9.9.9
nmcli con mod primary ipv4.dns 1.1.1.1 ipv4.dns 9.9.9.9 overwrite
nmcli con mod primary ipv4.dns "1.1.1.1 9.9.9.9"
explain: Multiple values for ipv4.dns are given as one space-separated quoted list in a single nmcli con mod. Repeating the property overwrites rather than appends in that form, device set has no such dns subcommand, and hand-editing resolv.conf is overwritten because NetworkManager manages that file.

q: A lab interface should never come up automatically at boot, though staff may raise it manually for tests. Which setting achieves this?
options: nmcli con mod labtest ipv4.method disabled
nmcli device disconnect labtest once
nmcli con mod labtest connection.autoconnect no
hostnamectl set-autoconnect labtest off
explain: connection.autoconnect no stops NetworkManager from activating the profile automatically while still allowing manual activation. Disabling the IPv4 method breaks the profile purpose, a one-time disconnect does not change boot behavior, and hostnamectl does not manage connection profiles.

q: After editing a profile with nmcli con mod, which action actually applies the new settings to the running interface?
options: nmcli con up <profile-name>
cat /etc/hostname
nmcli general status
nmcli con show <profile-name>
explain: nmcli con up activates or reactivates the profile so its settings take effect on the device. Showing a profile or general status only displays information, and reading the hostname file has no effect on interface configuration.

q: What is the key difference between a NetworkManager connection profile and a device?
options: A profile is hardware and a device is a file in /etc/hosts
A profile is a stored set of configuration settings; a device is the actual network interface hardware or virtual interface
Profiles exist only for Wi-Fi and devices only for Ethernet
A device can hold only one address while a profile holds routes only
explain: NetworkManager separates the configuration object, the profile, from the interface it is applied to, the device; one device uses one active profile at a time but can have several profiles defined. Profiles are not hardware, they apply to wired and wireless alike, and addressing is part of profile settings.

q: Which command changes only the runtime hostname until reboot, leaving the persistent hostname untouched conceptually, and which file holds the persistent value?
options: nmcli con mod changes runtime only; the persistent value is in /etc/fstab
hostname <name> changes runtime only; the persistent value is stored in /etc/hostname
Editing /etc/hosts changes runtime only; the persistent value is in /etc/passwd
hostnamectl set-hostname changes runtime only; the persistent value is in /etc/resolv.conf
explain: The hostname command sets the transient kernel hostname, while /etc/hostname holds the static hostname read at boot; hostnamectl set-hostname updates the static value persistently. The resolver, hosts, password and fstab files do not store the system hostname.

q: An admin runs hostnamectl set-hostname buildnode7.example.org. Where is the static hostname recorded and when does it take effect?
options: In /etc/resolv.conf, effective after NetworkManager restarts
In the connection profile, effective after nmcli con up
Only in memory until the next reboot writes it to /etc/hosts
In /etc/hostname, effective immediately for the static hostname without a reboot
explain: hostnamectl set-hostname writes the static hostname to /etc/hostname and applies it right away. It is not stored in the hosts or resolver files, nor in a NetworkManager profile, and no reboot or profile reactivation is required.

q: A name lookup returns the /etc/hosts entry even though DNS has a different address for the same name. Output of grep hosts /etc/nsswitch.conf reads: hosts: files dns myhostname. Why does the local file win?
options: The files source is listed before dns in the hosts lookup order
DNS is disabled whenever /etc/hosts is non-empty
getent forces /etc/hosts to be checked last
myhostname always overrides DNS and files equally
explain: nsswitch.conf is consulted left to right, so files, meaning /etc/hosts, is tried before dns and its match wins. DNS remains usable for names not in the file, myhostname handles local hostname resolution, and tools honoring nsswitch follow that stated order rather than reversing it.

q: Which tool queries DNS servers directly, bypassing /etc/hosts and nsswitch, to check what DNS itself returns for portal.example.net?
options: dig portal.example.net
ping -c1 portal.example.net
getent hosts portal.example.net
hostnamectl query portal.example.net
explain: dig talks straight to DNS and reports the authoritative lookup path, ignoring local files. getent deliberately follows nsswitch including files, ping resolves through the system resolver so it can reflect /etc/hosts, and hostnamectl has no such name-query function.

q: A user can ping 198.51.100.25 successfully but pinging updates.example.net fails with a name resolution error. What is the most focused next check?
options: Add a second default gateway in another subnet
Change the host MTU to 9000
Replace the network cable and renegotiate link speed
Check DNS configuration and test resolution with dig or getent hosts updates.example.net
explain: Successful ping by address proves IP connectivity and routing work, so failure only by name points at resolution: the resolver address, /etc/resolv.conf contents and a direct dig test. Physical link, MTU and extra gateways do not explain a pure name failure when numeric connectivity succeeds.

q: Inline output reads: default via 172.22.0.1 dev ens160 proto dhcp metric 100; 172.22.0.0/24 dev ens160 proto kernel scope link src 172.22.0.44 metric 100. What is the default gateway and source address?
options: Gateway 172.22.0.0 and source address 172.22.0.1 on lo
There is no default route in this output
Gateway 172.22.0.1 and source address 172.22.0.44 on ens160
Gateway 172.22.0.44 and source address 172.22.0.1 on ens160
explain: The line beginning with default via names the next hop 172.22.0.1 out ens160, and the connected route line lists src 172.22.0.44 as the local address. Reversing those values misreads the fields, the .0 entry is the subnet route not a gateway, and a default route is plainly present.

q: Inline ss output reads: tcp LISTEN 0 4096 0.0.0.0:22 0.0.0.0:* users:((sshd,pid=912,fd=3)). What does this show? (Choose two.)
options: The service is a UDP listener on port 4096
The service accepts only connections from 0.0.0.0 hosts with accounts
The listening process is sshd with process ID 912
A TCP service is listening on port 22 on all IPv4 interfaces
explain: In ss -tulpn output the first field is protocol tcp, LISTEN and local 0.0.0.0:22 mean listening on every IPv4 interface at port 22, and the users field names sshd pid 912. The 4096 value is the backlog queue, not a port, and 0.0.0.0 as peer means any remote address, not a restriction.

q: Inline ss output reads: udp UNCONN 0 0 127.0.0.1:323 0.0.0.0:* users:((chronyd,pid=701,fd=5)). Which interpretation is correct?
options: chronyd listens with UDP on localhost port 323 only
The socket is an established TCP connection to 0.0.0.0
Port 323 is open to every remote host for time service
chronyd listens with TCP on all interfaces port 323
explain: The proto is udp, the local address 127.0.0.1 restricts it to loopback, and the port is 323, owned by chronyd. It is not TCP, not bound to all interfaces, and UNCONN for UDP does not indicate an established connection.

q: An interface shows state DOWN in ip link output and no carrier. Which command attempts to bring the link up through NetworkManager for the profile bound to it?
options: nmcli device connect ens256 or nmcli con up on its profile
ip route list table main
nmcli con show --active
ss -tulpn
explain: Bringing a device up is done by connecting the device or activating its profile with nmcli. Listing active profiles, routes or sockets only reports state and will not change a down link or missing carrier condition by itself.

q: What does an MTU of 1500 on an Ethernet interface describe?
options: The maximum number of routes the interface can hold
The maximum number of hosts allowed in the subnet
The link speed in megabits per second
The largest IP packet payload frame size in bytes the interface sends without fragmentation on standard Ethernet
explain: MTU is maximum transmission unit in bytes, 1500 for standard Ethernet, affecting fragmentation. It is unrelated to host counts, which come from prefix length, to negotiated speed, or to routing table capacity.

q: An admin needs to inspect every setting stored in profile wan-uplink before changing it. Which command is appropriate?
options: nmcli device status wan-uplink
nmcli con show wan-uplink
getent hosts wan-uplink
ip addr show wan-uplink
explain: nmcli con show with a profile name displays the full stored configuration for that profile. Device status expects a device name and gives brief state, ip addr shows runtime addresses, and getent queries name databases, not NetworkManager profiles.

q: A host at 10.44.16.80/28 needs its gateway set. Which gateway address is valid for its subnet?
explain: A /28 block starting at .80 spans .80 to .95, usable .81 to .94, so .81 is a valid in-subnet gateway. The .95 address is that block broadcast, .79 belongs to the previous block, and .97 is in the following block and unreachable as a gateway.

q: How many usable host addresses does a /25 subnet provide, and what mask does it correspond to?
options: 62 usable addresses and mask 255.255.255.192
254 usable addresses and mask 255.255.255.128
126 usable addresses and mask 255.255.255.128
128 usable addresses and mask 255.255.255.128
explain: A /25 leaves 7 host bits, 128 total minus network and broadcast gives 126 usable, and the last octet mask is 128. Counting 128 usable forgets the reserved addresses, 254 belongs to /24, and 62 with mask .192 describes a /26.

q: Which nmcli command switches an existing profile named dhcp-wan to a static IPv4 configuration so DHCP is no longer used for IPv4?
options: nmcli con mod dhcp-wan ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.0.2.60/24 ipv4.gateway 192.0.2.1
nmcli con mod dhcp-wan ipv6.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.0.2.60/24
nmcli con mod dhcp-wan ipv4.method auto ipv4.addresses 192.0.2.60/24
nmcli device reapply dhcp-wan dhcp off
explain: ipv4.method manual tells NetworkManager to use only the statically listed IPv4 addresses and gateway. Leaving method on auto keeps DHCP active, changing only the IPv6 method does not fix IPv4, and reapply has no dhcp off syntax.

q: A profile was set with ipv4.method auto and no addresses. After activation the host receives 10.77.3.101/24 plus a gateway from a server on the LAN. What supplied those values?
options: The /etc/hosts file
SLAAC for IPv6
A DHCP server on the local network
The static hostname in /etc/hostname
explain: ipv4.method auto means DHCP for IPv4, so a DHCP server supplied the lease, mask and gateway. The hosts file maps names, SLAAC concerns IPv6 autoconfiguration, and the hostname file holds the machine name, none of which lease IPv4 addresses.

q: Inline ip addr output reads: 2: ens192: mtu 1500 qdisc mq state UP; inet 10.15.9.22/24 brd 10.15.9.255 scope global ens192; inet6 fe80::250:56ff:feaa:1122/64 scope link. Which statements are accurate? (Choose two.)
options: The interface has IPv4 address 10.15.9.22 with broadcast 10.15.9.255
The interface also has an IPv6 link-local address in fe80::/10
The MTU is 9000 and the link state is DOWN
The interface IPv4 address is 10.15.9.255
explain: The inet line gives address .22 and brd .255, and the inet6 line is a link-local address. The broadcast is not the host address, and the header clearly shows mtu 1500 and state UP, contradicting the jumbo DOWN reading.

q: An admin edits a profile that is assigned to ens224 while the device is actually running a different profile, then wonders why nothing changed on the wire. What explains this?
options: Inactive profiles are automatically deleted at boot
ip addr caches old addresses for 24 hours regardless of profiles
NetworkManager merges all profiles for a device into one runtime config
Only the active profile controls the running device; editing an inactive profile changes stored settings only
explain: A device runs exactly one active profile; edits to other profiles wait until that profile is activated. NetworkManager does not merge profiles, inactive profiles persist across boots, and ip addr reflects current kernel addresses rather than a day-long cache.

q: A server must resolve the name backup.internal locally to 10.60.0.40 even though no DNS record exists. Which approach works through the normal system resolver?
options: Set hostnamectl to backup.internal
Add a line 10.60.0.40 backup.internal to /etc/hosts
Add backup.internal to /etc/hostname
Create a NetworkManager profile named backup.internal
explain: Entries in /etc/hosts are consulted by the system resolver via nsswitch files source and need no DNS record. The hostname file and hostnamectl set this machine own name, and a connection profile configures an interface, not name mappings for other hosts.

q: An admin runs getent hosts db2.internal and gets no output, but dig db2.internal returns an address. /etc/hosts has a blank line only for that name. What is a plausible cause?
options: The blank line in /etc/hosts is a valid address record
getent never returns DNS results under any configuration
dig uses /etc/hosts while getent uses only DNS, so results should be reversed
The nsswitch hosts line may lack dns, or the files entry handling prevents reaching DNS for applications using getent
explain: getent follows nsswitch order; if dns is missing from the hosts line, applications using the system databases never query DNS even though dig, which bypasses nsswitch, succeeds. Dig does not use /etc/hosts, getent does return DNS when configured, and a blank line is not a record.

q: Why should an admin avoid treating hand edits to /etc/resolv.conf as permanent on a RHEL 10 NetworkManager system?
options: NetworkManager regenerates /etc/resolv.conf from profile DNS settings on activation and reboot
DNS servers are set in /etc/hostname instead
Only root can ever read /etc/resolv.conf
/etc/resolv.conf is stored in RAM only and never written to disk
explain: On NetworkManager-managed systems resolv.conf is generated from the active profile ipv4.dns and ipv6.dns values, so manual edits are replaced. The file does live on disk, root and other users can typically read it, and the hostname file has no DNS role.

q: A host cannot reach its gateway: ping to 172.19.0.1 reports Destination Host Unreachable from its own address 172.19.0.55/24, while ip link shows the interface UP. What should be checked next?
options: Only whether /etc/hosts contains the gateway name
Layer 2 connectivity to the gateway: cable or switch port, VLAN assignment, and that the gateway is powered and on the same segment
Whether hostnamectl shows the correct static hostname
Only the DNS server address in the profile
explain: Destination Host Unreachable from the host itself with the link up points to ARP and layer 2 failure on the local segment, so physical, switch and VLAN checks come first. DNS, hosts entries and hostname do not affect reaching a gateway by numeric address on the same subnet.

q: Which prefix describes a single host route in IPv4 and a single host address assignment with no subnet peers?
options: /32, a one-address prefix often used for loopback or a point identifier
/24, a one-address prefix for loopback only
/0, a one-address prefix matching one host
/30, a one-address prefix with two usable hosts
explain: A /32 has all 32 bits as network bits, leaving exactly one address. A /24 has 256 addresses, /0 matches everything as the default prefix, and /30 has four addresses with two usable, none of which is a single-address prefix.

q: An admin wants a RHEL 10 system to keep its current DHCP IPv4 setup but add a persistent secondary DNS server through NetworkManager. Which property should be extended?
options: ipv6.dns only, which automatically mirrors to IPv4
/etc/hosts, adding the DNS server as a host entry
ipv4.dns on the active profile, listing both servers in the space-separated value, then reactivating the profile
ipv4.gateway, adding the DNS address as a second gateway
explain: DNS servers for IPv4 belong in ipv4.dns as a combined list on the profile, applied on reactivation. Gateways are next hops not resolvers, hosts entries map names to addresses, and IPv6 DNS settings do not substitute for IPv4 resolver configuration.

q: Inline ip route output reads: default via 10.8.0.1 dev ens128 proto static metric 105; default via 10.8.8.1 dev ens224 proto dhcp metric 110. Which default route is preferred and why?
options: The route via 10.8.0.1 on ens128, because its metric 105 is lower than 110
The route via 10.8.8.1 on ens224, because DHCP routes always win
Both routes are used equally for every packet with no preference
Neither route is usable because two defaults cannot coexist
explain: When multiple default routes exist the kernel prefers the lowest metric, so 105 beats 110. DHCP origin does not override metric, traffic is not split equally per packet by default in this setup, and multiple defaults are allowed with metric deciding preference.

q: A connection profile sets ipv4.never-default yes on a secondary interface. What effect does this have?
options: DNS from that connection becomes the only resolver
The interface will never obtain an IPv4 address
That connection will not provide the system default route, even when active
The profile can never be activated manually
explain: never-default prevents the profile gateway from becoming the default route, useful for secondary or management links. The interface still gets its address, the profile can still be activated, and resolver behavior is controlled by DNS settings and priorities, not by this flag alone.

q: Which nmcli sequence correctly changes the DNS on profile office to 10.2.0.53 and makes the change live on an already connected device?
options: nmcli con mod office ipv4.dns 10.2.0.53 followed by nmcli con up office
Edit /etc/resolv.conf followed by nmcli con show office
nmcli con mod office ipv4.dns 10.2.0.53 followed by nmcli con show office
nmcli device status followed by hostnamectl set-hostname office
explain: Modifying a profile stores the value, and con up reactivates it so NetworkManager rewrites resolver state and applies it. Showing the profile does not apply anything, hand edits to resolv.conf are overwritten, and unrelated status or hostname commands do not activate network settings.

q: An IPv6-only test host should have no global IPv6 address until an admin assigns one manually later. Which ipv6.method is appropriate for the interim profile?
options: manual with no addresses listed as a permanent global method
dhcp, which is an IPv4-only method name in nmcli
auto, which keeps only fe80 link-local addressing
link-local, which keeps only fe80 link-local addressing
explain: ipv6.method link-local restricts the profile to link-local addressing. Auto would autoconfigure global addresses via SLAAC or DHCPv6, manual is meant for listed static globals, and the nmcli IPv6 method for DHCPv6 is expressed through auto or dhcp-only style values, not a bare dhcp token for this purpose.

q: What does the scope link label on an inet6 fe80 address in ip addr output indicate?
options: The address is globally routable across the internet
The address is a multicast group for all nodes
The address is valid only on the local link and is not routed off the segment
The address expires when the DHCP lease ends
explain: Link-local scope means routers do not forward traffic for that address beyond the local segment. It is a unicast host address, not multicast, not globally routed, and it is auto-derived rather than lease-based.

q: Which two checks best distinguish a routing problem from a DNS problem when a remote web name fails to load? (Choose two.)
options: Ping the remote host by its numeric IP address to test routing independently of names
Delete all connection profiles and recreate them
Use dig on the name to test whether DNS returns an address at all
Change the system hostname and retry the browser
explain: Pinging by address isolates IP routing from resolution, and dig isolates the DNS answer; together they show which layer fails. Changing the hostname does not affect remote resolution or routing, and deleting profiles is destructive without diagnostic value.

q: A subnet is written as 192.168.200.0/24 and a host is proposed at 192.168.201.15 as part of it. Why is that proposal wrong?
options: 192.168.201.15 is the broadcast of the 192.168.200.0 network
A /24 allows third octet values only up to 200 exactly
Hosts in a /24 must end in an even final octet
The third octet differs, so 192.168.201.15 is in a different /24 network entirely
explain: In a /24 the first 24 bits, including the third octet, are the network portion, so .200 and .201 networks are distinct. There is no cap tying the octet to the network label value, no even-octet rule, and the broadcast of 192.168.200.0/24 is 192.168.200.255.

q: An admin runs nmcli device disconnect ens192 for maintenance. What happens to the profile that was active on ens192?
options: The device is removed from ip link output forever
The profile is permanently deleted from NetworkManager
The profile is converted to a DHCP profile automatically
The device is deactivated, but the profile remains defined and can be brought up again later
explain: Disconnect deactivates the running connection without deleting its stored profile, so con up or device connect can restore it. Deletion requires con delete, no automatic conversion occurs, and the device remains present in link listings while down.

q: Given last-octet blocks for /26, which set correctly lists a complete subnet?
options: 192.168.7.192 network, usable .193 to .255, broadcast .192
192.168.7.192 network, usable .193 to .254, broadcast .255
192.168.7.128 network, usable .129 to .190, broadcast .192
192.168.7.64 network, usable .65 to .126, broadcast .128
explain: Wait check: /26 blocks are 64 wide; the .192 block runs network .192 to broadcast .255 with usable .193-.254, which matches the correct set. The .128 block broadcast is .191 not .192, and the .64 block broadcast is .127 not .128, so those readings shift the boundary by one block.

q: A new profile should use IPv6 static addressing only, with address 2001:db8:88::20/64 and gateway 2001:db8:88::1. Which nmcli fragment is correct?
options: ipv6.method disabled ipv6.addresses 2001:db8:88::20/64 ipv6.gateway 2001:db8:88::1
ipv4.method manual ipv6.addresses 2001:db8:88::20/64
ipv6.method manual ipv6.addresses 2001:db8:88::20/64 ipv6.gateway 2001:db8:88::1
ipv6.method auto ipv6.addresses 2001:db8:88::20/64 ipv6.gateway 2001:db8:88::1
explain: Static IPv6 requires ipv6.method manual together with the addresses and gateway properties. Auto would seek autoconfiguration, setting only the IPv4 method leaves IPv6 unmanaged in the intended way, and disabled prevents IPv6 addressing altogether.

q: Which two settings must both be present in a profile for a working static IPv4 setup with off-subnet access? (Choose two.)
options: ipv6.method set to manual with an IPv6 gateway only
ipv4.addresses with an address in CIDR notation such as 10.33.0.20/24
ipv4.method set to auto with no addresses listed
ipv4.gateway set to an address inside that same subnet, such as 10.33.0.1
explain: A static IPv4 setup needs the address itself in ipv4.addresses and a reachable in-subnet gateway in ipv4.gateway for off-subnet traffic. Leaving the method on auto with no addresses means DHCP, and an IPv6-only gateway does not provide IPv4 routing.

q: A new hire's account is created, and the admin wants them forced to set their own password at first login. Which command does this?
options: Deleting and recreating the account, because password expiry cannot be forced on first login
chage -d 0 username, which sets the last password change date to 1970-01-01 so the password is immediately expired; verify with chage -l username
chage -E 0 username, which expires the entire account
passwd -l username, which locks the password
explain: chage -d sets the date of the last password change; 0 means the epoch, so the password is considered expired and the user must change it at next login. chage -l displays the resulting policy for verification. Option D locks the account, preventing login entirely. Option C sets the account expiration date (-E), which disables the account rather than expiring just the password. Option A is unnecessary; chage handles this directly.

q: An admin runs usermod -G wheel alice. Afterwards alice has lost her docker group membership and still cannot sudo. What two mistakes were made?
options: usermod cannot modify group membership; only groupmod can
-G without -a replaced her entire secondary group list instead of appending (use usermod -aG), and the %wheel ALL=(ALL) ALL rule is commented out by default in /etc/sudoers, so enable it with visudo
The wheel group does not exist on RHEL and must be created first
Editing sudoers with vim directly is the recommended method and the syntax must be wrong
explain: usermod -G sets the exact secondary-group list, wiping docker; -aG appends instead, so the fix is usermod -aG wheel,docker alice. Separately, RHEL ships the %wheel sudo rule commented out, so membership alone grants nothing until the rule is uncommented via visudo (which also syntax-checks). Option C is wrong; wheel exists by default. Option A confuses usermod with groupmod's role. Option D is dangerous advice: always use visudo, which validates syntax before saving, since a broken sudoers can lock out all sudo access.

q: Practice scenario: which command creates user 'devops' WITH a home directory and /bin/bash as the login shell?
options: useradd -d /home/devops devops
useradd -m -M -s /bin/bash devops
useradd -m -s /bin/bash devops
useradd -M -s /bin/bash devops
explain: C is correct: -m creates the home directory (populated from /etc/skel) and -s sets the login shell. A uses -M, which explicitly suppresses home-directory creation, so SSH key auth and profile setup would break. B sets the home path with -d but never creates the directory, leaving a dangling path. C passes contradictory flags (-m create, -M do not create); never combine them - pick one.

q: Practice scenario: an admin ran 'usermod -G wheel jdoe' and jdoe lost membership in every other group, including docker. Which command puts jdoe in wheel AND docker without wiping anything else?
options: usermod -G wheel,docker jdoe
usermod -aG wheel,docker jdoe
gpasswd -d jdoe docker
useradd -G wheel,docker jdoe
explain: B is correct: usermod -G REPLACES the supplementary group list - that is the pitfall that wiped docker. The -a (append) flag preserves existing memberships while adding the new ones. A repeats the same destructive replace; it happens to list both groups, but any group not listed is still dropped. C deletes jdoe from docker - the opposite of the goal. D fails outright: useradd refuses to operate on a user that already exists.

q: Practice scenario: set carol's password to expire after 90 days, warn her 14 days beforehand, and lock the account 30 days after expiry. Which command does this?
options: chage -E 90 -W 14 -I 30 carol
chage -M 90 -W 14 -I 30 carol
usermod -e 90 -W 14 carol
passwd -M 90 -W 14 -I 30 carol
explain: B is correct: chage -M sets the maximum password age, -W the warning window, and -I the inactive grace period. B is wrong because passwd has no -M/-W/-I flags (it uses -x, -w, -i instead). C misuses -E, which sets an absolute account expiration DATE (YYYY-MM-DD format), not a password lifetime in days. D's usermod -e also sets an account expiry date, and usermod has no -W/-I options at all.

q: You need to create user 'bob' with a home directory, the bash shell, and supplementary membership in the wheel group. Which command is correct?
options: useradd -m -s /bin/bash -aG wheel bob
useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G wheel bob
adduser --disabled-password --gecos '' bob
useradd -m -s /bin/bash -g wheel bob
explain: B is correct: '-m' creates the home directory, '-s' sets the login shell, and '-G' (uppercase) adds supplementary group membership in wheel without changing bob's primary group. D is wrong because lowercase '-g' sets the primary group — bob's primary group would become wheel instead of a private 'bob' group, which is not what was asked. A is wrong because '-a' (append) is only valid with 'usermod -G'; useradd rejects the combination. C is wrong because '--disabled-password' is a Debian/Ubuntu adduser-ism that does not exist on RHEL's useradd. Set bob's password afterward with 'passwd bob'.

q: Company policy requires user passwords to expire every 90 days, with a warning starting 7 days before expiry. Which command enforces this for user 'alice'?
options: chage -m 90 -W 7 alice
chage -M 90 -W 7 alice
chage -E 90 -W 7 alice
passwd -l alice
explain: B is correct: '-M' (uppercase) sets the maximum number of days a password remains valid (90), and '-W' sets how many days in advance the user is warned (7). A is wrong because lowercase '-m' sets the minimum days between password changes — it controls how soon a password may be changed, not expiry. C is wrong because '-E' sets the account expiration date and expects a date in YYYY-MM-DD format, not a day count — '-E 90' is invalid. D is wrong because 'passwd -l' locks the account immediately, preventing login entirely. View the current policy with 'chage -l alice'.

q: You need to create a group called 'devs' and make existing user 'alice' a member of it without disturbing her other group memberships. Which sequence is correct?
options: groupadd devs && usermod -aG devs alice
groupadd devs && usermod -G devs alice
useradd -G devs alice
groupmod -A alice devs
explain: A is correct: groupadd creates the group, and 'usermod -aG' appends (-a) the supplementary group (-G) while preserving all existing memberships. B is wrong and dangerous: 'usermod -G' without '-a' replaces the entire supplementary group list, silently stripping alice of every other group she belonged to — a classic exam trap. D is wrong because groupmod has no '-A' option; it modifies group attributes like name (-n) or GID (-g), not membership. C is wrong because useradd creates new users — run against an existing username it fails (and '-G' there applies only at creation). Confirm with 'id alice'.

q: The '%wheel' line in /etc/sudoers is commented out on this system. What is the safe, correct way to grant user 'alice' full sudo privileges?
options: Append 'alice ALL=(ALL) ALL' directly to /etc/sudoers with echo >>
Run chmod u+s /usr/bin/sudo
Run visudo and add the line 'alice ALL=(ALL) ALL'
Run usermod -aG wheel alice
explain: C is correct: visudo locks the file and validates syntax before saving, so a typo cannot lock you out of sudo; adding a per-user line works regardless of the wheel group's commented-out state. D is wrong because merely joining wheel grants nothing while the '%wheel' sudoers line remains commented — group membership alone is not privilege. A is wrong because writing to /etc/sudoers without visudo's syntax check risks a parse error that disables sudo for everyone, including root's passwordless path. B is wrong because /usr/bin/sudo is already set-UID root by design; re-chmodding it changes nothing about who may invoke it. A cleaner variant is dropping a file in /etc/sudoers.d/ and checking it with 'visudo -c'.

q: Employee 'alice' has left. You need to delete her account AND her home directory and mail spool. Which command does this?
options: deluser --remove-home alice
userdel -r alice
rm -rf /home/alice
userdel alice
explain: B is correct: '-r' (--remove) tells userdel to delete the account along with the home directory and mail spool. D is wrong because plain 'userdel' removes only the account entry — /home/alice and her mail spool are left behind as orphaned data. C is wrong because deleting the directory leaves the account itself intact in /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow, which is a security loose end. A is wrong because 'deluser' is the Debian/Ubuntu tool; it does not exist on RHEL. Check for leftover files owned by her UID afterward with 'find / -uid -ls'. Section 9 — Security: Firewall, SSH & SELinux

q: chage -l alice shows: Last password change: Mar 05, 2026; Password expires: Jun 03, 2026; Password inactive: never; Account expires: never; Minimum number of days between password change: 7; Maximum number of days: 90; Number of days of warning before password expires: 14. What does this mean?
options: The account itself is deleted on Jun 03
Password expires means the account locks permanently on Jun 03 with no grace login
The user may change the password again immediately, any time
The password was last changed Mar 05 and, with a 90-day maximum, expires Jun 03; the user starts getting warnings 14 days before that
explain: chage -l reports aging: last change + maximum days (90) = expiry Jun 03. 'Password expires' is about the PASSWORD's age, not account deletion ('Account expires' is the separate field, set to never), and the 7-day minimum blocks an immediate re-change.

q: chage -l alice shows: Last password change: 0; Password expires: never (as listed after an admin ran chage -d 0 alice). What does this mean?
options: Alice's password was changed today and is fresh for the full maximum period
The password can never expire again because the last-change day is 0
Alice will be forced to change her password at her next login
Alice's account is locked until an admin resets it
explain: A last-change value of 0 is the special 'must change at next login' marker, not a date in 1970 arithmetic for aging purposes. The account is not locked; she logs in and is immediately pushed through a password change.

q: A line reads: alice:x:1025:1025:Alice A:/home/alice:/bin/bash. What does it tell you?
options: alice is a system account because her UID is four digits
The account expires on day 1025 and its group is named 1025
UID 1025, primary GID 1025, home /home/alice, login shell /bin/bash; the x means the password hash lives in /etc/shadow
UID 1025, password 'x', home /bin/bash, shell /home/alice
explain: The passwd fields are name:password:UID:GID:GECOS:home:shell. The literal x replaced real hashes long ago (they moved to /etc/shadow), and UID 1025 is a regular user (>= 1000).

q: A line reads: svc-backup:x:721:721:Backup service:/var/lib/backup:/sbin/nologin. What does it tell you?
options: A group account, because the UID and GID match
An account locked because its home is outside /home
A regular user whose password is 721
A service account (UID 721, in the system range) that cannot be used for interactive login because its shell is /sbin/nologin
explain: UIDs below 1000 are reserved for system/service accounts, and /sbin/nologin politely refuses interactive sessions while still letting services run as that identity. Matching UID/GID numbers are coincidental.

q: A line reads: id bob prints: uid=1030(bob) gid=1030(bob) groups=1030(bob),10(wheel),1005(devs). Which statement is correct?. What does it tell you?
options: bob's primary group is wheel because it is listed first among the extras
The groups output proves bob can sudo because devs is listed
bob has three primary groups
bob's primary group is bob (GID 1030); wheel and devs are supplementary groups
explain: The gid= field is the primary group; everything in groups= after the primary entry is supplementary membership. A user has exactly one primary group, and sudo rights come from sudoers rules (wheel is conventionally the sudo group, but id alone shows membership, not policy).

q: Which command will create user 'sam' with a home directory, bash shell, and supplementary membership in wheel?
options: useradd -m -G /bin/bash -s wheel sam
useradd sam -m -s /bin/bash --primary wheel
useradd -m -s /bin/bash -G wheel sam
useradd -m -s /bin/bash -g wheel sam
explain: -m creates the home, -s sets the shell, and -G adds SUPPLEMENTARY groups. Lowercase -g sets the PRIMARY group — making wheel sam's primary group is a different, wrong outcome.

q: Which command will add existing user 'erin' to the devs group WITHOUT touching her other group memberships?
options: usermod -g devs erin
usermod -aG devs erin
gpasswd -M devs erin (adds while preserving, per the flag shown)
usermod -G devs erin
explain: usermod -G REPLACES the supplementary list, silently dropping erin from her other groups; -a (append) must be combined: -aG. -g changes her primary group. (gpasswd -a erin devs is the equally correct alternative form; the -M variant shown overwrites the member list.)

q: Which command will force user 'tom' to choose a new password at his next login?
options: passwd -l tom
usermod -e 0 tom
chage -d 0 tom (or passwd -e tom)
chage -M 0 tom
explain: Setting the last-change day to 0 marks the password as expired-on-arrival, so the next login must set a new one. -M 0 would make the password expire every day forever, -l locks the account, and -e on usermod sets the ACCOUNT expiry date, not password aging.

q: Which command will delete the account of a departed employee INCLUDING her home directory and mail spool?
options: userdel -f --home maria
userdel -r maria
rmuser -r maria
userdel maria
explain: userdel -r removes the home directory and mail spool along with the account; plain userdel leaves them behind. The other spellings are not userdel forms on RHEL.

q: Which command will create a system account 'svcmon' with no login shell and no home directory?
options: useradd -r -s /bin/bash -m svcmon
useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin -M svcmon
groupadd -r svcmon
useradd --system svcmon (defaults give it /bin/bash and a home)
explain: -r allocates a system-range UID, /sbin/nologin blocks interactive logins, and -M suppresses home creation. useradd --system is the long form of -r but on its own still pairs with default shell/home behavior unless the other flags are given; the bash/-m variant is a normal interactive account.

q: Which command will see the default values useradd will use (shell, home base, skel) before creating accounts?
options: cat /etc/passwd | head
useradd -D (and /etc/login.defs for UID ranges and aging defaults)
systemctl cat useradd
useradd --show-defaults is not needed; defaults are in /etc/shadow
explain: useradd -D prints the compiled/file defaults from /etc/default/useradd; aging and UID boundaries live in /etc/login.defs. Shadow holds per-account data, not creation defaults.

q: Which command will grant user 'priya' full sudo rights in the conventional RHEL way, assuming the stock sudoers wheel rule is active?
options: echo 'priya ALL=(ALL) ALL' >> /etc/sudoers with a plain editor as the routine method
usermod -aG wheel priya
chmod u+s /usr/bin/sudo for priya's session
Add priya to the sudo group (the RHEL convention)
explain: On RHEL the wheel group is the sudo-enabled group in the stock sudoers, so membership is the clean grant. 'sudo' is the Debian-era group name, appending to sudoers with an editor bypasses visudo's syntax checking (a dedicated sudoers.d drop-in via visudo is the managed alternative), and setuid games are not administration.

q: Which command will check WHY the account 'oldacct' cannot log in even with the right password: faillock shows a tally of recent failures?
options: Delete /etc/shadow's oldacct line to reset the tally
The account's shell was changed to /bin/false by faillock
The password expired in 1970; run chage -d 0
The account is locked by pam_faillock after repeated failures; clear it with faillock --user oldacct --reset
explain: faillock tracks failed authentication attempts and locks accounts per policy; the faillock tool's --reset clears the tally. It is separate from password aging (chage) and account locking, and hand-editing /etc/shadow is never the fix.

q: A sudoers line reads: %devs ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart httpd. What does it grant?
options: devs may run any systemctl command without a password
Members of the devs group may run exactly that systemctl restart command as any user, without a password prompt
The devs group owns the httpd service account
All users may restart httpd without a password
explain: The leading % marks a GROUP rule. NOPASSWD applies to the listed command only — the full path and arguments as written; other systemctl verbs are not covered, and the rule is about privilege, not ownership.

q: Why must sudoers changes be made with visudo (or visudo-checked drop-ins) instead of a quick echo >> /etc/sudoers?
options: sudoers is regenerated from visudo's cache at boot, discarding editor changes
visudo encrypts the file; plain edits are stored unencrypted and ignored
visudo validates sudoers syntax before saving; a malformed sudoers can lock out ALL sudo elevation, including root's recovery path via sudo
There is no real reason; it is only a style convention
explain: sudo parses /etc/sudoers on every invocation and fails closed on syntax errors — one bad line can break sudo system-wide. visudo locks the file and refuses to save invalid syntax. Nothing is encrypted or regenerated.

q: Where should a NEW sudo rule for one application team live so package updates and audits stay clean?
options: Appended to /etc/passwd's sudo section
Only ever in /etc/sudoers itself; sudoers.d is ignored by sudo on RHEL
In its own file under /etc/sudoers.d/ (mode 0440, edited/checked with visudo -f)
In /etc/sudo.conf, which sudo reads first
explain: sudo reads /etc/sudoers.d drop-ins (via the includedir directive in the main file), which is the managed way to add rules. The file should be root-owned and not group/world-writable.

q: An /etc/login.defs file contains: PASS_MAX_DAYS 60; PASS_MIN_DAYS 1; PASS_WARN_AGE 7. A new user is created with useradd and no aging options. What aging applies?
options: The values apply only to root
No aging applies until an admin runs chage on the account
The numbers are in hours, so the password lasts 60 hours
Passwords may be used at most 60 days, must be kept at least 1 day before changing again, and expiry warnings begin 7 days ahead — these are the defaults written into the new account's shadow entry
explain: login.defs supplies the defaults copied into /etc/shadow at account creation: PASS_MAX_DAYS (maximum validity), PASS_MIN_DAYS (minimum between changes), PASS_WARN_AGE (warning window) — all in DAYS, for ordinary users too. Existing accounts are not retro-edited by changing login.defs.

q: /etc/login.defs defines UID_MIN 1000 and SYS_UID_MAX 999. What do these two values together guarantee?
options: Root's UID can be reassigned up to 999
Groups use the same fields with GID_MIN ignored
Regular user accounts start at UID 1000, and system accounts created with useradd -r are allocated below 1000
All UIDs above 999 are system accounts
explain: UID_MIN is the floor for normal accounts and the system range tops out just below it (SYS_UID_MAX 999), which is how scripts and admins tell service accounts from people at a glance.

q: An /etc/shadow line reads: carol:$6$rounds=5000$saltsalt$hash...:19800:0:90:7:14:: What does the trailing ':14:' field (inactive) do?
options: The account is deleted 14 days after creation
The password must contain 14 characters
Carol may change her password 14 times per day
After the password expires, carol gets 14 more days during which she can still log in and change it; after that the account is locked by aging
explain: Shadow fields run: last-change, min-days, max-days, warn, INACTIVE (grace days after password expiry), account-expire, reserved. The inactive value is the post-expiry grace period before the account becomes unusable.

q: An /etc/shadow password field shows '!!' for a freshly created account, and another account shows '*'. What is the difference?
options: '!!' marks a system account and '*' marks a regular user
'*' means the password is expired and must be changed at login
They are identical spellings of 'locked'

'!!' means no password has ever been set (locked, unusable for password login); '*' means password login is impossible for that field but the account may still authenticate by other means (e.g. SSH keys), a common state for service accounts
explain: A bare '!' locks the password hash; the doubled '!!' is useradd's untouched-account marker. '*' is a deliberately impossible hash value that blocks password authentication while keeping the account otherwise functional.

q: Which chage option sets the number of days AFTER password expiry during which the user may still log in and change it (the inactive period)?
options: chage -m <days> <user>
chage -E <days> <user>
chage -W <days> <user>
chage -I <days> <user>
explain: -I is inactive days (grace after expiry). -W is the warning period BEFORE expiry, -E is the absolute account expiration date, and -m is the minimum days between changes.

q: Which chage option sets an absolute date after which the ACCOUNT (not just the password) can no longer be used?
options: chage -I 30 <user>
chage -M 365 <user>
chage -E 2026-12-31 <user>
chage -d 0 <user>
explain: -E sets account expiration (a date or days since epoch) — the account stops working entirely. -M is password lifetime, -d 0 forces a password change at next login, and -I is the post-expiry grace window.

q: A contractor's account must stop working on 2027-01-15 no matter what, while his password should follow normal 90-day aging until then. Which pair of settings achieves this?
options: userdel --expire 2027-01-15 (a scheduled deletion)
chage -M 90 and chage -d 2027 for the account
chage -E 2027-01-15 for the account expiry, leaving -M 90 password aging untouched
Set the login shell to /sbin/nologin today
explain: Account expiration (-E) and password aging (-M/-m/-W) are independent controls. Nologin today would block the contractor immediately, and userdel has no scheduled-expire option.

q: On RHEL, an admin runs passwd -l dave to 'lock' the account, but dave can still log in with his SSH key. Why, and what is the stronger lock?
options: SSH keys bypass all account controls by design and cannot be blocked
The lock applies at the next reboot only
passwd -l is broken on RHEL 10 and must be reported
passwd -l only locks PASSWORD authentication (it prefixes the hash with !); key-based SSH still works. usermod -L plus expiring the account (chage -E 0) or a nologin shell is the robust block
explain: Password locking affects the password credential specifically; sshd can still authenticate by key (and sshd's handling varies with UsePAM). A complete lockout combines password lock, account expiry, and/or a non-login shell.

q: Which command expires a user's password immediately (forcing a change at next login) using the passwd tool itself?
options: passwd -e <user>
passwd --force-change <user>
passwd -l <user>
passwd -x <user>
explain: passwd -e expires the password now (equivalent to chage -d 0). -x is not the expire flag on RHEL's passwd, -l locks the password, and --force-change is invented.

q: A new hire's home directory is missing the standard .bashrc and profile files that other accounts have. What was skipped at creation?
options: The files are generated at first GUI login only
They live in /usr/share/skel on RHEL 10 and need a package install
The files come from /etc/skel, copied when the home is created with useradd -m; the account was probably created without -m or the home was made by hand
They are copied from /etc/profile.d by sshd at login
explain: /etc/skel is the skeleton directory whose contents seed every new home directory created with -m. Without -m (or with a manually created directory), the seed files never land.

q: Which file controls the default shell, home-directory base, and mail spool behavior that useradd uses when options are omitted?
options: /usr/lib/useradd/defaults
/etc/default/useradd
/etc/useradd.conf
/etc/passwd.defaults
explain: useradd -D reads and edits /etc/default/useradd (SHELL, HOME, INACTIVE, EXPIRE, SKEL defaults). The other paths are invented; per-account results land in /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow.

q: An admin needs every FUTURE account to be created with /bin/zsh by default. What is the persistent change?
options: Edit each new account with usermod -s after creation; defaults cannot change
useradd -D -s /bin/zsh (writes SHELL=/bin/zsh in /etc/default/useradd)
Change root's own shell with chsh and useradd inherits it
Set DEFAULT_SHELL in /etc/environment
explain: useradd -D edits the stored defaults, including the default shell, affecting later account creation. There is no DEFAULT_SHELL mechanism in /etc/environment for useradd.

q: An /etc/group line reads: devs:x:1005:alice,bob,carol. bob leaves the team. Which command removes ONLY bob from devs?
options: usermod -G '' bob (removes him from groups)
gpasswd -d bob devs
groupmod -d bob devs
gpasswd -r bob devs
explain: gpasswd -d removes a single member from a group. usermod -G '' would strip ALL of bob's supplementary groups, and the other two spellings are not how gpasswd/groupmod express member removal (-r with groupmod is a rename option in some tools, not member removal).

q: What does the fourth field of an /etc/group line (the comma-separated list) represent — and what does it NOT contain?
options: It lists users whose home directories live in the group directory
It lists every member including primary members
It lists the users for whom this group is a SUPPLEMENTARY group; users whose PRIMARY group it is are not listed there (their primary GID is in /etc/passwd)
It lists the group's sudo-capable users
explain: Group membership has two channels: primary (the GID field in each user's passwd entry) and supplementary (the member list in /etc/group). Tools like id merge both; the /etc/group list alone under-reports membership.

q: A user runs groups and sees 'devs' listed, but a process they start creates files with group 'users'. Why?
options: Their PRIMARY group is users (from /etc/passwd); devs is only supplementary and becomes the effective group for new files only after newgrp devs (or a fresh login with sg)
groups output is cached and wrong until reboot
The sticky bit on their home directory forces the users group
Supplementary groups never affect file creation at all
explain: New files take the process's EFFECTIVE GID, which starts as the primary group at login. Supplementary groups grant ACCESS rights but do not set the creating group until the user switches with newgrp/sg.

q: Which command switches the current shell's effective group to 'devs' (for a member) so new files are group-owned by devs?
options: chgrp -s devs
sgstart devs
usermod -g devs $USER --now
newgrp devs
explain: newgrp starts a shell with the chosen group as the effective GID (sg devs -c 'cmd' runs one command that way). chgrp changes existing files' ownership, and usermod -g permanently changes the primary group, taking effect at next login, not this shell.

q: passwd -S alice prints: alice PS 2026-03-01 0 90 7 -1. What does PS mean, and what does the trailing -1 mean?
options: PS = protected system account; -1 means the account never expires
PS = password suspended; -1 is her failed-login count
PS = password same-as-username warning; -1 disables the warning
PS = a usable password is set; the fields after the date are min/max/warn aging, and -1 for inactive means no post-expiry inactivity lock is set
explain: passwd -S status codes: PS password set, LK locked, NP no password. The numeric tail mirrors shadow aging fields; an inactive value of -1 disables that control.

q: A user wants to change THEIR OWN login shell to /bin/zsh, which is installed and listed in /etc/shells. Which command does it without root?
options: Edit their own line in /etc/passwd with a text editor
usermod -s /bin/zsh $USER (works unprivileged)
Add SHELL=/bin/zsh to ~/.bashrc
chsh -s /bin/zsh (the user authenticates and the shell must be listed in /etc/shells)
explain: chsh is the self-service tool and validates against /etc/shells. usermod needs root, /etc/passwd is not user-writable, and a .bashrc variable does not change the LOGIN shell the system launches.

q: An admin creates a user with useradd -N svc2. What does -N change?
options: The home directory is created under /nonexistent
The account gets no password field in shadow
The account is created without a UID
No user group is created: svc2 does NOT get a private group of the same name; the primary group falls back to the default group (users, GID 100)
explain: By default useradd creates a same-named private group (USERGROUPS_ENAB). -N suppresses it, leaving the account in the system default group — a meaningful difference for shared-service accounts.

q: After an admin edits /etc/skel/.bashrc to add a company banner alias, existing users report nothing changed. Why, and what is the correct expectation?
options: skel files apply only when the user next changes a password
Existing users must run useradd --refresh-skel
/etc/skel only seeds homes at CREATION time; existing homes already hold their own copies and are never re-synced
The banner needs a reboot to propagate
explain: Skel is a template copied once. Retro-fitting changes to live accounts means editing their files (or using config management). No refresh command or reboot propagates skel changes.

q: lastlog shows 'Never logged in' for a service account that definitely authenticates via SSH keys daily. Which tool gives the real recent-login picture, and why the discrepancy?
options: faillock --user shows successful logins
who -a reads lastlog and would show the sessions
last (from wtmp) and the journal/auth logs: lastlog only records INTERACTIVE password-style logins tracked by pam_lastlog, and key-based or session types may not register there
lastlog is authoritative; the account truly never authenticates
explain: lastlog's coverage depends on PAM session hooks and login types; wtmp via last, plus sshd journal entries, are the fuller evidence. faillock tracks FAILURES for lockout, not successes.

q: Which command shows the sudo privileges a specific user 'nadia' effectively has, as the admin (root)?
options: id nadia (groups imply the rights)
sudo -l -U nadia
grep nadia /etc/sudoers (complete because all rules are there)
visudo --list nadia
explain: sudo -l -U <user> evaluates the full sudoers policy (main file plus sudoers.d drop-ins and group rules) for that user. Grep of one file misses drop-ins and group-derived rights; id shows memberships, not policy.

q: faillock --user bob shows several failures from yesterday but bob logged in fine this morning. What reset the tally?
options: A successful authentication resets the failure tally (and the admin tool faillock --user bob --reset can clear it manually)
The tally never resets until an admin clears it
Tallies reset only at midnight by cron
Logging in from a new IP address clears it
explain: pam_faillock counts CONSECUTIVE failures within its window; a success clears the count. Manual clearing uses the faillock utility, and there is no midnight cron involved.

q: An account 'temp01' was created for a one-day task last month and never removed. Which audit command pair quickly lists such interactive-capable accounts?
options: useradd -D lists all created accounts
ls /home proves which accounts are real
grep -E '/bin/(ba)?sh' /etc/passwd to find login-shell accounts, cross-checked with lastlog for usage
rpm -qa lists locally created users
explain: Login shells in /etc/passwd mark interactive capability (system accounts carry nologin/false shells), and lastlog shows whether they were ever used. /home contents are not an account registry.

q: Which TWO changes make a departing admin's account unusable for login while PRESERVING the account and its files for audit? (Choose two.)
options: passwd -d (delete the password), which blocks all logins
usermod -L (lock the password) combined with setting the shell to /sbin/nologin
chage -E 0 (expire the account immediately)
userdel -r, which preserves files by moving them to /var/audit
explain: Locking the password plus a nologin shell (or an immediate account expiry) blocks password, key, and interactive paths while leaving the UID, home, and files intact for forensics. userdel -r DESTROYS the home, and passwd -d can leave the account passwordless-login-able — the opposite of a lockout.

q: Which command creates user martin with UID 1050, primary group developers, and a comment of Build Engineer?
options: useradd -u 1050 -g developers -c "Build Engineer" martin
groupadd -u 1050 -g developers martin
usermod -u 1050 -g developers -c "Build Engineer" martin
useradd -u developers -g 1050 -c martin "Build Engineer"
explain: useradd creates the account, with -u for UID, -g for the primary group which must already exist, and -c for the GECOS comment. Swapping the UID and group values breaks the syntax meaning, groupadd creates groups not users, and usermod modifies an existing account rather than creating one.

q: On RHEL 10, which UID range is used for regular human users created without an explicit UID, per /etc/login.defs?
options: 1000 and above, as set by UID_MIN
500 through 999 only
Any UID including 0
1 through 99 only
explain: login.defs sets UID_MIN to 1000 on RHEL, so regular users start at 1000 while system accounts use lower ranges below 1000. The low ranges are for system and reserved accounts, and UID 0 is root only, never a normal assignment.

q: Which command creates a system account named svcbackup with no login shell and no home directory creation beyond defaults for service use?
options: useradd -m -s /bin/bash svcbackup
groupadd -r svcbackup
useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin svcbackup
useradd -r -s /bin/bash -M svcbackup extra
explain: The -r flag creates a system account with a low UID and -s /sbin/nologin prevents interactive login, the standard service pattern. A bash shell with a home directory describes a human account, combining contradictory expectations, and groupadd does not create a user at all.

q: An admin wants new user priya to have home directory /data/priya instead of /home/priya, created automatically. Which command does this?
options: useradd -m -d /data/priya priya
useradd -d /home/priya -h /data/priya priya
usermod -d /data/priya priya before the account exists
useradd -M -d /data/priya priya
explain: useradd -d sets the home path and -m ensures it is created and populated from /etc/skel. The -M flag explicitly suppresses home creation, -h is not a useradd home option, and usermod cannot modify an account that has not been created yet.

q: What is the purpose of the files in /etc/skel on RHEL 10?
options: They are copied into a newly created user home directory when it is created with home creation enabled
They store password hashes for all new users
They define the default sudo policy for new users
They list groups that every new user automatically joins
explain: The skeleton directory holds default dotfiles and directories copied into new homes at creation. Password hashes live in /etc/shadow, sudo policy lives in sudoers files, and default group membership is governed by useradd defaults and explicit group options, not by skel contents.

q: Which file controls system-wide defaults such as PASS_MAX_DAYS, PASS_MIN_DAYS and PASS_WARN_AGE applied to new accounts?
options: /etc/login.defs
/etc/skel/login.defs
/etc/passwd
/etc/default/useradd only for aging values
explain: Password aging defaults and UID ranges are defined in /etc/login.defs. The /etc/default/useradd file holds defaults like HOME, SHELL and INACTIVE handling for useradd, skel holds home templates, and /etc/passwd stores account records, not policy defaults.

q: An admin runs usermod -G qa tomas to add a group, and tomas loses his existing release group. Which command should have been used and why?
options: usermod -G qa -replace tomas, because -replace preserves old groups
gpasswd -M qa tomas, because -M appends a single member
useradd -G qa tomas, because useradd edits existing users
usermod -aG qa tomas, because -a appends to supplementary groups instead of replacing the whole list
explain: Without -a, usermod -G replaces the entire supplementary group list; -aG appends the new group while keeping existing ones. There is no -replace flag for this, useradd creates rather than edits accounts in this context, and gpasswd -M sets the full member list, which would also drop others if only one name is given.

q: Which command safely moves user elena home from /home/elena to /srv/elena including moving the files?
options: useradd -d /srv/elena -m elena
mv /home/elena /srv/elena with no account change needed
usermod -d /srv/elena elena and then the files move automatically later
usermod -d /srv/elena -m elena
explain: usermod -d changes the home directory field and -m moves the contents to the new location in one operation. Without -m the record changes but files stay behind, useradd would try to create a duplicate account, and a plain mv leaves the passwd entry pointing at the old path.

q: An account must be renamed from oldlogin kfern to new login kfernandez without changing UID or home contents location initially. Which command renames the login?
options: usermod -l kfernandez kfern
passwd -l kfernandez
useradd -l kfernandez kfern
usermod -n kfernandez kfern
explain: usermod -l changes the login name while keeping UID and other attributes. The -n flag is not the rename option for usermod, useradd creates accounts, and passwd -l locks a password rather than renaming any account.

q: Which command deletes user nadia and also removes her home directory and mail spool?
options: userdel -f nadia keeps home and spool
userdel -r nadia
usermod -r nadia
userdel nadia
explain: userdel -r removes the account together with the home directory and mail spool. Plain userdel leaves those files behind, -f forces removal even when logged in but is not the home-removal flag by itself, and usermod has no account-deletion function.

q: Which sequence creates group analytics and adds existing user omar as a member without affecting his other groups?
options: groupadd analytics followed by usermod -G analytics omar
useradd analytics followed by groupadd omar analytics
gpasswd -M omar analytics before creating the group
groupadd analytics followed by gpasswd -a omar analytics or usermod -aG analytics omar
explain: Creating the group first, then appending membership with gpasswd -a or usermod -aG preserves other memberships. Using usermod -G without -a replaces the supplementary list, the reversed useradd/groupadd sequence mixes up object types, and setting members before the group exists cannot work.

q: Output of id for user sana reads: uid=1042(sana) gid=1042(sana) groups=1042(sana),1050(docker),1060(ops). What is her primary group and what are supplementary groups?
options: Her UID is 1050 and primary group is docker
Primary groups are docker and ops; sana is a supplementary group only
She has no primary group because groups are listed together
Primary group is sana; supplementary groups are docker and ops, with sana also listed in groups output
explain: In id output gid= names the primary group, here sana with GID 1042 matching her UID-named group, while the groups list includes the primary plus supplementary docker and ops. The UID is 1042, not 1050, which is a group ID for docker.

q: A user needs to work as a member of group reports immediately in a new shell without logging out entirely. Which command switches the effective primary group for that session if the user is a member?
options: usermod -g reports self permanently
newgrp reports
passwd reports
sudo groupadd reports
explain: newgrp changes the effective group ID for the current shell session to a group the user belongs to. Permanently changing primary group with usermod is a different administrative action, groupadd creates groups, and passwd changes passwords, not group context.

q: On RHEL, which method sets user ivan password non-interactively from a script using standard input?
options: passwd ivan --file newpass.txt
useradd --stdin ivan
echo "newpass" | passwd --stdin ivan, or chpasswd with user:password lines
echo ivan:newpass > /etc/shadow directly
explain: RHEL supports passwd --stdin to read a password from a pipe, and chpasswd reads user:password pairs for batch updates. There is no passwd --file mode or useradd --stdin password mode for this, and writing hashes or plaintext directly into shadow bypasses proper hashing and locking.

q: What does passwd -l do to an account, and what is an important nuance about alternative login methods?
options: It unlocks a previously expired password without changing it
It forces a password change at next login only
It locks the password by prefixing the shadow entry, but key-based SSH login may still be possible unless the account itself is handled separately
It deletes the account and its home directory immediately
explain: passwd -l disables password authentication by locking the hash; it does not delete the account and does not by itself block public-key SSH access. Forcing change is done with chage or passwd -e style aging, and unlocking is passwd -u, the opposite operation.

q: Which chage command sets user renata maximum password age 60 days, minimum age 7 days, warning 10 days, and account expiration on 2027-03-01?
options: chage -M 7 -m 60 -W 2027-03-01 -E 10 renata
usermod -M 60 -E 2027-03-01 renata
passwd -M 60 -m 7 -W 10 renata
chage -M 60 -m 7 -W 10 -E 2027-03-01 renata
explain: In chage, -M is maximum days, -m minimum days, -W warning days and -E account expiry date, matching the stated values. Swapping -M and -m reverses the policy, and neither passwd nor usermod uses this full chage flag set for aging.

q: Running chage -d 0 farid has what effect at farid next login?
options: His password is deleted and no password is required
His account is locked permanently until root unlocks it
He is forced to change his password immediately at next login
His password will never expire afterwards
explain: Setting the last-change day to 0 marks the password as aged out, so the system forces a change on next login. It does not delete the password, lock the account outright, or disable future aging; those are different operations such as passwd -d, usermod -L or chage -M -1 style settings.

q: chage -l output for user greta shows: Last password change: Sep 10, 2026; Password expires: Dec 09, 2026; Password inactive: never; Account expires: never; Maximum number of days between password change: 90. When was the password last changed relative to expiry and is it consistent?
options: Last change Sep 10 plus 90 days gives Nov 09, so expiry is inconsistent
Last change Sep 10 plus 90 days gives Dec 09 expiry, so the listing is consistent
Maximum days is ignored, so expiry should be Sep 10 itself
Account expires never contradicts a password expiry date
explain: Counting 90 days from Sep 10 lands on Dec 09, matching the shown password expiry, and password expiry is separate from account expiry, which can remain never. The November date miscounts the interval, and the maximum-days field is exactly what drives password expiry calculation.

q: Which file and tool should be used to edit sudo policy safely so a syntax error does not lock out sudo?
options: visudo, which validates syntax before saving /etc/sudoers or files in /etc/sudoers.d
Any text editor directly on /etc/shadow, which visudo also checks
nmcli, which validates sudoers on save
chmod 777 /etc/sudoers then edit with echo
explain: visudo edits sudoers with locking and syntax checking, preventing a broken file from disabling sudo. Editing shadow is unrelated to sudo policy, nmcli manages networking, and loosening sudoers permissions is itself a security failure that sudo will reject.

q: A sudoers line reads: %qa-team  ALL=(ALL)  NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart reporting. What does it grant?
options: User qa-team may run any command without a password
Members of qa-team may edit any file without a password
Members of group qa-team may run only that systemctl restart command via sudo without entering a password, as any runas user
Host qa-team may log in without a password from any machine
explain: In sudoers, a leading percent denotes a group, the host field is ALL, runas is (ALL), NOPASSWD removes the password prompt, and the command list restricts privilege to the single systemctl restart command shown. It is not a single user, not unrestricted, and not about login or file editing.

q: Where is the preferred place to add a local sudo rule for one application team without editing the main packaged file directly?
options: A new file in /etc/sudoers.d edited with visudo -f, included by the main sudoers configuration
The /etc/group file with NOPASSWD appended to the group line
A new line appended to /etc/passwd for the team lead
A file in /etc/skel named sudoers.local
explain: Drop-in files in /etc/sudoers.d are the standard modular location and should be edited via visudo -f for validation. Passwd, skel and group files do not define sudo policy, and appending sudo keywords there has no effect.

q: A locked account shows an exclamation mark at the start of its field in /etc/shadow. A user with a valid SSH key still connects. Which additional step fully prevents account use for a departure case, combined with locking?
options: Expire the account with usermod --expiredate 1 or chage -E 0 and terminate sessions, in addition to password locking
Only run passwd -l again a second time
Change the user shell comment with usermod -c
Add the user to the wheel group
explain: Password locking alone does not block key-based access; expiring the account prevents login by any method and sessions should be ended. Re-locking changes nothing new, a comment edit is cosmetic, and adding wheel would increase privilege, the opposite of offboarding.

q: An admin needs to see when user hugo last logged in and whether he has ever logged in since account creation. Which command reports this from the lastlog database?
options: lastlog -u hugo
last -f /etc/passwd hugo
chage -l hugo shows login sessions
id hugo shows last login time
explain: lastlog reports the most recent login per user and explicitly notes users who never logged in. The last command reads wtmp session history rather than the lastlog summary in that form, chage reports password aging, and id reports IDs and groups.

q: Which command lists currently and recently logged-in session history with user, terminal and login time from wtmp?
options: lastlog -a all sessions
groups
faillock --reset
last
explain: The last command parses wtmp to show session history with times and terminals. lastlog summarizes only the latest login per user, groups shows group membership, and faillock manages failed authentication tallies, not session history.

q: After several failed SSH password attempts, user mateo is blocked even with the correct password. Which tool inspects and can reset the tally on RHEL 10?
options: lastlog to view and userdel to clear
faillock, using faillock --user mateo to view and faillock --user mateo --reset to clear
chage -l mateo to view and passwd -d to clear
visudo to view and nmcli to clear
explain: pam_faillock tracks failed attempts and the faillock utility displays and resets them per user. chage handles aging, lastlog handles login times, and neither visudo nor nmcli manage authentication failure tallies.

q: Which useradd default value source determines whether a home directory is created and the default shell for new users when no flags override them?
options: /etc/hosts
/home directory listing itself
/etc/default/useradd together with /etc/login.defs CREATE_HOME related policy defaults on the system
/etc/sudoers.d defaults
explain: useradd reads its defaults from /etc/default/useradd for shell, home base and related settings, with login.defs supplying system policy such as home creation behavior. Hosts and sudoers files govern resolution and privilege, and the contents of /home do not configure future account creation.

q: An admin creates user test99 without -m on a RHEL system where home creation is not automatic in that invocation, then the user cannot get a home on login. Which flag was missing and what does it do? (Choose two.)
options: -r, which forces creation of a regular user home at /home
-m, which forces creation of the home directory
Population of the home from /etc/skel occurs when the home is created
-L, which creates and locks a home directory
explain: The -m flag forces home creation even when defaults would not create it, and created homes receive skeleton files from /etc/skel. The -r flag makes system accounts with low UIDs, and -L is not a useradd home flag; it is associated with locking in usermod context.

q: Which command changes user kwame login shell to /bin/bash and verifies shell choices are listed in /etc/shells consideration?
options: usermod -s /bin/bash kwame
usermod -s kwame /bin/bash
chage -s /bin/bash kwame
useradd -s /bin/bash kwame for an existing user
explain: usermod -s sets the login shell for an existing account, with the user name as the final argument. Reversing the arguments misplaces the values, useradd would attempt creation, and chage manages password aging, not shells.

q: A service account needs an expiration date set at creation so it stops working after a project ends on 2026-12-31. Which useradd flag sets account expiry?
options: useradd -E 2026-12-31 svcproject in lowercase form only
useradd -e 2026-12-31 svcproject
useradd -f 2026-12-31 svcproject
useradd -M 2026-12-31 svcproject
explain: useradd -e sets the account expiration date in YYYY-MM-DD form. The -f flag sets days after password expiry before the account is disabled, not a calendar date, uppercase -E is not the useradd expiry flag in this form, and -M suppresses home creation.

q: The -f option in useradd or chage context for password inactivity refers to what?
options: The frequency of password warnings in weeks
The number of days after a password expires before the account is disabled as inactive
The forced home directory path
The number of failed logins before faillock engages
explain: The inactive period counts days after password expiry until the account is disabled; in chage it is -I and in useradd defaults it is -f for new accounts. It is not a faillock threshold, a path, or a warning frequency, which are handled by PAM, -d and -W respectively.

q: Which groupmod command renames group olddevs to platform and changes its GID to 2090?
options: usermod -n platform -g 2090 olddevs
groupmod -n platform -g 2090 olddevs
gpasswd -n platform -g 2090 olddevs
groupmod -l platform -g 2090 olddevs
explain: groupmod uses -n for the new group name and -g for the new GID, with the existing group as the final argument. The -l rename flag belongs to usermod for users, gpasswd manages members and passwords, and usermod operates on user accounts, not group definitions.

q: An admin runs gpasswd -d lena qa. What happens?
options: lena is removed from group qa, leaving her other memberships untouched
lena account is deleted from the system
qa is removed from the list of primary groups for all users automatically
Group qa is deleted entirely
explain: gpasswd -d removes a single named user from a named group. It does not delete the group, which is groupdel, does not delete the user account, which is userdel, and does not rewrite primary group assignments for other users.
