q: Which gpasswd option sets the complete member list of group design to exactly users ana and boris, replacing previous members?
options: gpasswd -d ana,boris design sets the list
gpasswd -M ana,boris design
groupadd -M ana,boris design
gpasswd -a ana,boris design appends without replacing
explain: gpasswd -M defines the full membership list, so anyone not listed is removed. Using -a adds one user without replacement and -d removes a user, while groupadd has no member-list flag for an existing group in that form.

q: A user primary group is changed with usermod -g research for user dario. What must be considered about files he created earlier?
options: All his old files automatically change to research group instantly
Files previously created retain their old group ownership unless changed separately; the primary group change affects new files and his gid field
His UID changes to match the research GID
His supplementary groups are cleared by any -g change
explain: Changing primary group updates the account gid and the group of newly created files, but existing file group ownership stays until chgrp is run. It does not clear supplementary groups, that is the -G list, and UID and GID remain independent numbers.

q: Which two statements about primary versus supplementary groups are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A user has exactly one primary group recorded in /etc/passwd at a time
Supplementary groups replace the need for any primary group
A user can have several primary groups simultaneously in passwd
Supplementary groups are recorded in /etc/group member lists and grant additional access
explain: Each account has a single primary group stored as the GID in its passwd entry, while supplementary memberships are listed in /etc/group and add access. Multiple primaries at once is not how the model works, and a primary group is mandatory even when supplementary groups exist.

q: An expired password, as opposed to a locked account, produces what behavior at login?
options: The user authenticates with the old password and is then forced to change it before proceeding
Only SSH key login is allowed until expiry is extended
The user can never authenticate at all, even with the correct old password, until root resets it manually in all cases
The account is deleted after the first expired login attempt
explain: When a password is expired but the account is not locked or expired, the system allows authentication with the current password and forces an immediate change. A locked account blocks password authentication outright, expiry does not delete accounts, and key login rules depend on account expiry and locking, not password expiry alone.

q: Which command unlocks user selma password after it was locked with passwd -l, restoring password login?
options: chage -d 0 selma, which unlocks the hash
passwd -d selma, which sets a passwordless account as the unlock method
passwd -u selma or usermod -U selma
userdel -u selma
explain: Unlocking is passwd -u or usermod -U, removing the lock prefix if a valid hash remains. Deleting the password with -d would leave the account passwordless rather than restored, chage -d 0 forces a password change, and userdel removes accounts.

q: What risk does editing /etc/sudoers directly with a plain editor and introducing a typo create, and how is it mitigated?
options: There is no risk because sudo ignores syntax errors silently
The only risk is the file color scheme changing; visudo merely adds highlighting
A syntax error can break sudo for all users including admins; using visudo validates syntax and warns before saving a broken file
A typo deletes /etc/passwd automatically; visudo backs it up to skel
explain: Sudo parses the entire policy strictly, so one malformed line can deny sudo broadly; visudo checks syntax on save and refuses or warns on errors. The risk is operational lockout, not cosmetics or passwd deletion, and sudo does not silently ignore malformed policy.

q: A sudoers entry reads: fatima  web01=(root)  /usr/bin/dnf update. Which fields are correctly identified?
options: User fatima, host web01, run as root, command /usr/bin/dnf update
User web01, host fatima, run as dnf, command root
Group fatima, host root, run as web01, command update only without dnf
Host fatima, user root, run as web01, command /usr/bin/dnf
explain: Sudoers order is who, where, as whom, what: fatima is the user, web01 the host, (root) the runas user, and the full path command is dnf update. The percent sign for groups is absent, and reversing the fields misreads the policy entirely.

q: Which command sets a password for multiple existing users at once from lines in the form user:password in a file named creds.txt?
options: chage --file creds.txt
useradd -f creds.txt
chpasswd < creds.txt
passwd --batch creds.txt
explain: chpasswd reads colon-separated user and password pairs from standard input and updates each account with proper hashing. passwd has no such batch-file mode for multiple users, and useradd or chage do not consume credential pair files for password setting.

q: An admin wants user accounts created from now on to default to shell /bin/bash and home base /home, as stored defaults. Which file is edited for useradd defaults?
options: /etc/default/useradd
/etc/passwd
/etc/skel/shell
/etc/nsswitch.conf
explain: The SHELL and HOME defaults for useradd are kept in /etc/default/useradd. The passwd file stores existing accounts, skel holds home templates without a shell config file of that name, and nsswitch governs database lookup order.

q: Output of groups for user vera reads: vera : vera docker qa. If vera creates a new file with default settings, which group owns it by default?
options: docker, the first supplementary group listed
qa, the last group listed
vera, her primary group
root, because supplementary groups override primary for files
explain: New files take the user effective primary group, which for vera is her own group vera, unless the directory has setgid or the group was switched with newgrp. Supplementary groups grant access but do not determine default file group ownership.

q: Which two actions are appropriate when granting a contractor sudo for only a specific service restart? (Choose two.)
options: Grant NOPASSWD: ALL to the contractor for convenience during the project
Add a scoped sudoers.d rule naming the exact systemctl command with visudo validation
Limit the rule to the contractor user or their group rather than granting ALL commands
Add the contractor to root group with UID 0 as a shortcut
explain: Least privilege is achieved with a validated drop-in rule scoped to the exact command and to the named user or group. Granting all commands without a password or giving UID 0 equivalence far exceeds the stated need and creates standing risk beyond the project task.

q: A system account for an application should have UID below 1000 and no password-based login path used. Which creation pattern fits?
options: useradd -r -s /sbin/nologin appdaemon
groupadd -r appdaemon alone creates the login account
useradd -r -s /bin/bash -m -d /home/appdaemon appdaemon as a human style account
useradd -u 1500 -s /bin/bash -m appdaemon
explain: System accounts use -r for a low UID and nologin shell to prevent interactive use. A UID of 1500 with bash and a home is a human account pattern, groupadd alone creates no user, and dressing a system account as a human account defeats its purpose.

q: PASS_WARN_AGE in /etc/login.defs is set to 7 and PASS_MAX_DAYS to 90 for new accounts. What does the 7 control?
options: New passwords must be at least 7 characters long
Accounts lock 7 days after creation regardless of activity
Users begin receiving password expiry warnings 7 days before the 90-day maximum is reached
Passwords may be changed only every 7 days at minimum
explain: PASS_WARN_AGE is the warning window before expiration, while the minimum change interval is PASS_MIN_DAYS and length rules come from PAM quality settings. It does not lock accounts on a fixed creation schedule.

q: An admin runs sg reports -c "id" for user sessions. What is the purpose of sg compared with newgrp?
options: sg deletes a supplementary group after running a command
sg is an alias for sudo that grants root
sg sets the permanent primary group in /etc/passwd
sg runs a single command with the named group as effective group, similar to newgrp but for one command instead of a new shell
explain: sg, like newgrp, switches effective group for a member, but executes one specified command and exits. It does not delete groups, rewrite the passwd primary group permanently, or grant root privileges.

q: Which chage listing field tells an admin the date after which a password must be changed following inactivity lockout calculations? (Choose two.)
options: Password inactive date, after which the already-expired password locks the account
Groups listing, which shows inactivity timers per group
Last password change plus minimum days, which alone determines inactivity
Account expires date, which separately controls when the whole account stops working
explain: chage distinguishes password inactive, the grace end after password expiry, from account expires, the hard stop for the whole account. Minimum days govern how soon a password may be changed again, not inactivity lockout, and group listings carry no aging timers.

q: A helpdesk tech changed user omari shell to /sbin/nologin by mistake with usermod -s. What is the observed effect and fix?
options: omari loses all group memberships; fix with userdel -r omari
omari cannot get an interactive login shell; fix with usermod -s /bin/bash omari
omari becomes root; fix with passwd -l omari
Nothing changes because shell field is a comment only
explain: The shell field is the program run at login, so nologin politely rejects interactive logins; restoring a real shell with usermod -s fixes it. It does not grant root, affect groups, or serve as a comment, which is the separate GECOS field.

q: Which two facts are shown by the command id without arguments for the current user? (Choose two.)
options: The password expiration date for the current user
The sudo policy that applies to the current user
All supplementary groups the current session user belongs to
The current user UID and primary GID with their names
explain: id reports uid, gid and the full groups list for the invoking or named user. Password aging requires chage or passwd status, and sudo policy requires sudo -l, neither of which id displays.

q: A file moved with mv into /var/www/html returns HTTP 403, while an identical file copied in fresh with cp serves fine. ls -Z shows the moved file has user_home_t. What happened and what is the durable fix?
options: mv preserves the file's original SELinux context (user_home_t), while cp creates a new inode that inherits the destination directory's default context; run restorecon -Rv /var/www/html to reapply policy contexts
The correct fix is to disable SELinux so contexts no longer matter
mv corrupts file contents during the move, so the web server rejects it
Only chcon can fix this, and its changes are permanent
explain: mv keeps the same inode and therefore its SELinux context; cp creates a new file that gets the target directory's default context (httpd_sys_content_t under /var/www/html). Apache is denied by policy from serving user_home_t files. restorecon -Rv reapplies the policy-defined contexts, and because it derives from policy, the fix survives relabels. Option C is false; contents are untouched. Option D is wrong: chcon edits only the inode and is wiped out by the next restorecon or relabel. Option B is a sledgehammer that discards mandatory access control instead of fixing a label.

q: An admin runs firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http and tests immediately, but port 80 is still blocked. What went wrong?
options: A reboot is required before any --permanent change applies
The http service definition does not ship with firewalld and must be created first
--permanent only writes the stored configuration; run firewall-cmd --reload to apply it to the running runtime configuration
--permanent changes take effect instantly, so the firewall must be broken
explain: firewalld keeps two configurations: runtime (active now) and permanent (stored on disk). --permanent edits only the stored copy; --reload rebuilds the runtime from it, which is when the port actually opens. (Alternatively, omit --permanent to change the runtime directly.) Option B is wrong: http.xml ships with firewalld. Option D states the misconception that caused the confusion. Option A is unnecessary; --reload applies it immediately.

q: SSH key authentication fails and the server log says 'Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes for /home/bob/.ssh/authorized_keys'. The directory is 755 and the file is 644. What is the fix?
options: Run chmod 700 ~/.ssh and chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, and make sure the home directory itself is not group- or world-writable (sshd's StrictModes requires this)
Restarting sshd is the only fix; permissions on key files are irrelevant
Set both to 777 so the sshd process can always read them
Mode 644 on authorized_keys is correct and secure; the error must come from elsewhere
explain: sshd's StrictModes refuses key authentication when ~/.ssh or authorized_keys are writable by others (or the home directory is group-writable), because another user could then plant keys. The secure standard is 700 on ~/.ssh, 600 on authorized_keys, and a non-writable home directory. Option D is wrong: 644 leaves the file world-readable and, combined with a writable path, triggers the refusal. Option C is the opposite of secure. Option B ignores the explicit log message naming ownership/modes.

q: chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/web/index.html fixed a 403, but the problem returned after an autorelabel. What is the durable fix?
options: chcon changes are permanent, so the relabel must have been misconfigured
Set SELinux to permissive with setenforce 0 to stop contexts from being reset
chcon accepts a -P flag that makes its changes survive relabels
Record the context in policy with semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/web(/.*)?' and then apply it with restorecon -Rv /srv/web
explain: chcon writes the context onto the inode only; any restorecon or filesystem relabel reapplies contexts from policy and wipes the chcon change. semanage fcontext adds a persistent file-context rule to the local policy store, and restorecon -Rv applies it to the existing files. Option A states the exact misconception. Option B disables enforcement, throwing away mandatory access control instead of labeling correctly. Option C confuses chcon with setsebool, whose -P flag is the persistence mechanism for booleans.

q: setsebool httpd_can_network_connect on fixed a web app's outbound connections, but the setting reverted after a reboot. How is it made persistent?
options: Run setenforce 1, which commits all pending boolean changes
Run setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on: the -P flag writes the change to the policy store; verify with getsebool httpd_can_network_connect
Edit /etc/selinux/config to make the boolean permanent
Boolean changes can never survive a reboot; a startup script must reapply them
explain: Without -P, setsebool changes only the runtime value, which is lost at reboot. The -P flag commits the boolean to the on-disk policy store so it persists. getsebool (or getsebool -a | grep httpd) confirms the current value. Option D is false; -P exists precisely for persistence. Option C confuses /etc/selinux/config, which sets the SELinux mode (enforcing/permissive/disabled), not booleans. Option A is wrong; setenforce only switches the current mode.

q: The DocumentRoot was moved to /srv/web and Apache now returns 403 for every page. Which sequence durably fixes the SELinux labeling?
options: chcon -R -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/web alone, which is permanent
Moving the files back to /var/www/html, because custom docroots are unsupported
Running semanage fcontext alone is enough; restorecon is unnecessary
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/web(/.*)?' && restorecon -Rv /srv/web
explain: Files under the new docroot lack the httpd_sys_content_t type Apache's policy allows. The semanage fcontext rule (with the (/.*)? regex covering the directory and everything beneath it) records the correct context persistently in policy, and restorecon -Rv applies it to the existing files. Option A is temporary: the next restorecon or relabel would revert it. Option B avoids the task rather than solving it; custom docroots are fully supported once labeled. Option C is half the job: semanage only records the rule, restorecon applies it to files on disk.

q: Practice scenario: in the public zone, allow TCP 5432 ONLY from 10.0.0.0/24, persistently. Which command is correct?
options: firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="10.0.0.0/24" port port="5432" protocol="tcp" accept'
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-port=5432/tcp && firewall-cmd --reload
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="10.0.0.0/24" port port="5432" protocol="tcp" accept' && firewall-cmd --reload
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="10.0.0.0/24" port port="5432" accept' && firewall-cmd --reload
explain: C is correct: a rich rule with family, source, port plus protocol, and the accept action, made --permanent and activated with --reload. A opens 5432 to the entire internet, ignoring the source restriction entirely. B omits protocol="tcp" - a rich-rule port element requires a protocol, so firewalld rejects the rule. D omits --permanent, so the rule lives only in the runtime configuration and vanishes on the next reload or reboot.

q: Practice scenario: a RHEL 10 box routes between an internal zone and the external zone. Which firewalld command enables NAT masquerading persistently on the external zone?
options: firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=external --add-masquerade && firewall-cmd --reload
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=external --add-forward-port=port=80:proto=tcp:toport=8080 && firewall-cmd --reload
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=external --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" masquerade' && firewall-cmd --reload
sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1
explain: A is correct: --add-masquerade on the outbound zone is firewalld's NAT mechanism, and firewalld enables IP forwarding for masqueraded zones. B only flips the kernel forwarding flag - without masquerade, return traffic gets no NAT and connections break. C configures port forwarding, a different feature from outbound NAT. D is invalid: masquerade is not an action that rich rules support, so firewalld errors out.

q: Practice scenario: httpd returns 403 serving files you moved from /var/www/html to /srv/web. What is the correct FIRST diagnostic step?
options: yum reinstall httpd
restorecon -Rv /srv/web
setenforce 0
sealert -a /var/log/audit/audit.log
explain: D is correct: sealert parses the AVC denials and tells you whether you are facing mislabeled files, a boolean, or a genuine policy block - diagnose before treating. A (permissive mode) merely silences SELinux and masks the root cause; it is never a fix. B might be the eventual fix for moved files, but run blindly it teaches nothing - if the denial is actually a boolean (e.g. httpd_read_user_content), restorecon changes nothing. C reinstalls the package, which cannot fix a labeling problem on your data directory.

q: Practice scenario: sshd must also listen on TCP 2222. Which SELinux command labels the new port correctly?
options: semanage port -m -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 2222
semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 2222
semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 2222
semanage fcontext -a -t ssh_port_t "/etc/ssh(/.*)?"
explain: C is correct: -a adds a NEW port record with type ssh_port_t, which is what sshd is allowed to bind. A uses -m (modify), which fails because 2222 has no existing record to modify. C labels it http_port_t - the wrong type, so sshd still gets AVC denials. D manages FILE contexts, not ports; it does nothing for a listening socket. (You would still need firewall-cmd --add-port=2222/tcp separately.)

q: Practice scenario: httpd gets 'Permission denied' reading content from an NFS mount that root can read fine. Which fix is correct?
options: setenforce 0
setsebool -P httpd_use_nfs 1
chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /mnt/web
mount -o remount,rw server:/share /mnt/web
explain: B is correct: SELinux confines httpd from NFS by default; the httpd_use_nfs boolean (persistent with -P) is the designed toggle. B disables SELinux system-wide - a sledgehammer, not a fix. C cannot work: NFS has no local xattrs to label, and the denial is not a labeling problem anyway. D changes mount read/write options, but root already reads fine - the block is the SELinux boolean, not the mount options.

q: Practice scenario: SSH key auth fails for alice. ~/.ssh is 700 and authorized_keys is 600, but her home directory is mode 775. What is the fix?
options: chmod 755 /home/alice
Add 'StrictModes no' to sshd_config
Regenerate alice's key pair
chmod 600 /home/alice/.ssh
explain: A is correct: sshd's StrictModes refuses key auth when the home directory is group-writable (775) - 755 removes group write while keeping the directory usable. A is irrelevant: the key itself is fine; the server is rejecting the path. B breaks the .ssh directory (it needs the execute bit - 700, not 600). C disables a real security check to paper over a permissions bug; fix the permissions instead.

q: Practice scenario: ssh fails with 'WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!' for ~/.ssh/id_rsa. What is the cause and fix?
options: chmod 777 ~/.ssh/id_rsa so ssh can read it
The key is readable by others - chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_rsa
The public key is missing - regenerate with ssh-keygen
The key is encrypted - remove the passphrase
explain: B is correct: ssh refuses private keys with group/other permissions (here likely 644); 600 (owner read/write only) satisfies its strict check. A misreads it: passphrase-protected keys are fine and encouraged. B is unrelated - the error is about the private key's mode, not a missing pubkey. C does the exact opposite, making the key world-readable.

q: Practice scenario: you moved a vhost document root to /srv/www and fixed ownership, but httpd still gets AVC denials. chcon fixed it yesterday, but the denials are back after a relabel. What is the durable fix?
options: chcon -R -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/www
setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs 1
setenforce 0
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/srv/www(/.*)?" && restorecon -Rv /srv/www
explain: D is correct: chcon does not survive a relabel - semanage fcontext writes the policy mapping so the label persists, and restorecon applies it. A is what already proved temporary. B is for home directories, not /srv/www. D disables SELinux instead of fixing the label.

q: Practice scenario: a firewall rule added with 'firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=http' worked until the server rebooted, then vanished. What happened, and what is the fix?
options: firewalld does not support the http service
The rule needs --add-rich-rule instead
It was runtime-only - re-add with --permanent (or run firewall-cmd --runtime-to-permanent) and --reload
firewalld must be reinstalled after every reboot
explain: C is correct: without --permanent, firewall-cmd writes only the runtime configuration, which is discarded on reload/reboot - --permanent plus --reload makes it stick (--runtime-to-permanent can salvage current runtime rules). A is false; http is a stock service definition. B is unnecessary - services are the simpler, correct tool here. C is absurd; nothing about firewalld requires reinstallation. q: You need the firewalld service to start automatically at boot. Which command enables this persistence?
options: service firewalld enable
systemctl enable firewalld
chkconfig firewalld on
systemctl start firewalld
explain: B is correct: 'systemctl enable' wires firewalld into the boot target so it starts on every boot. D is wrong because 'start' only runs it in the current session — it will not survive a reboot. C is wrong because chkconfig is the RHEL 6 SysV utility; RHEL 9/10 manage services with systemd. A is wrong because 'service' does not accept an 'enable' action — that syntax comes from mixing SysV and systemd concepts. Use 'systemctl enable --now firewalld' to both persist and start it, and confirm with 'systemctl is-enabled firewalld'.

q: You need to allow HTTPS traffic through firewalld in the public zone, permanently, and apply the change. Which sequence is correct?
options: firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=https
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-service=https && firewall-cmd --reload
iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 443 -j ACCEPT
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-port=https && firewall-cmd --reload
explain: B is correct: '--permanent' writes the change to the on-disk configuration, '--add-service=https' opens the predefined service (port 443/tcp), and '--reload' applies permanent configuration to the running firewall without dropping existing connections. A is wrong because without '--permanent' the change is runtime-only and vanishes on the next reload or reboot. D is wrong because '--add-port' requires a numeric port/protocol pair like '443/tcp' — passing the service name 'https' is a syntax error. C is wrong because hand-inserted iptables rules bypass firewalld and are wiped out the next time firewalld reloads; always manage the firewall through firewall-cmd on RHEL. Verify with 'firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-services'. Section 8 — Users & Groups

q: You must allow HTTP traffic from the 192.168.1.0/24 subnet ONLY (not the whole internet) in the public zone, permanently. Which firewall-cmd sequence is correct?
options: firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.1.0/24" port port="http" protocol="tcp" accept' && firewall-cmd --reload
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-service=http && firewall-cmd --reload
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="192.168.1.0/24" service name="http" accept' && firewall-cmd --reload
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv6" source address="192.168.1.0/24" service name="http" accept' && firewall-cmd --reload
explain: C is correct: a rich rule combines family, source address, and service into one granular allow rule; '--permanent' plus '--reload' makes it persistent and active. B is wrong because '--add-service=http' opens HTTP to every source address — it fails the 'subnet only' requirement. D is wrong because family="ipv6" does not match 192.168.1.0/24, which is an IPv4 subnet, so the rule would never match the intended traffic. A is wrong because the 'port' element requires a numeric port ('port="80"') — passing the service name 'http' there is a syntax error; the 'service name="http"' form in D is the right way to reference a service. List rich rules with 'firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-rich-rules'.

q: You want new files created by users to default to 640 and new directories to 750. Which umask value produces this?
explain: B is correct: umask subtracts from the base permissions (666 for files, 777 for directories) — 666-027=640 for files and 777-027=750 for directories. C is wrong because 022 yields the traditional defaults: 644 files and 755 directories (group and others can read). D is wrong because 077 is the most restrictive: 600 files and 700 directories, with no group access at all. A is wrong because 002 yields 664 files and 775 directories (group-writable). Set it persistently in /etc/profile, /etc/bashrc, or ~/.bashrc depending on scope, and verify a test file with 'touch testfile && stat -c %a testfile'.

q: You set up SSH key authentication for a user, but logins still prompt for a password. Which permission set on the server is required for key auth to work?
options: ~/.ssh is 755 and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys is 644
~/.ssh is 700 and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys is 600
~/.ssh is 700 and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys is 666
~/.ssh is 777 and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys is 600
explain: B is correct: sshd's StrictModes requires that ~/.ssh be accessible only by the owner (700) and authorized_keys be readable/writable only by the owner (600); it also requires correct ownership by the user. A is wrong because a world-readable authorized_keys (644) is rejected under strict modes — sshd logs 'bad ownership or modes' and falls back to password auth. D is wrong because a world-writable ~/.ssh (777) is the textbook StrictModes violation; sshd will refuse to trust anything inside it. C is wrong because a world-writable authorized_keys (666) is equally rejected. Diagnose with 'sshd -T | grep strictmodes' and the server logs, and generate keys properly with 'ssh-keygen -t ed25519' plus 'ssh-copy-id user@host'.

q: The system is currently in permissive mode, but SELinux must be in enforcing mode after every reboot. Which change makes enforcing persistent?
options: Set SELINUX=enforcing in /etc/selinux/conf
Run setenforce Enforcing
Run setenforce 1
Set SELINUX=enforcing in /etc/selinux/config (and run setenforce 1 to apply it now)
explain: D is correct: /etc/selinux/config is read at boot and determines the mode SELinux starts in, so SELINUX=enforcing there survives reboots; 'setenforce 1' applies enforcing immediately without waiting for a reboot. C is wrong because setenforce only changes the runtime mode — after a reboot the system returns to whatever /etc/selinux/config says. B is wrong for the persistence requirement too: it is just another runtime invocation of setenforce (valid syntax, but still non-persistent). A is wrong because /etc/selinux/conf is not a real file — the configuration lives at /etc/selinux/config. Confirm the running mode with 'getenforce' and the configured mode by reading the config file.

q: You placed web content in /web, but httpd is denied access by SELinux. You need the httpd_sys_content_t context applied so it survives a filesystem relabel. Which sequence is correct?
options: setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on
chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /web
chmod -R 755 /web
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/web(/.*)?" && restorecon -Rv /web
explain: D is correct and persistent: 'semanage fcontext -a' writes a file-context rule into the SELinux policy store, and 'restorecon -Rv' applies it — because the rule is in the policy store, it survives relabels and restorecon runs. The '(/.*)?' regex covers /web itself and everything beneath it. B is wrong because chcon changes only the on-disk label with no policy-store rule; the next 'restorecon' or autorelabel silently reverts it — the classic temporary fix. C is wrong because chmod changes discretionary (DAC) permissions, which are unrelated to the SELinux type-enforcement denial. A is wrong because httpd_enable_homedirs concerns home directories, not /web, and booleans never change file contexts. Verify with 'ls -Z /web' and 'semanage fcontext -l | grep /web'. Section 10 — Ansible Core Components

q: An admin needs to make sshd's new listening port 2222 acceptable to SELinux policy (the port is not yet labeled for SSH). Which action is correct?
options: semanage port -m -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 2222
setsebool -P sshd_port_2222 on
chcon -t ssh_port_t 2222
semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 2222
explain: -a ADDS a new port label; the port has no existing ssh_port_t entry, so -m (modify) would fail with 'already/does not exist' style errors in the other direction: -m is for ports that ALREADY carry a type. chcon labels files, not ports, and the boolean named does not exist.

q: An admin needs to relocate a web site to port 8080 where semanage port -l already shows 8080 labeled http_cache_port_t; Apache must bind it as an HTTP port. Which action is correct?
options: semanage port -m -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 (modify, because the port already has a type)
semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080 --force
restorecon -Rv 8080
semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8080
explain: A port can carry only one type in policy: adding a second label for 8080 is rejected, so the existing label is MODIFIED with -m. --force is not a semanage port option, and restorecon works on files.

q: An admin needs to add a durable SELinux file-context rule so /srv/web and everything under it is labeled httpd_sys_content_t, then apply it. Which action is correct?
options: semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/web (no restorecon needed)
semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/web(/.*)?' followed by restorecon -Rv /srv/web
chcon -R -t httpd_sys_content_t /srv/web (durable across relabels)
touch /.autorelabel alone after editing the files
explain: semanage fcontext writes the POLICY rule (with the (/.*)? idiom to cover contents), and restorecon applies it to the live filesystem. chcon changes only live labels and is wiped by the next relabel; semanage alone does not relabel existing files.

q: An admin needs to check the current SELinux mode and whether the boot-time configuration agrees. Which action is correct?
options: getenforce for the running mode; grep ^SELINUX= /etc/selinux/config for the configured mode
cat /sys/fs/selinux/policy
ls -Z /etc/selinux/config
sestatus --mode only
explain: getenforce reports the live mode and the config file holds the persistent setting; the two can disagree after a setenforce (runtime-only) change. sestatus shows both current and config-file modes too — as a tool — but of the choices given, the getenforce+config pair is the direct check.

q: An admin needs to let Apache connect out to a backend database, persistently, via SELinux policy. Which action is correct?
options: setsebool httpd_can_network_connect on (without -P it survives, booleans are persistent by default)
chcon -t httpd_connect_t /usr/sbin/httpd
semanage boolean --enable httpd_network
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
explain: Booleans are runtime switches in policy; -P writes the value to the policy store so it survives reboot. Without -P the change is runtime-only, and there is no file context trick for a connect permission.

q: An admin needs to A file copied with cp from /tmp into /var/www/html serves fine, but an identical file MOVED with mv from a home directory returns 403. Why?. Which action is correct?
options: mv strips the file's read permission bit; cp restores it
SELinux relabels moved files to httpd_sys_content_t only at reboot
Apache cannot serve files whose inode predates the service start
mv preserves the file's original SELinux context (user_home_t), while cp created a new file that inherited the destination's httpd context; fix with restorecon
explain: mv within/across filesystems keeps the existing context (rename semantics), so the file keeps user_home_t, which httpd cannot read under targeted policy. cp creates a NEW inode in the destination, inheriting the directory's context. restorecon applies the expected label.

q: With umask 0022, what permissions do newly created files and directories get (assuming programs request 0666 for files and 0777 for directories)?
options: files 0640 / directories 0750
files 0644 / directories 0755
files 0600 / directories 0700
files 0664 / directories 0775
explain: New permissions = requested mode ANDed with the umask's complement: files 0666 & ~0022 = 0644; directories 0777 & ~0022 = 0755. The umask only REMOVES bits — it can never add execute to a file.

q: With umask 0027, what permissions do newly created files and directories get (assuming programs request 0666 for files and 0777 for directories)?
options: files 0600 / directories 0700
files 0664 / directories 0775
files 0640 / directories 0750
files 0644 / directories 0755
explain: New permissions = requested mode ANDed with the umask's complement: files 0666 & ~0027 = 0640; directories 0777 & ~0027 = 0750. The umask only REMOVES bits — it can never add execute to a file.

q: With umask 0077, what permissions do newly created files and directories get (assuming programs request 0666 for files and 0777 for directories)?
options: files 0640 / directories 0750
files 0664 / directories 0775
files 0644 / directories 0755
files 0600 / directories 0700
explain: New permissions = requested mode ANDed with the umask's complement: files 0666 & ~0077 = 0600; directories 0777 & ~0077 = 0700. The umask only REMOVES bits — it can never add execute to a file.

q: With umask 0002, what permissions do newly created files and directories get (assuming programs request 0666 for files and 0777 for directories)?
options: files 0644 / directories 0755
files 0664 / directories 0775
files 0600 / directories 0700
files 0640 / directories 0750
explain: New permissions = requested mode ANDed with the umask's complement: files 0666 & ~0002 = 0664; directories 0777 & ~0002 = 0775. The umask only REMOVES bits — it can never add execute to a file.

q: With umask 0037, what permissions do newly created files and directories get (assuming programs request 0666 for files and 0777 for directories)?
options: files 0600 / directories 0700
files 0644 / directories 0755
files 0640 / directories 0740
files 0640 / directories 0750
explain: New permissions = requested mode ANDed with the umask's complement: files 0666 & ~0037 = 0640; directories 0777 & ~0037 = 0740. The umask only REMOVES bits — it can never add execute to a file.

q: A user complains that files they create are world-readable. Their shell shows umask 0022. They want new files to be 0640 and new directories 0750. What umask achieves exactly that?
explain: Files start from 0666: 0666 & ~0027 = 0640. Directories start from 0777: 0777 & ~0027 = 0750. 0037 would give files 0640 but directories 0740, and 0077 gives 0600/0700 — stricter than requested.

q: An admin needs to allow HTTPS permanently in the default (public) zone and make it effective immediately. Which approach is correct?
options: firewall-cmd --add-service=https (this alone survives reloads and reboots)
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https followed by firewall-cmd --reload (or use --add-service=https in both runtime and permanent config)
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=https (this alone also changes the running firewall)
firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-port=https/tcp --permanent --now
explain: firewalld keeps separate runtime and permanent configurations: --permanent edits only the stored config, so a --reload is needed to activate it (reload drops runtime-only rules). A runtime-only add vanishes at the next reload/reboot, and ports are numbers or service names, not 'https/tcp'.

q: An admin needs to allow TCP port 8080 ONLY from the 10.10.0.0/24 network, permanently, in the public zone. Which approach is correct?
options: firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-port=8080/tcp then reload
firewall-cmd --add-rich-rule='rule source address=10.10.0.0/24 service name=http accept'
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family=ipv4 source address=10.10.0.0/24 port port=8080 protocol=tcp accept' then reload
firewall-cmd --permanent --add-port=8080/tcp then reload (the source restriction is implied by rich text elsewhere)
explain: Source-restricted allows are rich rules; --add-port opens the port to the WORLD. Moving the port to the trusted zone changes which interfaces/sources the zone matches (and trusted is far broader), and http is port 80, not 8080, plus the last form lacks --permanent.

q: An admin needs to check whether firewalld is running and which zone interface eth0 is assigned to. Which approach is correct?
options: firewall-cmd --state and firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
systemctl is-active firewalld shows the zones too
firewall-cmd --zone=eth0 --list-all
iptables -L lists firewalld zones
explain: --state reports the daemon's running state and --get-active-zones maps interfaces to zones. Zones are assigned to interfaces/connections, not named after them, and firewalld's nftables backend is not inspected with iptables -L.

q: An admin needs to make this server act as a NAT router for the internal zone. Which approach is correct?
options: firewall-cmd --zone=internal --add-forward-all
echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward only
firewall-cmd --zone=internal --add-masquerade (with --permanent and a reload for persistence)
firewall-cmd --add-service=nat
explain: Masquerading is a zone property in firewalld (--add-masquerade). IP forwarding sysctl alone does no address translation, and there is no nat service or --add-forward-all flag (plain forwarding between zones is handled with policies/rules separately).

q: An admin needs to A rule added with firewall-cmd --add-port=9090/tcp worked until the admin ran firewall-cmd --reload. Why did it disappear, and how is that prevented?. Which approach is correct?
options: Port 9090 is reserved and auto-removed
firewalld only keeps rules added while the daemon was stopped
The reload had a bug; rules must be re-added after every reload
The rule was runtime-only; --reload replaces runtime config with the permanent config. Add it with --permanent (and reload) to keep it
explain: Runtime changes are intentionally ephemeral: reload and restart discard them in favor of the permanent store. That is the designed behavior, not a bug or a port reservation.

q: Which TWO statements about firewalld configuration are true? (Choose two.)
options: firewall-cmd --reload discards runtime-only rules and activates the permanent configuration
The runtime and permanent configurations are the same store; --permanent is only a comment
Adding a service with --add-service opens every port that service might ever use, including future ones
Changes made with --permanent do not affect the running firewall until a reload or restart
explain: firewalld deliberately separates runtime from permanent config; reload reconciles runtime TO permanent. A service definition maps to specific known ports (e.g. https = 443/tcp), not an open-ended set.

q: ls -Z /var/www/html/index.html shows: unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0. Which field is the TYPE that targeted policy mainly uses to decide access?
options: The third field, httpd_sys_content_t (user:role:TYPE:level)
The fourth field, s0
The first field, unconfined_u
The second field, object_r
explain: An SELinux context is user:role:type:level. Under the targeted policy, access decisions hinge on the TYPE; s0 is the MLS/MCS level and roles matter little for ordinary confined services.

q: sestatus reports: SELinux status: enabled; Current mode: permissive; Mode from config file: enforcing. What happens at the next reboot, and what is the machine doing NOW?
options: It reboots into enforcing (the config wins at boot); right now it is permissive — denials are logged but not enforced
It reboots disabled because permissive and enforcing conflict
Right now it is enforcing; the 'current mode' line is a cache
It stays permissive forever because current mode overrides the config
explain: setenforce changes only the runtime mode; /etc/selinux/config decides the boot mode. Permissive mode logs AVCs without blocking, which is precisely why a permissive/enforcing mismatch matters for audits.

q: sshd refuses a user's key with 'Authentication refused: bad ownership or modes for directory /home/ivan'. The modes found are: home 777, .ssh 700, authorized_keys 600. Which single change fixes it?
options: chmod 755 (or stricter) /home/ivan — sshd's StrictModes rejects home directories writable by group/others
chmod 777 .ssh so sshd can read it
chown root /home/ivan/.ssh
chmod 644 authorized_keys
explain: StrictModes checks the home directory, .ssh, and authorized_keys for loose ownership/modes. A world-writable HOME (777) fails even when the inner files are perfect; authorized_keys 600 is already correct and .ssh 700 must not be loosened.

q: A user's private key file ~/.ssh/id_ed25519 has mode 644. ssh refuses to use it with 'WARNING: UNPROTECTED PRIVATE KEY FILE!'. What mode fixes it, and why?
options: 777 temporarily, then ssh secures it automatically
600 (or stricter): the ssh client ignores private keys readable by anyone else, by design
640 with group ssh-keys is the required mode
644 is fine; the warning means the key is corrupted and must be regenerated
explain: OpenSSH refuses identity files whose private key is accessible to other users — a deliberate safety check, not corruption. chmod 600 makes the owner the only reader.

q: Which statement about zones in firewalld is TRUE?
options: An interface can be in several zones and the most permissive wins
The default zone cannot be changed from public
A network interface belongs to exactly one active zone at a time, and connections not assigned elsewhere fall into the default zone
Zones are per-user firewall profiles
explain: Zone assignment is per connection/interface (or source), single-valued; the default zone (settable with --set-default-zone) catches the rest. Rules union across zones is not how firewalld evaluates traffic.

q: firewall-cmd --get-default-zone prints 'public', and --get-active-zones shows 'public: eth0' and 'internal: eth1'. A new service is added with --permanent --add-service=https and NO --zone. Where did it go?
options: Into the default zone (public), because commands without --zone apply to the default zone
Into both active zones
Into the internal zone, the last one listed
Nowhere; the command errors without --zone
explain: --zone omitted means the default zone. It never broadcasts to all zones, and the command succeeds — which is exactly how admins accidentally open services on the wrong (public) side.

q: Reading firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-all shows: services: dhcpv6-client ssh; ports: 8080/tcp; masquerade: no; rich rules: (none). What traffic can reach this host from the public side?
options: SSH (22/tcp), DHCPv6 client responses, and TCP 8080; everything else not matched is dropped by the zone's default target
Nothing; masquerade: no blocks inbound traffic
Only 8080; services listed are informational
All TCP ports, because ports: lists only examples
explain: list-all enumerates exactly what the zone allows: the named services' ports plus the explicit port list. Masquerade governs outbound NAT, not inbound reachability.

q: An admin wants a service open in the runtime firewall NOW but deliberately NOT after the next reboot. What is the correct shape?
options: Add it with --permanent and remove it manually before reboot; there is no runtime-only mode
Add it WITHOUT --permanent (runtime-only), and it will vanish at reload/reboot by design
Add it, then run firewall-cmd --runtime-save=off
firewalld has no runtime-only rules; use iptables directly
explain: Runtime-only changes are a first-class firewalld concept: they take effect immediately and are discarded on reload/restart — ideal for temporary access windows.

q: After switching SELinux from disabled to enforcing in /etc/selinux/config, what happens on the next boot and why?
options: SELinux stays permissive until an admin runs setenforce 1 once
The system refuses to boot until contexts are fixed by hand
A full filesystem relabel runs automatically (because /.autorelabel behavior is triggered for the disabled→enforcing transition) and the boot takes much longer; file contexts are rebuilt from policy
Nothing changes; enforcing only matters for new files
explain: Files created while SELinux was disabled lack contexts, so the transition forces a complete relabel at boot. The config file's mode then applies without further commands.

q: A confined service works when SELinux is permissive and fails when enforcing, and the audit log shows AVC denials naming the service's type. What is the WRONG response an auditor should flag?
options: Labeling the content with the correct type via semanage fcontext and restorecon
Checking for a boolean that governs the service's needed access
Setting SELinux to permissive (or disabled) permanently to 'fix' the application
Reviewing the AVC to see which file or port the service actually needed
explain: Permissive/disabled removes the protection instead of fixing the label, port, or boolean mismatch the AVC pinpoints. The other choices are the legitimate remediation paths.

q: Which command shows the SELinux type of running processes (for example, proving sshd runs confined)?
options: systemctl status sshd shows the context in the unit header
ls -Z /proc
ps -eZ (or ps auxZ) — the Z flag adds the context column
ps --selinux
explain: The Z option across ls/ps/id adds SELinux context output. For processes, ps -eZ shows domains like sshd_t. There is no --selinux flag and unit headers do not print contexts.

q: A web application runs as a systemd service and its files come out world-readable despite the admin's shell umask of 0027. Why?
options: RHEL 10 ignores umask for services entirely and uses ACLs instead
umask is per-file and was reset by the application's installer
The shell umask only applies to root's files
systemd services do not inherit a login shell's umask; the service's umask is controlled by the unit's UMask= setting or the manager default (0022)
explain: Umask is a per-process inherited attribute; services are children of PID 1, not of the admin's shell, so they get the manager's default unless UMask= is set in the unit. This is a common 'works in my shell' trap.

q: Which TWO remediations correctly fix an SELinux denial for a service reading content from a nonstandard path? (Choose two.)
options: Add a file-context rule with semanage fcontext for the path and run restorecon on it
Run chcon on the files and schedule a weekly relabel to maintain it
Enable the boolean that governs the service's access, if one exists for the behavior
Move the service's policy module to permissive with semanage permissive -a
explain: Durable fixes change POLICY (fcontext rules, booleans) and then apply them. chcon edits are erased by relabels, and making a domain permissive guts enforcement for that service instead of fixing the mismatch.

q: What is the practical difference between firewall-cmd --panic-on and stopping the firewalld service?
options: Panic mode only blocks inbound traffic
They are identical; panic is the service's stop alias
Stopping firewalld also drops all forwarded traffic by default

Panic mode drops ALL traffic (in/out/forward) immediately while the daemon keeps running and can panic-off cleanly; stopping firewalld removes its rules and typically leaves the host OPEN per the underlying nftables state
explain: Panic mode is the emergency brake: total drop, reversible with --panic-off. Stopping the daemon flushes firewalld's policy — usually the opposite of an emergency lockdown.

q: getsebool -a | grep httpd shows: httpd_can_network_connect --> off; httpd_can_sendmail --> on. An app under httpd cannot reach its database on another host. Which single command fixes it persistently?
options: setenforce 0 for the httpd domain only
semanage boolean -m httpd_can_network_connect --off
setsebool httpd_can_sendmail off
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
explain: The boolean gating outbound network connections for httpd is httpd_can_network_connect; -P persists it. sendmail is unrelated, the semanage boolean form shown flips the wrong direction, and domain permissive tricks are not setenforce options.

q: What does restorecon -F additionally do compared with plain restorecon?
options: -F fixes file permissions (mode bits), not contexts
-F relabels the entire filesystem from /
Nothing; -F is the recursive flag

It forces a reset of contexts to the policy defaults even for files whose types were customized with local fcontext entries marked as such (it also resets user/range parts in some flows) — plain restorecon skips files with custom types from local modifications
explain: restorecon respects 'customized' file contexts recorded by semanage; -F forces them back to the system defaults. Recursion is -r/-R, and contexts are not mode bits.

q: Before reloading sshd after editing /etc/ssh/sshd_config, which validation step prevents locking everyone out, and what does sshd use on reload?
options: No validation exists; restart and hope
ssh -t validates the server config from a client
sshd -t validates the config (exit status and messages); a reload (SIGHUP / systemctl reload sshd) applies it to NEW connections without dropping existing sessions
systemctl restart sshd drops no sessions, so reload is pointless
explain: sshd -t is the pre-flight check that catches syntax errors and bad directives BEFORE the daemon is touched; reload then re-reads config for new sessions while established ones continue. A restart does sever the listener (existing sessions usually survive, but reload is the safe path).

q: An audit asks whether a custom SELinux policy module built from denials (audit2allow) is a good blanket practice. What is the balanced truth?
options: audit2allow output is always safe because it is generated by the system

audit2allow is a legitimate LAST-resort tool for local policy gaps, but blanket-approving its output can silently grant dangerous access (it allows whatever was denied, including attacks); rules must be reviewed line by line
audit2allow is prohibited on RHEL and never appropriate
It only ever generates file-label rules, never access rules
explain: audit2allow turns AVC denials into allow rules verbatim — powerful for genuine gaps, dangerous as a reflex. The professional workflow is: fix labels/ports/booleans first, review any generated module carefully, and prefer targeted booleans and types.

q: Where do firewalld's built-in SERVICE definitions (the XML mapping a service name to its ports) live, and what is the correct way to define a custom service?
options: Services are defined inside /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf
Built-ins live in /etc/firewalld/services/ and should be edited in place
Built-ins live in /usr/lib/firewalld/services/; custom definitions go in /etc/firewalld/services/ (which overrides by name) — never edit the /usr/lib copies
Custom services can only be permanent port rules; XML services are fixed
explain: The /usr/lib tree is vendor-shipped (package updates overwrite it), while /etc/firewalld holds local configuration — the same precedence pattern as systemd units and SELinux local policy.

q: An authorized_keys line begins: from="10.0.0.5",no-port-forwarding ssh-ed25519 AAAA... What does the from= option accomplish?
options: It records where the key was generated, as a comment
It sets the address the server binds to for this key
It forces the session to be forwarded FROM 10.0.0.5 through a jump host
The key is accepted only when the connection originates from 10.0.0.5, adding a source restriction on top of key possession
explain: authorized_keys options constrain a key: from= matches the client source address, and options like no-port-forwarding/no-pty tighten what that key may do — defense in depth if a key leaks.

q: Which TWO things must be true before an SSH public key in ~/.ssh/authorized_keys is accepted by a stock RHEL sshd? (Choose two.)
options: The authorized_keys file must be mode 644 so sshd can always read it
The key must be listed in /etc/ssh/ssh_config on the server
StrictModes requirements hold: home directory, .ssh, and authorized_keys are owned by the user (or root) and not group/world-writable
The private key file on the client is not readable by group/others (or the client refuses to use it)
explain: Key auth fails closed on loose permissions at BOTH ends: the client protects the private key (600-style), and the server's StrictModes rejects sloppy ownership/modes on the home path. 644 is neither required nor the point (600 is typical), and server-side ssh_config is the CLIENT config file.

q: What does it mean when getenforce reports Enforcing on a RHEL 10 system?
options: SELinux is actively enforcing policy and will deny access that violates the loaded policy.
SELinux is enforcing only for network services and ignores local file access.
SELinux policy is not loaded and no SELinux checks or audit records are produced.
SELinux is only logging violations and allowing every access that violates policy.
explain: In Enforcing mode the kernel applies the loaded policy to each access check and denies non-matching access while also logging the denial. Logging-only behavior describes Permissive mode, and having no policy loaded describes Disabled mode, neither of which matches the Enforcing report.

q: Which command shows the current SELinux mode for the running system without changing it?
options: semanage login -l
getenforce
setenforce 1
firewall-cmd --state
explain: getenforce only reports whether the running kernel is in Enforcing, Permissive, or Disabled handling. Changing the mode requires a different tool, the login listing reports SELinux user mappings, and the firewall state command reports firewalld rather than SELinux.

q: An admin runs setenforce 0 to test a service fault. The service starts. After the next reboot the same fault returns. Why did the test result not persist?
options: setenforce changes only the running mode, so the mode stored in /etc/selinux/config takes effect again at boot.
setenforce changes firewalld to the runtime configuration, which is discarded when the system reloads.
setenforce also rewrites the file contexts database, so labels revert to their previous values at boot.
setenforce disables the audit daemon, so denials stop being recorded after the machine restarts.
explain: setenforce is a runtime switch and intentionally does not edit the persistent configuration file. If that file still selects Enforcing, the next boot returns to Enforcing regardless of the earlier test, while file labels and audit service state are separate concerns.

q: A system reports Permissive today and must be Permissive again after every reboot. A check of /etc/selinux/config shows SELINUX=enforcing. What change is required?
options: Edit /etc/selinux/config so the SELINUX line reads SELINUX=permissive, then the setting will apply at boot.
Create the file /.autorelabel so the kernel chooses Permissive during the next filesystem check.
Run setenforce 0 once each week so a scheduled job can keep the mode from changing at boot.
Remove the SELinux policy package so the boot loader falls back to Permissive handling.
explain: The SELINUX value in the configuration file is what the system reads during boot to select the initial mode. A one-time runtime switch is lost at reboot, an autorelabel marker controls labeling rather than mode, and removing policy is neither required nor a valid way to select Permissive.

q: A server has run with SELINUX=disabled for months. The admin changes the setting to enforcing and reboots. Why is the first boot expected to take much longer and possibly reboot again?
options: Every user password must be rehashed because disabled mode stores credentials without SELinux labels.
The firewall must rebuild every zone because enabling SELinux deletes all permanent firewalld configuration.
The filesystem must be relabeled because files created while SELinux was disabled carry no usable security contexts for enforcing policy.
The kernel must recompile every policy module from source because disabled mode deletes the compiled policy store.
explain: While Disabled, files are not labeled in a way Enforcing policy can rely on, so the system performs a full relabel before trusting the contexts. That relabel is a filesystem operation and does not rebuild firewall rules, recompile all policy source, or change password storage.

q: Output from ls -Z reads: -rw-r--r--. ana ana unconfined_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0 /opt/intranet/logo.png; Which field is the SELinux type for this file?
options: object_r, the second field of the context, which names the role assigned to the file.
httpd_sys_content_t, the third field of the context, between the role and the sensitivity level.
unconfined_u, the first field of the context, which names the SELinux user for the file.
s0, the final field of the context, which names the sensitivity level assigned to the file.
explain: A context is ordered user, role, type, then level, so the third component is the type. For files on a targeted-policy system that type is what policy rules match on, while the user, role, and level occupy the surrounding positions and do not name the type.

q: Output from ps -Z for a web process reads: system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 2314 ? 00:00:02 httpd; Which part of the context identifies the domain the process runs in?
options: httpd_t, the type field, which is the domain that targeted policy rules use for this process.
system_r, the role field, which alone decides every file the process is allowed to open.
s0, the level field, which selects the executable that the service manager started.
system_u, the user field, which replaces the Unix account the process is running as.
explain: For a process, the type field acts as its SELinux domain, and policy allow rules are written against that domain. The user and role fields add constraints in stricter policies, but on the targeted policy the day-to-day access decisions turn on the process type meeting the object type.

q: Why do most SELinux troubleshooting steps on RHEL targeted policy focus on the type field rather than the user or role fields?
options: The type field is the only field stored on disk, while user and role exist only in the audit log.
Changing the type also changes file ownership, which is why httpd can then read the content as its own user.
Targeted policy ignores types completely and grants access whenever the SELinux user matches the Unix user name.
Targeted policy bases most allow decisions on the process type and the object type, with user and role largely uniform for system objects.
explain: The targeted policy ships with a largely uniform user and role for system files and services, so matching types is what grants or denies most access. Types are stored as part of the full context on disk, and a type change does not alter Unix ownership or permissions.

q: Web content will live in /opt/intranet, outside the default document root. Which pair of steps applies httpd_sys_content_t durably so it survives a relabel?
options: Run chcon -t httpd_sys_content_t /opt/intranet/logo.png once and then disable future relabeling in the SELinux configuration.
Run setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on, because the boolean rewrites the file context database for custom paths.
Run touch /.autorelabel and reboot, because a full relabel invents the correct type for any custom directory it finds.
Run semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t "/opt/intranet(/.*)?" and then restorecon -Rv /opt/intranet to apply the stored rule.
explain: Recording the pattern with semanage fcontext writes the labeling rule into policy storage, and restorecon then applies that stored rule to the existing tree. A direct context change without a stored rule is overwritten by the next relabel, an autorelabel uses stored rules rather than guessing, and a boolean never edits context rules.

q: An admin extracts release notes from a tar archive into /srv/portal. The files arrive labeled default_t and the internal service that should read them is denied. Ownership and mode are correct. What is the durable correction?
options: Run setenforce 0 and leave the system permissive so the service can read the files for production use.
Run chcon on the top directory only, because a relabel will then copy that type down to every file below it.
Add a semanage fcontext rule assigning the type the reading service expects for /srv/portal and its contents, then run restorecon -Rv /srv/portal.
Run chmod -R 777 /srv/portal so the service can bypass the type check that is blocking reads.
explain: Extracted files keep whatever context they end up with, and only a stored fcontext rule plus restorecon makes the expected type stick across relabels. Loosening Unix modes does not satisfy a type mismatch, leaving the machine permissive removes protection rather than fixing labels, and a one-off context change is not stored.

q: A directory was labeled samba_share_t with chcon last month and sharing worked. After an administrator ran restorecon -Rv on the parent tree, sharing broke again. What happened?
options: restorecon disabled the Samba boolean, so the service lost permission to export any local directory.
restorecon changed the Unix group to root, so Samba could no longer traverse the directory.
restorecon reset the directory to the type recorded in the file contexts database because the earlier chcon change was never stored there.
restorecon converted the directory into a symbolic link, so Samba followed the link to an unlabeled target.
explain: restorecon applies the database of stored labeling rules; a context set only in memory of the filesystem with chcon has no database entry and is replaced. The command does not create links, toggle booleans, or rewrite ownership, which is why recording the intended type first is the lasting approach.

q: Output from semanage port -l includes: http_port_t tcp 80, 81, 443, 488, 8008, 8009, 8443, 9000; A second Apache instance must listen on TCP 8081. What must be done in SELinux before it will bind?
options: Edit the Apache configuration to use port 8008 in the URL only, leaving the actual listen socket on 8081 unchanged.
Add TCP 8081 to the ssh_port_t type so the web service inherits the network permission from sshd.
Add TCP 8081 to the http_port_t type with semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8081, because 8081 is not in the listed set.
Nothing, because any port above 1024 is automatically treated as an HTTP port by the targeted policy.
explain: The listing shows exactly which TCP ports carry the HTTP port type, and 8081 is absent, so httpd would be denied the bind until the port is labeled. High ports are not auto-labeled, labeling the port for a different service would not grant httpd the bind, and changing only the displayed URL does not change the socket.

q: A hardened sshd will listen on TCP 2022 instead of 22. Which SELinux command allows sshd to bind that port?
options: semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 2022
semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 2022
firewall-cmd --add-port=2022/tcp
semanage fcontext -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 2022
explain: sshd may bind only to ports labeled with the SSH port type, so the new port must be added with that type using the port management command. Labeling it as a web port would not authorize sshd, the file-context tool does not manage network ports, and opening a firewall port does not grant the SELinux bind permission.

q: Running semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 8009 fails with a message that the port is already defined. The port currently carries a different type and must be reassigned to sshd. Which command succeeds?
options: semanage port -m -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 8009, using modify because a type already exists for that port.
semanage port -a -t ssh_port_t -p tcp 8009 -f, using a force flag to overwrite the existing record silently.
semanage port -d -t http_port_t -p tcp 8009 followed by rebooting so the port record clears itself.
restorecon -Rv /etc/services, because port types are stored as file contexts on the services file.
explain: When a port already has a type, the add operation refuses to create a second record and the modify operation is the supported way to change the existing one. There is no force variant for this refusal, deleting an unrelated record or rebooting does not reassign the type, and port types live in policy rather than in a file context.

q: An admin wants to inspect boolean values before changing anything. Which two commands report current boolean state? (Choose two.)
options: setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on, which changes the value rather than only reporting it.
getsebool httpd_enable_homedirs, which reports the current value of that single named boolean.
getsebool -a, which reports the current values of all booleans on the system.
ausearch -m AVC -ts today, which searches audit events rather than reporting current boolean values.
explain: Both getsebool forms are read-only reports of current boolean state, one for a single name and one for the full list. The persistent set operation changes state instead of reporting it, and the audit search retrieves past events rather than the values in effect now.

q: Users report that http://server.example.net/~priya/ returns 403 even though /home/priya/public_html exists, permissions allow traversal, and getsebool shows httpd_enable_homedirs --> off. Which change fixes it persistently?
options: setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on, so Apache may serve user home content now and after reboot.
chmod 777 /home/priya, because home directory serving is controlled only by Unix traversal bits.
semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 80, because user content is served on a separate labeled port.
setsebool httpd_enable_homedirs on without persistence, accepting that the next reboot is out of scope.
explain: The named boolean is exactly the switch that permits httpd to read user home directories, and the persistence flag writes the value so it survives reboot. Without persistence the fix is temporary, loosening the home directory does not override a boolean denial, and the standard web port is already labeled for httpd.

q: A web application under httpd must open outbound connections to a remote database listener, and denials stop when that specific capability is allowed. Which persistent boolean change matches the need?
options: setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect off
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect_db on
setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on
setsebool -P allow_httpd_anon_write on
explain: The database-connect boolean is scoped to httpd initiating connections toward database ports, which matches an application reaching a remote database listener. The home-directory boolean governs a different kind of read, turning the general connect capability off would worsen the fault, and anonymous write access does not authorize outbound database connections.

q: A service fails with Permission denied in Enforcing mode, starts normally during a brief Permissive test, and its Unix permissions and firewall rules check out. What is the best-supported diagnosis?
options: The kernel has run out of file handles, so limits should be raised without checking the audit log.
The service binary is corrupt, so it should be reinstalled before any log is inspected.
The firewall is silently dropping the service traffic, so every zone should be set to trusted for production use.
An SELinux policy denial is blocking the service, so the audit log and the relevant contexts or booleans should be examined next.
explain: Behavior that changes only with the SELinux mode, while ordinary permissions stay correct, points directly at a policy denial recorded in the audit log. Jumping to firewall trust changes, reinstalling the binary, or raising limits ignores the one variable that reproduced and cleared the fault.

q: Which command lists recent SELinux denial records from the audit log for triage?
options: journalctl --list-boots
ausearch -m AVC -ts recent
firewall-cmd --list-all
ls -Z /var/log/audit
explain: The audit search tool filtered to the AVC message type and a recent start time returns the denial records an admin needs for triage. Listing boots, listing firewall configuration, and listing a directory with contexts do not retrieve the denial events themselves.

q: Output from firewall-cmd --get-active-zones reads: public; interfaces: enp1s0; What does this tell the admin?
options: The public zone contains no services, because active zones never list allowed services.
enp1s0 has been placed in panic mode, so all traffic on the interface is being dropped.
The enp1s0 interface is currently assigned to the public zone, so the public zone rules govern traffic arriving on that interface.
The public zone is the factory default zone, regardless of which interface is actually carrying traffic.
explain: Active-zone output pairs each zone in use with the interfaces or sources bound to it, so traffic on the named interface is judged by that zone. The report does not state the default zone, does not indicate panic mode, and says nothing about which services the zone permits.

q: Which two statements about firewalld runtime and permanent configuration are correct? (Choose two.)
options: A rule added without --permanent is written to disk automatically when the service is stopped cleanly.
Running firewall-cmd --reload discards runtime-only rules and loads the permanent configuration.
Adding a permanent rule also inserts it into the live ruleset at the same moment without any reload.
A rule added with --permanent is stored but does not affect live traffic until a reload or restart loads it.
explain: Permanent edits change the stored configuration and take effect only when that configuration is loaded, which a reload does by replacing the runtime ruleset with the stored one. Runtime-only rules are never saved to disk on shutdown, and a permanent edit alone does not change live filtering.

q: An admin runs firewall-cmd --add-port=1313/tcp and the probe works. Minutes later the admin runs firewall-cmd --reload for an unrelated change and the probe fails. What happened to the 1313 rule?
options: The reload restarted SELinux in Enforcing mode, which relabeled port 1313 to a different type.
The reload enabled panic mode automatically because a port above 1024 was opened at runtime.
The reload converted port 1313 into a service definition that only applies to the internal zone.
The reload replaced the runtime ruleset with the permanent configuration, and the runtime-only 1313 rule was not stored there.
explain: A reload is not a merge; it loads the permanent configuration and throws away changes that exist only at runtime. That behavior explains a working rule vanishing after a reload, and it has nothing to do with zone conversion, SELinux port labeling, or panic mode.

q: Cockpit must be reachable on its service in the public zone after reboots and immediately after the change is applied. Which sequence is correct?
options: firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-port=22/tcp, because cockpit shares the SSH service port on RHEL systems.
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-service=cockpit alone, because permanent edits apply to live traffic instantly.
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-service=cockpit followed by firewall-cmd --reload to load the stored change.
firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-service=cockpit alone, because a runtime service addition is saved when cockpit restarts.
explain: Storing the service addition permanently and then reloading is the combination that both persists the rule and activates it now. A runtime-only addition is lost on reload or reboot, a permanent addition alone waits for a load, and cockpit does not listen on the SSH port.

q: Only hosts on 172.16.8.0/24 may query the DNS service on this server in the public zone, and the rule must persist. Which firewall-cmd command is correct?
options: firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-port=53/tcp, because DNS uses only TCP and a port rule can name a source subnet.
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-rich-rule="rule family='ipv4' source address='172.16.8.0/24' service name='dns' accept"
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-service=dns, because a service addition can be scoped to one subnet in the same command.
firewall-cmd --zone=trusted --add-source=172.16.8.0/24, because moving the subnet to trusted is the only way to allow its DNS queries.
explain: A rich rule is the firewalld construct that binds a source network, a service, and an accept action together in one zone rule. A plain service addition opens the service to the whole zone, moving the source to another zone changes far more than DNS access, and DNS also uses UDP while a plain port rule carries no source condition.

q: An admin must verify whether masquerading is active for the external zone before troubleshooting outbound NAT. Which command answers that directly?
options: firewall-cmd --zone=external --query-rich-rule
firewall-cmd --zone=external --list-services
firewall-cmd --zone=external --query-masquerade
firewall-cmd --get-default-zone
explain: The masquerade query returns a yes or no answer for that specific zone setting. Listing services reports allowed services rather than NAT behavior, the default-zone query names a different property, and a rich-rule query tests a rule string the admin has not supplied.

q: All traffic originating from 192.0.2.0/24 must be handled by the trusted zone, persistently, while interfaces stay in their current zones. Which command does this?
options: firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-source=192.0.2.0/24
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-service=trusted
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --add-masquerade
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=trusted --change-interface=enp1s0
explain: Assigning a source network to a zone makes packets from that network be judged by the named zone without moving any interface. Changing the interface binding would affect every sender on that link, there is no service by that name for this purpose, and masquerade controls address translation rather than zone selection.

q: During an active intrusion attempt an admin runs firewall-cmd --panic-on. What is the immediate effect?
options: The public zone is deleted and rebuilt from the factory defaults at the next reload.
SELinux switches to Enforcing mode and the audit log is rotated immediately.
All incoming and outgoing network traffic is dropped until panic mode is turned off, leaving only local console work practical.
Only new incoming connections are logged, while established traffic continues to flow normally.
explain: Panic mode is an emergency stop that drops network traffic in both directions on the host. It does not merely log connections, rebuild zones, or change SELinux mode, and recovery is done from the local console by turning panic mode off.

q: Output from firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-all includes the line: services: dhcpv6-client ssh; ports: 8080/tcp 514/udp; A test shows TCP 8080 reachable. How was 8080 most likely opened?
options: By the ssh service, because sshd on RHEL also answers on TCP 8080 by default.
It was not opened at all, because --list-all hides port rules that are currently active.
By the dhcpv6-client service, because that service definition includes a web alternate port.
As a raw port addition, because 8080 appears under ports rather than being implied by a listed service name.
explain: The list-all report separates service-based openings from explicit port openings, so a port shown on the ports line came from a port rule. Neither listed service provides that web alternate port, and the report is specifically meant to show the active openings for the zone.

q: A vendor application listens on UDP 514 for syslog. Which permanent firewalld change opens exactly that, and how is it activated?
options: firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-service=syslog, using a built-in service name that ships with firewalld.
firewall-cmd --zone=public --add-port=514/tcp alone, because protocol choice does not matter for syslog.
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-port=514/udp followed by firewall-cmd --reload.
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-port=514/udp alone, with no reload needed for activation.
explain: A raw port rule must name the correct transport protocol, and storing it permanently still requires a reload before it filters live traffic.
