TCP would not match the UDP listener, there is no stock service entry that substitutes here, and skipping the reload leaves the stored rule inactive.

q: Key-based SSH logins for user erin fail. A listing shows /home/erin/.ssh as drwxrwxrwx owned by erin. Home and authorized_keys modes are correct. With StrictModes on, what is the fix?
options: chmod 777 /home/erin/.ssh/authorized_keys so sshd can read the key file under any SELinux context.
chown root:root /home/erin/.ssh so the directory is owned by a privileged account.
chmod 700 /home/erin/.ssh so only the owner can read, write, or traverse the SSH configuration directory.
Add erin to the wheel group so sshd relaxes its permission checks for administrators.
explain: sshd with StrictModes refuses key material when the SSH directory is writable or readable by others, and owner-only 700 is the expected mode. Making the key file world-accessible worsens the refusal, the directory must belong to the user rather than root, and group membership does not waive the strict checks.

q: On a client, ssh reports that permissions 0664 for /home/dave/.ssh/id_ed25519 are too open and ignores the key. What is the correct repair?
options: Move the key to /tmp and set mode 777 so ssh can always open it without prompts.
chmod 600 /home/dave/.ssh/id_ed25519 so the private key is accessible only to its owner.
chmod 644 /home/dave/.ssh/id_ed25519 so the shell can read the key during login.
chmod 400 /home/dave/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub so the private half inherits safer modes.
explain: A private key must not be accessible to group or others, and owner read-write 600 is the standard repair that ssh accepts. Keeping group read leaves the warning in place, changing the public half does nothing for the private file, and a world-accessible copy in a shared directory is both unsafe and still rejected.

q: A junior admin created /home/gina/.ssh with sudo, so the directory and authorized_keys are owned by root, both mode 700 and 600. Gina still cannot log in with her key. Why?
options: sshd requires authorized_keys to be mode 644, so the file is being skipped for being too restrictive.
sshd requires the .ssh directory to be a symbolic link to /etc/ssh/keys for every user.

sshd requires the .ssh directory and authorized_keys to be owned by the logging-in user (or root-managed in a way that still passes ownership checks for that user path), and files owned by root inside her home fail the ownership check when created incorrectly for her account, so ownership must be given to gina.
sshd cannot use Ed25519 keys when the home directory was created with sudo assistance.
explain: StrictModes checks ownership as well as modes: the key path in a user home must belong to that user, and root-owned files dropped in by an administrator fail that check until ownership is corrected. More permissive modes are not required, no link to a central directory is expected, and the key algorithm is unrelated to who created the folder.

q: After editing sshd_config an admin wants to be certain a typo will not lock out SSH on the next reload. Which validation step comes first?
options: Run firewall-cmd --reload so the new SSH port is opened before the daemon is tested.
Run systemctl restart sshd immediately so the running daemon reports errors in the journal.
Run ssh-keygen -A so new host keys overwrite any configuration mistake at startup.
Run sshd -t to test the configuration files and fix any reported error before reloading the service.
explain: The daemon test mode parses the configuration and reports bad options or values without applying them, which is the safe gate before any reload. Restarting first risks applying a broken configuration, the firewall does not validate daemon syntax, and regenerating host keys does not repair a typo.

q: An admin corrected PasswordAuthentication in sshd_config and validated it. How is the change applied while minimizing disruption?
options: Reboot the server, because sshd reads its configuration only during the boot sequence.
Delete /run/sshd.pid so a new daemon process is forced to start at the next login attempt.
Run setenforce 1, because SELinux enforces the new authentication setting on the daemon.
Run systemctl reload sshd so the daemon re-reads its configuration without a full service teardown.
explain: Reloading signals the running daemon to re-read its configuration and is the normal low-disruption way to apply sshd changes. A reboot is unnecessary, SELinux mode does not apply daemon configuration, and removing a PID file does not restart or reconfigure the service safely.

q: An admin sets PasswordAuthentication no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config, reloads sshd, yet password logins still work. A drop-in file /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/01-cloud.conf sets PasswordAuthentication yes. Why does the drop-in win?
options: Reloading sshd never applies authentication changes, so only a full reboot can enforce the setting.
The main sshd_config is ignored entirely whenever any drop-in directory exists on the system.
sshd uses the first obtained value for most options, and the included drop-in files are parsed before the main file body, so the earlier yes stands.
sshd averages duplicate settings, so yes and no together leave password authentication half enabled.
explain: For most sshd options the first value obtained wins, and the include directive sits at the top of the main file, giving drop-ins precedence in practice. Settings are not averaged, the main file still supplies every option the drop-ins omit, and a reload does apply a correctly resolved configuration.

q: Interactive users on a server run with umask 027, yet files written by a systemd service run as the same account appear as 644. Why does the service not follow the shell umask?
options: umask 027 only applies to directories, so files from any process always appear as 644.
systemd services do not inherit a login shell environment, so the service uses the manager default unless UMask is set in the unit.
The login shell umask is stored in the kernel and expires when the first service starts.
The service binary ignores umask because it was compiled without position-independent code.
explain: A umask set in shell startup files belongs to that shell session and is not passed to services started by the service manager. Service units need their own UMask setting to get the same creation mask, which explains different results for the same account in the two environments.

q: Where would an admin set a persistent umask for a single user interactive shell sessions on RHEL, rather than for every account at once?
options: In /etc/shadow, where per-user file creation defaults are stored beside the password hash.
In /etc/fstab, because mount options supply the creation mask for the home filesystem.
In the systemd unit for sshd, because every interactive session inherits the daemon unit mask.
In that user shell startup file such as ~/.bashrc, where the umask command runs when the user shells start.
explain: Per-user shell behavior belongs in the user own startup files, and a umask line there affects that user interactive sessions. The shadow file stores account and password data, a daemon unit controls only that service, and filesystem mount options do not set a process umask.

q: Postfix submission under httpd is denied when the web application tries to hand mail to the local mail system, and the audit log points to a boolean-guarded capability. Which persistent change matches this narrow need?
options: setsebool -P httpd_can_sendmail on
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
setsebool -P httpd_use_cifs on
setsebool -P httpd_enable_homedirs on
explain: The sendmail boolean is the narrow capability that lets httpd invoke the local mail transfer path for application-generated mail. Broader network access, home directory access, and CIFS access each govern unrelated operations and would grant more or different access than the denial requires.

q: A team share will be exported by Samba from /export/team, a nonstandard location. Which steps give it a durable SELinux label Samba can use?
options: Run setsebool -P samba_enable_home_dirs on, because that boolean relabels every exported directory.
Run semanage fcontext -a -t samba_share_t "/export/team(/.*)?" and then restorecon -Rv /export/team.
Run chcon -R -t samba_share_t /export/team once and record nothing, accepting the next relabel outcome.
Run chmod -R 777 /export/team, because Samba checks Unix modes before any SELinux label.
explain: A nonstandard export path needs its intended type recorded with the file-context tool and then applied with restorecon, the same durable pattern used for other services. An unrecorded context change is lost at relabel, the home-directory boolean does not relabel custom paths, and Unix modes cannot substitute for the required type.

q: An admin wants fixes that will still be correct after a full filesystem relabel and a reboot. Which two actions qualify? (Choose two.)
options: Switching the running mode with setenforce alone, without editing the boot configuration.
Recording a path rule with semanage fcontext and applying it with restorecon -Rv so the intended type is stored in policy.
Changing a file type with chcon alone, without recording any rule for the path involved.
Setting a needed boolean with setsebool using the -P flag so the value is written to persistent policy storage.
explain: Stored file-context rules and persistent boolean values are both written into policy storage, so relabels and reboots preserve them. A bare context change has no stored rule behind it, and a runtime mode switch has no boot configuration behind it, so both of those revert.

q: Anonymous uploads to an FTP drop directory fail in Enforcing mode. The audit denial is boolean-controlled and uploads are an approved requirement. Which change enables them persistently and narrowly?
options: chmod 777 /var/ftp/pub
setenforce 0
setsebool -P ftpd_full_access on
setsebool -P ftpd_anon_write on
explain: The anonymous-write boolean grants exactly the upload capability the denial concerns, and the persistence flag keeps it across reboots. Full access grants far broader read and write reach than approved, dropping to permissive removes enforcement for the whole system, and world-writable modes do not answer an SELinux boolean denial.

q: Inline audit output reads: type=AVC msg=audit(1730000000.123:881): avc: denied { read } for pid=2401 comm="httpd" name="rates.csv" scontext=system_u:system_r:httpd_t:s0 tcontext=unconfined_u:object_r:default_t:s0 tclass=file permissive=0; What is the core problem shown?
options: The target file carries default_t, a type httpd_t is not allowed to read, so the file needs a type httpd is permitted to access.
The audit subsystem denied the read because the message serial number exceeded the configured threshold.
The file rates.csv has the wrong name extension, and httpd is forbidden from reading comma-separated files.
The httpd process is running as the wrong SELinux user, and system_u must be changed to the webmaster account name.
explain: The record pairs a httpd domain as the source with a default_t file as the target, and that type pairing is what policy denies. The SELinux user on a system service is expected, the file name and extension do not drive the decision, and the audit serial is bookkeeping rather than a cause.

q: An admin touches /.autorelabel and reboots a server that has many custom-labeled application directories. What should the admin expect and verify afterward?
options: The marker file disables SELinux for one boot so services can recreate their own labels without denials.
The marker file only relabels /etc and /var, so application directories outside those trees are untouched.
The next boot converts every custom directory to httpd_sys_content_t automatically, regardless of the service that uses it.
The next boot relabels the filesystem from the stored file-context database, so any directory whose rule was never recorded will lose its custom type and must be checked.
explain: Autorelabel applies the stored labeling database to the filesystem, which restores recorded types and overwrites unrecorded manual changes. It does not guess a single web type for everything, does not disable enforcement, and is a full-filesystem operation rather than a two-directory one.

q: Subdirectories under /data/site keep reverting to a generic type after restorecon, while files directly in /data/site get the intended portal type. The stored rule was entered as "/data/site/*". What is wrong with the rule?
options: semanage fcontext cannot manage directories under /data at all, so the content must be moved under /var before labeling.
The rule uses a star where a question mark is required for file names, so restorecon ignores the rule for regular files only.
The pattern only matches a single level, so nested paths are not covered; the rule should use the "/data/site(/.*)?" form to cover the directory and everything beneath it.
restorecon processes directories in reverse alphabetical order, so deeper paths must be labeled with a separate reboot.
explain: The trailing-star pattern reaches only one path level, which matches the symptom of top-level files labeling correctly while nested content reverts. The recursive idiom covers the directory itself and all descendants, the tool can manage this location, and neither file-name punctuation nor processing order explains the level-limited result.

q: A custom service works after an admin labels its socket directory and sets a boolean at runtime, but fails again after both a relabel and a reboot on different occasions. Which review finds both root causes in one pass?
options: Set every boolean for the service domain to on permanently, because partial settings cannot survive a reboot.
Move the service socket into /tmp, because temporary directories are exempt from relabeling and boolean checks.
Compare semanage fcontext -l custom entries and getsebool values against persistent policy storage, checking that the path rule was recorded and the boolean was set with persistence.
Reinstall the service package twice, because only a reinstall writes both file contexts and boolean defaults.
explain: Two different resets point at two different non-persistent changes, and only inspecting the stored context rules and the stored boolean state confirms both. Reinstalling does not create custom rules, enabling every boolean is excessive and unrelated to the label loss, and moving a socket to a shared temporary area avoids neither mechanism.

q: Which two outcomes follow from running a production server with SELINUX=disabled rather than permissive? (Choose two.)
options: Re-enabling enforcing later requires a filesystem relabel, because files were created without proper contexts.
File contexts are maintained automatically in the background so a later switch needs no preparation.
Services run in permissive domains that still record every policy violation for later review.
No SELinux AVC denials are logged for blocked behavior, because the policy is not loaded to evaluate access.
explain: With the policy not loaded there is no evaluation and therefore no denial logging, and files created in that state lack trustworthy labels, forcing a relabel when enforcing returns. Recording violations while allowing access describes permissive mode, and disabled systems do not quietly maintain contexts in the background.

q: Logins for user heidi fail by key. A listing reads: drwxr-xr-x heidi heidi /home/heidi; drwxrwxr-x heidi heidi /home/heidi/.ssh; -rw------- heidi heidi /home/heidi/.ssh/authorized_keys; Which two entries violate StrictModes expectations and must be corrected? (Choose two.)
options: The .ssh directory at group- and world-writable modes, which must be tightened so only heidi can write there.
The authorized_keys file at owner-only 600, which must be loosened so sshd can read it as another user.
The ownership of every listed path, which must be transferred to root before sshd will use the key.
The home directory at group-writable mode, which must be tightened so the group cannot write into it.
explain: StrictModes rejects key paths when the home directory or the .ssh directory is writable by group or others, and both listed directories have that flaw. The key file at owner-only 600 is exactly what is expected, and transferring the user files to root would create an ownership problem rather than solve one.

q: A runbook says to avoid firewalld direct rules for a new port opening and to use zone configuration instead. What is the strongest reason that matches firewalld design on RHEL 10?
options: Direct rules can only open UDP ports, so any TCP opening must be written as a zone rule.
Zone rules apply instantly without a daemon, while direct rules require the kernel to be rebooted.
Direct rules are stored only in SELinux policy, so they disappear whenever a boolean is changed.
Zone and service rules are the managed, inspectable configuration model, while direct rules bypass that model and are deprecated in favor of native rules and policies.
explain: firewalld is designed around zones, services, and rich rules that can be listed and audited through the normal tools, and the direct interface is a legacy bypass of that model. Direct rules are not stored in SELinux policy, do not need a reboot, and are not limited to a single transport protocol.

q: A new interface with no explicit zone assignment must land in the internal zone instead of public on this server, permanently. Which command changes where unassigned interfaces go?
options: firewall-cmd --reload, which reassigns every interface to the internal zone as part of reloading.
firewall-cmd --zone=internal --add-service=ssh, which adds a service but does not change assignment defaults.
firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-masquerade, which enables translation but not zone assignment.
firewall-cmd --set-default-zone=internal, which changes the zone applied to interfaces that have no specific assignment.
explain: The default zone is the fallback for interfaces without their own binding, so changing that setting is the direct control for this requirement. Adding a service, enabling masquerade, and reloading each affect different properties and none of them changes the fallback zone.

q: The RHEL 10 installation ISO is mounted at /mnt/iso, and its top level contains the BaseOS and AppStream directories. An administrator writes a repository file so DNF can install packages from the AppStream content on the mounted image. Which baseurl line is correct?
options: baseurl=file:///mnt/iso/AppStream
baseurl=file:///mnt/iso
baseurl=http:///mnt/iso/AppStream
baseurl=file://mnt/iso/AppStream/
explain: A file-based repository must point at the directory that directly contains the repodata folder, which for installation media is the AppStream directory itself, and a local path uses the file scheme with three slashes. Pointing at the mount root fails because there is no repodata directory at that level.

q: An administrator creates a new repository definition for DNF on a RHEL 10 system. In which location and with which name will DNF actually load the definition?
options: /etc/yum.repos.d/custom.txt
/etc/dnf/repos.d/custom.repo
/etc/yum.repos.d/custom.repo
/etc/yum/custom.repo
explain: DNF reads repository definitions from files ending in .repo inside /etc/yum.repos.d, a path kept for compatibility even though DNF 5 is the package manager on RHEL 10. Files with other extensions or in other directories are ignored.

q: A repository file sets gpgcheck=1 but has no gpgkey entry, and the vendor's public key has never been imported into the RPM keyring. What happens on the first installation attempt from this repository?
options: DNF installs the packages and silently skips signature verification.
DNF disables the repository and continues with the remaining repositories.
DNF imports the key automatically from the first package it downloads.
DNF cannot verify the package signatures and the transaction fails until the signing key is available.
explain: With gpgcheck enabled, every package must carry a signature that chains to a key DNF can find, either through the gpgkey setting in the repo file or already imported in the RPM keyring. Without any source for the key, verification cannot succeed and the install is refused rather than quietly downgraded to unchecked.

q: A repository file contains both gpgcheck=1 and repo_gpgcheck=1. What does the repo_gpgcheck setting add?
options: It makes DNF verify the GPG signature of the repository metadata itself (repomd.xml), in addition to verifying each package.
It makes DNF verify each package twice, once at download and once at install.
It checks that the repository URL uses HTTPS before downloading anything.
It imports the repository key into the RPM keyring automatically at every run.
explain: The two settings protect different artifacts: gpgcheck covers the RPM packages, while repo_gpgcheck covers the signed repository metadata file, so tampered metadata is detected before DNF even trusts the package list. Neither setting fetches or imports keys on its own.

q: Which command creates a repository file in /etc/yum.repos.d from a .repo definition published at a URL?
options: dnf config-manager --install-repo https://repo.example.com/rhel10/example.repo
dnf repolist --add https://repo.example.com/rhel10/example.repo
subscription-manager --add-repo https://repo.example.com/rhel10/example.repo
dnf config-manager --add-repo https://repo.example.com/rhel10/example.repo
explain: The config-manager command family manages DNF configuration, and its add-repo action downloads the repo definition from the URL and stores it as a .repo file in /etc/yum.repos.d. The subscription tool manages entitlements rather than arbitrary repo URLs, and repolist only displays repositories.

q: An administrator wants to stop DNF from using one repository, without deleting its definition, so it can be switched back on later. What is the correct change?
options: Set gpgcheck=0 in the [repoid] section of its .repo file.
Set priority=0 in the [repoid] section of its .repo file.
Set enabled=0 in the [repoid] section of its .repo file.
Remove the baseurl line from its .repo file.
explain: The enabled flag is the on/off switch for a repository: with enabled=0 the definition stays on disk but DNF ignores the repository until it is switched back. Changing gpgcheck only affects signature verification, priority only orders repositories that provide the same package, and deleting baseurl breaks the definition instead of pausing it.

q: An administrator runs dnf repolist --all and the output lists three repositories: baseos (enabled), appstream (enabled), and internal-test (disabled). For a normal dnf install command, which repositories will DNF search for packages?
options: baseos and appstream only, because the disabled repository is skipped.
All three, because listing a repository makes it available.
baseos only, because it appears first in the output.
internal-test only, because it was listed most recently.
explain: The listing command with its all flag shows every defined repository, but install and search operations only use repositories whose enabled flag is on. A disabled repository stays invisible to normal transactions until it is explicitly enabled again.

q: On a registered RHEL 10 system, which command enables the official AppStream repository provided through the system's subscription?
options: dnf config-manager --set-enabled appstream
subscription-manager attach --repo=appstream
yum-config-manager --enable rhel-appstream
subscription-manager repos --enable=rhel-10-for-x86_64-appstream-rpms
explain: Repositories delivered by a Red Hat subscription are switched on with the subscription tool's repos action using the full repository ID. The generic config-manager works on repo IDs defined in local repo files, and the old yum-era config tool no longer exists on RHEL 10.

q: A repository file contains the line baseurl=https://cdn.example.com/rhel/$releasever/$basearch/. On a RHEL 10 x86_64 machine, how does DNF interpret the two variables?
options: Both variables must be exported as shell environment variables before DNF will run.
$releasever resolves to the version of the newest package in the repository.
$releasever resolves to 10 and $basearch resolves to x86_64, substituted automatically when the repository is used.
The variables are left literal, and the server is expected to redirect the request.
explain: DNF performs variable substitution in repository URLs at runtime: releasever comes from the system's distribution release and basearch from the machine architecture, so one repo file works across releases and architectures without editing.

q: Repository metadata on a system is still within its cache lifetime, but an administrator needs one DNF command to re-check the repositories for a package published minutes ago. Which invocation forces a metadata refresh for just that command?
options: dnf --refresh install <package>
dnf --force install <package>
dnf --no-cache install <package>
dnf install --refresh-metadata <package>
explain: The global refresh flag tells DNF to synchronize repository metadata before running the command, regardless of cache age, without changing any persistent setting. The other spellings are not DNF options.

q: Two enabled repositories both provide the same package at the same version. The administrator wants DNF to prefer the internal repository. Which repo-file setting accomplishes this, and how?
options: priority=1000 in the internal repository's file, because the highest number wins.
cost=1 in the internal repository's file, because DNF always picks the cheapest repository.
Listing the internal repository first in the file, because DNF reads sections top to bottom.
priority=1 in the internal repository's file, because a lower priority number wins over the default of 99.
explain: Repository priority is a numeric preference where the lowest value is preferred, and repositories without the setting default to 99. When the same package build is offered by several repositories, DNF selects it from the one with the lowest priority number.

q: Which statements about DNF repository definition files on RHEL 10 are true? (Choose two.)
options: A single .repo file may contain several [repoid] sections, each defining its own repository.
A custom repository file is usable only after it is registered with subscription-manager.
Setting gpgcheck=1 makes DNF verify package signatures against the key given by the gpgkey entry or already present in the RPM keyring.
The file extension does not matter as long as the file sits in /etc/yum.repos.d.
explain: One file can hold many repository sections, and gpgcheck ties signature verification to the configured key material. Custom repository files need no subscription registration, and DNF only loads files whose names end in .repo.

q: Which command installs the mandatory and default packages of the package group whose ID is devtools?
options: dnf groupinstall devtools
dnf install devtools
dnf group install devtools
dnf install @^devtools
explain: The group subcommand operates on package groups, and installing a group pulls in its mandatory and default packages. The single-word groupinstall form was a legacy alias that DNF 5 dropped, a bare name is treated as a package rather than a group, and the @^ prefix addresses environment groups, not regular groups.

q: Before installing a large package group, an administrator wants to see exactly which packages the group named web-server contains. Which command shows this?
options: dnf group show web-server
dnf list web-server
dnf info web-server
dnf group info web-server
explain: The group info action lists a group's mandatory, default, and optional packages before anything is installed. The plain info and list actions describe individual packages, and there is no group show action.

q: An administrator runs rpm -e libwidget and gets an error that package app-frontend requires libwidget.so.2. What is the correct way to remove libwidget together with everything that depends on it?
options: Run dnf remove libwidget and confirm, because DNF evaluates the whole dependency tree and removes the dependent packages as part of the transaction.
Run rpm -e --nodeps libwidget so the dependency check is skipped.
Run rpm -e --force libwidget to override the dependency error.
Delete libwidget's files manually and then remove its entry from the RPM database.
explain: The low-level rpm tool refuses to break dependencies, and forcing or bypassing the check leaves installed packages with missing libraries. DNF works at the transaction level, so removing a library also queues the packages that require it, keeping the installed set consistent.

q: The repositories offer httpd 2.4.62 and 2.4.63. An administrator must install the older 2.4.62 build for compatibility testing. Which command does this?
options: dnf install httpd --version=2.4.62
dnf install httpd-2.4.62
dnf get httpd@2.4.62
dnf install httpd --releasever=2.4.62
explain: Appending a version (and optionally release and architecture) to the package name in the install specification selects that exact build from the available ones. There is no version flag or get subcommand for this, and releasever refers to the distribution release, not a package version.

q: Immediately after a dnf upgrade transaction, a service breaks. Which command reverts exactly that most recent transaction, restoring the previous package versions?
options: dnf history delete last
dnf downgrade --all
dnf history undo last
dnf reinstall --transaction last
explain: DNF records every transaction, and the history undo action reverses a chosen transaction (here the latest one), reinstalling the earlier versions and removing what the transaction added. The downgrade action targets individual packages, not a whole recorded transaction.

q: A library was installed automatically as a dependency, but a locally written script now calls its tools directly. The administrator wants dnf autoremove to stop treating the library as removable. Which command accomplishes this?
options: dnf lock <library-package>
echo the package name into /etc/dnf/protected.d/custom
dnf group install <library-package>
dnf mark install <library-package>
explain: Packages carry an install reason, and autoremove only removes dependencies that nothing needs anymore. Marking a package as user-installed changes its reason so autoremove keeps it; the protected.d mechanism guards essential packages against removal in general, which is a different and blunter tool.

q: A monitoring script runs dnf check-update and inspects the exit code. The command exits with code 100. What does that mean?
options: Updates are available for installed packages.
One hundred packages are installed on the system.
The check failed with an error and no information was gathered.
The system is fully up to date.
explain: check-update uses its exit code as the report: 0 means no updates, 1 means an error occurred, and 100 specifically signals that updates are available, which is why scripts test for that value.

q: Policy requires applying only security fixes during a maintenance window, leaving feature and bugfix updates for later. Which command does this on RHEL 10?
options: dnf upgrade --advisory-type=all
dnf updateinfo apply security
dnf upgrade --security
dnf upgrade --only-security-fixes
explain: DNF's advisory data classifies updates, and the security option on upgrade limits the transaction to updates flagged as security fixes. The updateinfo command belonged to the older DNF generation, and there is no only-security-fixes option.

q: A kernel and glibc update just completed. Which command reports whether a reboot is needed for the running system to actually use the updated code?
options: dnf check-update --reboot
systemctl is-system-running
dnf history verify
dnf needs-restarting -r
explain: The needs-restarting action compares the running system against updated libraries and kernels, and its -r flag reports specifically whether a reboot is required. The other commands report update availability or general system state, not restart requirements.

q: A file belonging to the installed package coretool has been corrupted. The same version is still the newest in the repositories. Which command restores the package's files?
options: dnf reinstall coretool
dnf install coretool
dnf upgrade coretool
dnf repair coretool
explain: Reinstall replaces the currently installed build with the identical version from the repository, restoring any damaged or missing files. A plain install reports the package is already installed and does nothing, and upgrade only acts when a newer version exists.

q: A web application needs the htpasswd utility, which is not installed. Which command finds which available package ships /usr/bin/htpasswd?
options: rpm -qf /usr/bin/htpasswd
dnf search htpasswd
dnf provides /usr/bin/htpasswd
dnf list htpasswd
explain: The provides action searches repository file lists, so it can name the package that supplies a file even when nothing is installed yet. The rpm owner query only works against the local database of installed packages, and search and list match package names and summaries rather than file paths.

q: An administrator has a local file app-1.0-1.x86_64.rpm and wants to install it so that any missing dependencies are pulled from the enabled repositories. Which methods accomplish this? (Choose two.)
options: dnf install ./app-1.0-1.x86_64.rpm
rpm -ivh app-1.0-1.x86_64.rpm
rpm -Uvh --nodeps app-1.0-1.x86_64.rpm
dnf install /root/rpms/app-1.0-1.x86_64.rpm
explain: When DNF is given a local package file, by relative or absolute path, it treats it as part of the transaction and resolves its dependencies from the enabled repositories. The rpm tool installs local files on their own and either fails on missing dependencies or, with the nodeps flag, installs a broken package.

q: Package sensor was upgraded to version 3.2, which misbehaves; version 3.1 is still offered by the repositories. Which command returns the system to 3.1?
options: dnf install sensor-3.1
dnf upgrade sensor --to-version=3.1
dnf history undo sensor
dnf downgrade sensor
explain: The downgrade action is the dedicated path for moving to a lower available version. The install action refuses to replace a newer installed build with an older one, there is no to-version option, and history undo takes a transaction identifier rather than a package name.

q: Running rpm -qf /etc/passwd reports which package as the owner of the file?
options: bash
filesystem
shadow-utils
setup
explain: The owner query against the RPM database reports the setup package for /etc/passwd. The shadow-utils package owns the related shadow-password tooling instead, and filesystem owns the directory skeleton.

q: Which command lists every file that the installed chrony package owns?
options: rpm -ql chrony
rpm -qf chrony
rpm -qi chrony
dnf provides chrony
explain: The list query prints the file list recorded for an installed package. The owner query expects a file path rather than a package name, the info query shows package metadata instead of files, and provides searches repository data for capabilities rather than listing an installed package's files.

q: Which command lists only the configuration files belonging to the installed openssh-server package?
options: rpm -ql openssh-server
rpm -V openssh-server
rpm -qc openssh-server
dnf repoquery --config openssh-server
explain: The config-files query filters the package's file list to entries flagged as configuration files. The plain list query returns every file, the verify action checks files against the database rather than listing them, and repoquery has no config-file listing mode.

q: A package is not installed yet, and an administrator wants to inspect the exact files it would lay down before committing to it. Which approach works?
options: Run rpm -ql on the package name, which reads the file list from the repository.
Run dnf info and read the file list from the package description.
Extract the repository's repodata and search it for the package name.
Download the package with dnf download, then list its contents with rpm -qpl on the downloaded file.
explain: The list query only works for installed packages, so for a candidate package the file must be fetched first; the download action retrieves the RPM, and querying the downloaded file with the package-file variant of the list query shows its payload. Package metadata shown by info does not include the file list.

q: An administrator suspects that files from the installed sudo package were modified after installation. Which command checks the package's files against the RPM database and reports discrepancies?
options: rpm -V sudo
dnf check sudo
rpm --checksum sudo
dnf verify sudo
explain: The verify action compares each installed file's size, mode, digest, and other recorded attributes with the RPM database and prints coded flags for anything that differs. The dnf check action validates dependency consistency across the system, not file contents.

q: Before removing a library, an administrator wants every package that requires it, including packages that exist only in the repositories and are not installed. Which command gives the complete picture?
options: rpm -q --whatrequires <library-package>
dnf provides <library-package>
dnf repoquery --whatrequires <library-package>
dnf list --installed
explain: Repoquery evaluates the repository metadata, so its what-requires query also covers packages that are merely installable. The rpm database query only knows installed packages, provides answers the opposite question (who supplies something), and the installed list carries no dependency information.

q: Which command shows the exact download URL from which DNF would fetch a package in the repositories?
options: dnf info <package>
dnf repoquery --location <package>
rpm -qi <package>
dnf provides <package>
explain: Repoquery's location output is the resolved URL of the package file inside its repository. The info actions show descriptive metadata and repository names but not the file URL, and provides reports which package supplies a capability.

q: Which commands report information about an RPM package that is already installed on the system? (Choose two.)
options: flatpak info <package>
rpm -qi <package>
dnf download <package>
rpm -ql <package>
explain: The info and list queries read the local RPM database to show an installed package's metadata and file list. The download action only fetches a package file without reporting on the installed one, and the flatpak tool manages a completely separate software stack.

q: Which command registers the Flathub repository as a Flatpak remote, tolerating being run more than once?
options: flatpak repo-add flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo
dnf config-manager --add-repo flathub
flatpak remote-add --if-not-exists flathub https://dl.flathub.org/repo/flathub.flatpakrepo
flatpak remote-add flathub
explain: Registering a remote needs a name and the location of its repo definition, and the if-not-exists flag makes the command safe to repeat. The RPM config tool manages a different repository system, and omitting the URL leaves the remote undefined.

q: Which command installs the GNOME Calculator application from the flathub remote?
options: flatpak install flathub org.gnome.Calculator
flatpak get org.gnome.Calculator
dnf install org.gnome.Calculator
flatpak run org.gnome.Calculator
explain: Installing a Flatpak application names the remote and the application's reverse-DNS ID. The run action only launches an application that is already installed, and DNF installs RPM packages, not Flatpaks.

q: A Flatpak remote named testrepo exists but installs from it fail because the remote is disabled. Which command makes it usable again without re-adding it?
options: flatpak remote-add --force testrepo
flatpak install --enable testrepo
dnf config-manager --set-enabled testrepo
flatpak remote-modify --enable testrepo
explain: Existing remotes are adjusted with the remote-modify action, whose enable flag reactivates a disabled remote while keeping its configuration. Re-adding is for remotes that do not exist yet, and the DNF tool has no knowledge of Flatpak remotes.

q: Which command lists only the installed Flatpak applications, excluding runtimes and other components?
options: flatpak list --applications-only
flatpak apps
flatpak list --app
flatpak list --type=app
explain: The list action's app flag filters the output to applications. Without a filter it shows applications and runtimes together, and the other spellings are not Flatpak commands or options.

q: An application must be available to every user account on the machine, including accounts created later. How should the administrator install it with Flatpak?
options: Install it into the system installation (the default for root, or explicitly with --system), not with --user.
Install it with --user as root so the root account shares it with everyone.
Install it once per user, because Flatpak has no shared installation.
Install it with dnf so that it lands in the system paths.
explain: Flatpak keeps two installations: a shared system installation under /var/lib/flatpak that all users see, and a per-user one under the installing user's home directory. Only the system installation serves every account.

q: An administrator installed a Flatpak application while testing, and it launches fine in the administrator's session. A regular user on the same machine gets 'application not installed'. What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The regular user lacks execute permission on /var/lib/flatpak and needs a group change.
Flatpak applications are licensed per user and must be obtained separately for each account.
The application must be re-registered with subscription-manager for other users.
The application went into the administrator's per-user installation; install it with --system so all users can use it.
explain: An install performed into the per-user installation lands under that user's own home directory, which no other account can see. Installing into the system installation makes the same application available to everyone on the machine.

q: LibreOffice was installed as a Flatpak from flathub. Which command launches it from a terminal?
options: flatpak run org.libreoffice.LibreOffice
flatpak exec org.libreoffice.LibreOffice
flatpak start org.libreoffice.LibreOffice
libreoffice --flatpak
explain: Installed Flatpak applications are started with the run action followed by the application ID. There are no exec or start actions for launching applications.

q: Several Flatpak applications were removed, but disk usage barely dropped because their runtimes remain. Which command removes runtimes and extensions that no installed application needs anymore?
options: flatpak clean --runtimes
flatpak prune --all
flatpak uninstall --unused
rm -rf /var/lib/flatpak/runtime
explain: The unused flag on uninstall finds runtimes and extensions with no remaining application depending on them and removes just those. Deleting the runtime directory by hand would corrupt the installation's bookkeeping, and the other two commands do not exist.

q: A team wants to freeze a Flatpak remote: no installs or updates from it for now, but its definition must stay on the system for later. Which command does this?
options: flatpak remote-delete <remote>
flatpak remote-modify --remove <remote>
chmod 000 /var/lib/flatpak/repo
flatpak remote-modify --disable <remote>
explain: Disabling a remote keeps its definition while excluding it from installs and updates, and it can be re-enabled the same way. Deleting removes the definition entirely, and changing permissions on the repository directory breaks the installation instead of configuring it.

q: Where can an administrator drop a .flatpakrepo file so that the remote it describes is automatically defined as a system remote on the machine?
options: /etc/flatpak/remotes.d/
/etc/yum.repos.d/
/usr/share/doc/flatpak/
/etc/dnf/vars/
explain: Flatpak reads remote definitions from .flatpakrepo files placed in its remotes.d directories, with /etc/flatpak/remotes.d being the administrator's location for system remotes. The other directories belong to the RPM repository system and DNF variables.

q: Which statements about Flatpak on RHEL 10 are true? (Choose two.)
options: Flatpak applications are installed and removed through DNF, like RPM packages.
System-wide Flatpak installations live under /var/lib/flatpak, while per-user installations live under ~/.local/share/flatpak.
A Flatpak application is identified by a reverse-DNS application ID such as org.mozilla.firefox.
The flatpak uninstall --unused command removes runtimes even when installed applications still depend on them.
explain: Flatpak is a software stack separate from DNF and RPM, with its own system and per-user installation trees and reverse-DNS application IDs. The unused cleanup is specifically limited to components that no installed application depends on.

q: A transaction aborts with: file /usr/share/app/config.yml from install of app-2.0 conflicts with file from package app-plugins-1.0. What does this mean and what is the sound resolution?
options: The file is corrupted; delete it manually and the install will proceed.
The repository metadata is stale; cleaning the cache removes the conflict.
The packages have the same name; renaming one package file resolves it.
Both packages claim ownership of the same path; resolve it by removing or updating the conflicting package so only one package owns the file, then rerun the transaction.
explain: A file conflict means two packages in the transaction set ship the identical path, which RPM cannot reconcile. The fix is to change the package set (remove the conflicting package or move to a matching version of it); deleting the on-disk file does not help because the conflict is detected between the packages themselves.

q: An administrator copies a working appstream.repo file from another server into /etc/yum.repos.d, but DNF acts as if the repository does not exist and repolist does not show it. Inspecting the file reveals enabled=0 was set on the source server. What is the fix?
options: Run dnf clean all so the copied file is noticed.
Rename the file to appstream.repo.disabled so DNF scans it.
Enable it, either by setting enabled=1 in the file or with dnf config-manager --set-enabled appstream, after which DNF will use it.
Register the file with subscription-manager repos --import.
explain: A copied repo file carries its enabled state with it; a disabled repository is ignored by transactions and hidden from the default listing. Cleaning caches does not change enablement, and local repo files need no registration step.

q: Packages from a newly added third-party repository fail to install with a GPG check failure because the vendor's signing key is unknown to the system. What is the correct fix that keeps signature verification in place?
options: Point the repository's gpgkey entry at the vendor's public key (or import it with rpm --import) so DNF can verify the signatures.
Set gpgcheck=0 in the repository file and leave it that way.
Import the vendor's private key into the RPM keyring.
Delete the repository's cached metadata and try again.
explain: Signature verification needs the vendor's public key, supplied through the repo file's gpgkey setting or imported once into the keyring. Turning verification off removes the protection entirely, private keys are never distributed for this purpose, and the metadata cache is unrelated to key trust.

q: After a repository server migration, DNF reports it cannot download repomd.xml for the appstream repository even though the baseurl in the repo file already points at the new server and the server is reachable. What should the administrator try first?
options: Set skip_if_unavailable=1 so DNF silently ignores the repository.
Reinstall the appstream packages from local media.
Disable gpgcheck for the repository.
Clean the cached metadata (dnf clean metadata or dnf clean all) so DNF downloads fresh metadata from the new server.
explain: Stale cached metadata can keep DNF working from an outdated view of the repository after its location changes; expiring the cache forces a fresh metadata download from the configured baseurl. Silently skipping the repository would hide the problem and leave its packages unavailable.

q: The httpd package must stay at its currently installed version even when the team runs full system upgrades. Which DNF feature holds a package at its version in this way?
options: An entry in /etc/dnf/protected.d, which prevents the package from being upgraded.
The priority setting in the repository file where httpd came from.
A versionlock entry, created with dnf versionlock add httpd and reviewable with dnf versionlock list.
Marking httpd as a group with dnf group install httpd.
explain: Versionlock pins named packages so upgrade transactions skip them until the lock is removed. The protected.d list guards essential packages against removal rather than upgrades, and repository priority only chooses between repositories offering the same build.

q: Installing a package fails with a problem report: the package requires libsensor.so.3, but none of the providers can be installed, and the enabled repositories only carry libsensor.so.2. What is the correct conclusion and course of action?
options: The package build is not compatible with the current repository set; obtain a build made for these repositories or enable the repository that provides the required library version, rather than forcing the install.
Force the installation with rpm --nodeps so the missing library is ignored.
Add --allowerasing so DNF deletes the conflicting library.
Downgrade the application package even though it was never installed.
explain: A 'none of the providers' problem means a hard requirement cannot be satisfied from the enabled content at all; no solver flag manufactures the missing library. Forcing the install would leave a permanently broken package, and allowerasing only resolves conflicts between packages that do exist.
